articles.title: Rohingya: Historic International Court of Justice ruling finds Myanmar guilty of genocide
International Court of Justice finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
International court of justice ruling on Myanmar
World Court Finds Myanmar Committed Rohingya Genocide
articles.description: The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya is a historic milestone in their long quest for justice.
paragraphs: (The Hague) – The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya is a historic milestone in their long quest for justice, Human Rights Watch said today. On November 19, 2026, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations,” carried out by Myanmar’s military.

In the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (Genocide Convention), the court ruled for Gambia, with a nine to six vote by the judges, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. This is the first time that the ICJ found a country responsible for committing genocide. The court also found that Myanmar violated other obligations under the Genocide Convention, including the obligations to punish those responsible for genocide and to prevent genocide. The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

“The landmark International Court of Justice ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The ruling also provides a significant precedent for victims of genocide and other grave crimes across the world in their own search for justice.”

In August 2017, Myanmar’s security forces began a sweeping campaign of massacres, rape, and arson against ethnic Rohingya in northern Rakhine State that forced more than 700,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. In November 2019, Gambia filed a case before the ICJ alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya constitute genocide and violate the Genocide Convention. This was also the first time that a country without any direct connection to the alleged crimes used its membership in the Genocide Convention to bring a case before the ICJ.

The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, adjudicating disputes between states and issuing advisory opinions on international law. It consists of 15 judges elected by the UN General Assembly and Security Council for nine-year terms.

In its ruling, the ICJ found that the evidence before it established that Myanmar’s security forces, and other state organs, intentionally committed the genocidal acts of killing, causing serious bodily or mental harm, and imposing measures intended to prevent births against the Rohingya.

Considering the totality of the evidence, the court concluded that Myanmar committed these acts with the requisite genocidal intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population of Myanmar. To reach this conclusion, it considered an array of relevant factors, including the general context, the selective targeting of the Rohingya, acts that violated the foundations of the Rohingya group, such as sexual violence and targeting children, and the systematic nature of Myanmar’s actions.

Based on these factors, the court found that Myanmar’s genocidal intent was “the only reasonable inference” that could be drawn from the evidence before it. The judges rejected the possibility that other alternative intents, such as to carry out counterinsurgency operations or to forcibly displace the Rohingya, could reasonably explain Myanmar’s conduct.
articles.lede: The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya is a historic milestone in their long quest for justice.

‘Today the Truth Has Been Recognized’
articles.description: Thousands of Rohingya waited anxiously in refugee camps in Bangladesh as the International Court of Justice delivered its judgment in the landmark case brought against Myanmar for violating the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.
paragraphs: As the International Court of Justice in The Hague delivered its judgment on November 19 in the landmark case that Gambia brought against Myanmar for violating the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, thousands of Rohingya waited anxiously in refugee camps in Bangladesh.
In the Jamtoli Camp 15 in Cox's Bazar District, many crowded around a television. About two hours into the reading of the judgment, it started to rain. But no one moved.

The court’s president spoke in English, a language rarely heard in the crowded camps where over a million Rohingya sought refuge after fleeing Myanmar military attacks in 2017. At 5:13 p.m. local time, a community leader relayed the court’s ruling in the Rohingya language to the waiting crowd, telling them that, by nine votes to six, the court found Myanmar “committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State.”
“The Myanmar military tried to convince the world that we had lied,” said 58-year-old Monajat Alam, from Rathedaung Township. “Today, the truth has been recognized.”

The ruling was based on evidence showing that thousands of Rohingya civilians, including children, had been killed and that there was widespread sexual violence and destruction of villages during the 2017 military campaign. The court found the evidence also showed that Myanmar intended to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population.

Nemat Hussen from Maung Nu in Buthidaung Township, where Myanmar soldiers massacred hundreds of Rohingya villagers on August 27, 2017, brought along his son. Maung Nu was one of three villages that Gambia asked the court to examine for evidence of genocidal intent.
“In 2017, I lost my mother and eldest son,” Maung Nu said. “Since that day, I’ve been waiting for justice, and today I brought my son to hear the judgment.”

The court ordered Myanmar to investigate suspected perpetrators of genocide and prosecute them where warranted, compensate the Rohingya for the harm they suffered, and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of those displaced, among other measures.
“Today, my hopes have grown tremendously,” Monajat Uddin said. “I wish that we’ll be able to return to Rakhine and live in peace and our homeland will be safe so that we can return.”

articles.title: - Opinio Juris
Myanmar: World court issues historic first judgment recognizing Rohingya genocide
articles.description: The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and its member organizations Alternative ASEAN Network on Burma (ALTSEAN-Burma), Women’s (…)
paragraphs: The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and its member organizations Alternative ASEAN Network on Burma (ALTSEAN-Burma), Women’s Peace Network (WPN), Info Birmanie, and Odhikar welcome the historic International Court of Justice (ICJ) judgment, marking the first time an international court has recognized the genocide committed by Myanmar against the Rohingya, and the first time the ICJ has found a State responsible for committing genocide. They call on States to ensure full implementation of the Court’s judgment and to pursue all avenues of accountability and justice for the Rohingya.

The Hague, Paris. 19 November 2026. The ICJ today ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during the 2017 clearance operations in northern Rakhine State, in violation of the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (the “Genocide Convention”). The Court found that Myanmar’s security forces committed acts prohibited under Article II(a), (b) and (d) of the Convention, including killing, causing serious bodily or mental harm, and imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group, with the intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population. The Court also found that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide and to prosecute and punish those responsible for it. Significantly, the Court found that gender-based violence, including widespread rape and other forms of sexual violence, caused serious bodily and mental harm, contributed to measures intended to prevent births within the Rohingya group, and supported its finding of genocidal intent.

The Court ordered Myanmar to investigate suspected perpetrators of acts prohibited under the Genocide Convention during the 2017 clearance operations and, where warranted, prosecute and punish them. It also ordered Myanmar to enact implementing legislation, provide guarantees of non-repetition and adopt restitution measures, including the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced Rohingya, restoration of property, rehabilitation and protection against discrimination and persecution. Myanmar must also compensate victims for harm not remedied through restitution.

Under Article 60 of the ICJ Statute, the ICJ’s judgment is final and without appeal. It is legally binding on the parties under Article 59 of the Statute and Article 94(1) of the United Nations (UN) Charter. Should Myanmar fail to comply with the judgment, The Gambia may bring the matter before the UN Security Council, which may make recommendations or decide upon measures to give effect to the judgment.

The case was filed by The Gambia on 11 November 2019. It alleged that Myanmar had violated the Genocide Convention through acts committed against the Rohingya population in Rakhine State, including killings, causing serious bodily or mental harm, and imposing measures to prevent births within the group. These acts, alongside forced displacement, formed part of a campaign that the Gambia alleged was intended to destroy the Rohingya group, in whole or in part.

Choisir de résister, le podcast de la FIDH
articles.description: En collaboration avec Louie Media, la Fédération internationale pour les droits humains (FIDH) lance son podcast original : « Choisir de résister (…)
paragraphs: Paris, le 19 novembre 2026. Et si résister n’était pas un choix héroïque, mais une décision qui survient du jour au lendemain?

Partout dans le monde, des femmes et des hommes prennent des risques, parfois au péril de leur vie, pour défendre les droits humains. Mais qu’est-ce qui les pousse à s’engager? Une rencontre, un deuil, une lecture, une conviction profonde?

« La FIDH, c’est avant tout des centaines de personnes qui, partout dans le monde, choisissent de résister à l’oppression », raconte Alexis Deswaef, président de la FIDH. « Les combats pour les droits humains sont différents, d’un pays à l’autre, évidemment, mais ils ont tous un point commun: une décision. Une décision forcément intime, mais aux conséquences potentiellement tragiques. Le courage des activistes est une inspiration, mais il est aussi une invitation aux auditeurs et aux auditrices: rejoignez le combat pour les droits humains, car c’est avant tout le vôtre. »

D’Algérie à la Colombie, d’Israël et la Palestine au Sénégal, les quatre épisodes de la première saison de « Choisir de résister » racontent des trajectoires singulières, marquées par des choix, des ruptures et une même détermination à défendre les droits humains.

En Algérie, Aïssa Rahmoune, avocat et secrétaire général de la FIDH, raconte son combat pour la démocratie, la dignité et la liberté, jusqu’à l’exil forcé en France. Un départ qui ne marque pas la fin de son engagement, mais le début d’une reconstruction.

En Colombie, Yessika Hoyos Morales, avocate et membre du collectif Cajar, organisation membre de la FIDH, a transformé le meurtre de son père, syndicaliste assassiné par l’armée alors qu’elle avait 17 ans, en combat contre l’impunité et l’oubli. Malgré les menaces, elle poursuit sans relâche sa lutte pour la dignité et la justice.

En Israël et en Palestine, Yuli Novak, directrice de B’Tselem, organisation membre de la FIDH, a choisi de construire des ponts plutôt que des murs. Après cinq années passées dans l’armée israélienne, elle défend aujourd’hui la justice et l’égalité des droits entre Palestinien·nes et Israélien·nes, malgré les intimidations.

Au Sénégal, Abibatou Samb, avocate et défenseuse des droits humains, se bat pour la dignité des femmes, le droit à l’avortement médicalisé et la reconnaissance juridique du féminicide. À travers son association Voix de Victimes, elle mène un combat quotidien dans un contexte marqué par les mouvements anti-droits et les violences faites aux femmes.
Un nouvel épisode sera diffusé chaque jeudi, à partir du 19 novembre 2026 jusqu’au 10 décembre, jour de la Déclaration universelle des droits de l’homme.

articles.title: Milestone Crossed: 1,000 Cases Filed Against Trump Administration Policies
articles.description: Description of 1,000 cases filed against Trump administration policies, with charts showing success rates for plaintiffs and the government.
paragraphs: The landscape of civil litigation against Trump administration policies now includes over 1,000 cases, a sobering number by any account.

At Just Security, we have been closely and comprehensively monitoring the cases, providing the public with daily updates of significant court developments and documents. The Litigation Tracker launched on Jan. 29, 2025, and has been continually updated since. Plaintiffs include private citizens, civil society organizations, and state and local governments. (A recently added feature of the Tracker is the ability to sort by cases in which state attorneys general are involved as plaintiffs or amicus.)
Below are four charts with more nuanced information about this historic moment in American law. The charts are for public use (please credit Just Security).

The first chart shows that in cases where courts have issued a ruling, plaintiffs have succeeded 66% of the time in blocking the government’s actions. Examples include getting the courts to issue a temporary restraining order, a preliminary injunction or a permanent one. In other words, a plaintiffs’ success generally means the court determined the government action is likely unlawful or is unlawful, either as a violation of constitutional law or congressional statute or both.

The second and third charts break those figures down by district and appellate court levels. The charts show that plaintiffs succeeded 66% of the time at the district court level in blocking the government’s actions, and plaintiffs succeeded 67% of the time at the appellate level.
The final chart shows the distribution of plaintiff and Trump administration successes within specific issue areas. These are issue areas we use to organize the Litigation Tracker.

Readers may glean different insights from this final chart. Notable findings include that the Trump administration has greater success in cases involving the structure of government/personnel, winning 51% of the time. Plaintiffs’ greatest success rates are in the areas of the environment (83%) and diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility (71%). That said, those cases have a smaller n (overall size of that population of cases). And, in general, success rates may be driven partly by selection effects involving which cases plaintiffs decide to bring.
If you appreciate our nonprofit research and academic work, please consider a donation to support Just Security. We appreciate gifts of all sizes.

Ryan Goodman ( X - Bluesky - LinkedIn) is co-editor-in-chief of Just Security and Anne and Joel Ehrenkranz Professor of Law at New York University School of Law. He served as Special Counsel to the General Counsel of the Department of Defense.
articles.lede: Description of 1,000 cases filed against Trump administration policies, with charts showing success rates for plaintiffs and the government.

Litigation Tracker: Case Status Key and Glossary
articles.description: How to read the Litigation Tracker's case statuses, and what each ruling means for challenged executive actions.
paragraphs: This Case Status Key and Glossary explains how to read each case status in Just Security’s Litigation Tracker and how to interpret a given ruling’s effect on the challenged executive action. We hope these resources make it easier to follow individual cases, spot emerging trends, and understand how courts are responding.

A court has issued a ruling — at any stage of litigation, including on preliminary motions — that pauses or blocks the challenged government action for the plaintiff(s) who brought the case. This category reflects the current posture of the case, not necessarily a final outcome. A ruling in favor of plaintiff(s) on a preliminary motion does not mean plaintiffs have prevailed on the merits; litigation is typically ongoing.

A court has issued a ruling — at any stage of litigation, including on preliminary motions — that allows the government action to proceed. This category reflects the current posture of the case, not necessarily a final outcome. A ruling in favor of the government on a preliminary motion does not mean the government has prevailed on the merits; litigation is typically ongoing.

A court has issued a ruling that partially blocks the challenged government action and partially allows it to proceed. This category reflects the current posture of the case, not necessarily a final outcome.
The case has concluded without a ruling on the merits or without an explicit win or loss for either party.
Affirmed: When a higher court agrees with a lower court’s decision and leaves it in place, meaning the lower court’s ruling remains in legal effect.

Administrative Procedure Act (APA): A federal act that governs the procedures of administrative law. The APA establishes how administrative agencies make rules (“rulemaking,” which is defined as “the agency process for formulating, amending, or repealing a rule”) and how agencies adjudicate administrative litigation, meaning how they resolve specific agency matters by issuing orders. Under 5 U.S. Code § 706, federal courts may “hold unlawful and set aside” agency action that is arbitrary and capricious, contrary to law, or procedurally defective. Courts may also issue stays under Section 705 (see below).

Administrative Stay: A brief temporary pause, often lasting only a few days, that a court may grant alongside its own ruling or in response to an emergency motion. When issued by a district court, an administrative stay gives the losing party a short window to seek emergency relief from a higher court before the ruling takes full effect. When issued by an appellate court, an administrative stay gives the court time to consider an emergency motion — such as a motion for a stay pending appeal — before ruling on it. In either case, an administrative stay does not reflect the merits of the ruling itself.

Emergency Application: A request to the Supreme Court to act quickly — such as by staying a lower court’s ruling — without necessarily committing to a full review of the lower court’s ruling. These are often decided without full briefing or argument and with little or no published reasoning.
articles.lede: How to read the Litigation Tracker's case statuses, and what each ruling means for challenged executive actions.

Bukele’s Troops in Haiti: The Frontlines of an Eroding Rules-Based Global Order?
articles.description: The deployment of Salvadoran troops to Haiti entrenches a security model in the country beyond legal constraints and U.N. guardrails.
paragraphs: In recent weeks, thousands of Salvadoran troops have descended on Haiti in a sudden deployment ostensibly to counter the island nation’s gangs. They now outnumber the United Nations-authorized force. Initially presented as a rescue mission to recover four missing Salvadoran technicians, El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, is now casting himself as a strongman with a solution to Haiti’s intractable gang crisis.

This raises urgent questions about how Haitians’ human rights will be protected and who will answer for any abuses and civilian harms caused by the Salvadoran military. More broadly, it entrenches a security model in Haiti beyond legal constraints and U.N. guardrails, making Haiti a new frontline in the erosion of the rules-based international order.

Bukele’s troops are entering a deep governance, security, and humanitarian crisis that has been building for decades and was hastened by the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse. Armed groups have amassed and maintained power through collusion with state actors, and powerful elites that have long benefited from the support of the international community. These groups control significant territory through violent extortion and brutal assaults. The insecurity has spurred the worst humanitarian crisis in the Western Hemisphere — approximately 1.5 million people are internally displaced and more than half of Haitians need immediate humanitarian assistance.

U.N.-authorized stabilization missions have been in Haiti for most of the past 22 years, but Bukele’s deployment is the latest move away from U.N.-grounded security missions whose mandates and safeguards constrained the use of force and promised accountability, at least on paper. But the longest-running mission, MINUSTAH, became embroiled in accountability scandals related to use of excessive force, sexual exploitation and abuse, and the introduction of a devastating cholera epidemic. In October 2023, the United States co-authored a resolution adopted by the U.N. Security Council for a Kenyan-led Multinational Security Support Mission that would operate outside of U.N. oversight and accountability. When that severely underfunded mission failed to deliver, the United States pushed the Security Council in September 2025 to authorize an unprecedented Gang Suppression Force. The Force operates under its own command with an aggressive mandate to kill gangs. Like the controversial structure of the Trump administration’s “Board of Peace” in Gaza, the Gang Suppression Force for Haiti pilots a new model of U.N.-sanctioned operations governed by a small group of States outside of U.N. frameworks. The Force’s structure and militarized mandate have sparked criticism that it won’t be able to protect civilians, strengthen Haitian authorities’ capacity, or address the actual causes of the crisis.

More than a year into the Gang Suppression Force’s mandate, approximately 2,000 troops out of the envisioned 5,000 have deployed to Haiti. The troops draw from a number of countries, with Chad contributing the largest contingent, and smaller contributions coming from Sri Lanka, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, and Mongolia. The Salvadoran technicians ambushed on Oct. 18 were in the country as part of the original Salvadoran contribution to the Gang Suppression Force.
articles.lede: The deployment of Salvadoran troops to Haiti entrenches a security model in the country beyond legal constraints and U.N. guardrails.

articles.title: Remarks of Judge Kimberly Prost at ABILA’s International Law Weekend
articles.description: In her remarks at ABILA's International Law Weekend, Judge Kimberly Prost spoke of the resilience of international legal institutions.
paragraphs: These remarks were delivered virtually on Oct. 24, 2026, as the keynote address of the American Branch of the International Law Association’s International Law Weekend.

Though it is with great disappointment that the sanctions imposed by the United States preclude me from being with you in New York today, I am very grateful to the American Branch of the International Law Association for having given me the opportunity to be heard nonetheless. Please know I am also with you in spirit!

I am particularly pleased to be speaking just after my former boss and dear friend Silvia Fernandez de Gurmendi has received this well-deserved honor from ABILA. Her career and her continuing efforts are inspirational to us all.

It is a bit daunting to address you, after what must have been interesting but sober discussions throughout the weekend. Your program highlights the challenges. In different fields – climate, trade, arms control, health; so many precepts and systems we took as fundamental and given are under threat, across these legal disciplines. But I consider it my role today, while recognizing the seriousness of the challenges that we face, to direct our focus on to the way forward. We know that developing and maintaining international law, in particular international criminal law, was always going to be extraordinarily challenging. Currently, we are facing very turbulent times in that regard, as in an airplane, one of those moments when flight attendants are asked to take their seats. And we must act in the same manner to address this turbulence, as in an aircraft. We need to keep calm, steady the course, take any necessary corrective measures, and ride out the bumps, knowing, in due course, we will arrive if not to clear skies, at least calmer ones. I am confident that is how international law will emerge from this difficult period.

In that regard I love the conference theme – (R)evolution in the International Legal Order – which gives me options – revolution or evolution in international law? I strictly choose the latter. What we are seeing is an evolution – one that will unquestionably bring some changes and some losses but will not result in the overturn or discarding of the entire regime of international law – the rules-based order which we have fought so hard to attain.

In that spirit, while I will focus my comments today on international criminal law and the International Criminal Court, I know that all of us in our various fields face the same the same sense of horror, frustration and fear – that what we have long strived for is being summarily upended. I hope I convey a message today that resonates across all these fields and generates, albeit in different ways, motivation to find ways forward for international law, in all its manifestations.

In turning to my specific topic, I will not recount in any detail what is well known to this audience – the targeted strikes which have been aimed at the Court and the system which surrounds it. Individual judges and prosecutors subject to intimidation tactics, arrest warrants, in absentia convictions and debilitating sanctions for doing their jobs in accordance with their oaths of office. Civil society organizations and UN officials, providing critical support to the core work of the institution, similarly targeted. In a further escalation, on 9 th October, the International Criminal Court – the institution – was designated by the United States and added to a list designed for those implicated in terrorism, organized crime and human rights abuses. Even with the licenses which are granted for the moment, the reality is the Court is designated and will face disruptions. Moreover, the purpose is clear – to attack the Court through comprehensive economic sanctions aimed at crippling its operations.
articles.lede: In her remarks at ABILA's International Law Weekend, Judge Kimberly Prost spoke of the resilience of international legal institutions.

Norway reaffirms its commitment to victims: EUR 900,000 unrestricted contribution to the Trust Fund for Victims at the ICC
articles.description: The Trust Fund for Victims (TFV) at the International Criminal Court (ICC) has concluded a contribution agreement with the Kingdom of Norway, through the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation (Norad), for 10 million Norwegian kroner (approximately EUR 900,000). This unrestricted contribution advances the TFV's mandate to raise awareness of the plight of victims, mobilise resources for their benefit, and implement programmes that serve them -encompassing both ICC‑ordered reparations and other programmes for the benefit of the victims that address the physical, psychological, and material needs of victims and affected communities.H.E. Mr Espen Barth Eide, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Norway stated: "When the world responds to atrocities and holds those responsible to account, we must also remember the rights of victims. Through this contribution, we seek to support people affected by war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide by helping them access rehabilitation and rebuild their lives. At a time when international institutions are being challenged, it is essential to stand up for the rule of law. Norway’s support for the Trust Fund demonstrates our strong commitment to international criminal justice, to victims, and to the fight against impunity.”Mr Andres Parmas, Chair of the Board of Directors of the Trust Fund for Victims, stated: "Reparative justice belongs first and foremost to the victims themselves — to their courage, their understanding of what recovery requires, and their leadership within their own communities. Norway's contribution is significant because it demonstrates trust in that leadership and offers the steady, adaptable support that allows victims to shape their own recovery. Crucially, Norway treats reparations not as charity but as a right that victims already hold under the Rome Statute. It is my sincere hope that other States will recognise that same obligation, so that justice may be honoured wherever it is owed."Norway's continued partnership reflects a solidarity that the country has maintained for well over a decade: having contributed more than EUR 2.6 million since 2008, Norway stands among the Trust Fund's most steadfast partners.Background information about the Trust Fund for VictimsVoluntary contributions to the TFV enable the delivery of the reparative mandate of the ICC by funding services and activities that provide recognition, commemoration and material support through rehabilitative programmes.The TFV appeals to States Parties and other entities to contribute to the delivery of reparations to victims in urgent need, particularly in relation to the Ntaganda and Ongwen cases. The annual programme funding target of the TFV is set at a minimum of EUR 10 million.Contributions to the TFV qualify as Official Development Assistance (ODA)-eligible. TFV programmes for the benefit of victims of crimes under the jurisdiction of the ICC contribute to the broader impact of several United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including peace, justice, and strong institutions (SDG 16), poverty reduction (SDG 1), good health and well-being (SDG 3), gender equality (SDG 5), decent work and economic growth (SDG 8), reduced inequalities (SDG 10), and climate action (SDG 13).For more information about the Trust Fund for Victims at the ICC, please contact trustfundforvictims@icc-cpi.int or visit www.trustfundforvictims.org. You can also follow the TFV's activities on X, LinkedIn, Bluesky and Facebook.

articles.title: Afghanistan’s 80 Years at the U.N.: Keeping the Torch in Times of Darkness
articles.description: The Taliban represents an aberration in Afghanistan's long history of living up to its international obligations.
paragraphs: We have both held Afghanistan’s seat as permanent representative at the United Nations in Geneva, one (Dalil) as the first woman to lead our nation’s mission to the U.N., the other (Andisha) as the first diplomat of Afghanistan to serve as the vice-president of the Human Rights Council. In both cases, we represented the new generation of Afghanistan’s diplomatic service after the Taliban’s removal from power in late 2001.

This week, our country marks 80 years as a member of the U.N., having joined on Nov. 19, 1946 alongside Iceland and Sweden, among the first wave of nations admitted after the organization’s founding. Twelve years earlier, on Sept. 27, 1934, the League of Nations had welcomed Afghanistan here in Geneva, where we continue our work today. We defied the Taliban’s military takeover of our country, and we have rejected their policies and practices ever since, above all their assault on the human rights and dignity of our people. The Taliban refuse to honor Afghanistan’s international obligations, and the world, with the exception of Russia, refuses to recognize them. Our missions in Geneva, New York, and Vienna are therefore still led by diplomats who were accredited by the last constitutional government. We do not represent the Taliban and take no instructions from them; we serve the people of Afghanistan and adhere to the U.N. Charter and related conventions that our country signed over the past 80 years.

We invoke Geneva deliberately. Long before the emerging multilateral system was fully formed, a small, landlocked, and fiercely independent country was eager to be an active member of the League of Nations, choosing the rule of law early. Afghanistan understood what every vulnerable State eventually learns: for a small and geographically exposed nation in an anarchic world, international law is an affordable armor of recognition and protection.

Eighty years later, that armor is being systematically dismantled. Where invading armies and warring empires once posed a threat, today it comes from a radical extremist movement occupying Kabul that claims the apparatus of the State while repudiating every obligation attached to it internationally. Yet, there is much the international community can still do to help defend the dignity and rights of the people of Afghanistan in the face of the Taliban’s repression.

Through the Second World War, Afghanistan held to a strict neutrality while empires around it went to war. After the war, Afghanistan stood among founders of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) when the movement was conceived at the 1955 Bandung conference (Indonesia) and the 1961 Belgrade conference (former Yugoslavia). We defended self-determination and the sovereign equality of small States at the multilateral organizations.

Afghanistan fought hardest on issues where its geography hurt it most. From 1958, it pressed the case for the rights of landlocked States. The jurist Abdul Hakim Tabibi carried that argument through the 1958 Geneva conference on the law of the sea and served as vice-chairman of the 1965 New York conference on transit trade. The argument was included in Part X of the 1982 U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea. As a result, every landlocked country that invokes its right of access to the sea today draws on an argument Afghanistan pioneered. In his last years, Tabibi, once a civil servant of Afghanistan, lived in exile in Geneva, the city where he had won rights for countries like his own. We, too, live in Geneva now, not the first civil servants of Afghanistan to watch from afar as their home country is usurped by an extremist group. We are determined to be among the last.
articles.lede: The Taliban represents an aberration in Afghanistan's long history of living up to its international obligations.

articles.title: This is Not South Africa’s Definition: A New Report on Apartheid in the Draft Crimes Against Humanity Treaty
articles.description: [Lisa Davis is a professor of law at CUNY Law School, and the ICC special adviser on Gender and Other Discriminatory Crimes. Kirby Anwar is Visiting Associate Professor of Law at the Human Rights a…
paragraphs: [ Lisa Davis is a professor of law at CUNY Law School, and the ICC special adviser on Gender and Other Discriminatory Crimes.
Kirby Anwar is Visiting Associate Professor of Law at the Human Rights and Gender Justice Clinic, CUNY School of Law.]

The Trump administration’s Nov 2 notice that it will remove South Africa from the Africa Growth and Opportunity Act in 2027 is the latest in a series of punitive and often openly racist acts against the country. It tops off erratic tariffs, deadly aid cuts, discriminatory migration policies and false accusations of “ white genocide .” The administration’s characterization of South Africa’s mild 2025 land reform act and its affirmative action policies as “ racial discrimination” against Afrikaners works only by stripping racism of its social and historical context and reducing race to “objective” markers like skin color. This is the same discredited theory that apartheid’s perpetrators used to build their racist hierarchy. By that sleight of hand, the administration wrongly portrays the policies meant to repair decades of racist deprivation under apartheid as discrimination itself.

In addition to being a diplomatic insult, this portrayal demonstrates what can happen when law’s understanding of race is severed from context. A similar vulnerability sits at the heart of a treaty now being negotiated at the United Nations. States are drafting the first global treaty dedicated to preventing and punishing all recognized crimes against humanity, with the second session of the Preparatory Committee in April 2027 and a diplomatic conference in 2028. Among the crimes the draft treaty defines is apartheid, in a text that can be read to ground race in biology rather than in the systems perpetrators build. The draft definition also obscures apartheid’s full reality, including its gendered dimensions. Our new report for the New Lines Institute, Restoring Meaning, Ensuring Justice: The Definition of Apartheid in the Crimes Against Humanity Treaty, examines where that definition came from and how drafters can better ensure justice for all apartheid victims.

In the first round of proposals, released in June 2026, various states called for revising apartheid’s definition. Much of the discussion has centered on whether to add gender, in order to encapsulate what the Taliban has built in Afghanistan, namely an institutionalized regime of systematic oppression and domination against women, girls, and LGBTQI+ persons. We fully support that inclusion.

The current discussion, however, understates the definition’s problems. No one has yet been found guilty of the crime against humanity of apartheid. The compounded racial and gender oppression black women endured under apartheid in South Africa and Namibia was never legally recognized. Meanwhile, the Palestinian people have sought recognition of apartheid under international criminal law for decades.

It would be easy to see these gaps in justice as competing interests, with each impacted community required to press its own amendment to the same provision. The definition’s history, however, tells a different story. These struggles share a common problem. A movement built around their shared interests offers the best chance of changing the definition for the better.
articles.lede: The Trump administration’s Nov 2 notice that it will remove South Africa from the Africa Growth and Opportunity Act in 2027 is the latest in a series of punitive and often openly racist acts against the country.

articles.title: What the London Convention and Protocol’s New Assessment Frameworks Mean for Marine Geoengineering Governance
articles.description: [Stephanie Prufer J.D. has a Juris Doctor from Yale Law School and a Master in Environmental Management from the Yale School of the Environment. She was involved in negotiations at the London Conve…
paragraphs: [ Stephanie Prufer J.D. has a Juris Doctor from Yale Law School and a Master in Environmental Management from the Yale School of the Environment. She was involved in negotiations at the London Convention and London Protocol, and Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement). She also interned at the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea.

Dr James Kerry is Chief Scientist at OceanCare and an adjunct Senior Research Fellow at James Cook University. He was involved in negotiations at the London Convention and London Protocol on marine geoengineering.]

At this year’s LC/LP Governing Body meeting, via a resolution, the Parties adopted a Revised AF for Scientific Research Involving Ocean Fertilization (hereinafter, Revised Ocean Fertilization AF), along with two new AFs for scientific research in ocean alkalinity enhancement and biomass sinking. Each AF details procedures for evaluating the scientific justification, environmental risks, and uncertainties associated with the proposed research, and for determining whether the activities constitute legitimate scientific research and are consistent with the aims of the LC/LP. Together, these AFs provide detailed guidance for assessing the environmental risks and scientific uncertainties associated with marine geoengineering research and determining whether proposed activities constitute legitimate scientific research consistent with the aims of the LC/LP.

For almost two decades, Parties to the LC/LP have sought to regulate ocean fertilization. The LC/LP Parties first took up ocean fertilization, when they issued a “statement of concern” in 2007. In 2008, through a resolution, Parties agreed that ocean fertilization activities other than legitimate scientific research should not be allowed, and they directed the treaties’ Scientific Groups to develop an Assessment Framework for evaluating research proposals on a case-by-case basis. That framework was adopted in 2010 through Resolution LC-LP.2, as the Assessment Framework for Ocean Fertilization.

In 2013, Resolution LP.4(8) took the next step by proposing to amend the London Protocol to prohibit the placement of matter for marine geoengineering activities listed in Annex 4, which includes ocean fertilization, unless the listing provides that the activity can be authorized under a permit. The amendment also added Annex 5, which provides that activities listed in Annex 4 should be assessed using “specific assessment frameworks” tailored to each technique. To date, this amendment has not yet entered into force. Importantly, the 2013 resolution expressly reaffirmed the continued application of the 2008 and 2010 resolutions pending entry into force of the 2013 amendment.

Therefore, Parties to the LC/LP have not only agreed that ocean fertilization falls within the scope of the LC/LP through previous decisions but also have repeatedly established that only legitimate scientific research on ocean fertilization should move forward. These successive decisions establish an expectation that Contracting Parties apply the Revised Ocean Fertilization AF when assessing ocean fertilization research proposals, irrespective of whether the 2013 amendment has entered into force. While these resolutions are not themselves legally binding, they may help to define what due diligence requires under existing LC/LP obligations. A Party that authorizes such research without applying the Revised Ocean Fertilization AF, or undertaking an equivalent level of environmental assessment and precaution, could therefore face difficulties demonstrating that it has fulfilled its existing due diligence obligations.
articles.lede: [ Stephanie Prufer J.D. has a Juris Doctor from Yale Law School and a Master in Environmental Management from the Yale School of the Environment.

‘Losing the battle’: AI hands predators new ways to target children
articles.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is handing predators and criminal groups new ways to groom, extort and exploit children, while efforts to protect them are failing to keep pace, senior UN officials warned on Thursday.
paragraphs: “We lost the battle on social media because we were lagging behind, and we are now losing the battle on artificial intelligence because we are still lagging behind,” said Dr. Najat Maalla M’jid, the UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children.
She was speaking during a high-level event in the General Assembly on the risks and opportunities of AI to help end the scourge.

In the past year alone, at least 1.2 million children in 11 countries had their images manipulated into sexually explicit deepfakes, UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed told the event at UN Headquarters in New York, citing a recent study by the UN Children’s Fund ( UNICEF ).

Reports of child sexual abuse material linked to generative AI rose by 1,325 per cent between 2023 and 2024, according to the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, said Dr. M’jid, noting that most AI-facilitated crimes against children remain unreported and under prosecuted.

Chatbots are being used to gain children’s trust, gather personal information and coerce them into sharing explicit images, she said, while deepfakes made with “nudification” apps are used to humiliate, threaten and exploit them.
Profiling and predictive targeting allow predators, traffickers and criminal groups to reach vulnerable children more easily.
John Trenary who has worked on child exploitation investigations for more than 25 years, said predators have always sought ways of “weaponizing technology to exploit our kids”.

But because AI can scale so efficiently – automate and create wholly synthetic content – its weaponisation is “self-perpetuating”, he warned. As soon as investigators get a handle on one way predators misuse it, “something else comes out”.

Kay Chau of the Tech Coalition – a non-profit alliance focused on child protection – said perpetrators may be using chatbots to facilitate abusive role-play or generate grooming scripts, while agentic AI (systems that can carry out tasks independently) is introducing new risks.
articles.lede: Artificial intelligence (AI) is handing predators and criminal groups new ways to groom, extort and exploit children, while efforts to protect them are failing to keep pace, senior UN officials warned on Thursday.

articles.title: No government approval needed to form or join a group, UN rights committee says
articles.description: People do not need their government’s permission to form or join an association, the UN Human Rights Committee said on Thursday, issuing new guidance as civic space shrinks around the world.
paragraphs: General Comment No. 38 sets out how Article 22 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights should be interpreted. Article 22 guarantees the right to freedom of association.
The guidance comes at a time when civil society groups, human rights defenders, trade unions, political parties and grassroots movements face growing legal and administrative hurdles.

Freedom of association allows people to come together voluntarily – including at work – to pursue shared goals. The committee called it a cornerstone of democracy and essential to the enjoyment of other rights.
“ Attacks and infringements on the right to freedom of association are thus a crucial barometer of a broader crackdown on human rights, the rule of law and democracy ,” it said.
“The right to freedom of association is not conditioned by a State’s authorisation or acknowledgement. This means that no prior authorisation is needed for its enjoyment and exercise.”
The committee stressed that people must be free to choose whether to form or join registered or informal associations, a decision that “rests solely with the individuals themselves”.
Simply joining or belonging to an unregistered association “must not be criminalised or sanctioned”, it added.
The right also covers ideas and activities that may be seen as “controversial, dissent or disruptive”, including “peaceful collective civil disobedience actions”.
The committee warned against misusing counter-terrorism and national security laws, including vaguely worded laws targeting so-called “extremist” or “undesirable” organizations.
articles.lede: People do not need their government’s permission to form or join an association, the UN Human Rights Committee said on Thursday, issuing new guidance as civic space shrinks around the world.

articles.title: Détention de Moussa Kaka au Niger: l'Union des journalistes de RCA «appelle à la solidarité de toute la profession»
articles.description: Le 31 août, Moussa Kaka quittait les locaux de son média à Niamey pour regagner son domicile. Mais il n'y est jamais arrivé. Début octobre, après plusieurs semaines de silence, le ministre nigérien de…
paragraphs: Le 31 août, Moussa Kaka quittait les locaux de son média à Niamey pour regagner son domicile. Mais il n'y est jamais arrivé. Début octobre, après plusieurs semaines de silence, le ministre nigérien de la Justice avait affirmé à Reporters sans frontières (RSF) que le journaliste, que vous avez entendu raconter l'actualité nigérienne pendant des années sur notre antenne, était détenu et en vie. « Nous demandons aux autorités nigériennes la transparence, qu'elles disent où il se trouve, ce qu'on lui reproche et qu'elles garantissent ses droits fondamentaux », souligne aujourd’hui le président de l'Union des journalistes centrafricains (UJCA).

C'était le 31 août dernier au Niger. Ce soir-là, notre confrère Moussa Kaka quittait les locaux de son média à Niamey, la Radiotélévision Saraounia (RTS) pour regagner son domicile. Il n'y est jamais arrivé.

Après plusieurs semaines de silence, début octobre, le ministre nigérien de la Justice, Alio Daouda, a affirmé à Reporters sans frontières (RSF) que Moussa Kaka, que vous avez entendu raconter l'actualité nigérienne pendant des années sur notre antenne, était détenu et en vie. Il n'a toujours pas pu voir sa famille ni son avocat.

Organisations internationales et voix du continent continuent de dénoncer la violation des droits de notre confrère et d'appeler à sa libération, à l’instar d’Eustache Michael Mounzatela, président de l'Union des journalistes centrafricains (UJCA).

« Moussa Kaka est un journaliste respecté, une voix importante pour l'information au Niger et dans la sous-région, souligne-t-il au micro de Magali Lagrange. Le fait qu'il soit détenu sans que l'on connaisse clairement son lieu de détention, les motifs qui lui sont reprochés, ni qu'il puisse voir sa famille ou son avocat, est très préoccupant. Donc, nous demandons aux autorités nigériennes la transparence, qu'elles disent où il se trouve, ce qu'on lui reproche et qu'elles garantissent ses droits fondamentaux ».

Il poursuit: « La détention au secret d'un journaliste fragilise la liberté de la presse et le droit des citoyens à l'information. Donc, en tant que président de l'Union des journalistes centrafricains, j'appelle à la solidarité de toute la profession africaine. Moussa Kaka doit être retrouvé, protégé, et sa place est devant un micro ou bien dans sa rédaction, pas dans l'ombre. »
Ousmane Diallo, chercheur sur le Sahel pour Amnesty International: «On a de sérieuses appréhensions pour son intégrité physique»
articles.lede: Le 31 août, Moussa Kaka quittait les locaux de son média à Niamey pour regagner son domicile. Mais il n'y est jamais arrivé.

articles.title: Historic UN ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya is rare victory for survivors
articles.description: Responding to the ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ top court, that Myanmar authorities committed the crime of genocide in their clearance operations against Rohingya people in 2017, Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnes Callamard said: “Genocide. This is the unequivocal finding of the ICJ. After years of denial, impunity and…
paragraphs: “Genocide. This is the unequivocal finding of the ICJ. After years of denial, impunity and suppression of truth, this ruling is a historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya and a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families.

“For decades, Myanmar governments and military authorities have denied the Rohingya citizenship and subjected them to an institutionalized system of segregation, discrimination and persecution that amounts to the crime against humanity of apartheid. They have confined Rohingya to refugee camps, burned their homes and villages, and committed widespread unlawful killings and sexual violence, including during the horrors of the military’s 2017 campaign.

“This final judgment by the ICJ to must serve as a wake-up call to the international community at a critical juncture in Myanmar’s history. The findings of independent investigators and international courts must not simply be ignored. This decision comes only because the government of The Gambia set the wheels of justice in motion, exemplifying how all states can and should respond to crimes that shock the conscience of humanity.

“The Court’s clarification that genocidal intent can coexist with other goals, including military aims, is especially significant for other cases pending at the ICJ, such as the case brought by South Africa against Israel for alleged genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

“The man who oversaw a campaign of crimes against humanity and other crimes under international law against the Rohingya, the former head of the armed forces Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, is now Myanmar’s president following engineered elections. Governments should not welcome him on the international stage, especially as grave violations continue unchecked inside Myanmar. Instead they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar. The UN Security Council should impose a global arms embargo and refer the entire situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court.

“The Myanmar authorities must comply with the ICJ’s ruling immediately. All other states, including ASEAN Member States, must also act to uphold it by meeting their own obligations under the Genocide Convention and general international law and doing everything within their power to prevent and punish genocide. Failure to uphold this judgment would only embolden the Myanmar military’s defiance of international law and perpetuate the cycle of impunity.

“This should not be the end of the struggle for justice for the Rohingya. Survivors and victims are entitled to full and effective reparations for the harms they have suffered. They also need sustained international support, including humanitarian assistance, resettlement opportunities and strong political and financial backing for international accountability mechanisms.
articles.lede: This is the unequivocal finding of the ICJ.

articles.title: Ngaragba, le couloir de la mort: On taxe la nourriture des prisonniers pendant qu’ils meurent de maladie
articles.description: À la prison de Ngaragba à Bangui, les familles paient des taxes illégales sur la nourriture pendant que les détenus meurent de maladie sans soins.
paragraphs: À la prison centrale de Ngaragba, dans le 7e arrondissement de Bangui, les familles des détenus doivent désormais payer des taxes injustifiables pour faire entrer de la nourriture destinée à leurs proches incarcérés. Une pratique mafieuse dénoncée par les prisonniers, alors que l’établissement traverse une grave crise sanitaire et alimentaire. La tuberculose se propage comme une traînée de poudre dans les cellules, près de 50 % des détenus seraient contaminés et trois prisonniers, Nbassade Junior, Dawe Cyrille et Erick Bernard, viennent de perdre la vie en quelques jours, abandonnés dans un dénuement médical total.

La situation à la maison centrale de Ngaragba prend une tournure particulièrement scandaleuse. Alors que les détenus dépendent largement de leurs familles pour ne pas mourir de faim, des agents pénitentiaires véreux leur imposent des prélèvements financiers cyniques sur les moindres produits alimentaires apportés par leurs proches. Parmi ces agents impitoyables, les détenus pointent directement du doigt le redoutable agent Léonce Romuald Sépese, mais surtout l’agent Foxy Saze, qualifiée de « terrible de terrible », ainsi que Bengari Cristand Gérard et Sarakaba, qui font régner leur loi à coups de taxes et de restrictions.

Selon plusieurs témoignages accablants recueillis par la rédaction du CNC, chaque cuvette de manioc introduite dans la prison est soumise au paiement de 500 francs CFA. Un paquet de cigarettes coûte 250 francs CFA de taxe, tandis que le moindre paquet de sucre est également frappé d’un prélèvement de 500 francs CFA.

Ces sommes sont extorquées aux familles à l’entrée même de la prison, au moment où elles tentent désespérément d’apporter de quoi maintenir leurs proches en vie. Les restrictions absurdes se multiplient également. Le charbon est interdit d’entrée, tout comme les beignets préparés à domicile et d’autres produits de première nécessité. Autrement dit, les familles doivent payer pour avoir le droit de nourrir les leurs, tout en se heurtant à un mur d’interdictions qui compliquent davantage la survie des détenus.
À lire aussi: VAKAGA: après l’assassinat crapuleux de quatre Wagner noirs, la machine de propagande des mercenaires russes se mobilise pour tenter de les blanchir
À lire aussi: Le business de la propagande: comment des médias africains se font payer pour vendre le récit du Kremlin

Ces pratiques dénoncées prennent une dimension encore plus révoltante au regard du chaos sanitaire qui règne actuellement dans l’établissement. En quelques jours à peine, trois détenus ont rendu leur dernier souffle. Il s’agit de Nbassade Junior, décédé le vendredi 6 novembre, suivi de près par Dawe Cyrille et Erick Bernard, morts le dimanche 8 novembre.

Selon les informations recueillies par la rédaction du CNC, la tuberculose se propage à un rythme alarmant et incontrôlé. Le taux de contamination avoisinerait 50 % de la population carcérale. Les malades continuent d’être entassés avec les détenus encore sains, faute de structures adaptées permettant leur prise en charge et leur isolement.
articles.lede: À la prison de Ngaragba à Bangui, les familles paient des taxes illégales sur la nourriture pendant que les détenus meurent de maladie sans soins.

articles.title: International Court of Justice issues ruling on Myanmar genocide case
International Court of Justice to issue ruling on Myanmar genocide case
The International Court of Justice Finds that Myanmar Committed Genocide Against the Rohingya: A Preliminary Analysis
articles.description: A preliminary analysis of the International Court of Justice's judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar on genocide.
paragraphs: Today, the International Court of Justice found that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya ethnic group during its “clearance operations” in Northern Rakhine State in 2017. The Court applied its established interpretation of the Genocide Convention and its established standard of proof by fully convincing evidence. The Court found that Myanmar is legally obligated to offer restitution and compensation to surviving victims, with specific measures and amounts to be determined in future proceedings.

First, the Court found that Myanmar’s government and security forces committed acts of: (1) killing members of the Rohingya group, (2) causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the Rohingya group, and (3) imposing measures intended to prevent births within the Rohingya group under article 2(a), (b), and (d), respectively, of the Genocide Convention. In particular, the Court found that Myanmar’s security forces killed at least 10,000 Rohingya, including through “the direct targeting of civilians, including women and very young children, and killings with knives and burning of people in houses. They also included killing by widespread indiscriminate shooting.”

The Court further found that Myanmar’s security forces caused “injuries resulting from shooting, knife wounds and burning. Widespread acts of rape, including gang and mass rape, and other forms of sexual violence, often accompanied by beatings or mutilation, also resulted in serious physical harm.” The Court also found that:

At least 1,834 acts of rape caused severe suffering for the victims, as well as suffering for their family members and persons who witnessed the acts. Approximately 326,000 Rohingya had their homes burned, leaving them with no place to return to, and many personally experienced the burning of their homes and villages. Finally, while not all of the approximately 700,000 Rohingya who were forced to flee experienced extreme hardship during the journey to Bangladesh, the evidence establishes that many of them did, and those who fled have not been allowed to return. (internal citations omitted)

taken together, the restrictions on marriages and births on Rohingya in Maungdaw Township, where nearly 500,000 Rohingya resided, the denial of legal registration for Rohingya children and the commission of at least 1,834 acts of rape targeting the Rohingya population during the 2017 clearance operations, when viewed in the context of the Government’s messages regarding uncontrolled Rohingya population growth, establish an intent to impact the capacity of members of the Rohingya community to reproduce normally and thus an intent to prevent births within the group.
Accordingly, the Court found that the evidence conclusively establishes the commission of acts listed in article 2(a), (b), and (d) of the Genocide Convention

Second, the Court found that the “only reasonable inference” supported by the evidence is that Myanmar’s government and security forces acted with the specific intent to destroy the Rohingya group, in substantial part, as such. The Court inferred genocidal intent from several factors, including: the general context, including the perpetration of other culpable acts systematically directed against the group; selective targeting of the Rohingya; perpetration of acts that violate the foundations of the Rohingya group, including sexual violence and targeting children; and the systematic nature and scale of the relevant conduct. Notably, the Court found “that the fact that Myanmar did not take every opportunity it had to destroy members of the Rohingya group does not preclude an inference of genocidal intent.”
