Who Decides Who Pays for the AU Mission in Somalia? December’s Test for Resolution 2719
articles.description: [Lincoln Booth is an MSc candidate at the University of Oxford, a member of the Inner Temple and a research contributor to Oxford Pro Bono Publico, and spent more than two decades on cross-border i…
paragraphs: [ Lincoln Booth is an MSc candidate at the University of Oxford, a member of the Inner Temple and a research contributor to Oxford Pro Bono Publico, and spent more than two decades on cross-border infrastructure and investment transactions across Asia, Europe and the Middle East.]

Resolution 2719 was meant to give African Union peace operations a route to United Nations (UN) assessed financing. The African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) still depends on voluntary contributions for the mission’s own budget. In December, the UN Security Council must decide whether to renew AUSSOM. The mission’s mandate and United States funding both end on 31 December 2026. The question is whether the formal, step-by-step approach of the resolution and the UN’s structures for taking decisions hinder accountability and the development or implementation of the financing model AUSSOM needs.

On 1 July 2026 the United States told the African Union that funding would end with the mandate authorised by Resolution 2809. The three-year review of Resolution 2719 required by paragraph 17 falls in December 2026, alongside the decision on AUSSOM’s renewal.

Resolution 2719 does not itself oblige UN members to pay for AUSSOM. Article 17(2) of the UN Charter requires payment once the General Assembly apportions an expense. Before then, the African Union Peace and Security Council (AUPSC) must request support, and the UN Security Council must authorise access to assessed contributions. The question is whether these separate decisions allow AUSSOM to continue without anyone settling how the mission will be paid. The answer is yes. The Security Council can renew AUSSOM without opening the route to assessed financing. December will test whether the Council does so again.

Adopted on 21 December 2023, Resolution 2719 answered a durable grievance. UN peacekeeping is financed by assessed contributions that every member must pay, while African Union missions have relied largely on voluntary contributions for their own budgets. For AUSSOM, those contributions come from a few donors. The European Union approved a further EUR 75 million in April 2026, mainly for allowances, the United Kingdom pledged GBP 16.5 million for 2025, and the African Union contributed USD 40 million. The troop-contributing countries carry the shortfall, and their personnel have gone long periods without stipends.

Two paragraphs carry the mechanism. Paragraph 2 provides that the Security Council “agrees to consider on a case-by-case basis” requests from the AUPSC for assessed financing. Paragraph 6 caps this support at “not exceeding 75 per cent” of the mission’s annual budget, and provides for the remainder to be jointly mobilised by the African Union and the UN from the international community as extra-budgetary resources.

Several further acts are needed before assessed money reaches AUSSOM’s own budget, and paragraph 3 sets them out. Joint strategic assessment and planning by the African Union and the UN must come first. The AUPSC must then decide to request support. The Security Council must next decide whether the operation may receive assessed contributions. Only after this can a budget be proposed for the UN General Assembly to approve and apportion. Paragraph 4 sends the proposed budget through the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions and the Fifth Committee before the General Assembly decides whether to approve it under Article 17 of the UN Charter. Article 17(2) requires UN members to pay the expenses apportioned to them by the General Assembly. The obligation attaches to the apportionment, not to the authorisation of the mission.
articles.lede: Resolution 2719 was meant to give African Union peace operations a route to United Nations (UN) assessed financing.

articles.title: Haiti: Kenscoff violence highlights continued risk of killing, abduction and other abuses against children by gangs
articles.description: Children in Haiti remain at risk of killings, abductions, sexual violence and other abuses by armed gangs, Amnesty International said in new research ahead of World Children’s Day. Amnesty International interviewed witnesses to the Kenscoff gang raid on 23 August 2026, in which 55 people were killed and 15 more were injured, according to a…
paragraphs: Amnesty International interviewed witnesses to the Kenscoff gang raid on 23 August 2026, in which 55 people were killed and 15 more were injured, according to a municipal official. The UN said at least three boys and two girls were among those killed. A further 67 people, including 13 children, were abducted, according to municipal data.

Witnesses told Amnesty International that the attack began when dozens of gang members raided various parts of the commune of Kenscoff, south of Port-au-Prince. They attacked people in their homes, shooting them and setting houses on fire. They looted belongings and shot residents as they tried to escape. They also attacked displaced people who were taking shelter in the Ark of the New Covenant Church and shot many of them.

“Survivors of the Kenscoff August attack, which came just weeks after another massacre in the same commune, described how they watched as gang members killed their relatives and friends, and how they were raped, beaten and abducted,” said Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme.
“Children’s lives have been devastated by these horrors. Survivors must have access to mental health support and necessary protection services.

“On World Children’s Day, we are again calling for the Haitian authorities and the international community to urgently increase efforts to protect Haiti’s children as escalating gang violence continues to threaten their lives. Additionally, intensified security operations must not expose children to further harm.”

World Children’s Day, celebrated annually on 20 November, marks the anniversary of the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), which outlines the rights of every child and what governments must do to protect them. Haiti is a state party to the CRC.
Organized gangs – namely Grand Ravine, Ti Bwa, 5 Segon and 400 Mawozo – started attacking the mountainous commune of Kenscoff in January 2025. All four gangs are part of the Viv Ansanm coalition.

Kenscoff borders Pétion-Ville, where many government offices, embassies and key commercial interests are situated. The 23 August attack on the population, which began around 9pm and was primarily led by a group from the 5 Segon gang, further appeared to be a retaliation for intensified security operations against the gangs.
One teenage girl told Amnesty International that she hid under her bed as gunshots rang out: “When they came inside the house, they said everybody should get out [or else] they would kill us.”
articles.lede: Amnesty International interviewed witnesses to the Kenscoff gang raid on 23 August 2026, in which 55 people were killed and 15 more were injured, according to a municipal official.

articles.title: The Channel INTERPOL Has Chosen Not to Watch
cats: Commission for the Control of INTERPOL's Files
articles.description: In 2024 and 2025, INTERPOL restricted oversight of the largest channel of police cooperation it operates: direct messages between national police bureaus. Amendments to its rules now prevent INTERP…
paragraphs: In 2024 and 2025, INTERPOL restricted oversight of the largest channel of police cooperation it operates: direct messages between national police bureaus. Amendments to its rules now prevent INTERPOL’s General Secretariat and the Commission for the Control of INTERPOL’s Files (CCF), the organization’s independent oversight body, from accessing the content of those messages unless they have permission or become aware of a potential breach of the rules. Ironically, the change came while INTERPOL was introducing NEXUS, a new messaging platform that makes messages easier to search.

Consider the situation of a dissident living abroad whose Red Notice has been refused or deleted by the CCF because the case is political. No INTERPOL check now prevents the same government that sought a Red Notice from turning to INTERPOL’s messaging system the next day to ask its counterparts abroad to locate or arrest that person on the same facts. Unless the General Secretariat is copied in, neither it nor the CCF will see the message, and the dissident will ordinarily never know it exists. As legal experts on INTERPOL have argued, these facts could have serious implications for INTERPOL’s accountability and legal immunity.

Each member country has a National Central Bureau (NCB), its liaison office for INTERPOL matters. Notices are requested by an NCB and published by the General Secretariat after a compliance check. Diffusions, which an NCB sends directly to other members, are recorded in INTERPOL’s databases and usually also reviewed, though they reach other countries first.

Direct messages are INTERPOL’s third channel. Through INTERPOL’s secure communication system, I-24/7, an NCB writes to one or more counterparts on any operational matter, including requesting the location or arrest of a named person. Unlike notices and diffusions, these messages are not recorded in INTERPOL’s databases unless the General Secretariat is copied or the sender consents ( Rules on the Processing of Data (RPD), Article 9(4)). INTERPOL puts messages in the tens of millions a year, against 27,525 notices and 30,015 diffusions in 2025.

At its General Assembly in Glasgow in November 2024, INTERPOL adopted the current text of Article 22(6) of the RPD. Where the General Secretariat “is not a recipient of, or has not accessed the exchange”, its role is now primarily to keep the channel secure. It must act to examine compliance when it “becomes aware of a potential violation” of the rules, but otherwise may not access the content without “explicit authorization by the entity concerned”. The provision applies notwithstanding the General Secretariat’s obligations under Title 1, Chapter II of the RPD (Articles 10 to 18, including the rights of access in Article 18) and Article 22(5), under which it manages data processing in the system, including through spot checks. In other words, the General Secretariat cannot access direct messages it was not copied in on unless it has explicit permission or becomes aware of a potential breach of INTERPOL’s rules.
articles.lede: In 2024 and 2025, INTERPOL restricted oversight of the largest channel of police cooperation it operates: direct messages between national police bureaus.

articles.title: Beyond the blast radius: climate harm and IHL’s “widespread, long-term and severe” threshold for absolutely prohibited environmental damage
cats: Climate change, conflict and humanitarian action
articles.description: Beyond the blast radius, discover how climate harm challenges international humanitarian law and the protection of the natural environment.
paragraphs: Armed conflict can aggravate climate change through consequences that lie beyond an attack’s immediate physical footprint. Yet international humanitarian law’s prohibition of methods or means of warfare expected to cause widespread, long-term and severe damage to the natural environment is too often assessed through a temporally short and geographically bounded account of harm.

In this post, part of our series on Emerging Voices, Climate change, conflict and humanitarian action, and War, Law and the Environment, Giorgia Pane argues that foreseeable climate-related effects should enter that assessment, through a climate-informed approach to the existing cumulative test. It suggests that “long-term” should account for persistence and reversibility, “widespread” for broader spatial effects through climate-regulating systems, and “severe” for the impairment of ecological functions necessary for mitigation and adaptation. Drawing on the ICRC Guidelines’ recognition of cumulative and reverberating effects, the author proposes an evidence-based approach to planning and precautionary assessments, arguing for the application of the prohibition threshold compatibly with the climate knowledge now available.

International humanitarian law (IHL) has long recognized that war can damage the natural environment. The prohibition of the use of methods or means of warfare expected to cause “widespread, long-term and severe damage” to the natural environment remains the clearest expression of this concern ( Customary IHL – Rule 45. Causing Serious Damage to the Natural Environment ). IHL also protects the natural environment through the general rules governing the conduct of hostilities. These include the principle of distinction, under which parts of the natural environment are protected as civilian objects unless they become military objectives ( ICRC Guidelines, Rule 5); the rule of proportionality, which prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental harm excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated (Rule 7); and the obligation to take feasible precautions to avoid, and in any event minimize, incidental harm to the natural environment (Rule 8).

But even in cases where objects forming part of the natural environment could otherwise be targeted lawfully as military objectives, or could otherwise incur damage arising from a lawful application of the principle of proportionality, the high-threshold prohibition articulated in Articles 35(3) and 55 of Additional Protocol I establishes an “absolute ceiling of permissible destruction” that prohibits all widespread, long-term and severe damage to the natural environment regardless of considerations of military necessity or proportionality ( ICRC Guidelines, para. 49).

It is for this reason that a high threshold of damage is required to trigger this prohibition. Yet the climate crisis invites us to ask whether the way this threshold is understood is still adequate to the forms of environmental harm we are now able to identify.
articles.lede: Beyond the blast radius, discover how climate harm challenges international humanitarian law and the protection of the natural environment.

articles.title: Statement of Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang to the UN Security Council on the Situation in Libya, pursuant to Resolution 1970 (2011)
articles.description: Thirty-second report: EN | FR | Arabic(On 18 November 2026, ICC Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang addressed the United Nations Security Council on the Situation in Libya, remotely from The Hague. Below is a transcript of his remarks.)Madam President, thank you for the opportunity to address the Security Council today.Please allow me to also express my thanks to his Excellency the Permanent Representative of Libya to the United Nations.I regret that I am unable to join you in the Council because of the sanctions imposed by the United States Government.Madam President, Excellencies, the report that I submit to you demonstrates clearly: despite coercive measures, despite attacks, the ICC and its partners continue to deliver for victims in Libya, based on the mandate of this Council.And it is in the courtroom of the ICC that this progress has been seen most clearly. On 16 July, the Pre-Trial Chamber of the International Criminal Court confirmed 17 alleged counts of war crimes against Mr Khaled Mohamed Ali El Hishri, including murder, torture, persecution, enslavement and rape.This is a landmark moment for justice in Libya. And it is built on the courage of Libyan and other victims who have come forward to work with the ICC, to provide their accounts, to force open the black box of suffering at Mitiga prison and other detention facilities in Libya.The stories of these victims recounted here at the Court were harrowing. Men, women and children detained without lawful basis. Physical and psychological torture systematised. Children witnessing their parents being abused. People targeted for their race, their gender, their perceived sexuality, their religion – or for political reasons. Women, men and children raped.One courageous victim spoke to our Team about the profound impact that Mitiga had on him, and I quote, this is what he told us:“The arrest and torture were not just a fleeting incident that came and went, they were an earthquake that shattered everything I had believed to be stable in my life.The voices of the oppressed, the screams of the tortured, and the darkness of the cold cells still inhabit my mind and soul. I have not truly left the prison: my body left, but my spirit remained imprisoned within it.I carry those memories like a wound that will never heal, searching through this pain for justice, for a sense of fairness, for a light that could dispel the darkness they planted deep inside me.”This man, and so many victims of Mitiga, did not suffer only one crime, they suffered multiple crimes committed against them repeatedly throughout their detention.Our position is unambiguous. Mr El Hishri was an architect and chief perpetrator of this calculated abuse.The confirmation of all charges against Mr El Hishri shows that through our rigorous work, and with the help of our partners, we can honour the courage of the victims who have come forward.The opening of the trial of Mr El Hishri on 4 May 2027 will be a further milestone in the process of justice. An opportunity for the victims of the crimes of Mr El Hishri to tell their stories and to face him in Court. The Office of the Prosecutor is ready for trial to commence.Madam President, Excellencies, the progress seen in the ICC courtroom is a reflection of the dynamism of our work in this situation in Libya.Our investigations across key lines of inquiry into crimes related to the 2014-2020 operations and crimes against migrants also continue with focus and rigour.Through interviews with witnesses, collection of geolocation data, and advanced investigations, the Office has obtained key information and evidence to advance its work.The decisions by the Pre-Trial Chamber of the ICC in the period covered by the report submitted to you, confirming the jurisdiction of the Court in the cases of both Njeem and El Hishri, have also further strengthened our basis for action.Madam President, Excellencies, at this crucial moment, we must also reflect on how we got here, how we were able to show the world what has happened inside the walls of Mitiga.It is neither by this Court acting alone, nor by imposing its mandate on Libya or its people. It is through partnership. It is by working together, based on the mandate of this Council, unifying efforts between victims, Libyan authorities, civil society and all international partners.Our collaboration with civil society, in particular, has been central to this case, and our commitment to further strengthen our partnership with CSOs has never been more firm.In the last reporting period, our Office had over 143 engagements with civil society partners, including through the virtual roundtable with over 43 organisations that my colleague, the other Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan, participated in last July. I commend the continued willingness of these organisations to work with us, despite the hostile context.This highly fruitful collaboration in the case of Mr El Hishri is only going to be the first step. Our partnership is one built to last and to deliver more for victims across our various lines of inquiry.Madam President, Excellencies, in the last six months, that spirit of collaboration and partnership and has also been seen increasingly in our work with Libyan authorities.I wish to commend in particular the very strong dialogue we have developed with the offices of their Excellencies Mr Mohamed Younis Al-Menfi, President of Presidential Council of Libya, and with Mr Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, Prime Minister of Libya, and I also commend the cooperation of the Ambassador of Libya to the Netherlands.What I’m saying here is not just talk. It is cooperation that is delivering results in our investigations and is strengthening the basis for political processes and stability. Such is the spirit of the Council’s mandate.The recent request from Libya for the Office of the Prosecutor to provide assistance in relation to an alleged terrorist attack in Zawiya and Tripoli is further concrete evidence that this partnership is a two-way street. It shows that it is based on mutual support.As you will see in the report submitted to you, our collaboration with the Attorney-General of Libya has seen one recent concrete step, through receipt of the death certification of Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi. We naturally wish to see this cooperation with the office of the Attorney-General strengthened further.I specifically wish to call for more decisive action in relation to ICC suspect Mr Osama Elmasry Njeem.Our Office was informed of his conviction in Libya, but we know very clearly that Mr Njeem is a completely free man. He meets anyone he likes, including authorities and militias. He is with his family and friends. So we do not believe he is facing justice.There are undoubtedly enormous challenges facing local justice in Libya, we know, given the atrocities committed by militias such as RADA. It is our hope however, also based on recent constructive dialogue with the office of the Attorney General, that the trial of Mr El Hishri can serve as a catalyst, a moment in which the fear that grips so many is broken by the strength of the voices of Libyan victims.Our office will always stand ready to partner with the Attorney-General in this collective endeavour.Madam President, Excellencies, partnership is crucial in our efforts to deliver justice. The ICC is not the only place where it is delivered.As I noted, our investigation with respect to crimes against migrants from the Horn of Africa has benefited from the collaboration of with a range of national authorities as well as our Europol partners. And this collaboration continues to deliver very good results.On 28 October 2026, Mr Kidane Zekarias Habtemariam appeared before a Dutch court in a pro-forma hearing for participating in a criminal organisation involved in human trafficking, hostage-taking, extortion and violence, including sexual violence in Libya.Our Office has shared information with Netherlands authorities that has facilitated, that has directly supported national investigations. Our collective action has delivered more justice for victims.Our policy on complementarity and cooperation is having real impact, therefore. Results in the courtroom here or before domestic courts, based on collaboration across jurisdictions is delivering results in our courtrooms and in national courts alike. We are committed to further expanding the support we provide to national authorities across relevant situations.Madam President, Excellencies, to conclude, I would wish to offer one broader reflection, beyond the situation we address today.Because, ultimately, the story of progress made in Libya is, in many respects, also the story of the ICC as a whole. More victims and affected communities are coming forward and asking to work with us. More victims, having no other recourse, are placing all their hope in the Court’s ability to deliver justice for them.Here we can sense a strengthening spirit of creativity, dynamism and collaboration driving new partnerships with national actors, as well as a sense of humility and an acknowledgement of the primacy of national jurisdictions which deserve to be supported in their efforts.And through all of this, we show what international law can deliver for victims when we work together. It can deliver much. This spirit of togetherness, of progress and commitment to produce results for those affected by atrocities is what we see across situations.Here I would like to say that those who seek to undermine this Court should know that it is this collective work that allows a Libyan victim to stand before their abuser and demand justice. Ultimately, in fact, they are seeking to dismantle that also.On behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor I can however provide reassurance to this Council. Our work continues. Our work continues in the courtroom, with victims on the ground. Our work will continue with all our national partners.One victim, to quote another, one victim declared in their testimony, this is what they said. “I will be reborn when justice has been served.” That is what the victim said. It is with these words that I would like to conclude, because it is this sentiment that compels us to stay the course in the execution of our mandate.Thank you. articles.title: “We need to establish the truth for the sake of history”
articles.description: As the trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte is about to begin at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, a Philippine Truth Commission tries to uncover the truth about his “war on drugs”. We talked to its chair Raul Pangalangan.
paragraphs: RAUL PANGALANGAN: When I became an ICC judge in 2015, the editor-in-chief of the Philippine Daily Inquirer asked me why I was joining a court that will never have a case from the Philippines. This was a person legendary for her instinct for historical moments, leading a newspaper which had unseated two presidents of the Philippines. Indeed, who could imagine that by 2016, Duterte would be elected president on a campaign promise to kill drug users, and in such a spectacular way? There is a video where the killers are seen riding motorbikes. They stop, redirect the traffic, and shoot down a man in a public market in broad daylight. It was done in the open, no attempt to hide, no attempt at secrecy. It was brazen murder.

My impression is that during the entire Duterte period, from 2016 to 2022, while people were being killed left and right, the majority of Filipinos was cheering him on. To give you an example, a member of the staff of the parish of cardinal Pablo Virgilio David asked him: “Why are you attacking our president for the ‘war on drugs’? He’s just doing this for the good of the country.” The bitter irony is that this woman’s son was killed by the police during a drugs operation. Yet she complained merely that the police got the wrong person – she wasn’t objecting to the practice of killing.
“Now more people say: 'Duterte was doing all these bad things to solve the drugs problem. But if the problems are still here until today, maybe it’s not working.'”

Overall, popularity surveys show that many people still support Duterte and his ”war on drugs”, though I can say with confidence that today the number has gone down. Now more people say: “Duterte was doing all these bad things to solve the drugs problem. But if the problems are still here until today, maybe it’s not working.”

This is the last hope of traditional justice for the ”war on drugs”. The role of the ICC in the Philippine case is that we will have an authoritative record of the killings, presented in a legally careful way, with all the guarantees of fairness for the accused. If the trial ends with a guilty finding, it’s not just justice for the victims, it’s also educational for reforming our judicial system. Duterte kept on saying to the police: “Just kill them, because if you wait for the courts, nothing will happen”. The ICC will prove that it is possible to respect the rights of the accused and still punish the guilty.
“The Truth Commission is a completely different pathway to justice than the ICC. It’s parallel, but separate and independent.”

It was cardinal David, the bishop of Caloocan, the city where the biggest number of deaths were reported during the “war on drugs”. There were more deaths elsewhere, but in Caloocan more killings were documented because of cardinal David’s support for the victims’ families. He gave them sanctuary in his church, and they found the courage to speak up.

The Truth Commission is not part of the government. It is a civil society-led institution established to uncover and preserve the truth, give a voice and platform for victims and survivors, and foster societal healing to prevent this national nightmare from happening again. The Truth Commission is a completely different pathway to justice than the ICC. It’s parallel, but separate and independent.
articles.lede: As the trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte is about to begin at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, a Philippine Truth Commission tries to uncover the truth about his “war on drugs”. We talked to its chair Raul Pangalangan.

Centrafrique: après l’assassinat de deux jeunes parmi les douze arrêtés à Zemio, la tension monte, les miliciens Azandé menacent d’attaquer désormais la ville
articles.description: A Zemio en Centrafrique, l'assassinat de jeunes par des mercenaires russes provoque une flambée de violence et la menace d'une attaque imminente.
paragraphs: La tension est de nouveau montée à Zémio, dans la préfecture du Haut-Mbomou, après l’assassinat de deux jeunes miliciens Azandé parmi les douze personnes arrêtées par les mercenaires russes dans la nuit de dimanche à lundi.

Selon les informations recueillies par la rédaction du CNC, les deux hommes, qui se rendaient à Zémio pour déposer leurs armes dans le cadre d’un processus de désarmement, ont été capturés par les mercenaires russes avant d’être torturés puis tués. Depuis ces assassinats, d’autres miliciens Azandé ont repris les armes et se sont positionnés autour de la ville, menaçant de l’attaquer.

En effet, les événements trouvent leur origine dans les arrestations effectuées par une patrouille de mercenaires russes, accompagnés de soldats des Forces armées centrafricaines (FACA) et de leurs supplétifs Wagner noirs, dans la nuit de dimanche à lundi. Douze jeunes avaient été interpellés dans deux villages, notamment à Tamboura, situé à une vingtaine de kilomètres de Zémio.

À lire aussi: Leadership féminin: la Guinéenne Nanfadima Magassouba devient la première femme lauréate du Prix Panafricain d’Excellence du CPPAncienne ministre et députée guinéenne, Nanfadima Magassouba recevra en janvier 2027 une distinction continentale pour son engagement.

L’enquête menée par la rédaction du CNC permet aujourd’hui de mieux comprendre les circonstances de ces arrestations. Parmi les douze personnes interpellées figuraient des commerçants qui se rendaient dans la région pour acheter des marchandises destinées à leur activité. Deux autres personnes étaient des miliciens Azandé qui avaient décidé de se rendre aux autorités dans le cadre du désarmement.

À lire aussi: « Nous ne marchons pas pour le plaisir de marcher »: après la manifestation du 13 novembre, l’ancien Premier ministre Martin Ziguélé appelle à une révolution pacifique contre la tyrannie, la misère et la présence des mercenaires russes

Selon les informations recueillies par le CNC, les deux miliciens se dirigeaient vers Zémio avec des grenades. L’un d’eux en tenait une dans la main lorsqu’ils ont croisé la patrouille des mercenaires russes. Ces derniers les ont alors arrêtés avec les autres jeunes, avant de les soupçonner d’appartenir à la milice auto-défense Azandé.

Au lendemain de ces arrestations, le mardi, les mercenaires russes sont retournés dans un autre village situé à Gambara PK 10, sur l’axe Rafaï, à environ dix kilomètres de Zémio. À leur arrivée, ils n’ont trouvé aucun habitant. Alertée par le bruit des motos et l’approche des Wagner, la population avait fui et trouvé refuge dans la forêt.

Les mercenaires ont alors incendié une partie des habitations construites en paille, brûlé des greniers et saccagé plusieurs biens appartenant aux habitants. Les dégâts matériels sont importants. Les raisons précises de cette opération restent inconnues, mais elle est intervenue au lendemain des arrestations des douze jeunes.

Pendant ce temps, les douze personnes arrêtées avaient été conduites à Zémio. Dix d’entre elles, principalement des commerçants, ont finalement été remises à la gendarmerie, puis libérées après vérification de leur situation.
articles.lede: A Zemio en Centrafrique, l'assassinat de jeunes par des mercenaires russes provoque une flambée de violence et la menace d'une attaque imminente.

articles.title: Guantanamo Dispatches: USS Cole Bombing Trial Recesses With First 8 Jury Members Chosen
articles.description: On the selection of jurors in USS Cole trial before Guantanamo commission.
paragraphs: Jury selection in the USS Cole bombing case at Guantanamo Bay recessed until next month with the addition of an eighth member who recently served on a base in the Middle East that came under fire in the U.S. war against Iran.

Army Col. Matthew Fitzgerald, the judge, accepted the Air Force captain over the objections of a defense lawyer who argued that the officer should be disqualified because aspects of the juror’s recent wartime experience were similar to some of the facts in the Cole case.

The captain was sent to Saudi Arabia last year on a routine deployment, a peacetime mission as he saw it, before the U.S.-Iran war began. Then, this year, his base came under attack. Airmen under his command were injured by shrapnel and concussion injuries from either drone or missile fire.

In the Cole attack, the warship’s commander also believed he was on a peacetime mission, a routine refueling stop in the port of Aden, Yemen, when al-Qaeda struck on Oct. 12, 2000, killing 17 American sailors.

Casey Secor, a defense lawyer, told the judge that the jurors at the Cole trial will be shown disturbing images of U.S. sailors who were killed and wounded in the suicide bombing 25 years ago, and the Air Force captain’s reactions could be colored by the casualties experienced by his servicemembers.

At Guantánamo, a Saudi prisoner, Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, is accused of orchestrating the attack on the Cole by two al-Qaeda operatives who came alongside the ship in an explosives-laden skiff and ignited their load.

His is the first death-penalty case by military commission at Guantanamo Bay. The court is choosing a total of 20 U.S. officers. Twelve will serve as jurors and six as alternates. The prosecution and defense teams can each excuse one of the 20 without cause.

The Air Force officer who was added to the panel was 2 years old when the Cole was bombed. He underwent some of the most intensive questioning by defense lawyers since jury selection began on Nov. 4. He said he did not believe the death penalty was necessarily required in a case like the one against al-Nashiri.

But he also could not imagine sentencing someone convicted of all of the charges in the case to no prison sentence, the most lenient sentence available to the military jurors, if al-Nashiri is convicted at the trial, which starts in earnest next year.

“If they were guilty of all these charges,” he said, “getting no punishment would do a disservice to the legal system.” The Air Force officer juror said he believed al-Nashiri was probably guilty of something because he had been held at Guantanamo Bay for 20 years. He said he hoped the military had done “its due diligence” in keeping him so long without “a speedy trial.” It was not explained to the officer that al-Nashiri is held as an enemy combatant, and therefore the U.S. government considers him eligible for detention for the duration of the conflict with al-Qaeda, even if he is never convicted of any crime. Prospective jurors also have not been told about al-Nashiri’s first four years of detention by the CIA, during which he was tortured repeatedly.
articles.lede: On the selection of jurors in USS Cole trial before Guantanamo commission.

Global: Protesting children and young people face human rights abuses, including violence and discrimination
articles.description: Children and young people around the world face barriers, challenges and human rights abuses while exercising their right to protest.
paragraphs: Children and young people around the world face barriers, challenges and human rights abuses while exercising their right to protest, a new briefing from Amnesty International reveals, ahead of World Children’s Day on 20 November.

Sparking Change – Children’s Right to Protest: A Perspective from Children and Young Activists, is a briefing from Amnesty International developed in partnership with the Spark Club, a group of 11- to 17-year-olds from 12 countries across five regions. Drawing on research with more than 500 children and young people worldwide, the briefing examines why children protest, the risks they encounter, and what states and other actors must do to ensure that children can safely exercise their rights.

From the Gen-Z protests in Kenya to the Fridays for Future climate movement and recent youth-led demonstrations across Europe, young people have taken to the streets to make their voices heard. Yet many face violence, discrimination and other barriers when speaking out and putting forward their demands.

“Children and young people have led and participated in major protests around the world in recent years, demanding climate justice, racial equality, social justice and better education, among other important issues. Yet many have faced violence and exclusion, which points to the failure of states to adequately respect, protect and facilitate children’s right to protest,” said Carolina Roman, Amnesty International’s Senior Campaigner.
Through a series of questionnaires, group discussions and interviews, children and young people shared the reality of what it’s like to speak out.
We [young people] are encouraged to participate, but there is a difference between being given the opportunity to speak and having what you say taken seriously.

The findings show that while children are motivated to participate in protests and believe they can contribute to change, their ability to do so depends on the support, protection and opportunities available to them. Some reported feeling hopeful about their ability to affect change through protest and said that their protest experiences had been empowering. However, safety was a major concern for many child activists, with many reporting that they felt safer engaging in online forms of protest.

“Being a young activist has taught me that people are generally comfortable with young people having opinions until those opinions become difficult to accommodate. We are encouraged to participate, but there is a difference between being given the opportunity to speak and having what you say taken seriously. I have encountered spaces where young people are welcomed as representatives of the future yet treated as though we have little to contribute to decisions being made in the present.”
articles.lede: Children and young people around the world face barriers, challenges and human rights abuses while exercising their right to protest.

articles.title: Haiti: Kenscoff violence highlights continued risk of killing, abduction and other abuses against children by gangs
articles.description: Children in Haiti remain at risk of killings, abductions, sexual violence and other abuses by armed gangs, Amnesty International said in new research ahead of World Children’s Day. Amnesty International interviewed witnesses to the Kenscoff gang raid on 23 August 2026, in which 55 people were killed and 15 more were injured, according to a…
paragraphs: Amnesty International interviewed witnesses to the Kenscoff gang raid on 23 August 2026, in which 55 people were killed and 15 more were injured, according to a municipal official. The UN said at least three boys and two girls were among those killed. A further 67 people, including 13 children, were abducted, according to municipal data.

Witnesses told Amnesty International that the attack began when dozens of gang members raided various parts of the commune of Kenscoff, south of Port-au-Prince. They attacked people in their homes, shooting them and setting houses on fire. They looted belongings and shot residents as they tried to escape. They also attacked displaced people who were taking shelter in the Ark of the New Covenant Church and shot many of them.

“Survivors of the Kenscoff August attack, which came just weeks after another massacre in the same commune, described how they watched as gang members killed their relatives and friends, and how they were raped, beaten and abducted,” said Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme.
“Children’s lives have been devastated by these horrors. Survivors must have access to mental health support and necessary protection services.

“On World Children’s Day, we are again calling for the Haitian authorities and the international community to urgently increase efforts to protect Haiti’s children as escalating gang violence continues to threaten their lives. Additionally, intensified security operations must not expose children to further harm.”

World Children’s Day, celebrated annually on 20 November, marks the anniversary of the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), which outlines the rights of every child and what governments must do to protect them. Haiti is a state party to the CRC.
Organized gangs – namely Grand Ravine, Ti Bwa, 5 Segon and 400 Mawozo – started attacking the mountainous commune of Kenscoff in January 2025. All four gangs are part of the Viv Ansanm coalition.

Kenscoff borders Pétion-Ville, where many government offices, embassies and key commercial interests are situated. The 23 August attack on the population, which began around 9pm and was primarily led by a group from the 5 Segon gang, further appeared to be a retaliation for intensified security operations against the gangs.
One teenage girl told Amnesty International that she hid under her bed as gunshots rang out: “When they came inside the house, they said everybody should get out [or else] they would kill us.”
articles.lede: Amnesty International interviewed witnesses to the Kenscoff gang raid on 23 August 2026, in which 55 people were killed and 15 more were injured, according to a municipal official.

Sudan: Transfer War Crimes Suspects to ICC
articles.description: Sudanese authorities should immediately transfer former Interior Minister Ahmed Haroun to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to face charges in The Hague.
paragraphs: (The Hague) – Sudanese authorities should immediately transfer former Interior Minister Ahmed Haroun to the International Criminal Court ( ICC) to face charges in The Hague, Human Rights Watch said today. Haroun was recently taken into Sudanese custody and faces ICC war crimes and crimes against humanity charges, committed in Sudan’s Darfur region, in 2003 and 2004.

“For two decades, victims of atrocity crimes in Darfur have witnessed Haroun and others evading justice, leading to impunity-fueled cycles of violence that are claiming more victims every day.” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “If Sudan’s authorities transferred those sought by the ICC to the court in The Hague, as they are obliged to do, it would send a powerful message to those committing crimes today that they too may find themselves in the dock.”

Authorities should also transfer former President Omar al-Bashir —who is believed to be in Sudanese custody in Khartoum state as well—and locate, arrest, and transfer former Defense Minister Abdelrahim M. Hussein. The ICC has also issued arrest warrants for both of them, though there is no information available on Hussein’s location.

The ICC issued an arrest warrant against Haroun in 2007, and another against Hussein in 2012, for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2004. During that period, Sudanese government forces and allied militias carried out targeted attacks against civilians on the basis of their ethnicity, including killings, rape, forced displacement from their homes and land, and burning of their villages. In 2009 and 2010, the ICC issued two arrest warrants against al-Bashir for alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2008.
Following al-Bashir’s ouster in April 2019, Sudanese authorities held Haroun, al-Bashir, and Hussein in custody for charges not related to atrocities in Darfur but failed to transfer them to the ICC.

After fighting erupted between SAF and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on April 15, 2023, the authorities moved al-Bashir to Alia military hospital in Omdurman, Khartoum state, where he reportedly remained under guard, while Haroun left detention amid the collapse of prison security, and under circumstances suggesting coordination with judicial authorities.

On September 30, 2026, SAF granted al-Bashir initial approval to travel outside of Sudan for medical treatment. Based on media reports, al-Bashir continues to receive medical care at Alia military hospital and is yet to travel abroad.

UN Security Council Resolution 1593, referring the situation in Darfur to the ICC prosecutor, requires the government of Sudan to cooperate with the court even though it is not a party to the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty. In 2021, the ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor signed a memorandum of understanding with the Sudanese authorities addressing cooperation for arrests. The ICC lacks the ability to enforce its own orders and relies on state cooperation to conduct investigations and make arrests.
articles.lede: Sudanese authorities should immediately transfer former Interior Minister Ahmed Haroun to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to face charges in The Hague.

articles.title: Human Rights Watch Mourns Death of Activist Nabeel Rajab
articles.description: Nabeel Rajab, a prominent human rights activist from Bahrain and a close partner of Human Rights Watch, passed away on November 17, 2026, at the age of 62. He reportedly died in Türkiye following a heart attack.
paragraphs: (New York) – Nabeel Rajab, a prominent human rights activist from Bahrain and a close partner of Human Rights Watch, passed away on November 17, 2026, at the age of 62. He reportedly died in Türkiye following a heart attack.

Rajab rose to prominence as a human rights defender in Bahrain in the 1990s, and in 2000 he co-founded the Bahrain Human Rights Society, one of Bahrain’s first human rights organizations. He then co-founded and later became the president of the Bahrain Centre for Human Rights.

Rajab had served as a member of the Human Rights Watch Middle East and North Africa division’s advisory committee since 2010, playing a key role not only in supporting Human Rights Watch work in Bahrain, but also providing guidance to the documentation and advocacy work that Human Rights Watch carries out across the region.

Bahraini authorities unjustly detained and imprisoned him several times for his peaceful expression in the years following the 2011 pro-democracy protests in Bahrain. In 2018, he was sentenced to five years in prison for his comments criticizing torture at a Bahraini prison and the Saudi-led military campaign in Yemen. Even from detention, he continued his activism. In 2017, he wrote an op-ed for the New York Times from detention, titled “ Don’t Profit from Abuses by Bahrain ,” calling out US support of Bahraini authorities despite their abuses both in Bahrain and amid the conflict in Yemen. He wrote:

All our destinies are tied together. What will happen to Bahrain if everyone who supports peace, democracy and the rule of law is in jail? To whom will Bahrain’s disenfranchised youth turn to for support and guidance? These are the questions the Trump administration must ask itself before it sends my jailers another batch of fighter jets.

He was released from prison in 2020 and allowed to serve the rest of his sentence at home with his family, but only after his health deteriorated due to harsh detention conditions. In the years that followed, he continued to support the human rights movement and call out human rights abuses by Bahraini and other authorities across the world.

Sayed Ahmed al-Wadaei, the advocacy director at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy and a close friend, said that Rajab left Bahrain in March 2026 so that he could speak publicly on Bahraini human rights issues. He remained in exile until his passing, unable to return to Bahrain for fear of being rearrested.

Rajab’s death is a profound blow to the global and Arab human rights movements, which have lost a steadfast defender of freedom of expression and a voice of reason in a climate increasingly marked by hatred and polarization. Over many years, Rajab stood resolutely by his principles, despite being targeted, detained, and repressed for his unwavering commitment to universal human rights.

“Nabeel was a stalwart champion for human rights and democracy, not just for Bahrain but all of the Middle East,” said Sarah Leah Whitson, former Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “He paid a tremendous price for his advocacy, jailed and abused in prison, but always kept us hopeful and resilient. He played an essential role in guiding and supporting the work of Human Rights Watch’s MENA division. I considered him a true friend.”
articles.lede: Nabeel Rajab, a prominent human rights activist from Bahrain and a close partner of Human Rights Watch, passed away on November 17, 2026, at the age of 62. He reportedly died in Türkiye following a heart attack.

articles.title: Burkina Faso Targets Critics in Exile
articles.description: Journalists, activists and political opponents who fled Burkina Faso to escape the junta’s repression now risk arrest and prosecution abroad, as the country’s judicial authorities pursue dozens of individuals over alleged terrorism-related offenses.
paragraphs: Burkina Faso Prosecutor General Désiré Sawadogo announced on November 13 that a special court handling terrorism-related offenses had opened six cases against at least 45 people and entities. All those targeted exposed serious military abuses during counterinsurgency operations and include exiled journalists critical of the junta, among them Ahmed Newton Barry, Issaka Lingani, Inoussa Ouédraogo, Adama Ouedraogo, and Abdoulaye Barry; exiled social media activist Naïm Touré; former foreign affairs minister Alpha Barry, and international journalist Wassim Nasr. They face various charges, including complicity in terrorist associations and financing terrorism.

Burkina Faso sent international arrest warrants and extradition requests to Côte d’Ivoire, France, and the United States, said Sawadogo. He added that Burkina Faso asked the United States to use Meta to identify and prosecute Facebook page administrators accused of promoting terrorism.

The authorities are using counterterrorism laws to target critical voices and restrict independent reporting on military abuses. The extradition requests extend political repression beyond Burkina Faso’s borders, placing critics who sought protection abroad at risk of arrest, forced return, and further abuse. The government’s recent decision to reinstate capital punishment for offenses including terrorism, high treason, and espionage is also of grave concern.

Since seizing power in a September 2022 coup, the junta has restricted fundamental rights through media bans, suspension of unions and civil society organizations, dissolution of political parties, enforced disappearances, and the unlawful conscription of government critics.

Meanwhile, the conflict between government forces and allied militias and Islamist armed groups, ongoing since 2017, has involved widespread abuses by all parties, including war crimes and crimes against humanity, with no accountability. Human Rights Watch has documented serious flaws in the special terrorism court, including prolonged pretrial detention, and violations of fair trial guarantees.

Concerned governments should rigorously scrutinize all extradition and judicial cooperation requests from Burkina Faso. No journalist, activist or political opponent should be returned where there are substantial grounds to fear torture, arbitrary detention, an unfair trial, and the death penalty. International partners should condemn the targeting of critics at home and abroad and reject Burkina Faso’s attempts at transnational repression.

Cambodia’s Repression Hangs Over Francophonie Summit
articles.description: As world leaders recently gathered in Phnom Penh to celebrate the 20th Francophonie Summit with the theme of peace and shared prosperity, French President Emmanuel Macron took to the podium to call publicly for an investigation into the killing of former Cambodian lawmaker and French citizen Lim Kimya.
paragraphs: As world leaders recently gathered in Phnom Penh to celebrate the 20th Francophonie Summit with the theme of peace and shared prosperity, French President Emmanuel Macron took to the podium to call publicly for an investigation into the killing of former Cambodian lawmaker and French citizen Lim Kimya. It was a rare public rebuke of the Cambodian government by a foreign leader.
A gunman killed Kimya in Bangkok, Thailand in January 2025. Kimya had served as a parliament member with the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party before its 2017 dissolution.

A Thai court convicted the gunman, Ekkalak Paenoi, in October 2025 and issued arrest warrants for two Cambodian suspects, Ly Ratanakraksmey and Pich Kimsrin, both of whom have connections to high-ranking Cambodian officials. The Cambodian government—like many of its neighbors in Southeast Asia—is increasingly persecuting activists abroad.

The Cambodian government has yet to acknowledge the arrest warrants or start an impartial investigation. Both men remain at large. France has issued Interpol Red Notices for them on charges of complicity in premeditated murder.

Macron’s raising Kimya’s murder during a joint press conference with Prime Minister Hun Manet sends a strong message that the French government is taking Cambodian authorities’ attacks on activists abroad seriously. The Cambodian government should heed the call and independently and impartially investigate the murder.

But political repression by the Cambodian government runs deeper than one case. Ahead of 2027 local elections, the authorities are escalating their crackdown on the long suppressed political opposition. Young activists in particular, such as the five imprisoned Mother Nature Cambodia environmental activists, have been punished with baseless treason charges and lengthy prison sentences. Concerned governments should publicly and privately urge Cambodian authorities to release the more than 100 Cambodians currently imprisoned for exercising their fundamental freedoms.

Human Rights Watch was among the local and international organizations that pressed Cambodian authorities to release the Mother Nature activists and others ahead of the Francophonie Summit. The ruling Cambodian People’s Party, which exerts complete control over the country’s courts, was apparently unbothered by these efforts.

Other foreign leaders should amplify Macron’s message and publicly call on Cambodia’s government to reopen the space for the political opposition and respect the fundamental rights of all Cambodians, both at home and abroad.

articles.title: Rights Defender in Central African Republic Dies
articles.description: Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70.
paragraphs: Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70. One of the country's most respected rule of law advocates, his career spanned more than four decades.

Tiangaye first came into the spotlight as a young lawyer when he defended the former emperor, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, in 1986. Later he defended the future president, François Bozizé, when he was accused of plotting a coup.

For Tiangaye, the cardinal rule that all defendants must benefit from their right to a fair trial is one he lived by. By the early 1990s, Tiangaye was one of the leading Central African human rights advocates and served as the Bar Association president.

In 1996 he was the lead defense council for Jean-Paul Akayesu before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. Human Rights Watch strongly advocated for the prosecution of Akayesu hailing his 1998 conviction as a historic international precedent. I once discussed the seminal conviction with Tiangaye and he reiterated that a good lawyer must be willing to defend clients and insist on due process, even in highly charged circumstances.
Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, he spoke out for judicial independence and democratic governance. This often put him at odds with the government. But threats, he said, came with the job.

He regularly ended up at the heart of national politics. Following Bozizé's successful coup, Tiangaye helped draft the 2004 Constitution. In January 2013, then-president Bozizé appointed Tiangaye prime minister amidst national turmoil. He remained in the position after Seleka seized Bangui and committed widespread abuses. Tiangaye despised the Seleka’s crimes, he told me, and he resigned.

He returned to legal practice and his passion: defending the Constitution. He became an outspoken critic of President Faustin-Archange Touadéra's efforts to remove presidential term limits, insisting on constitutional safeguards and political pluralism.

His death is both a professional and personal loss for Human Rights Watch. More importantly, it occurs as independent voices and institutions remain under pressure in the Central African Republic. I spoke with him just last week about detained activists. I wish I asked how he would like to be remembered. I imagine he would have insisted that we not focus on the individual, but on his commitment to the rule of law and human rights—Tiangaye’s ultimate legacy.
articles.lede: Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70.

articles.title: Three Years’ Prison in Kyrgyzstan for Alleged Repost
articles.description: A district court in Bishkek on November 11 sentenced Baktybek Moldaliev, an activist, to three years in jail for allegedly reposting content produced by Kloop Media, which a court had previously declared “extremist”.
paragraphs: A district court in Bishkek on November 11 sentenced Baktybek Moldaliev, an activist, to three years in jail for allegedly reposting content produced by Kloop Media, which a court had previously declared “extremist”. The case sends a chilling message to social media users across Kyrgyzstan: simply clicking the repost button on a social media platform could land someone in prison.

Moldaliev, 49, who worked as a welder, and commented regularly on politics on Facebook was first detained for a day in November 2025, when police seized his phone as evidence and gained access to it, according to his wife, Elvira Zhusupova.

Six months later in May 2026 Moldaliev was charged with inciting "mass unrest"—vague charges frequently brought against social media users in Kyrgyzstan who are prosecuted for sharing or resharing content online. He was taken into custody where he has remained since. After a month and a half, authorities changed the charges to the production and distribution of extremist materials.
During the November 11 court hearing, Moldaliev denied the allegations, saying that police or other individuals could have used his account to share the content and frame him.

In July 2025, amid a crackdown on independent media, amendments to the criminal code and the code of offenses went into effect that toughen sanctions for production and distribution of materials authorities deem “extremist.” The crime is punishable by up to three years in prison, even without intent to disseminate the materials. The amendments also criminalize using the internet or mass media to make public calls for extremist activity, which carries a three to five-year prison sentence.

In October 2025 a district court in Bishkek declared the activities of Rinat Tukhvashin, Kloop's co-founder, and investigative journalist Bolot Temirov, founder of Temirov LIVE and Ait-Ait Dese, as well as materials produced by their media outlets, “ extremist ”. It was the first time a court had declared the content of media outlets extremist, Kloop said.

The Kyrgyz authorities should drop the case against Moldaliev, vacate his unjust conviction and release him, and the government should reverse course on its assault on the right to freedom of expression, stop weaponizing the criminal justice system to silence critics, and reform laws on extremism.
articles.lede: A district court in Bishkek on November 11 sentenced Baktybek Moldaliev, an activist, to three years in jail for allegedly reposting content produced by Kloop Media, which a court had previously declared “extremist”.

articles.title: GC IV Commentary Series
articles.description: The Commentary’s unqualified statement that NIACs may take place at sea and that CA 3 applies in such situations is unconvincing.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

The 2025 Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention states that non-international armed conflicts (NIACs) may “take place, and have taken place, in part or in entirety, at sea or on other bodies of water” and that “[w]ithin the framework of the Geneva Conventions, Article 3 applies to such conflicts.” As phrased, the statement suggests that NIACs can be entirely sea-borne and that Article 3 applies at sea without restrictions. These claims are difficult to reconcile with the historical record and with the terms of Common Article 3 (CA 3).

As the updated Commentary to the Second Geneva Convention observes, “[n]ot many non-international armed conflicts with a naval dimension have taken place since the adoption of the Geneva Conventions.” This Commentary offers the Sri Lankan civil war as the most prominent example, though the only authority it cites in support is an arbitral award concerned with combat operations on land (paras. 61-64).

Beyond Sri Lanka, the examples are few indeed. The Newport Manual mentions the Spanish civil war, which of course pre-dates the Geneva Conventions of 1949, Israel’s blockade of Gaza, and the Houthi attacks on shipping in the Red Sea. Others have cited the blockades of Abkhazia by Georgia, of East Timor by Indonesia, and of Yemen by the Saudi-led coalition. The classification of some of these conflicts as non-international is open to question. In any event, none of these conflicts were entirely sea-borne, since in each case the action at sea formed part of a conflict with a base on land. In fact, no entirely sea-borne NIAC appears to have ever taken place.

Perhaps the closest thing to an entirely sea-borne NIAC is the campaign of strikes the United States has conducted since September 2025 in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific against vessels it says are operated by drug traffickers. The United States has portrayed this campaign as part of a NIAC between itself and two drug cartels, the Tren de Aragua and Cartel de Los Soles. Putting aside the question of whether the conditions for the existence of a NIAC are actually satisfied in this case, the United States itself has not claimed that the conflict is entirely sea-borne, because its position rests on the argument that the two cartels have caused the deaths of tens of thousands of Americans within the United States. The Commentary’s claim that NIACs have taken place entirely at sea is therefore not borne out even in this instance.

The suggestion that CA 3 applies at sea runs into another difficulty. CA 3 applies to an armed conflict not of an international character “occurring in the territory of one of the High Contracting Parties.” Whether “territory” extends to the sea is not obvious. The answer turns on the rules of treaty interpretation in Articles 31 to 33 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, which the Commentary adopts as its guiding methodology (para. 98). The general rule of interpretation under Article 31(1) requires a treaty to “be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to the terms of the treaty in their context and in the light of its object and purpose.”
articles.lede: The Commentary’s unqualified statement that NIACs may take place at sea and that CA 3 applies in such situations is unconvincing.

El Salvador: condena a 15 años de prisión contra el defensor Fidel Zavala
articles.description: Nueva Información SLV 001 / 0425 / OBS 012.2 Condena / Detención arbitraria / Hostigamiento judicial El Salvador 18 de noviembre de 2026 El (…)
paragraphs: El Observatorio para la Protección de las Personas Defensoras de Derechos Humanos, programa conjunto de la Organización Mundial Contra la Tortura (OMCT) y la Federación Internacional por los Derechos Humanos (FIDH), ha recibido nueva información y solicita su intervención urgente ante la siguiente situación en El Salvador.

El Observatorio ha sido informado de la condena contra el Sr. Fidel Antonio Zavala Pérez, defensor de derechos humanos y vocero de la organización Unidad de Defensa de Derechos Humanos y Comunitarios de El Salvador (UNIDEHC), cuya labor se ha centrado en denunciar la corrupción, la tortura, los malos tratos y las muertes bajo custodia en los centros penitenciarios durante el régimen de excepción, así como en acompañar a comunidades amenazadas con desalojos forzosos. El Sr. Zavala inició esta labor tras haber permanecido 13 meses en prisión preventiva, entre febrero de 2022 y marzo de 2023, y haber sido absuelto y puesto en libertad.

El 10 de noviembre de 2026, según información publicada por la organización de derechos humanos, Cristosal y recogida el 13 de noviembre por el medio Infodemia, el Tribunal Tercero de Sentencia de San Salvador condenó al Sr. Fidel Zavala a 15 años de prisión por el delito de “estafa agravada”, en un juicio sometido a reserva judicial. La acusación se refiere a supuestos hechos cometidos entre 2018 y 2021, en perjuicio de tres personas, por un monto de 4.025 dólares estadounidenses (aproximadamente 3.655 euros). Su defensa ha señalado que recurriría la sentencia y que dispondría hasta el 24 de noviembre de 2026 para interponer la apelación.

Cabe recordar que el Sr. Zavala ya había sido absuelto en 2023 en un proceso por este delito, por falta de pruebas. Sin embargo, a finales de 2024, la Sala de lo Penal ordenó la repetición del juicio, meses después de que el defensor presentara, en julio de 2024, una denuncia ante la Fiscalía General de la República contra el entonces Director General de los Centros Penitenciarios de El Salvador, el Sr. Osiris Luna, por presuntas torturas y actos arbitrarios que afirmó haber presenciado durante una detención anterior.

El Observatorio recuerda que el 25 de febrero de 2025 el Sr. Fidel Zavala fue detenido durante un operativo policial en las oficinas de UNIDEHC, en el marco de actuaciones que también afectaron a otras personas defensoras vinculadas a esa organización. Desde entonces, el Sr. Zavala permanece privado de su libertad, acumulando, además de la reapertura del proceso por “estafa agravada”, supuestos delitos de “agrupaciones ilícitas”, “comercialización ilegal de parcelas” y “ejercicio ilegal de la profesión”, en relación con su labor de acompañamiento a las familias de la comunidad La Floresta, quienes defendían su derecho a la tierra, y cuyos líderes comunitarias también fueron criminalizados.

Posteriormente, el Observatorio advirtió sobre su traslado al Centro Penal La Esperanza, conocido como Mariona, y sobre los riesgos para su integridad debido a la presencia de personal penitenciario que denunció por presuntos actos de tortura y otros abusos; por lo que, tras la presión internacional, fue retirado de dicho penal y trasladado a las bartolinas del Centro Judicial “Dr. Isidro Menéndez” en la Ciudad de San Salvador, donde se encuentra detenido actualmente.

articles.title: What to Look for in Thursday’s ICJ Judgment on Genocide
The United States’ Missile Strike on Minab’s Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School Part II
articles.description: Experts consider U.S. accountability for the Iranian elementary school strike under international humanitarian law.
paragraphs: At 10:30 on the first morning of the U.S.-Israel-Iran war, a missile strike destroyed the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in the southern Iran city of Minab. More than 150 persons were killed – schoolgirls and schoolboys aged 6 to 13 years old, plus a handful of school personnel, nearly all of them women. (¶93) Months after that Feb. 28, 2026, strike, mourners continued to pay daily visits to graves marked by poster-sized photos of the children. Although all public evidence indicates that the U.S. military launched the strike, to this day the United States has neither acknowledged this nor credibly shown that some other actor was responsible. We have undertaken a legal analysis of the strike and its aftermath, initially in our essay just published in the October issue of the American Journal of International Law, and now in this two-part series of Just Security articles.

Our Part I article analyzed the available evidence against international humanitarian law, especially IHL’s rules on the protection of civilians and civilian objects, including children and schools. We found a powerful case that the Minab school strike violated the principle of distinction (requiring belligerents to distinguish between civilian and military persons or objects, directly attacking only the latter and never the former) as operationalized through the rule on doubt. We found a similarly compelling case that the United States violated its IHL obligations to take precautions, including the duty to undertake feasible verification of potential targets. Finally, we drew a link between these violations and the United States’ institutional and rhetorical shifts away from preventing and mitigating civilian harm – to quote Secretary of Defense-renamed-War Pete Hegseth, shifts away from “tepid legality” and toward “maximum lethality.”

In this Part II article, we consider questions of accountability for the strike and its horrific aftermath. In the weeks since our AJIL essay went to final proof, the United Nations’ Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Islamic Republic of Iran (“Iran IIFFM”) found “reasonable grounds to believe” that the strike constituted a “war crime” ( ¶ 126 ). That body’s report, summarized below, raises accountability questions that we consider in turn: Is it clear that the United States was responsible? If so, what forms of accountability are available? What has the United States done before in the wake of unintended attacks in other conflicts? How does the Iran IIFFM’s conclusion compare with our own findings of apparent violations of IHL? Does its war-crimes determination pertain to state responsibility under international law, to individual criminal responsibility, or both?

Before considering these questions, we note that multiple ex post accountability forums are authorized to deal with conduct of the kind under analysis here. Adjudicative forums include international criminal courts and tribunals, national criminal courts and military courts-martial, and civil lawsuits or administrative disciplinary proceedings. Additional forums include: fact-finding missions like the Iran IIFFM; state and international commissions of inquiry, claims commissions, and investigatory mechanisms; international treaty bodies and United Nations special mandate holders; regional human rights courts; and initiatives, like the Safe Schools Declaration, which bring together states, international organizations, and civil society. Within this array of options, the substantive areas of focus, applicable legal characterizations, evidentiary and proof requirements, procedural obstacles, and consequences of violation vary widely.
articles.lede: Experts consider U.S. accountability for the Iranian elementary school strike under international humanitarian law.

Philippine Police Detain Hundreds Protesting Trump Visit
articles.description: Police in the Philippines arrested and detained at least 245 people protesting the visit of US President Donald Trump to Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit.
paragraphs: Protests in Manila started on November 15 opposing the Philippine government’s plan to build a technology manufacturing hub in Capas, Tarlac province, under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative. The construction will displace hundreds of Indigenous people and small farmers from their homes and farmlands.

An estimated 6,000 people joined the protests despite police efforts to contain demonstrations by banning them everywhere except in “freedom parks” – designated areas where rallies can be held without a permit.

Yet police arrested 236 people on the outskirts of Metro Manila who were traveling from the Southern Tagalog region to the main protest site. Among those detained were 29 farmers including members of the Indigenous Mangyan tribe, 19 journalists, 9 environmental defenders, and 6 human rights workers. Ephraim Cortez of the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers said 19 children were detained.

“This is the largest mass arrest we’ve seen under [President] Marcos,” protest leader Renato Reyes told Human Rights Watch. “Our whole delegation was arrested and taken to a police camp where lawyers were not given immediate access.”
Detainees are being held inside a police camp in a hall with poor ventilation, insufficient drinking water, and inadequate restroom facilities, according to activists and lawyers.

The protesters have been detained for three days without charge. Lawyers representing them expressed concern that they could face criminal charges of illegal assembly, alarms and scandals, and disobedience to authority.

Police detained without charge another nine protesters at the main protest site on November 15 for attempting to march to the ASEAN summit venue. News footage shows police officers slapping and kicking a protester on the ground.

International human rights law protects the right to peaceful assembly. Law enforcement may not carry out indiscriminate mass arrests even if a protest violates local laws or becomes disorderly. Arrests need to be based on individualized grounds and comply with the requirements of legality, necessity, and proportionality. Police can arrest people responsible for specific unlawful conduct but not just for taking part in a protest. All those arbitrarily detained for exercising their basic rights should be immediately released.
articles.lede: Police in the Philippines arrested and detained at least 245 people protesting the visit of US President Donald Trump to Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit.

articles.title: Russia’s Strikes on Ukraine’s Energy Infrastructure as a Crime Against Humanity
articles.description: An expert examines whether Russia’s strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure constitute a war crime and crime against humanity.
paragraphs: Russia’s campaign against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, which supplies electricity and heat, has entered its fifth winter. Overnight strikes on Nov. 7-8 on energy facilities left more than 600,000 residents in the Dnipropetrovsk region without electricity as winter temperatures approached freezing. [1] The campaign has intensified every winter since it began in October 2022. Last winter, as temperatures fell below 0 degrees F, Russian strikes reduced thermal capacity to 30% in the hardest-hit areas. A single attack in January disabled three of Kyiv’s five combined heat and power plants, leaving most households in the region without power or heat. [2]

On Oct. 26, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, which was established by the Human Rights Council in 2022, submitted its latest report (dated Oct. 19) to the General Assembly’s Third Committee. [3] The report concluded that Russian authorities have committed the war crime of intentionally directing attacks against civilian objects and the crime against humanity of “other inhumane acts.” [4]

It is self-evident that the Russian attacks constitute war crimes on various grounds. But the crime against humanity finding is significant, for in 2023, the Commission found only that the attacks “may have amounted” to that international crime. [5] The 2026 report makes that conclusion definitive. It also brings the Commission into line with the International Criminal Court (ICC) Pre-Trial Chamber, which in 2024 found reasonable grounds to believe that four senior Russian officials had committed that very crime. [6]

But the characterization merits deeper legal unpacking than was possible in the Commission’s report. Accordingly, after briefly surveying the war crimes that the attacks likely constituted, I turn to the crime against humanity (there are numerous types) that has been alleged. The critical issue is whether the Russian attacks satisfied each requisite element of that offense. As the report explains, the Commission members agreed that they did, although they did not detail how they reached that conclusion. Nevertheless, I believe their conclusion was sound, at least as to strikes on facilities that were not military objectives. In this piece, I explain why, and where the Commission’s reasoning falls somewhat short.

At the outset, it is important to distinguish between (1) violations of the law of armed conflict (LOAC), committed by States through their organs, including the military, and (2) war crimes and crimes against humanity, which lead to individual criminal responsibility. In an earlier Articles of War piece published in October 2022, I addressed the former, [7] finding that at least some of the strikes violated LOAC under Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions (AP I), [8] to which both belligerents are Party, and customary international law. Here, the issue is whether the attacks violate international criminal law, opening the door to prosecuting those involved.
articles.lede: An expert examines whether Russia’s strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure constitute a war crime and crime against humanity.
