Litigation Tracker: Legal Challenges to Trump Administration Actions
articles.description: A public resource tracking the legal challenges to Trump administration executive orders and actions.
paragraphs: This living, searchable resource tracks legal challenges to Trump administration executive actions. If you think we are missing anything, you can email us at [email protected]. The Tracker is part of Just Security’s Collection: Coverage of the Trump Administration’s Executive Actions.
Case Name Filings Date Case Filed State A.G.'s Case Status Issue Executive Action Last Case Update Case Summary Case Updates National Association of the Deaf v. Trump (D.D.C.) 1:25-cv-01683

In January 2025, the administration stopped providing ASL interpreters at public press briefings and other similar events. The federal government had provided ASL interpretation for all coronavirus press briefings following a court order in October 2020 and began voluntarily providing interpretation services at all press briefings by key administration officials in January 2021.

The National Association of the Deaf (NAD), a civil rights organization, and two members of NAD are suing President Donald Trump, Susan Wiles, the White House Chief of Staff, Karoline Leavitt, the Press Secretary to the President, and a number of offices within the White House to challenge the decision to stop providing ASL interpretation. Plaintiffs argue that without such services, deaf and hard of hearing individuals are unable to meaningfully access federal government programs and services or participate in American society. Plaintiffs claim that Defendants are violating the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which prohibits executive agencies from discriminating against individuals with disabilities when conducting any program or activity. Plaintiffs also allege that Defendants are violating the First Amendment, arguing that freedom of speech includes the right to receive information and that this deprivation impinges on their ability to petition the government. Plaintiffs further argue that the Fifth Amendment is violated because Plaintiffs are being denied equal protection under the law by being treated differently and because the Plaintiffs’ fundamental rights under the First Amendment are being impinged upon. Plaintiffs seek preliminary and permanent injunctive relief requiring Defendants to provide ASL interpreters at press briefings and other similar events. They also seek a court declaration that Defendants are violating the Rehabilitation Act and the First and Fifth Amendments.

Nov. 4, 2025: Judge Amir H. Ali granted plaintiffs’ motion for a preliminary injunction in part, ordering the administration to provide a simultaneous and publicly accessible feed with American Sign Language (ASL) interpretation for “all publicly announced White House press briefings conducted by the President or White House Press Secretary that are captured by White House communication channels.” The court found that the administration’s decision to end ASL interpretation likely violated the Rehabilitation Act, which prohibits excluding people with disabilities from participation in, denying them benefits of, or discriminating against them in Executive agency programming. The court did not grant the plaintiffs’ request to require ASL interpretation for Vice President, First Lady, or Second Lady press briefings or events and that interpretation be provided for all videos on the White House website and social media pages.
articles.lede: A public resource tracking the legal challenges to Trump administration executive orders and actions.

articles.title: How Much Weight for ILO Supervisory Bodies? The ICJ’s One-Size-Fits-All Approach
articles.description: [Leonardo David Lima Valdés is a Mexican lawyer in the Legal Adviser’s Office of Mexico’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, where he works on international litigation and legal issues before internation…
paragraphs: [ Leonardo David Lima Valdés is a Mexican lawyer in the Legal Adviser’s Office of Mexico’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, where he works on international litigation and legal issues before international courts and organizations. He was a member of the Mexican delegation in the ICJ advisory proceedings on the right to strike under ILO Convention No. 87. The views expressed are personal and do not necessarily reflect those of the Government of Mexico or any institution with which the author is affiliated.]

During its 349 th bis (special) session, the Governing Body of the International Labour Organization (“ILO”) decided to request an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice (“ICJ”): Is the right to strike of workers and their organizations protected under the Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise Convention, 1948 (No. 87)?

On 21 May 2026, the ICJ delivered its Advisory Opinion. By ten votes to four, the Court affirmed that the right to strike of workers and their organizations is protected under Convention No. 87. Although this treaty does not expressly mention strikes, the Court held that the ordinary meaning of its relevant terms, in particular Articles 2, 3(1), and 10, read in good faith, in their context and in light of the object and purpose of the treaty, indicates that protection of the right to strike is encompassed in the protection of freedom of association.

The problem is not that the Court ignored differences between ILO supervisory bodies and human rights treaty bodies; it expressly acknowledged them. The problem is that it did not explain which differences matter, or how those differences affect the degree of interpretative weight to be accorded to their pronouncements. This post argues that a contextual assessment should distinguish two related questions: what institutional grounds and State acceptance support reliance on a pronouncement, and how persuasive is the particular interpretation? The first inquiry considers institutional origin, mandate and State reception; while the second examines independence, expertise, procedures and reasoning. Their interaction should explain the weight attributed, rather than leave “great weight” as a label whose implications remain uncertain.

The Court treated ILO supervisory bodies as important but not authoritative interpreters of Convention No. 87. It considered that their pronouncements do not themselves create “subsequent practice” under VCLT Article 31(3)(b), contrary to what some participants argued (Advisory Opinion, paras. 78-83). But it affirmed that they matter in two ways. First, if States react to or adopt them, they may help show State practice. Second, even without full State agreement, they may be used as supplementary means of interpretation under VCLT Article 32. The Court then said it could ascribe “great weight” to their pronouncements, while stressing that it was not bound to follow them.

The ILO supervisory system includes regular supervision by the Committee of Experts on the Application of Conventions and Recommendations (“CEACR”) and the Conference Committee on the Application of Standards (“CAS”). The CEACR, composed of 20 experts serving in their individual capacity, reviews State reports on the application of the fundamental ILO conventions, including Convention No. 87, and issues observations, direct requests, and General Surveys. The CAS has a tripartite composition, comprising governments as well as employers’ and workers’ organizations, and reviews States’ compliance with their obligations pursuant to ILO Conventions, including through the consideration of individual cases.
articles.lede: During its 349 th bis (special) session, the Governing Body of the International Labour Organization (“ILO”) decided to request an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice (“ICJ”): Is the right to strike…

articles.title: IMPACTO. Sudán: La labor de incidencia de la FIDH contribuye a que la Unión Europea sancione a agentes extranjeros que alimentan las atrocidades
articles.description: La situación de la población civil en Sudán sigue deteriorándose más de tres años después del inicio del conflicto armado. En 2026, la guerra se (…)
paragraphs: – La situación de la población civil en Sudán sigue deteriorándose más de tres años después del inicio del conflicto armado. En 2026, la guerra se ha cobrado 150.000 vidas, ha desplazado a 15 millones de personas y ha sumido a otros 20 millones en una situación de hambre aguda. – Desde 2023, la Federación Internacional por los Derechos Humanos (FIDH) y sus organizaciones miembros instan a la Unión Europea a adoptar medidas concretas para poner fin a las atrocidades y conseguir que agentes extranjeros dejen de alimentar la guerra en Sudán. – En julio de 2026, se escuchó por fin ese llamamiento: el Parlamento Europeo aprobó una resolución sobre la situación en El Obeid y el Consejo de la Unión Europea decidió imponer nuevas sanciones a agentes externos que vulneran el embargo de armas impuesto por las Naciones Unidas a Sudán.

El 15 de abril de 2023 estalló en Sudán un conflicto entre las Fuerzas Armadas Sudanesas (SAF) y las Fuerzas de Apoyo Rápido (RSF), enfrentadas por el poder. Desde el primer día, se han sucedido los ataques contra la población civil que en algunas ocasiones han sido deliberados.

En estos tres años, la población civil ha sido el blanco de la guerra, que ha dejado un rastro de atrocidades: ejecuciones masivas, desplazamientos generalizados y violencia sexual y de género. Activistas, periodistas, personal médico y humanitario, personas defensoras de los derechos humanos y quienes se oponen a la guerra sufren ataques, hostigamiento, detenciones y asesinatos perpetrados por ambas partes del conflicto.

Las regiones de Darfur y Kordofán son las más afectadas. El 26 de octubre de 2025, la toma de El Fasher por las Rapid Support Forces (RSF) marcó una escalada del conflicto. El asedio, que duró 18 meses, ha dejado a cientos de miles de víctimas de crímenes graves y de crímenes de lesa humanidad, como ejecuciones masivas, depuración étnica, secuestros, detenciones arbitrarias, violencia sexual generalizada y el uso del hambre como arma de guerra.

En 2026, los crímenes contra la población civil son cada vez más graves. La intensificación de los ataques con drones y los bombardeos de artillería en Kordofán del Norte y Kordofán del Sur desde el 18 de junio hace temer que en El Obeid, se repitan los crímenes cometidos en El Fasher y se destruyan los servicios esenciales para la supervivencia, con consecuencias humanitarias catastróficas.

En estos tres años, la FIDH ha pedido que se ponga fin al conflicto, que se proteja a la población civil y que se adopten medidas para que las personas responsables rindan cuentas. Desde abril de 2023, la FIDH y sus organizaciones miembros y asociadas denuncian los crímenes cometidos contra la población civil y piden que se ponga fin al ciclo de violencia e impunidad.

La diplomacia puede ser un instrumento eficiente para prevenir la guerra y poner fin a los crímenes de lesa humanidad y los crímenes de guerra. Desde el principio del conflicto, la FIDH pidió a la Unión Europea que interviniera. En una reunión del Consejo de Asuntos Exteriores celebrada en abril de 2024, instó a la Unión Europea y a sus Estados miembros a adoptar medidas urgentes para proteger los derechos humanos y hacer frente a la crisis humanitaria que se avecinaba en Sudán. En abril de 2025, la FIDH y otras 12 organizaciones no gubernamentales reiteraron su petición a la Unión Europea de que protegiera a la población civil.
articles.lede: La situación de la población civil en Sudán sigue deteriorándose más de tres años después del inicio del conflicto armado.

articles.title: IMPACT. Soudan: le plaidoyer de la FIDH contribue à obtenir des sanctions européennes pour les acteurs étrangers qui alimentent les atrocités
articles.description: La situation de la population civile au Soudan continue de se détériorer, plus de trois ans après le début du conflit armé. En 2026, la guerre a (…)
paragraphs: – La situation de la population civile au Soudan continue de se détériorer, plus de trois ans après le début du conflit armé. En 2026, la guerre a provoqué 150 000 morts, engendré le déplacement de 15 de personnes d’autres et plongé 20 millions d’autres dans une famine aiguë. – Depuis 2023, la Fédération internationale des droits de l’homme (FIDH) et ses membres plaident pour que l’Union européenne prenne des mesures concrètes afin de mettre un terme aux atrocités et d’empêcher les acteurs étrangers de continuer à attiser la guerre au Soudan. – En juillet 2026, cet appel à l’action a enfin été entendu. Le Parlement européen a voté une résolution sur la situation à El Obeid et le Conseil de l’Union européenne a décidé de nouvelles sanctions à l’encontre des acteurs extérieurs qui enfreignent l’embargo sur les armes décrété par les Nations unies au Soudan.

Le 15 avril 2023, un conflit a éclaté au Soudan entre les Forces armées soudanaises (SAF) et les Forces de soutien rapide (RSF), dans une lutte pour le pouvoir. Dès le premier jour de cette guerre, les attaques contre les populations civiles sont courantes, certaines étant délibérées.

Depuis trois ans, les populations civiles sont les cibles d’une guerre qui se caractérise par ses atrocités: des massacres, des déplacements massifs de population et des violences sexuelles et basées sur le genre. Les militant⸱es, les journalistes, les professionnel⸱les de santé, les travailleur⸱ses humanitaires, les défenseur⸱es des droits de l’homme et les opposant⸱es à la guerre sont victimes d’agressions, de harcèlement, de détentions et d’assassinats, de la part des deux parties au conflit.

Les régions du Darfour et du Kordofan sont particulièrement touchées. Le 26 octobre 2025, la chute d’ El Fasher aux mains des Forces de soutien rapide (RSF) a marqué une escalade du conflit. Un siège de 18 mois a fait des centaines de milliers de victimes de crimes graves et de crimes contre l’humanité, tels que des massacres, des nettoyages ethniques, des enlèvements, des détentions arbitraires, des violences sexuelles généralisées et le recours à la famine comme arme de guerre.

En 2026, la gravité des crimes commis contre les civil⸱es ne cesse de s’aggraver. L’intensification des frappes de drones et des bombardements d’artillerie dans les Kordofans du Nord et du Sud depuis le 18 juin fait craindre que les crimes commis à El Fasher ne se reproduisent à El Obeid, et que la destruction des services essentiels à la survie ne conduise à une catastrophe humanitaire.

Depuis trois ans, la FIDH appelle à la fin du conflit et à la protection des populations, ainsi qu’à l’adoption de mesures visant à traduire les responsables de ces crimes en justice. Depuis avril 2023, la FIDH et ses organisations membres et partenaires dénoncent les crimes commis contre les civil⸱es et appellent à briser le cercle vicieux de la violence et de l’impunité.

La diplomatie peut être un outil puissant pour prévenir la guerre et mettre fin aux crimes contre l’humanité et aux crimes de guerre. Très tôt, la FIDH a appelé l’Union européenne à intervenir. Lors d’une réunion du Conseil des affaires étrangères en avril 2024, elle a exhorté l’Union européenne et ses États membres à prendre des mesures urgentes pour protéger les droits humains et faire face à la crise humanitaire qui menace le Soudan. En avril 2025, la FIDH et 12 ONG ont de nouveau appelé l’Union européenne à protéger les civil⸱es.
articles.lede: La situation de la population civile au Soudan continue de se détériorer, plus de trois ans après le début du conflit armé.

articles.title: IMPACT. Sudan: FIDH advocacy contributes to European Union sanctions against foreign actors fueling atrocities
articles.description: The situation for the civilian population in Sudan continues to deteriorate, more than three years after the start of the armed conflict. In 2026, (…)
paragraphs: – The situation for the civilian population in Sudan continues to deteriorate, more than three years after the start of the armed conflict. In 2026, the war claimed 150,000 lives, displaced 15 million people, and left 20 million people suffering from acute famine. – Since 2023, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and its members have been advocating for the European Union to take concrete measures to put an end to the atrocities, and to make foreign actors stop fueling the war in Sudan. – In July 2026, the call to action is finally being heard. The European Parliament voted a resolution on the situation in El Obeid and the Council of the European Union decided on new sanctions for external actors breaching the United Nations arms embargo in Sudan.

The 15 April 2023 erupted a conflict in Sudan between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), in a quest for power. Since the very first day of this war, attacks on civilians have become a regular occurrence and some are deliberate.

During three years, the war has targeted civilians and claimed atrocities as mass killings, widespread displacement, sexual and gender-based violence. Activists, journalists, medical professionals, humanitarian workers, human rights defenders, and any opponent to the war face attacks, harassment, detention and killings, from both sides of the conflict.

Darfur and Kordofan regions are particularly affected. On 26 October 2025, the fall of El Fasher to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) marked an escalation of conflict. An 18-month siege has left hundreds of thousands of victims of serious crimes and crimes against humanity, such as mass killings, ethnic cleansing, abductions, arbitrary detentions, widespread sexual violence and the use of starvation as a weapon of war.

In 2026, the severity of crimes against civilians continues to increase. Intensifying drone strikes and artillery shelling North and South Kordofan from 18 June are raising fears that the crimes committed in El Fasher could be repeated in El Obeid, and the destruction of life-sustaining services, leading to a humanitarian catastrophe.

During three years, FIDH has been calling an end to the conflict and for the protection of civilians, as well as measures to hold perpetrators accountable. From April 2023, the FIDH and its member and partner organizations have denounced the crimes committed against civilians], the FIDH and its member and partner organisations have denounced the crimes committed against civilians and call to break the cycle of violence and impunity.

Diplomacy can be a powerful tool for preventing war and stopping crimes against humanity ans war crimes. Soon FIDH called for the European Union to intervene. At a Foreign Affairs Council meeting in April 2024, it urged the European Union and its Member States to take urgent measures to protect human rights and address the looming humanitarian crisis in Sudan. In April 2025, FIDH and 12 NGOs called again on the European Union to protect civilians.
articles.lede: The situation for the civilian population in Sudan continues to deteriorate, more than three years after the start of the armed conflict.

Général Bienvenue Zokoué confirme lui aussi que « les mercenaires russes ont aussi versé leur sang ici en RCA». Ah bon? Ces criminels russes peuvent aussi mourir? Lisez ici ce que le ministre Zokoué dit à propos des Wagner
articles.description: Écouter l'articleTélécharger Le général Bienvenue Zokoué assume pleinement le partenariat sécuritaire entre Bangui et Moscou. Dans son entretien
paragraphs: Le général Bienvenue Zokoué assume pleinement le partenariat sécuritaire entre Bangui et Moscou. Dans son entretien accordé à la télévision de propagande russe RT en français, le ministre centrafricain de la Sécurité publique présente les Russes déployés en Centrafrique comme des alliés ayant pacifier le pays et ayant payé également leur engagement de leur sang.

« On a des compatriotes centrafricains mais on a aussi des alliés russes qui ont aussi versé leur sang ici pour sauver, pour protéger, pour défendre notre vaste territoire, la République centrafricaine », affirme-t-il.
À lire aussi: Centrafrique: La COSCIPAC pilonne le régime Touadéra et dénonce une cabale contre Anicet Georges Dologuélé

Cette déclaration résume le discours défendu par le gouvernement sur la présence russe en Centrafrique. Moscou n’est pas présenté comme un simple partenaire militaire. Le ministre parle d’« alliés » et associe directement leur présence à la défense du territoire national.
À lire aussi: Elysée Nguimalé: « Les autorités issues des élections n’ont pas la capacité intellectuelle suffisante pour tenir un appareil étatique. »
Pour Bienvenue Zokoué, la coopération avec la Russie n’est pas une réponse temporaire à la crise sécuritaire.

Le ministre rappelle que les relations entre Bangui et Moscou ne seraient pas nouvelles et affirme qu’elles remontent aux années 1970. Il souhaite surtout leur donner une nouvelle dimension dans les années à venir.
La sécurité reste le principal domaine de cette coopération. Les instructeurs russes participent, selon le ministre, à la formation des FACA, des policiers et des gendarmes.
Les formations portent notamment sur les opérations, l’utilisation des armes, le combat, la tactique et le droit international humanitaire.

Des policiers et des gendarmes centrafricains bénéficient également de formations dans les académies russes. Le ministre cite notamment une dizaine de policiers et gendarmes ayant obtenu récemment un master 2 dans différents domaines.
articles.lede: Le général Bienvenue Zokoué assume pleinement le partenariat sécuritaire entre Bangui et Moscou.

Jakup Krasniqi granted custodial visit to Kosovo (November 2026)
articles.description: Due to compelling humanitarian reasons, the Trial Panel has instructed the Registry to manage a custodial visit to Ko
paragraphs: Due to compelling humanitarian reasons, the Trial Panel has instructed the Registry to manage a custodial visit to Kosovo for Jakup Krasniqi.
This is the 15th such visit by a detainee to Kosovo ordered by the judges of the Specialist Chambers for humanitarian reasons and managed by the court to date.

Such custodial visits are granted under Rule 56 of the KSC’s Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which were adopted by the judges and are based on international human rights law, including Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights and the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners.

When a detainee makes a request of this nature, the judge or judges dealing with the case assess all of the circumstances at the time that the request was made with the urgency and compassion that such situations require. They decide based on the KSC’s legal framework and international human rights standards.

articles.title: EXPLAINER – What to know ahead of ICJ ruling in Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
Human Rights by Renvoi? Not So Fast, Says ITLOS
cats: International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea
articles.description: [Agathe Niveleau is a PhD candidate in public international law at the University of Angers and a member of the Jean Bodin Research Centre. Her research focuses on renvois to external rules in the …
paragraphs: [ Agathe Niveleau is a PhD candidate in public international law at the University of Angers and a member of the Jean Bodin Research Centre. Her research focuses on renvois to external rules in the Montego Bay Convention.

Romain Degorgue is a PhD candidate in public international law at the University of Angers and a member of the Jean Bodin Research Centre. His research focuses on the legal regime of disputed territories in international law.]

On 27 May 2026, a Special Chamber of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (“The Special Chamber”) delivered its judgment in the M/T “Heroic Idun” (No. 2) case between the Marshall Islands and Equatorial Guinea. This dispute addresses the thorny issue of the content and normative functions of the so-called renvois contained in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (“UNCLOS”), i.e. a technique by which a legal text points to another rule through explicit reference rather than restating its content.

A growing trend has emerged over the past several years, whereby claimant States increasingly resorted to this legal technique in their pleadings (see for instance Chagos, South China Sea, and San Padre Pio cases). Through these claims, States sought to obtain a declaration that norms falling outside the material scope of UNCLOS had been infringed. Given ITLOS had never previously ruled on this matter in detail, this judgment could have provided much-needed clarification. Most notably, this decision raised the question of whether the jurisdiction ratione materiae of a tribunal competent to interpret and apply UNCLOS could be extended to cover human rights rules set out in other instruments such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (“ICCPR”).

The Special Chamber, in this case, declined to extend its jurisdiction to any rule of international law falling outside the scope of the UNCLOS. The reasoning has already been discussed by Lan Nguyen and Danae Georgoula. These two authors consider that the Special Chamber has adopted a “restrictive and perhaps one-dimensional reading” which tends to add complexity to the functioning of the renvois. The present authors differ on two points. First, they consider that the substantive renvoi clauses do not extend the Special Chamber’s jurisdiction. Second, while they agree that the Special Chamber’s reasoning blurs the line between jurisdiction and applicable law, they consider that this stems from the Special Chamber’s reliance on the Arctic Sunrise award without any attempt to justify the difference between the substantive renvoi clauses and the applicable law clause.

The M/T “Heroic Idun” is a crude carrier flying the flag of the Marshall Islands. In August 2022, it was denied the right to load crude oil in Nigeria’s EEZ. As a Nigerian Navy vessel approached, the crew of the M/T “Heroic Idun”, mistaking it for a pirate ship, fled. After passing through Equatorial Guinea’s EEZ, the vessel was intercepted in the waters of São Tomé and Príncipe by vessels of the Equatorial Guinean navy on suspicion of involvement in an illegal fuel supply operation. The crew members were subsequently arrested and detained in Equatorial Guinea before being transferred to Nigeria.
articles.lede: [ Agathe Niveleau is a PhD candidate in public international law at the University of Angers and a member of the Jean Bodin Research Centre. Her research focuses on renvois to external rules in the Montego Bay Convention.

articles.title: One Secretariat, Two Continents? On the Chile-Belgium Merged Bid for the BBNJ Secretariat
One Secretariat, Two Continents? On the Chile-Belgium Merged Bid for the BBNJ Secretariat
articles.description: On 6 November 2026, nine weeks before the first Conference of the Parties (COP1) to the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use o…
paragraphs: On 6 November 2026, nine weeks before the first Conference of the Parties (COP1) to the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement, which now counts 105 Parties and 145 signatories) convenes in New York, the foreign ministries of Belgium and Chile announced that the two countries would join their candidatures for the seat of the BBNJ Secretariat, “ also as a contribution to facilitate an effective decision at COP1 ”. Under the combined application, the Secretariat would be based in Valparaíso, Chile, from which its main functions, “ including the operationalization of the financial mechanism ”, would be delivered. However, the Clearing-House Mechanism (CHM), which the Secretariat shall manage, would have its physical and technical infrastructure in Brussels, and Brussels would host the meetings of the Agreement’s subsidiary bodies, offering “continuity” in their organization. With this maneuver, what had been a three-way race between Valparaíso, Brussels and Xiamen has become a choice between two institutional models: a transcontinental, two-city secretariat, and China’s single-city alternative Xiamen.

While the stakes may seem modest in bureaucratic terms, they are considerable in political ones. Headquarters arguably shape what international bureaucracies do. They work within local ecosystems of diplomats, experts and civil society ( Dairon and Badache ), shape staff composition and national representation ( Badache ), and the physical location of a Secretariat is “ consequential for how states relate to, and act through it” with respect to a variety of matters, including those related to funding ( Forster ). As Youdon suggests, Secretariats can operate as norm-shaping entities, and hosting the BBNJ Secretariat would allow early, informal influence over agenda-setting, technical guidance and capacity-building priorities, and help construct or consolidate an image of responsible stewardship of the global commons (points Youdon makes about China, but which arguably apply to any host). Indeed, the Secretariat of the BBNJ Agreement is expected to help orchestrate a fragmented ocean governance architecture ( Kim ). And then there is international prestige. So, the stakes are potentially quite high. Against this background, this blog offers an analysis of some of the political, institutional and legal implications of this merged bid.

Chile signaled its interest in hosting the BBNJ Secretariat while the Agreement was still being negotiated. Chile subsequently formalized its proposal in March 2023. Belgium announced its candidacy in January 2025 and formalized it in November 2025, while China nominated Xiamen in January 2026, just when the Agreement was entering into force. Each offer comes with significant material, infrastructural and diplomatic backing (see the offers of Chile, Belgium and China ), and with different claims to legitimacy.

articles.title: Vakaga: après l’enlèvement de deux jeunes à Ndiffa, les mercenaires russes menacent les familles et les chefs de village
articles.description: Dans la Vakaga, les mercenaires Wagner terrorisent les familles de Ndiffa et menacent les chefs de village après l'enlèvement arbitraire de deux jeunes.
paragraphs: L’enlèvement de deux jeunes habitants de Ndiffa, dont l’un souffre de troubles mentaux et présente un handicap auditif, a provoqué une nouvelle vague de menaces contre les populations civiles. Les mercenaires russes, qui affirment que les deux victimes sont des rebelles, exigent désormais des familles qu’elles retrouvent l’un des jeunes qu’ils disent s’être évadé de leurs mains.

Le 26 octobre dernier, des mercenaires russes du groupe Wagner se sont rendus dans le village de Ndiffa, situé non loin de Gordil, dans la préfecture de la Vakaga. Sur place, ils ont arrêté deux jeunes habitants qu’ils soupçonnaient d’appartenir à un groupe rebelle. Parmi eux se trouve un jeune sourd souffrant également de troubles mentaux. Les deux hommes ont ensuite été emmenés en direction de Gordil, avant d’être conduits vers une destination inconnue.

Deux jours plus tard, les mêmes mercenaires sont revenus dans le village. Cette fois, ils ne venaient pas chercher de nouveaux suspects. Ils étaient à la recherche de l’un des deux jeunes qu’ils avaient eux-mêmes arrêtés. Selon leurs explications, celui-ci se serait évadé pendant sa détention.

Mais au lieu de fournir des explications sur les circonstances de cette prétendue évasion, les mercenaires ont commencé à exercer des pressions sur les familles des deux jeunes, les chefs de village et les chefs de quartier. Ils leur ont ordonné de faire sortir le jeune qu’ils affirmaient avoir perdu. À défaut, les parents et les responsables communautaires risquaient d’être arrêtés à leur tour.

Les menaces ont provoqué l’incompréhension des habitants. Les familles ne comprennent pas comment elles pourraient retrouver une personne qui a été arrêtée et emmenée par les mêmes hommes qui viennent maintenant leur réclamer sa présence.

« C’est vous-mêmes qui avez arrêté notre enfant. Vous l’avez emmené et, deux jours après, vous revenez nous dire qu’il s’est évadé. Comment voulez-vous que nous sachions où il se trouve? Sommes-nous Dieu pour connaître sa destination? Si vous voulez que nous vous remettions cet enfant, il faudrait alors nous demander de le faire naître à nouveau et de le faire grandir jusqu’à aujourd’hui », ont fait comprendre des habitants aux mercenaires, selon les informations recueillies par la rédaction du CNC.

La pression exercée sur les populations a commencé à monter. Les familles redoutaient désormais de nouvelles arrestations, tandis que les chefs de village et les responsables de quartier se retrouvaient directement menacés pour une affaire dont ils ne maîtrisent ni les circonstances ni les suites.

C’est dans ce climat de peur que l’embuscade tendue par des éléments rebelles contre les mercenaires et leurs supplétifs à proximité de Boromata est venue interrompre les pressions exercées sur les habitants de Ndiffa.

À la suite de cette attaque, plusieurs combattants ont été tués ou blessés. Parmi les blessés figurent notamment Dogo, un responsable des Wagner noirs, grièvement touché à la jambe, ainsi que d’autres éléments du dispositif. Les blessés ont été évacués vers Birau pour recevoir des soins.
articles.lede: Dans la Vakaga, les mercenaires Wagner terrorisent les familles de Ndiffa et menacent les chefs de village après l'enlèvement arbitraire de deux jeunes.

Centrafrique: douze jeunes arrêtés par les mercenaires russes près de Zémio, trois portés disparus
articles.description: Douze jeunes arrêtés par les mercenaires de Wagner près de Zemio en Centrafrique. Trois personnes portées disparues dans une base militaire.
paragraphs: Douze jeunes hommes ont été arrêtés dans la nuit de dimanche à lundi par les mercenaires russes et leurs supplétifs centrafricains dans deux villages situés à proximité de Zémio, au sud-est de la République centrafricaine. Neuf ont été remis à la gendarmerie, dont un dans un état physique particulièrement grave après des actes de torture. Les trois autres, conduits dans une base des mercenaires russes, restent sans nouvelles depuis leur arrestation.

En effet, selon les informations recueillies par la rédaction du CNC, les faits se sont produits dans la nuit de dimanche à lundi. Les mercenaires russes ont quitté la ville de Zémio en direction d’Obo, chef-lieu de la préfecture du Haut-Mbomou, accompagnés de soldats des Forces armées centrafricaines (FACA) et de leurs supplétifs communément appelés Wagner noirs.
Image d’illustration des jeunes centrafricains arrêtés par les mercenaires russes du groupe Wagner, appuyés par des gendarmes, policier et FACA

Arrivés au village de Tamboura, situé à une vingtaine de kilomètres de Zémio, les Wagner et leurs supplétifs se sont arrêtés avant de commencer à tirer dans le village. Les habitants, surpris par les détonations, ne comprenaient pas ce qui se passait. Les mercenaires ont ensuite commencé à interpeller des jeunes, notamment ceux qui présentaient des traces de rasoir sur le corps.
À lire aussi: Contrats expirés et cours maintenus: la formule magique du ministère pour flouer les enseignants et détourner leurs salaires

Neuf jeunes ont ainsi été arrêtés à Tamboura. Le cortège de la mort a ensuite poursuivi sa progression jusqu’à un autre village, situé à moins d’une quarantaine de kilomètres de Zémio. Là encore, des tirs ont retenti avant que trois autres personnes soient interpellées. Le bilan des arrestations dans les deux villages s’élève donc à douze jeunes.

À lire aussi: Enquête exclusive: à l’ENERCA, un audit anti-corruption de la primature découvre un vaste réseau de vol et du détournement, mais le rapport de l’enquête est avalée par un décret présidentiel signé par Touadera. Incroyable!

De retour à Zémio, les mercenaires russes ont remis huit des douze personnes arrêtées à la gendarmerie. Les gendarmes les ont placées en détention. Les quatre autres jeunes ont été conduits directement dans la base des mercenaires russes.

Lundi matin, les mercenaires ont ramené l’un de ces quatre captifs à la gendarmerie. Le jeune homme présentait de graves traces de torture sur le corps et était couvert de sang. Son état physique a provoqué une vive réaction du commandant de la brigade de gendarmerie.

Devant les mercenaires russes, le commandant de brigade leur a reproché de lui présenter un détenu dans un état aussi grave. Il leur a notamment fait remarquer que lorsqu’ils décidaient de remettre des personnes à la gendarmerie, ils devaient les présenter dans un état physique acceptable. Il a expliqué que si un détenu venait à mourir dans les locaux de la gendarmerie, les gendarmes pourraient être tenus responsables devant la justice, alors qu’ils ne seraient pas à l’origine des sévices subis.
articles.lede: Douze jeunes arrêtés par les mercenaires de Wagner près de Zemio en Centrafrique. Trois personnes portées disparues dans une base militaire.

articles.title: Sudan: Devastating RSF drone strikes on civilians in El Obeid should be investigated as war crimes
articles.description: Drone strikes by Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which hit residential areas and civilian infrastructure in El Obeid city, in Sudan’s North Kordofan State, killing dozens and disrupting essential services, should be investigated as war crimes, Amnesty International said today. The organization investigated nine RSF drone strikes in El Obeid and its surroundings, which killed 37…
paragraphs: The organization investigated nine RSF drone strikes in El Obeid and its surroundings, which killed 37 civilians and injured 10 between June and August 2026. Three of the strikes hit residential areas; four struck key civilian infrastructure, including El Obeid’s power plant, fuel stations, and the main market; and two targeted moving vehicles. In all incidents, interviewees said they either saw or heard the drones, moments before or after the strikes. Amnesty International’s investigation did not identify military objectives in the vicinity of the sites at the time they were struck.

El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan State, remains under the control of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and their allied forces. The RSF first launched drone attacks in the city in October 2025 and continued intermittent attacks in the following months. In June 2026, the RSF dramatically escalated its drone strikes on El Obeid as it reportedly prepared to launch a ground offensive on the city – raising fears that the atrocities committed when it seized El Fasher a year ago would be repeated.

“The RSF drone attacks we’ve documented must be investigated as war crimes. They indicate how the Sudan conflict is moving into a new phase where all parties are increasingly using drones and other advanced weapons not only to kill and injure civilians, but also to disrupt essential and lifesaving services,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.

“There is no time to wait. With deadly drone attacks on civilians on the rise, immediate action is needed. The UN and the African Union must urgently work together to propose and implement concrete civilian protection measures, including deployment of a protection force to Sudan.”

Amnesty International has previously documented how the United Arab Emirates (UAE) supplied weapons, ammunition, armoured personnel carriers, and drones to the RSF. The organization also found that the RSF used Chinese drones including Wing Loong II and FeiHong-95, both of which have been provided by the UAE.

“This is a war on civilians which is being sustained by third parties including the UAE, the primary backer of the RSF. All those manufacturing and supplying drones and other military equipment to the warring parties must immediately cease doing so. The UN Security Council must also extend the arms embargo covering Darfur to the rest of the country and ensure that drones are included as part of the military materiel subject to the Sudan arms embargo,” said Agnès Callamard.

Between July and September 2026, Amnesty International interviewed 29 people from El Obeid including victims, relatives of victims, eyewitnesses and residents. The organization has also analyzed five photos and videos and reviewed satellite imagery and various reports of humanitarian and UN agencies.
articles.lede: The organization investigated nine RSF drone strikes in El Obeid and its surroundings, which killed 37 civilians and injured 10 between June and August 2026.

articles.title: Centrafrique: après 100 jours, Fidèle Gouandjika juge le gouvernement Moloua 3 totalement en échec
articles.description: Le gouvernement Moloua écope d'un zéro sur vingt en Centrafrique après cent jours d'exercice jugés totalement infructueux par Fidèle Gouandjika.
paragraphs: Le ministre conseiller à la présidence Fidèle Gouandjika estime que le gouvernement Moloua 3 a échoué à répondre aux attentes pendant ses 100 premiers jours. Dans sa déclaration publiée sur Facebook, il attribue la note de 0 sur 20 à cette première période et reproche aux ministres de ne pas avoir apporté de réponses concrètes aux difficultés économiques et sociales du pays.

Le verdict de Fidèle Gouandjika est sans appel. Pour évaluer les premiers résultats du gouvernement Moloua 3, il retient le critère du court terme, correspondant aux 100 premiers jours de l’équipe dirigée par Félix Moloua. À ses yeux, cette période devait permettre aux ministres d’engager des mesures immédiates dans leurs secteurs respectifs.
« Ils ont échoué à court terme. Court terme, là, c’est 100 jours. Ils ont échoué. Ils ont échoué totalement. 0 sur 20 », déclare-t-il dans son intervention.
À lire aussi: Martin Ziguélé: plus de 60 ans après les indépendances, dès que la lettre de félicitations de l’Élysée tombe, le problème des élections est bouclé

Le ministre conseiller ne limite pas ses critiques à un seul département. Il évoque plusieurs problèmes liés aux finances publiques, au carburant, au commerce, à l’agriculture et à l’éducation. Il reproche aux responsables gouvernementaux de multiplier les déclarations sans apporter, selon lui, des réponses suffisantes aux difficultés rencontrées par les populations.
À lire aussi: Bataille autour de la Mosquée du 6e arrondissement: à qui appartiennent réellement les droits revendiqués sur l’édifice?

Fidèle Gouandjika estime que le gouvernement aurait dû agir rapidement sur les recettes publiques. Il cite les pertes liées à la contrebande de l’or, du diamant et du bois, les pratiques de corruption dans les douanes ainsi que les recettes fiscales qui pourraient provenir des logements en location et des activités commerciales.

Selon lui, un meilleur recouvrement des taxes permettrait à l’État de disposer de ressources supplémentaires. Il considère que ces mesures peuvent être engagées rapidement, sans attendre des réformes à moyen ou long terme.

La hausse des prix du carburant constitue un autre point de désaccord. Le ministre conseiller demande aux autorités d’expliquer clairement cette décision aux consommateurs. Il estime que le gouvernement doit aussi examiner les moyens d’augmenter les recettes publiques avant de faire peser de nouvelles charges sur les ménages.

Dans sa déclaration, Fidèle Gouandjika interpelle également les responsables du Commerce, de l’Agriculture et de l’Éducation. Il évoque notamment le transport de la viande dans des pousse-pousse, les difficultés des producteurs de coton et les conditions d’apprentissage dans certaines écoles de Bangui.
articles.lede: Le gouvernement Moloua écope d'un zéro sur vingt en Centrafrique après cent jours d'exercice jugés totalement infructueux par Fidèle Gouandjika.

articles.title: Touadéra et le Cartel du Carburant en Centrafrique: Enquête sur une Spoliation Organisée
articles.description: Découvrez comment le cartel du carburant pille l'économie de la Centrafrique à travers un système opaque orchestré au sommet de l'État.
paragraphs: Une enquête approfondie sur les mécanismes de formation des prix des produits pétroliers en République Centrafricaine dévoile l’existence d’un système structuré de captation de rentes, soigneusement organisé au plus haut niveau de l’État. Le rapport d’audit définitif du CPCS, commandé par le PNUD et publié le 21 octobre 2025, documente un mécanisme sophistiqué qui transfère chaque année des milliards de FCFA des consommateurs et de l’État vers une oligarchie politico-économique gravitant autour du pouvoir de Faustin-Archange Touadéra.

Cette enquête, fondée sur l’analyse exhaustive du rapport, démontre que les dysfonctionnements du secteur pétrolier ne relèvent pas de simples erreurs administratives ou de contraintes logistiques. Ils constituent les pièces d’un dispositif délibérément conçu pour maximiser les profits d’un petit nombre, au détriment de l’intérêt général.

L’histoire commence en 2023. Le marché pétrolier centrafricain, jusque-là structuré autour d’un duopole composé de TOTAL et TRADEX, fonctionnait avec ses imperfections mais dans un cadre concurrentiel minimal. Cette année-là, le régime de Faustin-Archange Touadéra prend une décision lourde de conséquences: accorder un contrat d’exclusivité d’importation à la société Neptune Oil.
À lire aussi: Centrafrique: « À une loi injuste, nul n’est tenu d’obéir », déclare un centrafricain qui défend la ville morte du 12 octobre contre la hausse chaotique du prix du carburant

Officiellement, cette décision vise à résoudre les pénuries récurrentes, à améliorer l’autonomie nationale et à sécuriser l’approvisionnement. Le rapport du CPCS documente une réalité différente. Cette exclusivité couvre l’ensemble des produits pétroliers, à l’exception du Jet Al, concentrant entre les mains d’un seul opérateur l’approvisionnement d’une ressource vitale pour l’économie nationale.
À lire aussi: Koumboli, village de plus de 2000 habitants à 5 km de Zemio, privé de structures sanitaires depuis près de 3 ans

Le rapport qualifie cette transformation de “changement radical de la structure concurrentielle”. Derrière cette formulation technique se cache une réalité brutale: la création d’un monopole de fait, sans contre-pouvoir, sans régulation effective, sans transparence.
L’enquête révèle que ce monopole s’appuie sur un ensemble de mécanismes interconnectés, chacun contribuant à la spoliation organisée des ressources nationales.

Le décret n°24.157 du 17 juin 2024 fixe une méthodologie précise pour déterminer le prix de référence: la moyenne arithmétique des cotations publiées sur la plateforme S&P Global Commodity Insights pour une période définie. Cette méthodologie vise à garantir que le prix reflète les conditions réelles du marché.

Le rapport révèle que cette méthodologie est ouvertement violée. Depuis novembre 2024, la structure de prix utilise une référence basée sur un stock acheté en juillet 2024, période où les cours mondiaux avaient atteint un pic. Le rapport note que “le carburant consommé en RCA en septembre 2025” est supposé avoir été “livré au Cameroun en juillet 2024”.
articles.lede: Découvrez comment le cartel du carburant pille l'économie de la Centrafrique à travers un système opaque orchestré au sommet de l'État.

articles.title: Entre viols à ciel ouvert et impunité des mercenaires russes: Le fiasco de la loi en RCA
articles.description: Écouter l'articleTélécharger Les interventions juridiques de la MINUSCA sur les ondes de Guira FM décrivent une République centrafricaine idéale,
paragraphs: Les interventions juridiques de la MINUSCA sur les ondes de Guira FM décrivent une République centrafricaine idéale, dotée de codes, de lois de protection de la femme et de traités internationaux directement applicables par les tribunaux. Ce discours institutionnel veut rassurer, mais il se heurte à une vérité destructrice: la loi n’existe que sur le papier, effacée par la terreur que les hommes armés imposent aux civils.

Dans les villes de province, les militaires des forces armées nationales envoyés en détachement ont transformé leur statut de protecteurs en celui d’agresseurs. Libérés de tout contrôle, ils s’en prennent aux membres les plus vulnérables de la communauté. Les viols et les agressions sur des filles de 12 ou 13 ans se font sous le regard impuissant des habitants. L’uniforme sert de bouclier contre toute poursuite, installant un ordre basé uniquement sur la force.

En parallèle, les mercenaires russes déploient leur propre violence, sans aucune retenue. Leurs exactions se déroulent au grand jour, y compris dans le centre de la capitale, Bangui. Les sorties nocturnes de ces troupes se transforment fréquemment en chasses à l’homme, où les femmes et les filles mineures sont emmenées de force. Le souvenir de l’attaque survenue au quartier Benz-Vi montre le degré d’arrogance de ces forces: un mercenaire a tiré avec son arme de guerre en plein quartier pour disperser la foule et kidnapper une jeune fille, avant de s’engouffrer dans une voiture avec ses partenaires. Personne n’intervient, personne ne parle.

Ce silence complice dévoile publiquement la grande contradiction du système actuel. De quelle loi parle-t-on lorsque les auteurs des exactions les plus lourdes commettent leurs forfaits à ciel ouvert sans jamais être inquiétés? La rigueur de l’appareil judiciaire ne semble s’abattre que sur la population locale démunie. C’est ainsi que des enfants de 10 à 14 ans se retrouvent enfermés en cellule pour des affaires mineures ou non prouvées, pendant que les grands criminels et les forces étrangères jouissent d’une totale liberté de mouvement.

Les rappels hebdomadaires de la MINUSCA sur la gratuité des plaintes ou l’inutilité du certificat médical initial apparaissent ainsi comme un mirage. La justice centrafricaine reste paralysée par la peur et la complicité politique, laissant les populations sans autre choix que de subir la violence de ceux qui détiennent les armes.
Note: les deux premiers groupes sont réservés uniquement aux publications officielles du CNC
articles.lede: Les interventions juridiques de la MINUSCA sur les ondes de Guira FM décrivent une République centrafricaine idéale, dotée de codes, de lois de protection de la femme et de traités internationaux directement applicables…

The Law on Brain Technologies in Warfare Series – The Brain Firing: Lawfulness and Liability of Weapon Control through BCI
cats: Law on Brain Technologies in Warfare Series
articles.description: After sketching possible BCI-enabled set-ups for weapon control, this post highlights legal challenges the technology poses to LOAC and ICL.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: This post is an entry in our series on Air Commodore (ret.) William H. Boothby’s book, The Law on Brain Technologies in Warfare published by Elgar International.

Soldiers may soon direct weapon systems using only their thoughts. Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) can connect a person’s brain to a computing device. The computer picks up neural signals generated by the brain and translates them into a command for a physical gadget, allowing the user to mentally control that gadget. Employing BCIs to direct weapons has already been researched and has even earned a patent.
After sketching possible BCI-enabled set-ups for weapon control, this post highlights legal challenges the technology poses to the law of armed conflict and to international criminal law.

Various scenarios for weapon control are conceivable: a commander may remotely direct a ground vehicle equipped with a gun, a weaponized drone, or a missile firing mechanism aboard a vessel, to name just a few. In principle, there are two types of BCIs: active and reactive.

Active BCIs require the soldier to focus on giving a certain command. For example, the computer may recognize the neural signals evoked when the soldier imagines pressing a button with his hand. Thereupon, the computer transmits the instruction to fire to the connected weapon. This manner of control demands an intense, conscious effort.

Reactive BCIs decipher neural signals generated subconsciously, before the operator becomes aware of them. Imagine that you accidentally place your hand on a hot stove top. Your brain will elicit signals to immediately retract it. These signals are an instantaneous, subconscious reaction. For military BCIs, such signals can be provoked by rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP). The soldier, tasked with spotting a target, is shown images of the battlefield at very short intervals. Upon recognizing the target, the soldier’s brain emits a subconscious neural response, which the BCI then decodes and transmits to the weapon.

Weapon control is arguably one of BCI’s most promising applications for militaries. It permits remote command without depending on a physical control station. Reactive BCIs, on top, enable ultrarapid decisions. Target engagement based on subconscious neural signals is possible in 250 to 500 milliseconds after visual perception, which is the fastest method currently imaginable to operate any device.
Because thought-controlled weapons are unprecedented, I first address their general legality under weapons law and then turn to relevant aspects of targeting law.

Initially, the question arises whether such a system can be legally used in armed conflict under any circumstance. Considering the man-machine collaboration constitutes a weapon system, i.e. a means of warfare, a review under Article 36 of Additional Protocol I (AP I) (considered customary international law) is in order. Accordingly, the BCI must be capable of complying with international humanitarian law a priori, independent of a specific operational context. Closer scrutiny is demanded to determine whether the technology is inherently indiscriminate or incapable of ensuring proportionate targeting decisions.
articles.lede: After sketching possible BCI-enabled set-ups for weapon control, this post highlights legal challenges the technology poses to LOAC and ICL.

articles.title: Italy: “A bleak day for freedom of expression” as parliament votes through repressive definition of antisemitism into law
articles.description: Reacting to a vote by Italy’s parliament to formally adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism, Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Research, Policy, Advocacy and Campaigns, said: “Today marks a bleak day for freedom of expression as Italy explicitly makes the IHRA working definition of antisemitism legally binding.…
paragraphs: “Today marks a bleak day for freedom of expression as Italy explicitly makes the IHRA working definition of antisemitism legally binding. The new law, based on a definition that has long raised serious concerns because it conflates antisemitism with legitimate criticism of Israel, heightens the risk of far-reaching forms of censorship and self-censorship. Its application across schools, universities, social media platforms and beyond threatens a chilling effect and infringe on the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.
The new law, based on a definition that conflates antisemitism with legitimate criticism of Israel, heightens the risk of far-reaching forms of censorship and self-censorship

“Instead of strengthening the implementation of existing legislation in Italy, which already contains robust provisions to address antisemitism, hate crimes and discrimination, Italian authorities have chosen to introduce this law. While it may not introduce new criminal offences, it could be instrumentalized to punish legitimate criticism of the Israeli government’s policies and target solidarity with Palestinians.

“By blurring the distinction between antisemitism and criticism of a state´s actions, the law also risks undermining efforts to identify and effectively address genuine antisemitism. While stronger measures to prevent and address racism and discrimination are needed, the new law is not the answer. Protecting people from antisemitism and protecting freedom of expression are complementary obligations, not competing ones, and neither should come at the expense of the other.
“Italy must ensure that all groups including Jewish communities are equally protected from discrimination, and advocacy of hatred

“Branding criticism of Israel’s brutal occupation, its system of apartheid, and its ongoing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza as antisemitic – which could happen under the new law – also risks shielding state policies and practices from legitimate public scrutiny and debate.

“Italy must uphold its international obligations to protect freedom of expression and peaceful assembly for all and ensure that all groups including Jewish communities are equally protected from discrimination, and advocacy of hatred.”

The new law, “Measures for countering antisemitism and for the adoption of the working definition of antisemitism”, contains provisions for preventing and combating antisemitism and introduces into domestic law the “working definition of antisemitism”, adopted in May 2016 by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA), expressly including the indicators (“contemporary examples of antisemitism”).

After being passed by the Italian Senate on 2 March, the bill received final approval by the Chamber of deputies today, without any amendments being accepted, including those seeking to replace the IHRA definition with the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism. Developed by hundreds of scholars of antisemitism, Holocaust studies, Jewish studies and Middle East studies, the Jerusalem Declaration is less open to being misused to stifle debate and activism.
articles.lede: “Today marks a bleak day for freedom of expression as Italy explicitly makes the IHRA working definition of antisemitism legally binding.

articles.title: France: la LDH attaquée par l'extrême droite
articles.description: Lors d’un débat télévisé tenu le 16 novembre 2026, Marine Le Pen, la candidate du Rassemblement national (RN) à l’élection présidentielle de 2027, (…)
paragraphs: Paris, 17 Novembre 2026. Intimidée comme de nombreuses associations et mouvements de défense des droits humains en Europe, la LDH a montré sa pertinence et son rôle vital dans une démocratie tout au long de son histoire plus que centenaire. Ses bénévoles se sont encore illustré·es ces derniers mois au cœur des manifestations et des mouvements de revendication, brutalement réprimés par le gouvernement français.

« En attaquant de la sorte la LDH, Marine Le Pen conjure une tradition de l’extrême droite française, profondément autoritaire. Elle cherche à assouvir une vieille rancœur », commente Alexis Deswaef, le président de la FIDH. « Par ailleurs, en attaquant une organisation née de l’affaire Dreyfus, Marine Le Pen renoue avec une vieille obsession de l’extrême droite française anti-dreyfusarde, qui resurgit dans les temps de crise. Honte à elle. »

La LDH est régulièrement attaquée pour ses combats en faveur des droits humains. En avril 2023, le ministre de l’Intérieur de l’époque, Gérald Darmanin, avait mis en doute la probité de l’organisation et menacé de retirer son financement. Tout comme en 2023, la FIDH apporte son soutien sans faille à la Ligue, et, à la veille d’échéances électorales majeures, appelle tou·tes les candidat·es à la responsabilité.

« Les organisations de défense des droits humains jouent un rôle essentiel dans toute démocratie: elles permettent de responsabiliser le pouvoir, défendent les libertés fondamentales et donnent une voix à celles et ceux dont les droits sont en danger. Cibler publiquement une organisation telle que la Ligue des droits de l’homme/droits humains et menacer ses financements envoie un message très inquiétant », analyse Stéphanie David, secrétaire générale de l’OMCT. « Les divergences politiques ne doivent en aucun cas servir de prétexte pour intimider ou réduire au silence les organisations de défense des droits humains. »

Cette attaque violente contre la LDH s’inscrit dans un contexte de rétrécissement de l’espace civique en France, comme ailleurs en Europe. Dans un rapport, sorti à l’automne 2025, l’Observatoire et la LDH documentent une dégradation alarmante des libertés publiques en France. Narratifs hostiles, dissolutions administratives, réduction des financements publics, criminalisation des mobilisations, conduisent à un étouffement de la société civile et mettent en péril la liberté d’association et le droit de manifester.

Par ailleurs, plusieurs mairies détenues par le parti de Marine Le Pen, le Rassemblement National, ont déjà attaqué frontalement la LDH, privant ses sections de locaux. En avril 2026, Christophe Barthès, maire RN de Carcassonne, a mis fin à une subvention municipale à la section locale de la LDH, ainsi qu’au prêt d’un bureau, tout en lui interdisant de participer, comme c’était jusqu’ici l’usage, au forum des associations de la ville.

L’Observatoire appelle ainsi les autorités françaises à condamner fermement ces intimidations et menaces à l’encontre d’organisations de défense des droits humains et à respecter leurs obligations internationales en matière de protection de la liberté d’association, consacrée notamment par l’article 22 du Pacte international relatif aux droits civils et politiques et l’article 11 de la Convention européenne des droits de l’homme, et qui qui comprend le droit à chercher et à obtenir des financements publics.

articles.title: 1964–2026, Nabeel Rajab, human rights defender
articles.description: Nabeel Rajab died on 17 November 2026. He was 62 years old. Nabeel Rajab was a visionary who embodied a movement and championed its causes, a (…)
paragraphs: Nabeel Rajab was a visionary who embodied a movement and championed its causes, a leading figure in the defence of human rights in the Gulf and a key figure in the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), where he served as Deputy Secretary-General from 2010 to 2020. On the international stage, on the national stage, but also in every moment of a rich, adventurous and, above all, committed life. Co-founder and president of the Bahrain Centre for Human Rights, and founding director of the Gulf Centre for Human Rights, his role within the Federation reflected his commitment: at the heart of the international human rights movement.

His activism has led to many years of persecution, arbitrary detention, solitary confinement and illness. In September 2016, speaking from his prison cell, he told the New York Times that the authorities had threatened him, in front of his children, with a 15-year prison sentence if he did not cease his activities. It was a futile attempt. When they tried to force him to publicly retract an open letter addressed to US President Barack Obama, they failed. " I refused ," he explained tersely. Prison did not break his determination or his courage.
Released in June 2020, he never ceased to defend human rights, despite the restrictions that continued to weigh upon him.
With his passing, the FIDH has lost a friend, a colleague, an inspiration and a source of strength, whose influence radiated throughout the entire human rights movement.

paragraphs: Figure majeure de la défense des droits humains dans le Golfe, figure centrale de la Fédération internationale pour les droits humains (FIDH) dont il a été secrétaire général adjoint de 2010 à 2020, Nabeel Rajab était un bâtisseur qui savait incarner un mouvement et porter ses combats. Sur la scène internationale, sur la scène nationale, mais aussi dans tous les instants d’une vie riche, aventureuse et surtout, engagée.

Cofondateur et président du Bahrain Center for Human Rights, directeur fondateur du Gulf Centre for Human Rights, sa place dans la Fédération était à l’image de son engagement: au cœur du mouvement international des droits humains.

Son activisme lui a valu de longues années de persécution, des détentions arbitraires, l’isolement et la maladie. En septembre 2016, depuis sa cellule, il racontait dans le New York Times que les autorités l’avaient menacé, devant ses enfants, d’une peine de 15 ans de prison s’il ne cessait pas son action. Peine perdue. Lorsqu’elles avaient voulu faire renier publiquement une lettre ouverte, destinée au Président étasunien Barack Obama, ce fut en vain. « J’ai refusé », expliquait-il laconiquement. La prison n’a eu raison ni de sa détermination, ni de son courage.
Libéré en juin 2020, il n’a jamais cessé de défendre les droits humains, malgré les restrictions qui continuaient de peser sur lui.
La FIDH perd avec lui un ami, un collègue, une inspiration et une force, qui irradiaient sur l’ensemble du mouvement pour les droits humains.

articles.description: Ahead of the start of a hearing tomorrow in the case against the founders of the LGBTI organization Social Policy, Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation Studies Association (SPoD), the Human Rights Defenders Solidarity Network – a network of 38 organizations including Amnesty International Türkiye – have issued a joint statement. Esther Major, Amnesty International’s Deputy…
paragraphs: Ahead of the start of a hearing tomorrow in the case against the founders of the LGBTI organization Social Policy, Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation Studies Association (SPoD), the Human Rights Defenders Solidarity Network – a network of 38 organizations including Amnesty International Türkiye – have issued a joint statement. Esther Major, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for Europe, said:

“It is deeply disturbing that four founding members of this organization, which has fought tirelessly against discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, are facing prison sentences for doing this vital work. These could be the first of many such prosecutions in the wake of a new LGBTI crackdown that threatens the existence of dozens of other organizations.

“Prosecutions of LGBTI human rights defenders and actions to dissolve associations mark a dangerous escalation in efforts by Türkiye’s authorities to criminalize LGBTI rights and must be condemned and rejected. These actions threaten not only the organizations directly targeted but can also have a chilling effect on independent civil society organizations and human rights defenders more broadly in Türkiye. People must be able to defend LGBTI rights without fear of punishment.
These could be the first of many such prosecutions in the wake of a new LGBTI crackdown that threatens the existence of dozens of organizations

“Turkish authorities must drop all charges brought against these human rights defenders, immediately and unconditionally release everyone detained solely for exercising or defending human rights and end attempts to dissolve associations for their human rights work.”
SPoD is a prominent LGBTI organization that provides legal and psychosocial support and runs campaigns against discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.

Since the launch of the operation dubbed ‘My Family Is Safe’ by the Turkish authorities on 12 September 2026, dozens of human rights defenders have been imprisoned and subjected to criminal investigations under the Law on Associations and other criminal code provisions such as ‘obscenity’. Criminal prosecutions have been initiated against human rights defenders – at least three of these cases include a request for the dissolution of their respective associations, namely SPoD, Hevi LGBTI+ and Lambdaistanbul in Istanbul.

Indictments have been issued against founders and executives of LGBTI+ rights organizations in Istanbul and Ankara. As well as the four founders of SPoD, five founders of HEVİ LGBTI+ and six founders of Lambdaistanbul LGBTI+ Solidarity Association also face prosecution under Article 32/1-p of the Law on Associations on charges of “establishing associations for purposes prohibited by law”. We are also aware that LİSTAG, an association formed by parents and relatives of LGBTI people, as well as 7 Renk LGBTİ+ Association and Muamma LGBTİ+, both based in Mersin, are facing criminal proceedings in connection with the “My Family Is Safe” operations.

articles.title: El Salvador: Public debt is mortgaging the country’s future without guaranteeing rights today
articles.description: Amnesty International examines how public debt and a lack of budgetary transparency affect the protection of social rights in El Salvador.
paragraphs: The increase in public debt and indebtedness in El Salvador over the last decade has not led to a proportional and sustainable improvement in access to economic and social rights, according to Amnesty International’s new report, “When the budget does not guarantee rights”.

The report analyses the evolution of the public budget between 2015 and 2025, documenting how the increasing debt burden, lack of transparency and a concentration of decision-making power within the executive branch have reduced the state’s capacity to mobilize the maximum of its available resources to uphold rights such as the right to health, to education and to social protection.

“The findings highlight an alarming contradiction: the Salvadoran state is spending more and increasing its indebtedness, but these available resources do not manifest as equivalent improvements for the population. When debt servicing accounts for a larger proportion of the budget than health or education, it is legitimate to question where the money is going and why,” said Ana Piquer, Americas director at Amnesty International.

The findings highlight an alarming contradiction: the Salvadoran state is spending more and increasing its indebtedness, but these available resources do not manifest as equivalent improvements for the population.”

Over the last ten years, public debt servicing has become the largest budget expenditure within the national budget. In 2025, two out of every ten dollars in the budget were allocated to debt interest payments and amortizations, an amount higher than planned spending on health and greater than combined spending on education, social protection and pensions.

Evidence shows that debt servicing has tripled in real terms over the last decade while the Salvadoran economy has grown by an average of just 2.5% per year, which means that the debt ratio exceeds the size of the economy. This gradually reduces the fiscal space available for funding basic public services and increases the risk of future adjustments that will negatively impact the Salvadoran population, particularly those already experiencing poverty, inequality or discrimination.

The report also highlights serious issues of transparency and accountability in the management of public resources. Among these are the difficulty in tracking execution of key budget lines, the limited availability of information on contracts and procurements, and the increasing centralization of public investment.

One of the most significant changes observed by Amnesty International is the replacement of the long-standing system of municipal transfers with mechanisms administered by the executive branch through the National Directorate of Municipal Works (DOM). This change has concentrated the selection and implementation of infrastructure projects, with no public prioritization criteria or robust mechanisms for citizen participation in defining priorities and holding the authorities to account.

“Transparency is not a secondary administrative requirement. It is an essential condition for the general public to understand how resources are used and demand accountability. With no accessible information or effective controls, the risk of arbitrary decision-making, corruption and inefficiency increases,” added Ana Piquer.
articles.lede: Amnesty International examines how public debt and a lack of budgetary transparency affect the protection of social rights in El Salvador.

articles.title: The United States Has Space Weapons: How Should It Use Them?
articles.description: U.S. leadership has the opportunity to actively shape space warfare, expanding beyond the current legal framework into a holistic approach.
paragraphs: The idea of warfare in space has been present at least since the first Gulf War was declared the “ first space war ,” but the potential for armed conflict in the space domain has been growing for over a decade in both urgency and public consciousness. The inception of the U.S. Space Force brought with it open discussion of space as a warfighting domain, and Russia’s aggression in Ukraine brought with it explicit discussion of potentially targeting commercial satellites on orbit. In this context, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink recently announced that, for the first time, “ the Space Force now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.” One initial question with this announcement may be whether such weapons are legal. They are, as comprehensively discussed here.

This leaves us not just to consider what would be lawful targets for counter-space weapons in an armed conflict, but also what the United States, as a whole, wants the answer to be. A particular consideration is the legitimacy of commercial satellites as potential targets.

A starting point to answering these questions is the legal framework already in place. However, the law only provides a floor, or minimum requirement. It is a baseline, and the law of armed conflict–albeit with some clear red lines–contains fairly permissive rules that are focused on process for competent decision authorities (often commanders, but in the highly strategic context of space, more often senior policymakers and civilian leaders) rather than a specific outcome in a particular targeting scenario. Moreover, there are no space-specific laws for targeting; instead, rules for space are derived from general practice and rules that transcend the domains of conflict (that is, laws that apply to land, air, sea, cyber, and space generally), with domain-specific nuance either coming from explicit domain-specific agreements or the factual application of the unique aspects of the domain to the broader law.

Given this, the United States has an opportunity to shape the development and understanding of the norms, rules, and law related to what does, and does not, constitute a legitimate military objective in space. It is important to remember that the military objective test is only one part of a targeting decision, along with a proportionality and precautions analysis, any rules of engagement, or other policy requirements; but it is a foundational, essential part of the analysis and one the United States should not take lightly as it considers what is both responsible and reasonably workable behavior in the space domain.

So, under the law of armed conflict, what is a legitimate target (that is, a lawful military objective)? Fortunately, there is great consensus on this matter—or at least on the legal test —among parties to Additional Protocol I of the Geneva Conventions (the vast majority of states, including China and Russia, but not including the United States), the United States under the DoD Law of War Manual (section 5.6.3), and the International Committee of the Red Cross’s widely-accepted assertion of customary international law:
articles.lede: U.S. leadership has the opportunity to actively shape space warfare, expanding beyond the current legal framework into a holistic approach.

articles.title: The United States’ Missile Strike on Minab’s Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School: Part I
articles.description: Experts examine the available evidence to determine whether the Minab strike was a violation of international humanitarian law.
paragraphs: Nine months have passed since a missile strike on the first day of the U.S.-Israel-Iran war hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, destroying the structure and killing at least 150 persons – schoolgirls and schoolboys, plus a handful of school personnel. All public evidence indicates that the U.S. military launched that Feb. 28, 2026, strike. Yet, to this day, the United States has neither acknowledged its own responsibility nor credibly demonstrated that some other actor was responsible. We aim, in this and a subsequent article: first, to analyze the available evidence against international humanitarian law (especially IHL’s rules on the protection of civilians, including children); second, to situate that evidence within the context of shifting U.S. positions on law’s role in restraining warfare; and third, to consider what paths to accountability (criminal or otherwise) might exist were the strike fully attributed to, or acknowledged by, the United States.

This Part I article concentrates on the first two of those points. We begin by summarizing the IHL analysis of the Minab school strike that we have just published as part of a special Contemporary Practice of the United States section in the October issue of the American Journal of International Law. We then address information in investigative reporting published after our analysis was in final proof. Ultimately, we assess that the strike violated fundamental IHL rules.

In our Part II article, we consider questions of accountability: are there “reasonable grounds to believe” the strike was a “war crime” – as the United Nations’ Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Islamic Republic of Iran determined after our essay went to press? And besides adjudication, what forms might accountability take?

In assessing the strike pursuant to IHL, our AJIL essay emphasized U.S. interpretations of that body of law. The United States has assumed the obligation to comply with IHL through its ratification of the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and its acceptance of many customary IHL norms. But compared with many other states and commentators, the United States’ interpretations of IHL often have been more permissive, asserting greater leeway in the waging of war. Notwithstanding our concerns regarding such permissiveness, we found that, even when measured against the United States’ own positions:

We conclude that if the attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh school does not catalyze a political and institutional reversal of current trends, it is destined to be a devastating marker of the intensifying U.S. rejection of legal restraint in war.

Doubt and the Principle of Distinction: One of IHL’s “cardinal principles” ( ICJ ¶78) is that of distinction: at all times, belligerents must distinguish between civilian persons, the civilian population, and civilian objects, on the one hand, and combatants, persons directly participating in hostilities, and military objects, on the other. Military operations, including attacks, must be directed only at the latter, never at the former. Under the view that prevails globally, if there is uncertainty – doubt – regarding the status of a person or object, that person or object is to be presumed civilian (see Arts. 50(1), 52(3), Additional Protocol I).
articles.lede: Experts examine the available evidence to determine whether the Minab strike was a violation of international humanitarian law.
