articles.title: Azerbaijan: Abzas Media staff endure three years behind bars for independent journalism
articles.description: The reprisals do not end with unfounded imprisonment. Relatives and lawyers report increased use of solitary confinement, denial of health care, beatings and other ill-treatment against the Abzas Media journalists and others jailed for critical journalism and dissenting views.
paragraphs: Ahead of the third anniversary of the earliest arrests of Abzas Media journalists in Azerbaijan, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director, said:

“Three years on, seven Abzas Media journalists remain behind bars in desperate conditions, far from their families. They were among the first targets in what has become a sweeping crackdown on independent journalism in Azerbaijan.

“The reprisals do not end with unfounded imprisonment. Relatives and lawyers report increased use of solitary confinement, denial of health care, beatings and other ill-treatment against the Abzas Media journalists and others jailed for critical journalism and dissenting views.

“The Azerbaijani authorities must immediately and unconditionally release all those imprisoned solely for the exercise of their right to freedom of expression. They must provide all prisoners with adequate health care, promptly investigate reports of abuse and put an end to all forms of ill-treatment.”

Ulvi Hasanli, director of Abzas Media, was arrested on 20 November 2023. Six other journalists from the outlet were subsequently arrested. All seven were sentenced on 20 June 2025 to up to nine years in prison on fabricated financial charges. Similar charges have been later brought against journalists with Toplum TV, who were sentenced to between 12 and 15 years in prison in July 2026, and Meydan TV, whose staff were arrested shortly after Azerbaijan hosted COP29 in November 2024. Ilgar Aliyev, also arrested in connection with his work for Abzas Media, died in prison in May 2026.

On 2 November, Abzas Media director Ulvi Hasanli was placed in solitary confinement at Prison No. 10 following threats from the prison’s deputy head Kamran Shahsuvarov, his wife Rubaba Guliyeva told Amnesty. Prison officials have reportedly pressured Hasanli to delete Abzas Media’s investigative articles exposing conditions and alleged abuses inside the facility, and to halt any further reporting on the prison. Hasanli has been on hunger strike in protest.

Amnesty International has also received reports of increased pressure against other imprisoned journalists and activists. On 5 November, police detained Agil Aliyev, nephew of National Council of Democratic Forces chair Jamil Hasanli, reportedly pressuring him to appear on television to denounce his uncle and another jailed opposition leader, Ali Karimli.

Meanwhile, Meydan TV editor-in-chief Aynur Elgunash – arrested on 6 December 2024 as part of the Meydan TV case – underwent emergency kidney surgery on 13 November. Courts had repeatedly refused to release Aynur Elgunash, who has a physical disability and 20 prior surgeries, on medical grounds.
articles.lede: The reprisals do not end with unfounded imprisonment.

À la première audience, le procureur général a requis la peine de travaux forcés à perpétuité contre l’accusé Patrick Abo. La Cour l’a finalement condamné à dix ans de réclusion criminelle en requalifiant les faits de coups et blessures volontaires à coups et blessures involontaires ayant entrainé la mort. Retour sur l’audience d’hier avec Privat Rodrigue Lekpanga.

Beyond the Binary of War and Peace: Why the U.S., Israel, and Iran Must Return to Legal Intermediacy
articles.description: [Hadi Dadmehr is an Assistant Professor of international law at the University of Zabol, Iran. He holds B.A in political science from Allameh Tabatabai University (Iran), M.A. in international rela…
paragraphs: [ Hadi Dadmehr is an Assistant Professor of international law at the University of Zabol, Iran. He holds B.A in political science from Allameh Tabatabai University (Iran), M.A. in international relations from Tehran University (Iran) and PhD in international law from National University of Iran (SBU).]

The United States, Israel, and Iran, which had previously cooperated strategically within a common public order system, became adversaries following the 1979 Islamic Revolution, finding themselves in a new relationship that defies classification within the conventional peace–war binary. Decades ago, Georg Schwarzenberger, Philip Jessup, and Myres McDougal emphasized the need to recognize a legal state of intermediacy or status mixtus, between peace and war. Professor Jessup identified three characteristics of this intermediate state which I argue aptly describe post-revolutionary relations among the United States, Israel, and Iran:

Prior to the 2025–2026 war, all criteria of intermediacy were present in relations among Iran, Israel, and the United States. The hostility between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the United States dates back to the 1979 hostage crisis and the subsequent severance of their diplomatic relations. The crisis was reinforced by imposing U.S. sanctions on Iran and Washington’s support for Iraq during the Iran–Iraq War. Despite occasional diplomatic initiatives, relations between the two states were never normalized in the decades following the Islamic Revolution. Iran’s relations with Israel have likewise remained persistently hostile, influenced by the strategic partnership of U.S.–Israel and also the Islamic Republic’s support for the Palestinian cause. Taken together, the first characteristic of Jessup’s intermediacy state was present before the outbreak of the 2025–2026 war.

Second, the disputes separating these states are rooted in so fundamental antagonisms that cannot be overcome through the resolution of isolated issues. The recent failure of mediation efforts to secure a peaceful settlement underscores the depth of the underlying hostilities and the formidable obstacles to resolve them through diplomatic means. Iran’s enmity toward the United States is rooted primarily in the Islamic Republic’s ideological opposition to Western imperialism. Its hostility toward Israel likewise stems from religious and ideological considerations and manifested in its rejection of a Jewish state in the Middle East.

From its very beginning, anti-Americanism became an integral part of the Islamic Revolution’s identity. In line with the leftist discourse of the period, the revolutionaries framed the United States as an imperialist power and the embodiment of capitalism. Ayatollah Khomeini added a religious dimension to this antagonism by designating the United States as “the Great Satan” and denouncing its perceived role in promoting secularism among Muslims. The confluence of these ideological and religious narratives cemented the U.S as the Islamic Republic’s foremost adversary. In this regard, it is sufficient to note that the hostage crisis was of such importance that it came to be dubbed the “Second Revolution” – not merely a manifestation of 1979 Revolution, but a momentous event with its own distinctive impact (see Iran’s Grand Strategy, p.53).

articles.title: Haiti: ‘Atrocious abuses’ continue as UN warns anti-gang operations must priortise civilian protection
articles.description: The UN human rights office, OHCHR has urged greater protection for civilians in Haiti amid ongoing “atrocious abuses” committed by gangs and intensified security operations.
paragraphs: OHCHR has documented 4,595 people killed and 2,050 injured due to armed violence between January and 31 October, Spokesperson Marta Hurtado told journalists in Geneva.

During the same quarter, at least 340 women and girls were subjected to sexual violence, mainly gang rape, bringing the total number of cases from January to September to 1,497. Victims ranged from ages seven to 80.
Asked how 2026 figures overall compare with previous years, Ms. Hurta said that although some numbers “have gone down a little”, killings, rapes and child recruitment by gangs remain “awfully high”.

“I always refer to the report that we issued in February, where we had several examples of mothers saying, ‘I prefer to give my daughter to a gang member so she's only raped and not gang raped,’” she said.
Violent armed groups continue to control large areas of Haiti’s capital Port-au-Prince, and beyond. A Gang Suppression Force, authorised by the UN Security Council, has yet to be fully deployed.

Meanwhile, as security operations ramp up, gangs have adapted their tactics. Armed groups have carried out retaliatory attacks on residents suspected of cooperating with security forces, targeted kidnappings, increased forced recruitment of children and young people and placed tighter restrictions on freedom of movement.

They have also sought to influence upcoming elections through violence. Ms. Huerta noted that the leader of the ‘Brooklyn’ gang in the Cité Soleil neighbourhood allegedly prepared a candidate list to gain municipal positions. Two residents who denounced the scheme were shot dead.

OHCHR found that between July and September, at least 514 people were killed and 235 injured during security operations conducted by national security forces against gangs, at times with the support of a private military company.
Another 44 people were reported killed in extrajudicial killings by police officers outside anti-gang operations.
articles.lede: The UN human rights office, OHCHR has urged greater protection for civilians in Haiti amid ongoing “atrocious abuses” committed by gangs and intensified security operations.

articles.title: Azerbaijan Jails Parliamentary Watchdog Activists
articles.description: An Azerbaijani court sentenced two activists affiliated with Meclis.info, an independent platform monitoring the country’s parliament, to lengthy prison terms on dubious financial crime charges on November 12, 2026. These are the latest convictions as part of a wider crackdown that has seen scores of journalists, human rights defenders, and civic activists prosecuted on politically motivated charged since late 2023.
paragraphs: The Baku Grave Crimes Court sentenced Imran Aliyev, Meclis.info’s co-founder, to 10 years in prison, and Elgiz Gahraman, another co-founder and data analyst, to nine years. A third defendant, the platform’s accountant Tamella Musayeva, received a suspended prison sentence. All three were convicted of illegal entrepreneurship, money laundering, currency smuggling, tax evasion, and document forgery.

Launched in 2023, Meclis.info published analyses of Azerbaijan's parliament, scrutinizing lawmakers’ attendance, voting records, and public statements. Aliyev has been in detention since his arrest in April 2024. Gahraman and Musayeva were placed under police supervision in February 2025; Gahraman was taken into custody in the courtroom after the verdict.

During the trial, Aliyev acknowledged receiving foreign grants, but denied any criminal wrongdoing, maintaining that the prosecution was retaliation for Meclis.info’s work. His lawyer argued that failure to register grants constituted, at most, an administrative offense. Human Rights Watch has documented how Azerbaijani authorities use restrictive legislation and arbitrary registration practices to make it virtually impossible for independent groups to operate and receive foreign funding lawfully.

Aliyev testified in April that police had beaten him, subjected him to electric shocks, and pressured him to sign documents without a lawyer present following his arrest. The Interior Ministry failed to effectively investigate the allegations.

This is not Gahraman’s first politically motivated prosecution. Arrested on drug charges in 2016, he was sentenced to prison in 2017 and released by presidential pardon in March 2019. The European Court of Human Rights found in January that his earlier detention had been intended to punish him for his civic and political activism.

Azerbaijani authorities should immediately release Aliyev, Gahraman, and all others imprisoned on politically motivated charges, overturn the unjust convictions, and end the misuse of foreign funding regulations to silence independent civic groups and media.
articles.lede: An Azerbaijani court sentenced two activists affiliated with Meclis.info, an independent platform monitoring the country’s parliament, to lengthy prison terms on dubious financial crime charges on November 12, 2026.

articles.title: ICC: Afghanistan Decision Risks Narrowing Access to Justice
articles.description: An International Criminal Court (ICC) decision risks hindering a path to justice for victims of grave crimes committed in Afghanistan.
paragraphs: (The Hague) – An International Criminal Court (ICC) decision risks hindering a path to justice for victims of grave crimes committed in Afghanistan, Human Rights Watch said today. On November 12, 2026, an ICC pretrial chamber, citing a lack of activity, effectively closed the court’s situation dealing with crimes by US, Afghan government, and other forces prior to the Taliban’s August 2021 takeover.

The ICC prosecutor’s office on November 13 sought to appeal the decision and to seek a stay of the closure decision. Research by Human Rights Watch and others over many years has documented war crimes and crimes against humanity by the Taliban; the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP), an ISIS-affiliated group; Afghan government forces; and US military and Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) forces.

“Victims of serious international crimes committed by warring parties during Afghanistan’s long conflict have faced many roadblocks to justice,” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “The ICC judges’ decision threatens to compound barriers to future accountability for US and Afghan government forces.”

In its initial 2017 request to open an investigation in Afghanistan, the prosecution cited alleged crimes by US military and CIA forces including torture and cruel treatment, outrages upon personal dignity, and rape and other forms of sexual violence “pursuant to a policy approved by the US authorities.” Regarding Afghan government forces, it cited alleged torture, sexual violence against detainees and civilians, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial executions.

With respect to the Taliban’s forces, the crimes included directing attacks on the civilian population and other protected entities, murder, political and gender-based persecution, and the use of child soldiers. During the 20-year conflict, none of the warring parties demonstrated the will to meaningfully deliver justice for crimes committed by their personnel, Human Rights Watch said.

In March 2020, ICC judges authorized the court’s prosecutor to investigate all alleged crimes falling within the ICC’s jurisdiction in Afghanistan, an ICC member country, since May 1, 2003. The prosecutor was also authorized to investigate crimes if sufficiently linked to the situation and the armed conflict that were committed in the territory of another ICC member country since July 1, 2002. The investigation was paused while the prosecution, and subsequently, the court’s judges considered a request by the then-Afghanistan government to defer ICC proceedings in favor of prosecutions the government asserted it was pursuing. The court’s judges concluded in 2022 that any cases pursued by the former government were at best a “very limited fraction” of those that would be covered by an ICC investigation.

Since investigations resumed in 2022, the prosecution has indicated it would focus on alleged crimes by the Taliban and the ISKP, while deprioritizing alleged crimes by Afghan security forces and US personnel. In November 2024, in what is known as a state referral, six countries requested the ICC prosecutor to investigate “crimes committed against women and girls after the Taliban takeover in 2021” within the existing investigation. The investigations have yielded four arrest warrants against senior Taliban officials, including its supreme leader, for gender persecution, spotlighting the Taliban’s brutal repression of women, girls, gender non-conforming persons, and their allies.
articles.lede: An International Criminal Court (ICC) decision risks hindering a path to justice for victims of grave crimes committed in Afghanistan.

articles.title: Specialist Prosecutor welcomes verdict, pledges to maintain obstruction-of-justice investigations and prosecutions
articles.description: Specialist Prosecutor Kimberly West welcomed today’s verdict and convictions in the trial of Hashim Thaçi, Bashkim Smakaj, Isni Kilaj, Fadil Fazliu and Hajredin Kuçi, and pledged to continue to investigate and prosecute all cases of obstruction of justice to ensure the integrity of proceedings.
paragraphs: The Court found Messrs Thaçi, Smakaj and Fazliu guilty of offenses against the administration of justice, including attempt to obstruct official persons in performing official duties and contempt of court for unlawful attempts to influence protected witnesses. The Court specifically noted Mr Thaçi’s leadership role in coordinating these obstruction efforts and also found him guilty of violating the secrecy of proceedings. The Court also convicted Mr Kuçi of one count of contempt of court and found Mr Kilaj not guilty.

Commenting on today’s judgment, the Specialist Prosecutor said: “I welcome today’s verdict and convictions, which send a clear message: those who attempt to subvert the rule of law, reveal confidential court materials or interfere with witnesses will be held accountable, no matter their status or position.

“These attempts undermine the integrity of the judicial process and must be confronted head on,” Ms West continued. “The SPO will remain steadfast in investigating and prosecuting offenses against the administration of justice to uphold the rule of law.”

The charges in the Thaçi et al. administration-of-justice trial arose from targeted, judicially authorised, covert recordings and seized materials demonstrating that Mr Thaçi, while in detention in The Hague, issued unlawful instructions to visitors to contact SPO witnesses in Mr Thaci’s own ongoing war crimes proceedings.

articles.title: UN Committee Proposes Drastic Cuts to Afghanistan Investigations
articles.description: A United Nations budgetary advisory committee has proposed sweeping cuts to the Afghanistan accountability mechanism, established by consensus by the UN Human Rights Council in October 2025 following years of negotiations.
paragraphs: The Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan was created to support efforts to hold the Taliban and others responsible for international crimes in Afghanistan to account. It is expected to include a focus on the Taliban’s crimes against humanity of gender persecution. Like similar mechanisms for Myanmar and Syria, it was designed to collect and preserve evidence and prepare files to support criminal prosecutions. Its formation followed years of campaigning by Afghan and international human rights groups on the basis that it could be a key tool in securing justice for victims of grave abuses. Its investigations could also act as a deterrent for current Taliban commanders.

In a report prepared for the UN General Assembly’s Fifth Committee, which makes budget decisions, the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (ACABQ) recommended cutting 7 of 17 posts for 2027 with little explanation – including investigators, legal officers, security personnel, and administrative staff.

Together with cuts made last year based on its recommendations, implementation of these recommendations would mean cutting by over a third the mechanism’s staffing for 2027, significantly hampering its ability to deliver on its mandate. The cuts would hit particularly hard given the original budget proposal was already scaled back by states negotiating its creation, mindful of the UN financial crisis, as compared to similar mechanisms for Syria and Myanmar.

The budget advisory committee’s recommendation that the mechanism rely on other parts of the UN for communications, security and administrative support, rather than its own dedicated staff, also risks undermining its independence, a key feature of any criminal probe. The mechanism’s operational independence is intended to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of its work, and security of its staff, witnesses and victims. It is vital given the sensitive nature of its investigations and the risk of political interference.

UN member states should reject these proposed cuts and approve the original modest budget requested by the secretary-general — something the General Assembly has done in the past. They should respect the Human Rights Council’s decision and ensure the mechanism can begin its investigations safely, securely and effectively—without further delays.
articles.lede: A United Nations budgetary advisory committee has proposed sweeping cuts to the Afghanistan accountability mechanism, established by consensus by the UN Human Rights Council in October 2025 following years of negotiations.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia/UN: Closure of ILO complaint a blow for migrant workers facing persistent abuse and discrimination
articles.description: Responding to the closure of the labour rights complaint filed against Saudi Arabia under Article 26 of the International Labour Organization (ILO) Constitution, following an agreement reached between Saudi Arabia and workers’ representative to the ILO, Iain Byrne, Amnesty International’s Head of Economic and Social Justice, said: “The premature closure of the formal complaint at…
paragraphs: “The premature closure of the formal complaint at the ILO against Saudi Arabia is a blow for the millions of migrant workers in the country.

“The concerns that gave rise to the complaint remain unresolved. They include serious abuses linked to the persistence of the kafala system, which continues to leave migrant workers dependent on their employers and enables forced labour, exploitation and racial discrimination, while imposing substantial barriers to accessing justice.

“While the agreement reached between the trade unions and the government sets out broad areas for future engagement, it fails to detail any specific legal or policy changes that Saudi Arabia has committed to undertake. It also fails so far to provide clear timelines for action, publicly available benchmarks or an independent monitoring mechanism.

“By closing the complaint at this stage, the ILO Governing Body has removed an important source of international scrutiny and pressure on the Saudi authorities before there is evidence that the agreed framework is delivering real improvements in workers’ rights.

“Just yesterday, Amnesty International released a report highlighting that migrant workers at Amazon are still facing exploitation, with the kafala system remaining a key driver of their abuse despite years of promised government reforms. Workers do not need more assurances that their conditions may improve in the future. They need a credible agenda for change, with concrete reforms deadlines for implementation, measurable outcomes, transparent monitoring and meaningful accountability when commitments are not met.

“Ultimately, this process should be judged not by the meetings it convenes or the discussions it generates, but by whether it delivers tangible improvements for migrant workers. The closure of this complaint should not be confused with the resolution of the abuses that prompted it.”

In June 2025, African trade union groups filed a formal complaint against Saudi Arabia at the ILO under Article 26 of its Constitution, alleging persistent and widespread violations and abuses of migrant workers’ rights in breach of Saudi Arabia’s obligations under several ILO conventions. The complaint requested a commission of inquiry be established. The complaint was deemed receivable by the ILO Governing Body in November 2025 and in March 2026, Amnesty International and other human rights organizations called on it to reject Saudi Arabia’s request to prematurely close the complaint.

The agreement, announced yesterday, establishes a five-year “framework for engagement and technical cooperation” between the government of Saudi Arabia and workers’ representatives to the ILO, focused on six priority areas, including labour mobility, recruitment, wage protection, occupational safety and health, labour inspection, non-discrimination and fundamental rights at work. It sets out a high-level process for identifying, implementing and monitoring labour reforms between 2027-2031, including through “structured tripartite dialogue”, six-monthly reviews by a Joint Technical Working Group and annual reporting to the ILO Director-General.
articles.lede: “The premature closure of the formal complaint at the ILO against Saudi Arabia is a blow for the millions of migrant workers in the country.

articles.title: Terms of Reference: Capitalization of FIDH's International Advocacy Experiences
articles.description: 1. Context FIDH is a federation whose added value lies in its ability to facilitate advocacy by its member organisations (MOs) before regional and (…)
paragraphs: 1. Context FIDH is a federation whose added value lies in its ability to facilitate advocacy by its member organisations (MOs) before regional and international human rights protection mechanisms. Its role is to support MOs in identifying, accessing, and strategically leveraging the relevant tools (UPR, treaty bodies, special procedures, regional bodies, private actors, diplomatic channels, etc.). This function was confirmed by the external evaluation of the Expanding comprehensive advocacy to influence local human rights change programme funded by Irish Aid (December 2025), which highlights that FIDH facilitates the link between the field and international bodies, ensuring that advocacy strategies are defined based on the needs and realities of MOs. This approach is part of the current phase of the advocacy programme supported by Irish Aid (01/06/2024 – 31/05/2027) and of the Global Programme to Strengthen the FIDH Network’s Intervention to Multiply the Agency of Human Rights Defenders and Local Human Rights Organisations funded by the Agence Française du Développement (AFD), whose Tranche 2 covers years 3 and 4 (01/08/2026 – 31/07/2028). Faced with the shrinking of national civic space, MOs are increasingly turning to international spaces. FIDH responds to this need by facilitating direct access for defenders to relevant bodies and mechanisms, by organising interfaces with MOs, and by engaging with and feeding protection mechanisms. To avoid over-soliciting MOs and stakeholders, this approach pools the lessons from both programmes into a single in-depth investigation. 2. Objectives and capitalization questions This capitalization exercise pursues two complementary logics: • Operational relevance: consolidate existing approaches to produce an operational strategic reference, identify best practices, and reorient mobilisations towards the most relevant mechanisms according to national contexts. • Strategic adaptation: enable FIDH to mobilise its teams around updated influence strategies, legitimised by evidence of their past usefulness in diverse contexts. Problem statement To what extent and according to what criteria can FIDH and its MOs articulate national and international advocacy to produce concrete change, and how to decide on the most relevant lever to mobilise in a given situation? Capitalization questions 1. Trajectory based on the intended change: How do MOs decide to activate the international level in their advocacy, and according to what logic? 2. Decision criteria for investing in a lever: On what criteria do MOs arbitrate and combine different types of levers, considering their respective relevance, potential impact, risks involved, and resource implications in a given context? 3. Return effect of international advocacy on national change: When and how are outputs from international engagement (recommendations, decisions, reports, statements) effectively reappropriated by MOs in their national strategies? Expected results • Identify what each lever can achieve and what MOs can do with its outputs in their national strategies. • Formalise decision criteria to make engagement with a mechanism useful. • Produce capitalisable lessons by transforming the analysis of experiences into operational tools reusable by the federation and its network. 3. Methodological framework 3.1 Case study approach This approach falls within the case study framework, defined as empirical research that investigates a phenomenon in a real-life context and draws on multiple empirical sources. The case study allows each advocacy strategy to be placed in its context (spatial, historical, social, temporal) rather than isolating the international mechanism as a variable. The operational guiding principle follows: reconstruct the change trajectory from the objective pursued by the MO, rather than from an inventory of activities carried out. For each case, the exercise starts from a concrete change objective, then reconstructs the path of change: MO’s change objective → Obstacles and opportunities in the national context → Choice of international mechanism(s) → Result obtained at the international level → Reuse of this result by the MO and/or other actors → Observable changes or opportunities 3.2 Tools The method combines three complementary tools: • Trajectory reconstruction (timeline): overlaying the chronology of international interventions and the evolution of the national political context, to identify windows of opportunity, measure follow-up work, and spot inflection points. • Visualisation of influence flows (knowledge mapping): identification of key actors in the dissemination of outputs (embassies, media, national human rights institutions, regional organisations, peers) and analysis of the nature of their exchanges. • Comparative synthesis of multiple cases to draw cross-cutting lessons. 3.3 Scope Four contrasting case studies will be selected internally by FIDH, covering a diverse spectrum of national contexts, types of mechanisms mobilised (classic and alternative), and situations (acute crisis, constrained context, mobilisation of non-traditional actors). The unit of analysis is a specific advocacy strategy, defined by an objective pursued by several MOs. 3.4 Establishing contribution The contribution of FIDH and the MO is established through triangulation, based on convergence between: documentary evidence, trajectory reconstruction, and consistent testimony from key actors. This triangulation follows the principle of case study analysis, which consists of improving the reliability and validity of results through the multiplicity of data sources. 3.5 Validation The reconstructed trajectories are submitted in writing to interviewees and MOs for review and correction. A collective validation workshop brings together the MOs concerned and the geographic desks to jointly validate the consolidated trajectories, cross-cutting lessons, and the updated strategic framework. 4. Deliverables # Deliverable Description 1 Updated strategic framework Decision-support tool ("Which mechanism for which objective in which context?"), tested against actual trajectories 2–5 Four case study fact sheets Each study presents the context, the reconstructed trajectory, and the lessons learned 6 Presentation materials Webinar presenting the results, open to MOs, FIDH teams, and financial partners 5. Indicative timeline & budget The process will run between November 2026 and May 2027, i.e. approximately 5 calendar months, for a total budget of €15,000. Phase Period Main activities Framing and case selection November 2026 Internal selection of case studies, document gathering, securing MO engagement Data collection preparation December 2026 Document review, design of analytical tools, workshop preparation Data collection January/February 2027 Individual interviews, trajectory reconstruction workshops, transcription Analysis and synthesis March/April 2027 Cross-analysis of the four cases, collective validation workshop, drafting of deliverables Presentation and sharing May 2027 Presentation webinar, network ownership

articles.title: Trial Judgment pronounced in Thaçi et al. obstruction of justice case
articles.description: Today, 17 November 2026, a Single Trial Judge of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) pronounced the Trial Judgment in the case of The Specialist Prosecutor v. Hashim Thaçi, Bashkim Smakaj, Isni Kilaj, Fadil Fazliu and Hajredin Kuçi.
paragraphs: The case concerns offences against the administration of justice and public order, in relation to a different trial before this court (Thaçi et al., known as Case 6,) in which Mr Thaçi was a defendant facing charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

The Single Trial Judge found that Mr Thaçi had disclosed confidential information about several witnesses in his war crimes trial to persons visiting him in detention in 2023, and that he had conveyed instructions through visitors to witnesses about how they should testify in his war crimes trial. Mr Thaçi’s co-accused in this case were persons visiting him in detention.

The Single Trial Judge found Hashim Thaçi guilty of attempted obstruction of official persons in performing official duties, violating the secrecy of proceedings, and contempt of court, for which he was sentenced to 17 months of imprisonment, to be served separately from any sentence imposed for his conviction in the Thaçi et al. war crimes case.

Bashkim Smakaj was found guilty of attempted obstruction of official persons and assisting contempt of court, for which he was sentenced to 12 months of imprisonment. With credit for time served, the Single Trial Judge considered that his sentence had been served and discharged him.

Fadil Fazliu was found guilty of attempted obstruction of official persons and assisting contempt of court, for which he was sentenced to 12 months of imprisonment. With credit for time served, the Single Trial Judge considered that his sentence had been served and discharged him.

Hajredin Kuçi was found guilty of one count of contempt of court for which he was sentenced to one month, suspended for a period of one year and to be discharged if he does not commit any other offence under the Kosovo Criminal Code during that period.

In pronouncing the Trial Judgment, the Single Trial Judge emphasized the inherent gravity of the offences committed. He noted that obstruction of official duties relating to ongoing trial proceedings was an attack on the integrity of the judicial system, which is an essential foundation for the rule of law.

Fazliu Group The Single Trial Judge found that during a visit by Fadil Fazliu to the Detention Centre on 2 July 2023, Mr Thaçi communicated to Mr Fazliu certain instructions to be conveyed to a witness, Rrustem Mustafa concerning his imminent testimony in Case 6. The day after this visit, Mr Fazliu met with the witness and communicated those instructions. The instructions included advising the witness to deny, if asked by the Prosecution, that he had received any communications from Mr Thaçi.
Mr Thaçi and Mr Fazliu were found guilty of having attempted, by common action, to obstruct official persons in performing official duties.
articles.lede: Today, 17 November 2026, a Single Trial Judge of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) pronounced the Trial Judgment in the case of The Specialist Prosecutor v. Hashim Thaçi, Bashkim Smakaj, Isni Kilaj, Fadil Fazliu and Hajredin Kuçi.

articles.title: In the Philippines, citizens are taking the lead in truth-telling
articles.description: The church and the civil society have set up a Truth Commission on the violent “war on drugs” unleashed by former president Rodrigo Duterte, whose trial begins at the International Criminal Court in The Hague on November 30.
paragraphs: In a shiny hall at the huge Pope Pius XII catholic center in Manila, the members of a Philippine Truth Commission are getting ready for the next public truth-telling session. In front of them sits Lorna Carina Pepaño, a lady with short greyish hair and glasses. In the middle of the room, a photo of her son, Christian Pepaño, is placed on a wooden chair. The picture shows him as a young, serious man, who looks straight into the camera. A branch of pink lilies near the picture is there to honor him.

On this day, October 9, 2026, Pepaño will tell the story of her beloved son, the life and violent death of her dear Christian. She is surrounded by women who came to support her. As the session will be broadcast, some are wearing face masks in order not to be recognized. One young woman has pulled up the hoody of her sweater. Next to Pepaño sits priest Flaviano Antonio Villanueva, well known for his support for victims of the “war on drugs”.

In 2016, Rodrigo Roa Duterte ran for president, promising that, if elected, he would act exactly as he did as mayor of Davao: in that city, he enforced a ruthless anti-drugs policy, established a death squad that liquidated addicts and dealers, while presenting those killings as a solution to societal problems and crimes. “Forget the laws on human rights,” he said. “If I make it to the presidential palace, I will do just what I did as mayor. You drug pushers, hold-up men, and do-nothings, you better get out because I’ll kill you.”

In predominantly catholic Philippines, more than 16 million people, including many priests and church leaders, voted for Duterte as their new president. Immediately after his installation, on July 1, 2016, Duterte launched his national “war on drugs”, called “Operation Double Barrel”, aimed at suppressing the use and sale of illegal drugs by cracking down on drug personalities and syndicates. Tortured and dead bodies were found on a daily basis in poor neighborhoods of Manila, the capital city.

This policy had two major components. “Operation Tokhang” tasked the police to knock on doors of the houses of suspected drugs users, runners and street pushers, to encourage them to stop, surrender and participate in rehabilitation programs. When people resisted, the order was: shoot to kill. Duterte even encouraged citizens to join in: “If you know of any addicts, go ahead and kill them yourself as getting their parents to do it would be too painful.” The second component was “Operation High Value Targets”, targeting suspected drug lords who have a higher-impact and allegedly corrupt local officials, such as mayors.

During Duterte’s term, from 2016 until 2022, according to official figures, police and hitmen of vigilante groups killed at least 6,250 people. However, civil society groups estimate that at least 30,000 people were extrajudicially executed in the Philippines. The vast majority were living in poor areas across the country.

Currently, Duterte is being prosecuted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, in the Netherlands, where his trial starts on November 30, 2026. Meanwhile, in May 2026, the church and the civil society created the Philippine Truth Commission as a parallel and separate initiative.
articles.lede: The church and the civil society have set up a Truth Commission on the violent “war on drugs” unleashed by former president Rodrigo Duterte, whose trial begins at the International Criminal Court in The Hague on November 30.

articles.title: Beyond Only Intent
articles.description: [Dr. Gregory Stanton is Founding President of Genocide Watch, was Professor of Genocide Studies at George Mason University, President of the International Association of Genocide Scholars, and in t…
paragraphs: [ Dr. Gregory Stanton is Founding President of Genocide Watch, was Professor of Genocide Studies at George Mason University, President of the International Association of Genocide Scholars, and in the State Department drafted the UN Resolutions to create the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the Rules for the Khmer Rouge Tribunal.
Fitry Hamidah, Htet Htet Hliang, Anita Lesniak, Maximilian Millington, Emma Op het Veld, Tami Tasaki, Aymen Zehra, Natalie Kasper, and Omar Kausar are part of the Genocide Watch Legal Team.]

Article II of the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide ( Genocide Convention ), requires a determination that acts of genocide are committed by an individual or a state with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group, as such.

Unlike other international crimes, the occurrence of one or more of the prohibited acts of genocide is not enough to prove commission of the crime of genocide. A disputing state accusing another state of violating the Genocide Convention must also prove that such acts were committed with the specific intent ( dolus specialis) to destroy a protected group.

Since evidence of genocidal intent is often not evident in statements by an individual or the leaders of a state, the ICTY, ICTR, and other international courts have recognized that intent to destroy a protected group may be inferred from patterns of conduct and the surrounding circumstances of actions.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro (2007), the International Court of Justice (ICJ) held that, when genocidal intent is inferred from a pattern of conduct, the intent to destroy a group in whole or in part must be the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence. This doctrine has come to be known as the only intent test.

The Court repeated this test of intent in Croatia v. Serbia (2015). The only intent test sets a very high evidentiary threshold, making it almost impossible to prove genocidal intent to destroy a specific group. Especially for states, such specific intent usually coexists with military, political, or territorial intents.
The only intent test raises a crucial question: should the existence of another reasonable intent by a State automatically rule out genocidal intent?

To understand the ‘only reasonable inference’ standard, it is necessary to look at the laws of evidence in proving genocidal intent. The ICTR and ICTY only tried individuals, not states. These courts characterized the specific intent for genocide as “the conscious desire to achieve the destruction of the targeted group through the commission of the prohibited acts.” ( Akayesu, paras. 544-547; Kupreškić, para. 636; Krstić, para. 584).

Establishing specific intent to destroy a group presents considerable evidentiary challenges. Direct evidence or explicit manifestations of genocidal intent are rarely available ( Krstić Appeals, para. 32).
articles.lede: Fitry Hamidah, Htet Htet Hliang, Anita Lesniak, Maximilian Millington, Emma Op het Veld, Tami Tasaki, Aymen Zehra, Natalie Kasper, and Omar Kausar are part of the Genocide Watch Legal Team.]

articles.title: Electing the Fourth ICC Prosecutor: Preliminary Observations on the Process
articles.description: Introduction On 27 October 2026, the Bureau of the Assembly of States Parties announced the procedure for electing the fourth Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court and published draft term…
paragraphs: On 27 October 2026, the Bureau of the Assembly of States Parties announced the procedure for electing the fourth Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court and published draft terms of reference of an Advisory Committee and a vacancy announcement. According to an indicative timeline, applications close on 31 January 2027, and the election is to take place at the 26 th Session of the Assembly in December 2027 in The Hague, ‘unless the Bureau decides otherwise’. The Office of the Prosecutor will therefore have been without an elected head for at least 17 months after the removal of Karim Khan on 24 July 2026—an unprecedentedly long period without a principal of an organ in the Court’s history. To say that much is at stake in the upcoming elections would be an understatement. The procedure for the election of the next Prosecutor draws on lessons learnt from past experience and constitutes an improvement in several respects. However, it neglects the one lesson all three previous elections have taught. Political consultation, the key phase through which the Prosecutor is chosen, remains unregulated and unstructured, and this may defeat the purpose of the proposed procedure.

The first ICC Prosecutor, Luis Moreno Ocampo, was elected in April 2003 as the sole nominee, after months of informal consultations had produced a consensus candidate. In 2011, a Bureau Search Committee evaluated 51 candidates and shortlisted four. Ocampo’s Deputy Prosecutor, Fatou Bensouda, nominated by 66 States Parties, was elected by acclamation, although Article 42(4) Rome Statute requires a secret ballot. According to the Assembly’s evaluation, States were divided on nearly everything. Some considered that the Committee had added extra-statutory criteria and encroached on the right of States to nominate candidates. The Bureau conceded that it could present no conclusive recommendations (para 20).

In 2020, a Committee on the Election of the Prosecutor, assisted by a Panel of Experts, produced an unranked shortlist of four candidates. The Bureau’s ‘Way Forward’ of 13 November 2020 added five more, including Mr. Karim A. Khan. The troubled process ended with four failed rounds of consultations, and Khan was elected by secret ballot on 12 February 2021. The lessons-learnt report by the facilitators, drawing on separate reports of the former Presidency, the Committee, and the Panel, recorded the view of some States Parties that ‘politics, and lobbying, still played an influential role’ (para 104). The Justice Initiative’s review found that, although the terms of reference had been adopted more than 18 months before the vote, States began negotiating on actual candidates only weeks before it. Each election was decided by bypassing the agreed procedure—a tradition likely to continue this time around.

The Bureau deserves credit for improving the election procedure in at least three areas. First, vetting now precedes the assessment of candidates. All formally qualified candidates must undergo a due diligence check under a permanent procedure. An Independent Oversight Mechanism (IOM) confidential channel to communicate misconduct allegations will be open from 20 February to 20 April 2027, an IOM report will be due on 20 June, and interviews may take place only after the final report is received (draft terms of reference, para 10). That sequencing precludes the same failure that left the Advisory Committee on Nominations of Judges (ACN) unable, in its 2026 report, to make a conclusive determination on high moral character for any of the judicial candidates, having received only a preliminary IOM report. Second, a single candidate selection body—Advisory Committee on the Election of the Prosecutor (ACEP)—replaces the awkward pairing of Committee on the Election of the Prosecutor and the Panel of Experts, as many States had proposed with reference to the ACN model —an idea first floated in 2013. Third, there is a fixed end to consensus-building consultations among States, which a majority of States had requested, along with the publication of applications of the candidates the ACEP deems qualified and of the Committee’s report.

articles.title: Bangladesh: Education Crisis for Rohingya Refugee Children
articles.description: Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding.
paragraphs: (Bangkok) – Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding, Human Rights Watch said today. Donors should fully fund the education programs, while Bangladesh should recognize and the United Nations should support a separate Rohingya-led school network.

Humanitarian education programs have enrolled 312,000 out of approximately 500,000 school-age Rohingya children in the Bangladesh refugee camps. But the programs, which aid cuts had shuttered for months in 2025, are barely adequate even for the children they reach and may close again, humanitarian officials told Human Rights Watch. While resources are shrinking, about 90,000 more refugee children need schooling this year, due to population growth and new arrivals fleeing atrocities in Myanmar. The donor-supported programs have largely ignored the schools that Rohingya teachers set up in the camps, which are well-regarded by refugees for their quality of education, but lack legal status and reach only about 30,000 students.

“Donor governments have turned their backs on education for half a million Rohingya students stuck in the world’s largest refugee camp, but so much could be done to mitigate this crisis,” said Bill Van Esveld, associate children’s rights director at Human Rights Watch. “Bangladesh should accelerate steps to end bans on education for refugees, and humanitarian agencies should work with the Rohingya-led schools.”

On November 19, 2026, the International Court of Justice will deliver its judgment in the case brought by Gambia alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations” constitute genocide and violate the Genocide Convention.

Bangladesh’s Awami League government, overthrown in 2024, had banned Rohingya children’s access to certified education and higher education in the camps or in the Bangladesh school system. It allowed donor-funded education programs but prohibited Rohingya community-led schools, demolished several, and threatened teachers with exile to Bhasan Char, a remote island.
The current government has taken positive steps and should lift remaining restrictions on refugees’ access to education amid the donor funding crisis, Human Rights Watch said.

In October, Bangladesh for the first time allowed a few dozen Rohingya primary students to take an internationally recognized primary school examination, supported by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

Also for the first time, Bangladesh in October approved a Rohingya nongovernmental organization’s plans to build a primary school in the camps for 240 students and to provide a structured curriculum. The Rohingya Centre UK, set up by the diaspora Rohingya community, said that the 10-subject curriculum will be taught from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., significantly more instruction than students receive in donor-funded education programs. The organization is also running training on the new curriculum for other Rohingya-led schools in the camps.
articles.lede: Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding.

articles.title: EU: Countries Plan Rwanda Deportation Centers
articles.description: Negotiations to set up an offshore deportation center in Rwanda, which has a shocking human rights record, are a particularly cruel departure from the founding values of the European Union, Human Rights Watch said today.
paragraphs: (Brussels) – Negotiations to set up an offshore deportation center in Rwanda, which has a shocking human rights record, are a particularly cruel departure from the founding values of the European Union, Human Rights Watch said today.

After months of speculation, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands, alongside Rwanda’s interior minister, confirmed the negotiations on November 16, 2026, on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference organized by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development. The five EU countries confirmed their plan to send people whose asylum claims have been rejected in the EU to Rwanda starting in 2027.

“History has shown that third country transfers violate rights and cause suffering,” said Judith Sunderland, senior associate refugee and migrant rights director at Human Rights Watch. “The choice of a country that has an abysmal human rights record and resists international scrutiny tracks with that history and evokes deep skepticism that any nominal rights safeguards will be respected.”

The recently enacted EU Return Regulation allows member states to set up deportation centers, “return hubs,” in countries outside the EU where people, including families with children, will be sent if they cannot be deported directly to their country of origin. The regulation states that agreements should be reached only with countries that respect international human rights law. Rwanda does not meet this requirement, Human Rights Watch said, yet the five European countries did not provide any human rights or due diligence assessment during the announcement.

The Rwandan government has a well-established record of repressing dissent, including attacks on rights defenders. Its arrests of critics and dissidents, their ill-treatment in detention, and the government’s interference with the judiciary and failure to investigate suspicious deaths have contributed to a widespread climate of fear and self-censorship. In addition, the Rwandan military provides critical support to and exercises overall control over the M23 armed group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Both Rwandan forces and the M23 are responsible for serious abuses and war crimes.

As recently as January, Germany, Greece, Denmark, and the Netherlands raised concerns about Rwanda at its UN human rights review. A similar UK-Rwanda deal raised serious human rights concerns before it was abandoned, an Israel-Rwanda deal led to documented abuse, and the situation of recent deportees from the United States to Rwanda remains largely unknown.

In addition to the threat of harm to those deported to Rwanda, the deal risks financing and giving political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad, Human Rights Watch said. It could lead the EU to downplay Rwanda’s problematic human rights record or shy away from pressing for measurable improvements.

Human Rights Watch has consistently found that deportations to third countries expose people to arbitrary detention, ill-treatment, destitution, and onward returns to harm in their home countries, as well as other serious human rights abuse. The United Nations special rapporteur on the rights of migrants, the Council of Europe commissioner for human rights, and the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights have all cautioned against forcible third-country transfers. The EU countries involved in the deal with Rwanda are bound by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights.
articles.lede: Negotiations to set up an offshore deportation center in Rwanda, which has a shocking human rights record, are a particularly cruel departure from the founding values of the European Union, Human Rights Watch said today.

articles.title: Morocco / Western Sahara: Siege of Sahrawi human rights defender Sidi Mohamed Dadach's home and neighbourhood in El Aaiún
articles.description: MAR 003 / 1126 / OBS 058 Harassment / Intimidation / Restrictions on freedom of peaceful assembly / Restrictions of the right to privacy / (…)
paragraphs: MAR 003 / 1126 / OBS 058 Harassment / Intimidation / Restrictions on freedom of peaceful assembly / Restrictions of the right to privacy / Restrictions on freedom of movement Morocco / Western Sahara 16 November 2026

The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT) and the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Western Sahara.

The Observatory has been informed of the ongoing surveillance and intimidation of Sahrawi human rights defender Mr Sidi Mohamed Dadach, President of the Committee for the Defence of the Right to Self-Determination for the People of Western Sahara (CODAPSO). He is also a former political prisoner who spent more than 24 years in detention and was awarded the Rafto Prize in recognition of his human rights activities in 2002.

On 28 October 2026, at approximately 5:15 p.m., a security operation was launched when Moroccan police surrounded Mr Dadach’s home in the aftermath of a meeting of the Coordination Mechanism for Sahrawi Human Rights Action. The security cordon extended across the entire Lirak neighbourhood, with security personnel deployed at its four entrances and around its perimeter. The operation involved police officers and local authority personnel, including individuals in civilian clothing, who were deployed at the four entrances to the Lirak neighbourhood and around its perimeter, where they monitored access to and movement within the neighbourhood.

The following day, on 29 October 2026, at approximately 8 p.m., two international observers, Marianne Bugge Stavik, a Norwegian national, and André Christopher Belleteste, a Norwegian-American national, were intercepted by six Moroccan police officers as they were returning to their hotel in El Aaiún. The officers reportedly told them that their presence in the city was unwelcome and instructed them to leave for Agadir. Both observers, 22-year-old university students studying in Norway, had met with Mr Dadach, other Sahrawi human rights defenders and relatives of Sahrawi political prisoners earlier that day. Their forced departure prevented them from completing their planned programme of meetings, including further exchanges with Sahrawi human rights defenders and families of political prisoners on 30 October 2026.

On 31 October 2026, the security siege imposed around Mr Dadach’s home in the Lirak neighbourhood of El Aaiún remained ongoing. Individuals whom he identified as local authority personnel wearing civilian clothing continued to monitor his movements and those of his family members, raising serious concerns regarding their safety, privacy and freedom of movement.

The Observatory recalls that it has repeatedly documented acts of surveillance, intimidation and restrictions on freedom of movement targeting Sahrawi human rights defenders in Western Sahara. In its statement of 31 July 2026, the Observatory reported renewed restrictions on movement, surveillance and intimidation targeting several members of the Collective of Sahrawi Human Rights Defenders (CODESA), including the continued siege and surveillance of the homes of its President, Ali Salem Tamek, and Vice-President Khadijetou Douih. In an earlier urgent appeal published on 28 February 2025, the Observatory also documented the siege and attack on the home of CODESA member Hassan Zerouali while international visitors were meeting with him to collect testimonies of human rights violations. These incidents illustrate a recurring pattern of surveillance and intimidation targeting Sahrawi human rights defenders in their homes and in connection with their legitimate human rights activities.

articles.title: Liberia Lifts a Major Barrier to Education
articles.description: “Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a new government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade.
paragraphs: “Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a new government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade. The policy is already helping families who struggled to pay the fees, removing a longstanding barrier to their children's education.

Since the policy took effect in September, Liberian child advocates have interviewed parents in four counties to assess whether schools were complying with the ban. The findings offered encouraging early indications: nearly all 20 parents interviewed knew about the policy and had enrolled their children without paying registration fees.

Parents described the difference the policy was making. “The decision by the ministry is so good,” said a parent in Bong County. “It enables our children to go to school free without worry.” Another parent whose children had previously been out of school said, “For some of us that don’t have money, it helps us a lot.”

A Human Rights Watch investigation in late 2025 and early 2026 found that registration fees caused severe hardship for many Liberian families and put education out of reach for others. Some parents told us they had delayed enrolling their children for years because they could not afford the fees. Children described being sent home from school over unpaid fees. Others said they had dropped out of school or turned to child labor.

The new policy has the potential to benefit nearly half a million families, helping children start school on time, stay in school, and avoid child labor. But ensuring that all schools comply will be essential. One parent said that despite the policy, a primary school demanded registration fees for his three children. When he said he couldn't pay, he was told, “No registration, no school.”

The government should monitor and enforce compliance with the fee ban, extend the policy to junior and senior secondary schools, and address other costs—including transportation, uniforms, and textbooks—that keep children from attending school.

Liberia has taken a significant step toward making the right to education a reality for all children, regardless of their financial circumstances. Making education accessible to all children will help reduce inequality and create opportunities for generations to come.
articles.lede: “Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a new government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade.

articles.title: The Weapon Passed Legal Review, Then the Software Changed
articles.description: For an AI-enabled weapon, the facts that matter most to a lawyer now live in software, not necessarily in hardware.
paragraphs: Every legal opinion rests on a statement of facts. A weapon’s legal review is no exception. Under U.S. Army Regulation (AR) 27-53, the program office that wants a weapon reviewed supplies a description of the system, its intended use, its anticipated effects, and the technical information behind them. The judge advocate’s opinion answers the question those facts pose. If the facts later change, the opinion does not become wrong. It becomes an opinion about a different weapon.

For most of the Army’s history, changing the facts meant changing the hardware, and changed hardware is hard to miss. Here, “software” includes executable code, trained artificial intelligence (AI) models and their weights, and the rules and parameter settings that govern the weapon’s behavior; it does not include physical hardware or live sensor observations. For an AI-enabled weapon, the facts that matter most to a lawyer now live in software: what the system treats as a target; how confident it must be before it acts; where it will and will not operate; and how much room a soldier has to stop it. Software of that kind is updated often, and an update leaves the launcher, the airframe, the serial number, and the name exactly as they were. This post is about the gap that opens when the legal review stays attached to the hardware while the facts move with the code, and about a short document that would close it.

Consider a hypothetical counter-drone interceptor that passed Army legal review before fielding. The review request described a system that detects small quadcopters, engages only inside a geofence (a boundary drawn in software beyond which the system will not act), fires only after a soldier confirms the target, and aborts within two seconds of a stop command. The opinion found the weapon lawful on those facts.

The first repairs a display fault. Engineers re-run the tests the weapon passed before fielding and confirm that target recognition, soldier confirmation, and the abort command behave as before. The facts in the review request are unchanged.

The second retrains the recognition model, the part of the software that decides what the sensors are looking at. After retraining, the weapon can also classify small fixed-wing aircraft as targets. Nothing about the launcher changed. The description of what the weapon identifies, which the opinion took as a given, has changed.

The third shortens a timing delay to make the system more responsive. It also has a side effect: the abort command now takes effect in four seconds, not two. The engineer who made the change recorded it as a performance fix.

A judge advocate would see at once that the second and third updates alter facts the opinion relied on, and that the third is the dangerous one, because nobody thought of it as a change to the weapon. The law can handle all three. The open question is whether anyone in the program will put the facts in front of a lawyer before the new version reaches the field.

AR 27-53 anticipates changed weapons. Paragraph 6f provides that if a fielded weapon is changed so that it is no longer the system or capability described in the review request, including a substantial change to its intended use or anticipated effects, the earlier review is no longer valid and a new review is required. Paragraph 6g addresses substantial changes in a weapon’s effects or accuracy. Paragraph 9 allows a program that is unsure whether review is required to put the question, through its servicing judge advocate, to the office The Judge Advocate General (TJAG) has designated for weapons reviews, ordinarily the National Security Law Division. The same paragraph bars fielding or employment of a weapon that needs a review and has not had one.
articles.lede: For an AI-enabled weapon, the facts that matter most to a lawyer now live in software, not necessarily in hardware.

articles.title: Belgium: An intimidation lawsuit has been brought against Alexis Deswaef, a lawyer and president of the FIDH
articles.description: On 18 November 2026, Alexis Deswaef, a lawyer, former president of the Ligue des droits humains (LDH) and current president of the International (…)
paragraphs: – On 18 November 2026, Alexis Deswaef, a lawyer, former president of the Ligue des droits humains (LDH) and current president of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), is due to appear before the Ghent Court of Appeal on charges of abuse of the right of access to files in a legal case – These proceedings relate to a case of police violence which led to the death of Lamine Bangoura, a 27-year-old footballer, in Roeselare in 2018. – The LDH, the Liga voor Mensenrechten (LVM) and the Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership between the FIDH and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), have condemned this as a Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation (SLAPP) against Alexis Deswaef, the lawyer representing Mr Bangoura’s family.

Brussels, Paris, Geneva, 17 November 2026. In the trial opening before the Ghent Court of Appeal, Alexis Deswaef, the lawyer representing Mr Bangoura’s family, is being prosecuted for misuse of the right of access to a court file. The prosecution accuses him of having passed on information from Lamine Bangoura’s court file to journalists. Alexis Deswaef denies this charge.

Lamine Bangoura was a 27-year-old man who died of suffocation whilst pinned under the knees of police officers during an incident in Roeselare in 2018. These circumstances are reminiscent of the death of George Floyd in the United States of America in 2020. The Roeselare police were assisting a bailiff tasked with evicting the young man from his home due to rent arrears. The country’s Dutch-language press reported his final moments in detail, based on a video from the court file.

The police officers involved were not prosecuted; the Indictment Division had ruled that there were " insufficient grounds for referral to the criminal court ". However, these same officers had taken legal action to denounce the leak of a video of their operation to the press. The newspaper De Morgen had been questioned by the authorities but had not revealed its source, in accordance with the law on the protection of sources. The courts, defying all logic, ruled that there were sufficient grounds to refer Alexis Deswaef to a criminal judge.

Alexis Deswaef faces a Level 2 sentence, which could take the form of a prison term of between six months and three years, and an order to pay damages in excess of €50,000. This is a particularly worrying case, as these proceedings appear to be targeting a lawyer and a prominent human rights defender because of his work. The position taken by the public prosecutor’s office also raises questions, given that the police officers involved in the young man’s death are not facing any charges.

The LDH, the LVM and the Observatory have condemned a SLAPP order aimed at intimidating a human rights defender. The LDH, the LVM and the Observatory also call on the Belgian judicial authorities to drop the proceedings against Alexis Deswaef and reiterate that lawyers must be able to carry out their duties without intimidation, in accordance with the United Nations Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers and Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.
articles.lede: On 18 November 2026, Alexis Deswaef, a lawyer, former president of the Ligue des droits humains (LDH) and current president of the International (…)
