Europe: Disgraceful Rwanda deportation deal repeats mistakes of the past
articles.description: Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced plans to carry out deportations to so-called “return hubs” in Rwanda.
paragraphs: Reacting to today’s announcement from the Vienna Migration Conference where Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced plans to carry out deportations to so-called “return hubs” in Rwanda, Aimée Stuflesser, the asylum and migration expert at Amnesty International Austria, said:

“Today’s disgraceful deportation deal between European countries and Rwanda repeats mistakes of the past. Sending people to a country they have never been to is irresponsible and there is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights.

“Undocumented people must not become pawns in a politics of deterrence. The harms of these types of migration deals are well documented. From the Italy–Albania deal and the UK’s attempt to forcibly send people to Rwanda, to Australia’s offshore detention system, past attempts to send people to countries to which they have no connection have proven unlawful, unworkable and expensive.

“Wherever such schemes have been put in place, they have resulted in catastrophic human rights violations, while having a ruinous impact on asylum systems. The EU’s past cooperation with countries such as Libya on migration, moreover, have shown its inability – or unwillingness – to effectively uphold human rights, despite theoretical safeguards.

“The irony that this is happening in Vienna must not be lost. In this city, in 1993, states came together to affirm the universality of human rights. Today, this same city witnessed how those rights are being hollowed out piece by piece. Any responsible government should abandon these plans outright.”

According to the unveiled plans, under a “pilot project”, a first group of people without the right to stay in the EU are expected to be transferred to Rwanda in 2027. Amnesty International calls on the Austrian, German, Dutch, Greek and Danish governments to withdraw from the scheme.

“Return hubs” involve a heightened risk of refoulement, including in return hubs or through onward deportations, and raise concerns regarding the prohibition of torture, inhumane or degrading treatment or punishment which could occur during and after transfers. The uncertainty over which state’s jurisdiction is engaged and which state is responsible for protecting returnees, could also impact people’s access to effective judicial remedy for violations experienced in “return hubs”.

The UN Special Rapporteur on the human rights of migrants has also pointed out that outsourcing migration control to third countries and private actors makes it harder to attribute legal responsibility for human rights violations. It does not, however, release states from their human rights obligations.

The new EU Return Regulation only permits deportation centres in states that comply with international human rights standards. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention noted in 2026 that Rwandan authorities “suppress opposition and dissent, prosecuting political opponents, journalists and human rights defenders” for vague crimes. In 2023, the UK Supreme Court ruled the UK–Rwanda scheme unlawful and contrary to the principle of non-refoulement.
articles.lede: Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced plans to carry out deportations to so-called “return hubs” in Rwanda.

articles.title: Can EU Action Against TikTok Rabbit Holes Lead to Real Social Media Design Change?
articles.description: The EU found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for failing to mitigate the risk of harmful rabbit holes but will that lead to social media design changes.
paragraphs: The European Union’s executive preliminarily found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for failing to adequately assess and mitigate the risk of users falling into rabbit holes that could harm their well-being. The Commission particularly raised concern about young users’ and vulnerable adults’ repeated exposure to content that can negatively affect people’s mental health.

The findings closely echo Amnesty International research, which documented in two major studies how TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed can draw children who engage with mental health-related videos into rabbit holes of depressive and suicidal content. Young people and bereaved parents shared with us how TikTok’s feed normalized and exacerbated teenagers’ struggles with depression and self-harm, with devastating consequences.

TikTok has led the charge in steering social media away from centering on people’s real-world connections towards algorithmically recommended content from strangers and celebrities, based on deeply privacy-intrusive user profiling. The platform takes pride in tailoring each “For You” feed to the individual user within minutes.

In some cases, as our research shows, that can mean taking a child’s account from initial contact with a few sad videos to a stream of depressive videos including suicidal ideation content within less than an hour. Research from the Molly Rose Foundation similarly warned of an increase in risks to children’s safety on the platform between 2023 and 2025, despite the increased scrutiny the platform had come under. All of this underlines that solutions focused solely on “bad users,” parental controls, or teen bans will inevitably fail to create the kinds of safe and privacy-friendly platforms we all deserve, no matter our age.

TikTok has repeatedly disputed such findings, pointing to safety measures such as its Community Guidelines and user tools. Responding to the European Commission’s findings, a TikTok representative told the legal news platform MLex: “The Commission has made a series of statements that are fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety […] We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience.”
The company now has to formally respond to the Commission proceedings, adding to previous EU findings on addictive design and children’s safety.

The preliminary findings come amidst a heated global debate on how to ensure children’s online safety. Over 170,000 people mobilized around Amnesty International’s petition to make TikTok safer following the publication of our research in 2023.

Young people have been at the forefront of campaigning for design changes. Recently, multiple high-profile legal cases against Meta and TikTok in the United States reinvigorated optimism amongst campaigners after years of political deadlock in the US Congress. Yet over the last year, as pressure mounted, governments around the world, including a majority of EU member states, have pivoted towards teen social media bans as a quick-fix solution. They are choosing to “regulate children” rather than companies in a setback to more systemic reform approaches tackling the design and business model of Big Tech platforms.
articles.lede: The EU found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for failing to mitigate the risk of harmful rabbit holes but will that lead to social media design changes.

articles.title: Belgique: une procédure-bâillon vise Alexis Deswaef, avocat et président de la FIDH
articles.description: Ce 18 novembre 2026, Alexis Deswaef, avocat, ancien président de la Ligue des droits humains (LDH) et actuel président de la Fédération (…)
paragraphs: – Ce 18 novembre 2026, Alexis Deswaef, avocat, ancien président de la Ligue des droits humains (LDH) et actuel président de la Fédération internationale pour les droits humains (FIDH), comparaît devant la Cour d’appel de Gand pour abus de droit de consultation dans un dossier judiciaire. – Cette procédure est liée à une affaire de violences policières, qui ont causé la mort de Lamine Bangoura, un jeune footballeur de 27 ans, à Roulers, en 2018. – La LDH, la Liga voor Mensenrechten (LVM) et l’Observatoire pour la protection des défenseur·es des droits humains, un partenariat de la FIDH et de l’Organisation mondiale contre la torture (OMCT), dénoncent une procédure-bâillon à l’encontre d’Alexis Deswaef, avocat de la famille de M. Bangoura.

Bruxelles, Paris, Genève, le 17 novembre 2026. Dans le procès qui s’ouvre devant la Cour d’appel de Gand, Alexis Deswaef, avocat de la famille de M. Bangoura, est poursuivi pour abus de droit de consultation dans un dossier judiciaire. Le parquet l’accuse d’avoir transmis à des journalistes des informations issues du dossier judiciaire de Lamine Bangoura. Alexis Deswaef conteste cette accusation.

Lamine Bangoura était un homme de 27 ans, mort étouffé sous les genoux de policiers lors d’une intervention à Roulers en 2018. Des circonstances qui rappellent la mort de George Floyd aux États-Unis en 2020. La police de Roulers assistait un huissier chargé d’expulser le jeune homme de son logement pour un arriéré de loyer. La presse néerlandophone du pays a rapporté ses derniers instants en détail à partir d’une vidéo issue du dossier judiciaire.

Les policiers impliqués n’ont pas été poursuivis; la Chambre des mises en accusation ayant estimé qu’il n’y avait « pas de charges suffisantes pour un renvoi devant le tribunal correctionnel ». Cependant, ces mêmes policiers avaient saisi la justice pour dénoncer la fuite d’une vidéo de leur intervention dans la presse. Le journal De Morgen avait été interrogé par les autorités, mais n’avait pas révélé sa source, conformément à la loi sur la protection des sources. La justice a, contre toute logique, estimé que les charges étaient suffisantes pour renvoyer Alexis Deswaef devant un·e juge pénal·e.

Alexis Deswaef risque une peine de niveau 2, pouvant prendre la forme d’une peine d’emprisonnement de six mois à trois ans, et une condamnation à des dommages et intérêts de plus de 50 000 €. Une affaire particulièrement préoccupante, puisque cette procédure semble viser un avocat et un défenseur des droits humains en vue en raison de son travail. La position du parquet pose également question, puisque les policiers impliqués dans la mort du jeune homme ne sont pas inquiétés.

La LDH, la LVM et l’Observatoire dénoncent une procédure-bâillon visant à intimider un défenseur des droits humains. La LDH, la LVM et l’Observatoire appellent également les autorités judiciaires belges à mettre fin aux poursuites contre Alexis Deswaef et rappellent que les avocat·es doivent pouvoir exercer leurs fonctions sans intimidation, conformément aux Principes de base des Nations unies relatifs au rôle du barreau et à l’article 10 de la Convention européenne des droits de l’homme.
articles.lede: Ce 18 novembre 2026, Alexis Deswaef, avocat, ancien président de la Ligue des droits humains (LDH) et actuel président de la Fédération (…)

articles.title: Philippines: US Tech Hub to Displace Hundreds
articles.description: The Philippine government’s impending construction of a technology manufacturing hub under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative will displace hundreds of Indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province.
paragraphs: (Manila) – The Philippine government’s impending construction of a technology manufacturing hub under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative will displace hundreds of Indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province, Human Rights Watch said today.

The Philippine government will provide the land—including territory inhabited for generations by the Indigenous Aeta tribe—while investors, including US companies, will finance the infrastructure and facilities. The framework agreement between the Philippines and the United States is yet to be signed.

“Indigenous communities and small farmers fear they will be unlawfully displaced by the semiconductor hub,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government should follow domestic laws and international standards that protect land rights.”
Human Rights Watch visited two affected sites in Capas in October 2026—Sapang Kawayan in Barangay Aranguren and Sitio Binyayan in Barangay O’Donnell—and spoke to 11 residents.

Pax Silica is a US initiative that began in December 2025 to secure US technology supply chains. Under Pax Silica, the US State Department has brokered agreements with other countries and international entities on issues including mineral extraction, technology hardware manufacturing, communications infrastructure, software and platforms, and trade. The Philippines joined Pax Silica in April 2026 and agreed to host a 1,618-hectare semiconductor hub in the town of Capas in Tarlac province, north of Manila, largely for mineral processing and semiconductor manufacturing.

The hub development is led by the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), a Philippine government body created by law in 1992 that owns and administers areas previously used as US military bases, including territory occupied and used by the Aeta communities. The Pax Silica hub will be inside New Clark City, a government and residential complex built by BCDA in 2018. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said the government was “terribly excited” about Pax Silica.

Under the 1997 Indigenous Peoples Rights Act (IPRA), Indigenous peoples have the right to lands, inland waters, coastal areas, and natural resources that they have “occupied [and] possessed since time immemorial” and can receive Certificates of Ancestral Domain Title. Extended delays in processing titles have left many Indigenous communities vulnerable to encroachment.

The Aeta Hungey tribe in Sapang Kawayan has been seeking recognition of its ancestral domain since 1994 and refiled in 1999 after the Indigenous Peoples Rights Act took effect, but has not yet received title.

In early July 2026, BCDA officials sent letters to Sapang Kawayan residents, informing them that the land they were occupying would be “affected by the project New Clark City” and inviting them to discuss it at their Clark office without mentioning the planned hub. These letters and BCDA personnel visits to measure their lands caused immediate concern among residents.
articles.lede: The Philippine government’s impending construction of a technology manufacturing hub under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative will displace hundreds of Indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province.

articles.title: Regret Is Not a Defence: The Assembly of States Parties and the Sanctioning of the International Criminal Court
Regret Is Not a Defence: The Assembly of States Parties and the Sanctioning of the International Criminal Court
articles.description: [Ezequiel Jimenez Martinez is an Adjunct Professor at the Pompeu Fabra Law Faculty, and a Senior Fellow at the Center for International Law Research and Policy. He is the author of Governing the In…
paragraphs: [ Ezequiel Jimenez Martinez is an Adjunct Professor at the Pompeu Fabra Law Faculty, and a Senior Fellow at the Center for International Law Research and Policy. He is the author of Governing the International Criminal Court: the History and Practice of the Assembly of States Parties to the Rome Statute (Brill, 2025).]

On 9 October 2026 the United States designated the International Criminal Court itself under Executive Order 14203. The general licence permitting dealings with the Court to be maintained or wound down expires on 7 April 2027, and the State Department has presented that window as time for States Parties to make progress on resolutions addressing United States concerns. The Bureau of the Assembly said it “regrets” the measure and called for its revocation, eight foreign ministers of States Parties declared themselves committed to “constructive and inclusive dialogue with non-States Parties” ahead of the 25th session of the Assembly of States Parties, which opens in The Hague on 30 November. One can understand the difficult position diplomats are in when it comes to defending the International Criminal Court from the United States, the superpower. Yet, if States Parties will not defend the institution besides political solidarity, then their governance role which equips them to act in tangible ways, is at risk of becoming irrelevant.

The Assembly is the Court’s international judicial governance institution, or injugovin. Article 112(2)(b), (d) and (g) confer on it management oversight, the budget and any other function consistent with the Statute. Together they ground what Bergsmo and others have called a “non-waivable duty of care” towards the institution States Parties created. The Assembly has said so much itself when in December 2025 it reaffirmed “the incompatibility of the consequences of coercive measures against the Court” with States Parties’ obligations under the Statute, the Agreement on Privileges and Immunities and the Headquarters Agreement. Having said so, it cannot treat the response against the United States and other non-State Parties like Russia as optional.

When Executive Order 14203 was signed in February 2025, 79 of 125 States Parties endorsed a joint statement of support. By October 2026, only 35 States Parties voiced some concern. Nonetheless, at its 24th session in 2025, the Assembly adopted by consensus a Declaration that names no State and “encourage[s] dialogue between States Parties and Non-States Parties”. The undisputed Declaration was adopted as the President of the Court explained to States Parties that nine elected officials, “ including one third of the Judges, as well as the totality of the ICC Presidency ,” were subject to Russian arrest warrants. Yet only the Declaration was passed as a political decision on the matter. A few days later, on 12 December 2025, the Moscow City Court convicted the Prosecutor and eight current and former judges in absentia, and on 8 October 2026 Russia sent extradition requests for all nine to the Netherlands and other States. The Presidency of the Assembly had responded to earlier Russian measures under its previous President. I have found no statement on the verdict or the requests by the current Presidency. By August 2026 the United States had designated nine of the eighteen judges, the President among them, both Deputy Prosecutors and the former Prosecutor. While much protective work is rightly confidential, it that does not explain why public texts and statements only speak of concern, regret and dialogue in the face of such blatant attack on the rule of law.
articles.lede: On 9 October 2026 the United States designated the International Criminal Court itself under Executive Order 14203.

articles.title: ‘Peace begins in our hearts’: Children close Muscat forum with a message to the world
articles.description: Children from across the world sent a message of peace from the Omani capital Muscat on Monday, calling for an end to hatred, respect for diversity and the protection of human rights.
paragraphs: Their message closed the two-day Muscat Plan of Action Forum, held on the International Day for Tolerance, marked by the UN every 16 November.

“Peace begins in our hearts, and in our belief that we all belong to one humanity,” the children said, describing understanding as the bridge between peoples and coexistence as the foundation for a safe and prosperous future.
They pledged to build bridges of solidarity, stand up for children’s rights, protect the planet and act as ambassadors for peace in their own communities.

On the forum’s second day, UN officials, religious and traditional leaders and experts discussed how to turn the goals of the Muscat Plan of Action – launched at UN Headquarters in New York in June – into practical programmes and partnerships.

Mohamed bin Said bin Khalfan Al Mamari, Oman’s Minister of Endowments and Religious Affairs, said the plan aims to strengthen the role of religious and traditional leaders and Indigenous Peoples in preventing conflict and combating hate speech.
“Difference in itself does not create conflict, just as similarity does not guarantee peace,” said Mr. Al Mamari.
Peace “is not merely the absence of violence or the cessation of conflicts and wars,” he continued, but needs a system built on justice, trust and security.
The minister called for stronger local mediators, a better link between early warning and institutional response and a bigger role for women and young people.

Chaloka Beyani, the UN Special Adviser on the Prevention of Genocide, said tolerance is the basis for peace, human rights and coexistence, warning that discrimination and exclusion can escalate into incitement to violence and crimes against humanity.
articles.lede: Children from across the world sent a message of peace from the Omani capital Muscat on Monday, calling for an end to hatred, respect for diversity and the protection of human rights.

articles.title: Ecuadorian Courts Expose Flaws in US High-Seas Arrests
articles.description: Between August 28 and September 16, US military forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels, alleging that they served as floating refueling stations for drug-trafficking boats.
paragraphs: Between August 28 and September 16, US military forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels, alleging that they served as floating refueling stations for drug-trafficking boats. They detained 146 of the 160 crew members and transferred them to Ecuadorian authorities, who charged 90 with “unlawful association.”

Since Human Rights Watch reported on the operations, Ecuadorian courts have acquitted 40 people. In an October 29 judgment reviewed by Human Rights Watch, a Manta judge acquitted eight fishermen from a vessel named the Don Rufo. The prosecution’s own witnesses, including Ecuadorian police and Navy officials, testified that no illicit items were recovered, and that they knew of no prior investigation linking the fishermen to organized crime.
The judge said the prosecution rested on a “chain of successive presumptions.” He admonished the prosecutor for pursuing an unsupported case and closed it.

The ruling follows an October 7 decision acquitting another 32 crew members from the Conquista II and María Candelaria on similar grounds. The judge found no evidence supporting the unlawful association charge and admonished prosecutors for pursuing the case without even minimal evidence.

Out of the 160 crew members intercepted by the US, 110, that is 70 percent, are now free and without charges. Fourteen were not brought before Ecuadorian authorities, 56 were released without charge by a judge, and 40 were acquitted. Fifty others are awaiting trial.

Neither Ecuador nor the United States has publicly disclosed the operation’s legal basis, including the criteria used to intercept the vessels, and in some cases destroy them, or evidence linking the boats to drug trafficking.

The US Congress should ensure oversight over these and other US security operations in and near Ecuador, where people have been detained without evidence and, in some cases, tortured by Ecuadorian personnel. Organized crime in Ecuador is a serious threat that should be addressed with an effective and rights respecting security and justice policy, not with human rights violations.
articles.lede: Between August 28 and September 16, US military forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels, alleging that they served as floating refueling stations for drug-trafficking boats.

articles.title: ICC: How far does a UN Security Council referral extend?
articles.description: In the Njeem case, the International Criminal Court has confirmed its jurisdiction over the situation in Libya. However, the judges were divided on the basis for jurisdiction. This is a sensitive debate that also concerns Sudan.
paragraphs: In a decision of November 2, 2026, a Pre-Trial Chamber of the International Criminal Court (ICC) unanimously confirmed its jurisdiction in the case concerning Osama Elmasry Njeem, also known as Osama Almasri Njeem. This unanimity, however, masks a significant divergence of opinion amongst the judges. For Judges Iulia Antoanella Motoc and Reine Alapini-Gansou, the crimes with which Njeem is charged fall within the Court’s jurisdiction because they remain covered by the United Nations Security Council’s 2011 referral of the situation in Libya. Judge María del Socorro Flores Liera, on the other hand, deemed that the Court’s jurisdiction is based on a declaration submitted by Libya in 2025.
This divergence fuels a sensitive debate, which also concerns Sudan: how long can a Security Council referral remain in force?

On February 26, 2011, whilst Muammar Gaddafi’s regime was violently suppressing a popular uprising in Libya, the Security Council adopted Resolution 1970. Acting under Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, it decided to refer to the ICC Prosecutor “the situation in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya since 15 February 2011”.

This referral had a key distinguishing feature: Libya was not – and still is not – a party to the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty. The Court’s jurisdiction was therefore not based on ratification of the Statute by the State concerned, but on a provision of the Statute itself allowing the Security Council to refer a situation to the Prosecutor.

In this context, a Pre-Trial Chamber issued an arrest warrant for Njeem on January, 18, 2025. He is suspected of having run detention centres in Tripoli in which thousands of people have allegedly been detained for long periods. The warrant relates to war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder, acts of torture, cruel treatment, rape and other sexual violence, as well as acts of imprisonment and persecution committed at Mitiga prison from February, 15, 2015 onwards.

According to the prosecution, these crimes were committed personally by Njeem, on his orders or with his assistance, and by members of the Special Deterrence Force, also known as SDF/RADA. The victims were reportedly detained on religious grounds, due to their alleged opposition to the ideology of SDF/RADA or their alleged links with other armed groups.

Arrested in Turin, Italy, on January 19, 2025, Njeem was released and returned to Libya two days later by the Italian authorities, under highly controversial circumstances. This led the ICC to find that Italy had breached its obligations to cooperate, and to refer the matter to the Assembly of States Parties, which is due to consider this issue at its next session from November 30 to December 7, 2026, in The Hague.

The defence contested both the ICC’s jurisdiction and the admissibility of the case. In its view, Resolution 1970 relates to a specific crisis: the violence committed in 2011 by the state apparatus of the Gaddafi regime. The acts of which Njeem is accused, committed several years later in a different political and institutional context, do not, it argued, have a sufficient link to that initial situation.
articles.lede: In the Njeem case, the International Criminal Court has confirmed its jurisdiction over the situation in Libya. However, the judges were divided on the basis for jurisdiction.

articles.title: International Law for a Fragile World: Political Risk – Authoritarianism, Information Warfare, and Democratic Fragility (Part II)
articles.description: [Dr Sergey Sayapin is Visiting Principal Research Fellow at the NUS Centre for International Law and Professor of Law at KIMEP University (Almaty, Kazakhstan; on leave).] Part I of this post argued…
paragraphs: [ Dr Sergey Sayapin is Visiting Principal Research Fellow at the NUS Centre for International Law and Professor of Law at KIMEP University (Almaty, Kazakhstan; on leave).]

Part I of this post argued that contemporary democratic decline proceeds less through dramatic ruptures than through the cumulative, often formally lawful erosion of the institutions that allow political systems to correct themselves, and that international law – organised around discrete rights and flagrant violations – struggles to perceive this process until it is far advanced. This second part examines the dimension of political fragility that has been most profoundly transformed by technology – the information environment – before turning to the paradox that confronts democracies seeking to defend themselves, and to the elements of a legal approach capable of governing political risk before the threshold of irreversibility is crossed.

Propaganda and political manipulation are not new. States have always sought to influence foreign publics, and political actors have always deployed misleading claims. What has changed is the architecture through which influence operates. Digital platforms permit political communication at unprecedented scale and speed; recommender systems amplify emotionally provocative material irrespective of its accuracy; generative artificial intelligence has collapsed the cost of producing persuasive synthetic text, images, audio, and video; networks of inauthentic accounts allow narratives to be repeated across platforms until they acquire the appearance of consensus; and microtargeting fragments political communication so that different citizens encounter different versions of political reality. Foreign operations need not create domestic divisions – they exploit and amplify those that already exist.

Recent practice illustrates the range of techniques. In September 2024, the United States Department of Justice seized 32 internet domains used by the so-called “Doppelganger” operation, run by Russian companies acting at the direction of the Presidential Administration, which cloned the websites of established news outlets to disseminate fabricated articles and amplified them through influencers and paid social media advertising. Two days before Slovakia’s parliamentary elections in September 2023 – during the legally mandated pre-election moratorium on campaigning – an AI-generated audio recording purporting to capture the leader of a liberal opposition party discussing electoral fraud with a journalist circulated widely, at a moment when neither the media nor the parties concerned could effectively respond. In Moldova, the OSCE/ODIHR observation mission to the 2024 presidential election and constitutional referendum on European integration found that contestants campaigned freely “despite concerns over illicit foreign interference and active disinformation efforts”, and called for stronger action against vote-buying and illicit campaign finance – practices that national authorities attributed to a network directed from Russia. Information manipulation, financial inducements, and the exploitation of distrust are no longer separate techniques but components of integrated campaigns.

articles.title: International Law for a Fragile World: Political Risk – Authoritarianism, Information Warfare, and Democratic Fragility (Part I)
articles.description: [Dr Sergey Sayapin is Visiting Principal Research Fellow at the NUS Centre for International Law and Professor of Law at KIMEP University (Almaty, Kazakhstan; on leave).] The preceding posts in thi…
paragraphs: [ Dr Sergey Sayapin is Visiting Principal Research Fellow at the NUS Centre for International Law and Professor of Law at KIMEP University (Almaty, Kazakhstan; on leave).]

The preceding posts in this series have examined fragility in ecological, technological, human, and economic systems. All of these forms of risk, however, converge upon a further system whose resilience international law has largely taken for granted: the political institutions through which societies decide how every other risk is to be governed. Climate adaptation requires governments capable of planning beyond the electoral cycle; pandemic preparedness depends upon public trust in credible institutions; technological governance presupposes authorities able to regulate powerful private actors; and economic resilience requires governments capable of making contested distributive choices under uncertainty. When political institutions themselves become fragile, the capacity to govern every other category of risk deteriorates with them. Democratic erosion should therefore be understood not merely as a problem of constitutional design or domestic political organisation but as a form of systemic risk – and, in a sense, as the meta-risk of a fragile world.

The empirical evidence is difficult to dismiss. Freedom House reported in March 2026 that global freedom declined in 2025 for the twentieth consecutive year, with 54 countries deteriorating and only 35 improving; the share of the world’s population living in countries rated “Free” has fallen from 46 to 21 per cent in two decades. International IDEA’s Global State of Democracy 2025 found that 94 of the 173 countries it assesses – 54 per cent – had declined in at least one key dimension of democratic performance compared with five years earlier, that its indicator of credible elections had fallen to its lowest level in thirty years, and that press freedom had suffered its most far-reaching decline since the dataset began in 1975. The V-Dem Institute’s Democracy Report 2026 counts 92 autocracies against 87 democracies and estimates that almost three-quarters of humanity now lives under autocratic rule. These assessments differ in method, but they converge on a single conclusion: decline is no longer confined to fragile or transitional states. It is a structural feature of the contemporary international order.

This two-part post argues that international law is insufficiently equipped to understand this phenomenon because it protects democracy primarily through individual rights, electoral standards, and the prohibition of unlawful external interference. These protections remain indispensable. Yet democratic fragility increasingly develops through processes that are cumulative rather than episodic, informational rather than territorial, and frequently lawful when each measure is considered in isolation. Part I examines how democratic erosion operates and why the architecture of international law struggles to capture it. Part II turns to information warfare, the paradox of democratic self-defence, and the contours of a legal approach to democratic risk governance.
articles.lede: The preceding posts in this series have examined fragility in ecological, technological, human, and economic systems.

articles.title: Pre-Trial Chamber II of the ICC Closes (or Attempts to Close?) the Afghanistan Investigation
Pre-Trial Chamber II of the ICC Closes (or Attempts to Close?) the Afghanistan Investigation
articles.description: In our previous post, we discussed a curious set of procedural developments at the International Criminal Court (ICC), with Pre-Trial Chamber II (the PTC) ordering the Prosecution to open a second …
paragraphs: In our previous post, we discussed a curious set of procedural developments at the International Criminal Court (ICC), with Pre-Trial Chamber II (the PTC) ordering the Prosecution to open a second investigation in relation to the Situation in Afghanistan. The PTC also ordered the transfer of court records, including the four arrest warrants it had already issued within the ambit of the ongoing investigation, to the new ‘Situation in Afghanistan II’. We noted too that the PTC appeared to act on its own initiative, without any basis in the Court’s statutory framework, and without submissions from the Prosecution or anyone else. The Prosecution has appealed both decisions; these appeals are currently pending before the Appeals Chamber (AC). In the meantime, and seemingly without heed to the ongoing appeals, the PTC has now, on 12 November 2026, ordered the closure of the ongoing investigation into the Situation in Afghanistan. With that, as captured in immediate reporting, is the closure of any ‘ investigation into US war crimes in Afghanistan ,’ among other alleged crimes, including by Islamic State.

The best that can be said of the latest decision is that it at least makes clear what was driving the initial, procedurally irregular, decision to split the ongoing investigation into two. The latest decision asserts a motivation of securing ‘the objectives of legal certainty, transparency and the proper administration of judicial proceedings’ (para 22). The pursuit of these values is difficult to take at face value. After setting out the PTC’s reasoning, we raise technical, institutional, and strategic difficulties with the decision.

As a starting point, Pre-Trial Chamber II again invokes its own ‘inherent judicial powers’, which it proposes are necessary to ‘safeguard the fairness and legality of the proceedings’ (para 14). This aside, the legal basis suggested by the Chamber is Regulation 66 ter (2) of the Regulations of Court, adopted by the Court’s judges. Notably, Regulation 66 ter, which addresses the ‘[c]losure and reopening of case and situation records’, was included in the Regulations by way of amendment less than a month before the PTC’s decision to split the Situation in Afghanistan in two. The Regulation states, in the relevant part:

(a) When the Prosecutor, having provided information in accordance with regulation 45, sub-regulation 1, decides not to initiate an investigation, or determines that he or she does not anticipate any further investigatory or prosecutorial activities in a situation in relation to which an investigation has been initiated, he or she shall inform in writing the Pre-Trial Chamber to which the situation has been assigned.

(b) Having been so informed, the Pre-Trial Chamber may, upon application or proprio motu, order the Registrar, when appropriate, to close the record of the situation. The Pre-Trial Chamber shall be responsible for judicial matters of a residual nature in this situation, unless otherwise provided in the Statute, the Rules or these Regulations or such matters are assigned to another Chamber by the Presidency.

articles.title: UAE: 5 Shia Residents Arrested Arbitrarily
articles.description: UAE authorities have arbitrarily detained at least five Shia Muslim foreign residents since the United States and Israel carried out military strikes on Iran in February, 2026.
paragraphs: (Beirut) – Emirati authorities have arbitrarily detained at least five Shia Muslim foreign residents since the United States and Israel carried out military strikes on Iran in February 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The detentions appear to be based on the detainees’ religious identity.

Emirati authorities detained the residents, who had been in the UAE between 2 and 40 years, between March and May. They have not been brought before a judge or formally charged, three informed sources said.

“Emirati authorities appear to be rounding up residents simply based on their religious beliefs as Shia Muslims in a largely Sunni country rather than providing any evidence of wrongdoing, while trampling over people’s due process rights,” said Joey Shea, senior UAE researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately release anyone targeted because of their religion.”

Between September and October, Human Rights Watch interviewed the three sources and reviewed CCTV footage of a raid on the company that one of the detainees owned. The detainees’ and sources’ names are withheld for fear of reprisals against them and their relatives.

The sources said that security authorities asked at least one of the detainees about his religious affiliation before his arrest and interrogated at least one family member about their religious views. Another Shia community member warned at least one detainee and a relative to leave the UAE.
On March 23, Emirati state security arrested one man, 44, in Sharjah, as he was in his car near his home at midnight, a relative said. He was not allowed to contact a lawyer or his family that night.

The following night, Emirati security forces took the man to his family home for a search. The officers took money, jewelry, books, and credit cards, his relative said. Security forces did not inform him or his family of any charges against him.

The relative said that a worker at the mosque they attended had warned him to leave the country in June 2025. The government “viewed us Shias as sleeper cells,” he said. The relative left the UAE two days later.

The same mosque worker asked the man on March 20, 2026, whether he had “any problems with the police.” The relative said this was how the man had been warned, but he did not understand it as a warning and stayed in the UAE.

Emirati security forces also raided the man’s company. Human Rights Watch reviewed CCTV footage reportedly from the site, timestamped March 24. The footage shows two men, one in a baseball cap and the other in traditional clothing, entering the man’s company at around 9:19 p.m. and searching offices. One enters a room with computers and appears to tamper with the equipment.
articles.lede: UAE authorities have arbitrarily detained at least five Shia Muslim foreign residents since the United States and Israel carried out military strikes on Iran in February, 2026.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia: Amazon warehouse workers still facing exploitation despite company initiatives
articles.description: Migrant workers hired to work in Amazon’s operations in Saudi Arabia continue to face abuses from the third-party labour supply companies that employ them.
paragraphs: Migrant workers hired to work in Amazon’s operations in Saudi Arabia continue to face abuses from the third-party labour supply companies that employ them. They are also subjected to harsh working conditions in Amazon’s warehouses and the risk of the company ending their assignment at will, despite Amazon’s attempts to improve other aspects of their recruitment and living conditions, Amnesty International said in a new briefing today.

Amazon in Saudi Arabia: Why migrant workers remain at risk of exploitation documented some important improvements, including reduced recruitment-fee abuses, better accommodation standards and improved access to grievance mechanisms. Following Amnesty International’s 2023 investigation, Amazon also r eimbursed more than USD 2.45 million to 1,180 workers in Saudi Arabia. Nevertheless, migrant workers remain vulnerable to exploitation under Amazon’s hiring model.

“Three years on, workers are still describing some of the same abuses and vulnerabilities. Despite steps taken by Amazon to improve some conditions for workers and reimburse illegal recruitment costs, its outsourcing of the recruitment and employment of migrant workers for its warehouses continues to leave such workers dependent on labour supply companies for their income, legal status and ability to change jobs or leave the country,”said Marta Schaaf, Programme Director for Climate, Economic Social Justice and Corporate Accountability at Amnesty International.

“When workers are no longer needed by Amazon, they can be left without work or pay for weeks or months, yet unable to return home or move freely to other jobs. Such experiences reflect deeper problems in the way migrant workers are employed through labour supply companies within Saudi Arabia’s kafala system.”

This briefing draws on follow-up research conducted by Amnesty International between September 2025 and March 2026, including interviews with 24 migrant workers from India and Nepal who, at the time of interviews were currently or had recently been employed by three labour supply companies to work in one Amazon warehouse in Riyadh. Amnesty International has shared details of the investigation with Amazon and the Saudi Arabian government. Amazon’s responses can be accessed here. At the time of publication, the government had not responded.

Despite reforms to Saudi Arabia’s kafala sponsorship system, the experiences of contracted workers demonstrate that Amazon’s labour suppliers continue to exercise significant control over their employment, job mobility and freedom of movement.

Similar to Amnesty International’s previous findings, many workers said recruiters had misled them into believing they would be employed directly by Amazon on two-year contracts, only to discover shortly before departure that they would in fact be employed by third-party labour suppliers, something that many said they would not have agreed to had they known from the outset.
[Amazon] can expel us from work anytime they want. It’s unclear when they will kick us out from work – today or tomorrow. We’re temporary workers!”
articles.lede: Migrant workers hired to work in Amazon’s operations in Saudi Arabia continue to face abuses from the third-party labour supply companies that employ them.

articles.title: Two Weeks in Review: 2—13 November 2026
Two Weeks in Review: 2—13 November 2026
articles.description: Over the last two weeks, it is chiefly the institutions of international law that have been in focus. There have been a number of responses to the judicial elections at the International Court of J…
paragraphs: Over the last two weeks, it is chiefly the institutions of international law that have been in focus. There have been a number of responses to the judicial elections at the International Court of Justice, from congratulations to the incoming benchers, to consternation at the growing disparity in global representation, and a look forward to the election of the President next year. Commentators have also turned to the ICC’s decision to split the Afghanistan investigation, and the UN Security Council’s failure to renew MINURSO’s mandate in Western Sahara. Meanwhile, State practice following the recognition of Palestine has raised problems concerning Palestinian nationality and statelessness, in particular the protections for Palestinians under international law. And the updated ICRC Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention continues to struggle to address fully persons with disabilities. Not to mention a critical look at EJIL’s AI policy, and the use of the global carbon budget in climate litigation before domestic courts.
Marko Milanovic congratulates EJIL:Talk’s very own Dapo Akande on his election to the International Court of Justice—replete with AI-generated video laudatio.

Eric Chan turns our attention from who is in, to who is out. The United Kingdom may have regained a seat, restoring representation of all five permanent Security Council members, but the elections have left Latin America and the Caribbean with only one judge for the first time in the Court’s history. Take a look at voting patterns in the General Assembly and Security Council, and this outcome illustrates the tensions between informal regional seat allocations, the privileged position of the P5, and the requirement under Article 9 of the ICJ Statute to represent the world’s principal legal systems and forms of civilisation. This raises a deeper question, whether preserving established patterns of representation adequately reflects the diversity of international legal traditions—particularly given the historical contributions and contemporary under-representation of the Global South.

And looking ahead, Noam Morris examines the forthcoming February 2027 election of the ICJ’s President and Vice-President, distinguishing the President’s institutional and diplomatic responsibilities from their procedural and judicial functions under Article 21 of the ICJ Statute and the Court’s Rules. Drawing on historical election patterns, he identifies the influence of judicial seniority, re-election cycles, geographical representation, and gender diversity on the selection of the Court’s leadership. The growing complexity and political sensitivity of the Court’s docket make judicial experience, administrative competence, diplomatic skill, and the ability to manage deliberations especially important considerations in the election.

Miles Jackson and Priya Urs criticise the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber’s decision to require a separate investigation into crimes committed against women and girls following the Taliban’s return to power in 2021, notwithstanding existing arrest warrants issued within the Afghanistan situation. They question the Chamber’s reliance on inherent judicial oversight powers under Articles 15 and 53 of the Rome Statute, arguing that its intervention lacks a clear statutory basis, contradicts the Appeals Chamber’s approach to the scope of investigations, and creates uncertainty over the validity and jurisdictional basis of existing warrants. The decision risks undermining prosecutorial independence under Article 42, introducing procedural inconsistency and delaying justice for victims.
articles.lede: Over the last two weeks, it is chiefly the institutions of international law that have been in focus.

paragraphs: 1. Call for Papers: 20th Polar Law Symposium. Organised under the leadership of Associate Professor Liu, this symposium will be held at SMU Yong Pung How School of Law, Singapore, on 14 – 16 September 2027, under the theme “Polar Law in a Multipolar World: Connections, Diversity, and Adaptation”. It will examine legal and governance challenges facing the Arctic and Antarctic, including geopolitical shifts, environmental change, private law and industry, and the contributions of non-state actors and Indigenous peoples. Connections between emerging ASEAN economies and the polar regions will be a particular focus. The organisers welcome abstracts of up to 250 words and panel proposals of up to 500 words. The submission deadline is 31 March 2027, 11:59 pm Singapore time. Further details are available on the conference website, including the full Call for Papers and submission forms. 2. Call for Submissions: International Water Law in the Post-2030 Era. The International Water Law Academy (IWLA) and Northumbria University are inviting submissions for upcoming events in Newcastle, UK. The main conference (3 -4 June 2027) will be exploring the future of international water law amid the approaching SDG timeline. Accepted abstracts will be considered for the IWLA’s “Maverick Award” and for inclusion in a later special issue of a journal. Submissions of a 600-800 word abstract are invited by 31 January 2027. PhD students and early-career researchers are also invited to a pre-conference Emerging Scholars Workshop (2 June 2027) to share works-in-progress and receive mentorship. Workshop submissions are due 1 March 2027. For full event and submission details, visit the IWLA website.

articles.description: To have your event or announcement featured in next week’s post, please send a link and a brief description (1-2 paragraphs) to ojeventsandannouncements@gmail.com. Calls for Submissions Workshop &#…
paragraphs: Workshop – The Board of Peace and its Role in International Law: The Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and International Law invites submissions for a workshop to be held on 5 February 2027 on The Board of Peace and its role in international law: Challenge, continuity or a new global legal order? Looking back at the first year of the Board of Peace’s existence, this workshop intends to explore whether the Board challenges or even violates international law, how far it is genuinely new in the governance of peace, security and peacebuilding, and what to expect from it in the coming years, given its limited activity so far. We welcome papers from a variety of legal and interdisciplinary perspectives, particularly from Early Career Researchers. Abstracts should be submitted by 30 November 2026. The full CfP can be found here.

Conference – New Beginnings: Foundations for the Future: The ANZSIL Conference Organising Committee invites paper and panel proposals for the 34 th ANZSIL Annual Conference, to be co-hosted by Western Sydney University Law School, Parramatta, New South Wales, Australia, 30 June – 2 July 2027. Submissions on a wide range of areas are welcomed, with a specific focus on the Conference theme, ‘New Beginnings: Foundations for the Future.’ Participants are invited to reflect on how international law continues to adapt, innovate and renew. For the full Call and for the abstract submission process, see here. In addition, applications are open for the Alice Edwards Breakthrough Researcher Award, designed to assist one or two early career researchers or PhD students to present at the conference: see here for eligibility and benefits. Deadline for the Call for Papers and Panels and for the Alice Edwards Breakthrough Researcher Award: 8 February 2027.

Conference – ‘Freedom of the Seas: Past, Present and Future’: SOAS University of London and the British Institute of International and Comparative Law (BIICL) are co-convening a conference on 1 December 2026 as part of the British Academy project ‘Freedom of the Seas and Human Rights Protection’. Freedom of the seas is a fundamental principle that has shaped international law since its inception, framing patterns of commerce, human mobility, communication, access to resources, and security. Freedom, which in principle should allow all to benefit from the seas and oceans, has however resulted in access only for a few and in lack of regulation and control, that has promoted practices to the detriment of many States and people. The conference proposes to engage with contemporary challenges and to address some fundamental questions related to these themes, bringing together leading academics and practitioners. To attend, please register using this online form.

PhD Position – Upholding the Right to a Fair Trial in the Digital Age: Are you interested in pursuing a PhD on the intersections of criminal law, human rights, and new technologies? If so, consider applying to do a Department for the Economy (DfE)-funded PhD at Queen’s University Belfast – School of Law! This project, titled ‘Upholding the Right to a Fair Trial in the Digital Age’, will examine how new developments related to digital evidence, AI, deepfakes and inequalities in technological capacity can affect the integrity and fairness of criminal proceedings. Funding is subject to final DfE approval. If you are interested and have a proposal in mind, feel free to reach out to me via email for more information. The closing date for applications is 14 January 2027. More information here.
