articles.title: Israel Bans Travel for Prominent Palestinian Rights Defender
articles.description: Israeli authorities on November 13, 2026, imposed an international travel ban on Shawan Jabarin, the head of Al-Haq, a leading Palestinian human rights organization in the occupied West Bank.
paragraphs: (Beirut) – Israeli authorities on November 13, 2026, imposed an international travel ban on Shawan Jabarin, the head of Al-Haq, a leading Palestinian human rights organization in the occupied West Bank. The travel ban comes in the context of increasing attacks against Palestinians and civil society groups in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

Al-Haq, along with the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights and Al-Mezan Center for Human Rights, are continuing their critical human rights work despite US sanctions for engaging with the International Criminal Court. Human Rights Watch, with three other human rights organizations, filed a lawsuit in US federal court on August 11 seeking to have the sanctions struck down.
The following quote can be attributed to Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch:

“Israeli authorities’ travel ban against Shawan Jabarin, among the most prominent human rights defenders in Palestine, reflects a vindictive effort to punish those advocating for victims of serious crimes. The ban is the latest escalation of Israel’s campaign to silence Palestinian rights groups that document violations of international law and seek accountability. Governments should act to support and protect Palestinian civil society and ensure that they’re able to continue their invaluable work.”
articles.lede: Israeli authorities on November 13, 2026, imposed an international travel ban on Shawan Jabarin, the head of Al-Haq, a leading Palestinian human rights organization in the occupied West Bank.

articles.title: London Calling: The Customary Law of Naval Blockade and Contemporary Practice
articles.description: The employment of naval blockades in recent conflicts confirms that States continue to view them as an important method of warfare.
paragraphs: Naval blockade has long occupied a distinctive place within the law of naval warfare. Until very recently some commentators regarded it as a relic of an earlier era, however, the employment of naval blockades in recent conflicts has confirmed that States continue to view them as an important method of warfare. Although the fundamental principles of blockade law were set out in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, notably in the 1856 Declaration of Paris and the 1909 London Declaration Concerning the Laws of Naval War (which States never ratified and therefore never entered into force), its legal foundation has always rested principally upon customary international law. The classical requirements that a blockade be declared, notified, effective, impartial in its application, and respectful of access to neutral ports have remained remarkably stable for more than a century. These core criteria have been consistently reaffirmed in naval manuals and, more importantly, reflected in State practice.

Nevertheless, the use, and potential abuse, of blockade in situations where vulnerable civilian populations may face harm has led human rights advocates, humanitarian organizations, and some legal scholars to question whether blockade, in its current form, is compatible with contemporary international humanitarian law. The expression of such humanitarian concerns raises a fundamental question about the current state of blockade: does contemporary State practice confirm the validity of the customary law of blockade, as reflected in the 1909 London Declaration, or does it indicate that the Declaration’s traditional requirement of effectiveness is being reshaped by modern humanitarian norms?

This post argues that contemporary maritime practice demonstrates that the essential legal characteristics of blockade, as outlined in the 1909 London Declaration, have neither been abandoned nor transformed; rather, recent conflicts reveal a remarkable continuity in the customary law of blockade. States continue to declare blockades, enforce them through naval, air and other assets, intercept neutral shipping, and justify such measures by reference to established principles of the law of naval warfare. That which has changed is not the belligerent right to conduct naval blockades but rather the broader legal environment within which the law of naval blockade exists.

Naval blockade is a distinct belligerent maritime operation intended to prevent vessel traffic from all States from entering or leaving specified coastal areas that are under the sovereignty, occupation, or control of an enemy. Such areas may include ports and harbors, the entire coastline, or parts of it. As a distinct operation, it is governed by a body of rules that have evolved over five centuries and has been shaped through the practice of maritime powers, interpreted and refined by the jurisprudence of prize courts, and accepted as part of the belligerent right to wage war at sea.

Historically, blockade emerged from the broader doctrine that a belligerent was entitled to deny an adversary the use of the sea for military and economic purposes. By the late eighteenth century, British and American prize courts had recognized blockade as a lawful means of warfare, so long as certain minimum conditions were satisfied. These conditions reflected a balance between the legitimate military interests of belligerents and the rights of neutral States to engage in maritime commerce.
articles.lede: The employment of naval blockades in recent conflicts confirms that States continue to view them as an important method of warfare.

articles.title: Hungary Pledges to Ratify European Treaty to Protect Women from Violence
articles.description: On November 12, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that his government intends to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combatting violence against women and domestic violence, also known as “Istanbul Convention."
paragraphs: On November 12, Hungary's Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that his government intends to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combatting violence against women and domestic violence, also known as “Istanbul Convention,” as part of a comprehensive package of measures seeking to strengthen protection and dignity of women and girls. It is a welcome and timely step.

In 2013, I interviewed 37-year-old Lívia from Budapest for Human Rights Watch’s report Unless Blood Flows which documented domestic violence in Hungary. She told me she had repeatedly called the police about her husband’s abuse and that the police even witnessed him beating her. Officers told her they could do nothing “unless blood flows.” Other women described similar responses, some telling me they had stopped calling for help.

The new government package would strengthen enforcement of restraining orders, make misuse of intimate images a distinct criminal offense, and provide special protections for victims and survivors of intimate partner violence in criminal proceedings.

Parliament, then controlled by a two-thirds majority from the Fidesz/KDNP ruling coalition, blocked an earlier ratification effort in 2020. Ratification commits Hungary to binding standards on preventing violence, protecting victims and survivors including those without secure immigration status, and holding perpetrators accountable.

Alongside ratifying the convention, authorities should develop an implementation plan in consultation with victims, survivors and women’s rights organizations; Police should receive specialized training on intimate partner violence, how to assess risks and to act on credible threats, and how to work with the courts to enforce protection orders. And the government should adequately fund sufficient numbers of shelter spaces, legal aid, and counseling services nationwide. To ensure reforms are effective, authorities should collect and publish data on police responses and breaches of protection orders to facilitate assessment.
The real test of these reforms will be when a survivor like Lívia next calls the police for help. No one should have to bleed before police and authorities act.
articles.lede: On November 12, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that his government intends to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combatting violence against women and domestic violence, also…

articles.title: 6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Closing Remarks
articles.description: [Alessia Corti holds an MSc in Human Rights from LSE and currently works in the NGO sector and as a research assistant at the University of Rome ‘La Sapienza’.] Five days, nine posts an…
paragraphs: [ Alessia Corti holds an MSc in Human Rights from LSE and currently works in the NGO sector and as a research assistant at the University of Rome ‘La Sapienza’.]
Five days, nine posts and some sharks with a laser beam attached to their heads later, the 6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law comes to an end.

We opened the symposium on Monday by saying that we hoped it could show that international law can be (forgive us one last time for saying it out loud) cool. Having read this year’s contributions, we can say that international law can also be honest about what it does not know yet (which makes it even cooler, if you ask me)

Christine Bianco opened the week in the Hogwarts World. She showed how the International Statute of Secrecy, a rule written to protect a persecuted minority, ends up casting non-magical people as objects of the law rather than its subjects. Her reminder that international law is “a product and a weapon of power” echoed through the week. Mia Colliard asked: what status would Dr. Evil’s sharks have in international humanitarian law? She found a gap: while IHL protects animals indirectly as objects, it does not recognise them as full subjects in armed conflicts. Laurence Atkin-Teillet examined what is consider real and worthy of legal protection in international law by asking whether the painted people of Lumière could be victims of genocide. Her conclusion is that international law “does not currently provide a clear affirmative answer,” but that the videogame invites us to ask if it should. Nivedita S. closed the week by analysing Monstress to argue that legal subjecthood and extractability are mutually constituted, rather than sequential: dehumanisation enables extraction, and extraction sustains dehumanisation. Until the law sees this loop it will continue to punish only one half of the mechanism, or to regulate the other, while the mechanism itself continues.

Through Attack on Titan, Himani Jha and Garima Tiwari showed that law says little about when and to whom a confession must come to make a deception lawful. With no court to test the difference, the line between a clever ruse and the war crime of perfidy is left to the storytellers. Shaoxuan Xu, writing on The Three-Body Problem, distinguishes having control over communication from having the authority to speak for more than oneself. What if safeguards are established after one has already spoken for all? Shaoxuan tells us that this is not sufficient: “later disclosure can support accountability but cannot retrieve a signal.” Lu Yaoyao’s article showed how Once Upon a Time in the Middle East turns a foreign war into a Chinese story. Through the film, Lu asked: whose experiences and perspectives shape the understanding of a conflict?

Through the destruction of Ohara in One Piece, and the later recovery of its books, Estéfany Rocha Monteiro showed that rescuing a library’s books does not settle the scope of the harm: the records and scholarly practices through which its content could be interpret may be lost too, and require their own legal and evidentiary assessment. Lakshmidevi Somanath found a similar pattern in Ghibli-style AI trend. Lakshmidevi explained that copyright covers an expression, not an idea: it can judge whether a particular image copies protected work, but a visual style is beyond its reach. Even if the terms of copyright were extended to fill this gap, since copyright is territorials, the answer would likely change from country to country. The contradiction is inevitable: “a borderless tool will have to live with bordered answers”:
articles.lede: Five days, nine posts and some sharks with a laser beam attached to their heads later, the 6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law comes to an end.

articles.title: 6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Made Monstrous, Made Available – Monstress and the Law of Extractable Life
articles.description: [Nivedita S is a Research Fellow with the Centre for International Law, National University of Singapore and an avid reader.] The political economy of resource extraction in international law typic…
paragraphs: [ Nivedita S is a Research Fellow with the Centre for International Law, National University of Singapore and an avid reader.]

The political economy of resource extraction in international law typically focuses on tangible resources such as land, minerals, energy, and biological materials. The vocabulary that international law appears to have developed is a vocabulary of things. The likes of permanent sovereignty of natural resources, the seabed regime, investment protection for mining concessions, and the emerging law of critical minerals presuppose a sub-surface resource that lies beyond the people who claim it. Scholarship on extractivism pushes against this boundary by showing how the “ extractive zone” reorganises land, labour and life. Marjorie Liu and Sana Takeda’s Monstress confronts this framework by making this resource a person, shifting the analysis of extraction from the subsurface to the living body.

This post argues that Monstress reveals legal subjecthood and extractability as mutually constituted rather than sequential. International criminal law separates bodily subordination from extraction, treating persecution and enslavement as distinct crimes against humanity. Yet the comic depicts them as mutually reinforcing practices. International law’s separate categories risk obfuscating this structural relationship. Monstress therefore challenges us to recognise the production of extractable life through the recursive relationship between persecution and bodily commodification. I use the comic as a thought experiment to view a world in which this mechanism can be seen as a whole.

Monstress is set in a fantasy matriarchal world fracturing by conflict between the Federation of Man and the Arcanics, a race of “monstrous” beings who are hybrids of humans and “Ancients”. The Federation is dominated by the Cumaea, an order of witch-nuns who have systematically subjugated the Arcanics by incrementally harvesting “lilium,” a valuable, purple-coloured magical substance, from the bones of captives, who are kept alive and thus permanently maimed to maximise extraction yield over time, and ultimately killed. Lilium not only enhanced human minds and bodies, but it also had miraculous regenerative powers, and in concentrated forms could even extend human lifespans. The Arcanics are bought and sold at auctions, fitted with collars and assigned to laboratories, where Cumaean novices dissect Arcanic children as part of their training. ( Monstress Vol. 1, “Awakening”)

The design and illustrations in the comic are also significant here. Takeda renders Cumaean spaces in a lavish, art nouveau-like style such that the ornamentation of a civilisation and the infrastructure of its harvesting share the same frame. Lilium is not hidden but lights up the city. Liu’s stated inspiration of World War II and colonial atrocities highlights the historical relevance of the comic: a fantasy format that brings to the consciousness a history of racially targeted experimentation.
articles.lede: The political economy of resource extraction in international law typically focuses on tangible resources such as land, minerals, energy, and biological materials.

articles.title: Genocide and Myanmar at ICJ
articles.description: “It’s the World Court and it’s genocide: you don’t really get any bigger than that especially when it comes from reporting in The Hague,” says Stephanie van den Berg, cohost of our podcast partners at Asymmetrical Haircuts.
paragraphs: On 19 November the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will be ruling in a really significant case against the government of Myanmar, which is accused of committing genocide ‌against the minority Muslim Rohingya. Gambia brought the case to the ICJ under the Genocide Convention in 2019. During the hearings Gambia argued that ⁠a 2017 offensive by Myanmar government forces that forced at least 730,000 Rohingya into neighbouring Bangladesh constituted a genocide. Myanmar denies the charge and has said the offensive was a counter-terrorism campaign and therefore legitimate and definitely not genocide.

It’s the first time the UN court may rule that a state is liable for genocide. Melanie O’Brien, Professor of International Law at the University of Western Australia Law School and former President of the International Association of Genocide Scholars explains the challenging legal issues that make this case so important in the field of international justice.
articles.lede: “It’s the World Court and it’s genocide: you don’t really get any bigger than that especially when it comes from reporting in The Hague,” says Stephanie van den Berg, cohost of our podcast partners at Asymmetrical Haircuts.

articles.title: In the digital realm of the “RD4U”
articles.description: The Register of damages caused by Russia in Ukraine – also known as RD4U – has begun to operate. It has already received about 200,000 claims. Its executive director explains its current operations and future hopes.
paragraphs: With a Star Wars style acronym – RD4U – the ‘Register of Damage Caused by the Aggression of the Russian Federation Against Ukraine’, to give it its official name, is now completely open for business. All 43 categories of claims for compensation for “damage, loss or injury caused by the internationally wrongful acts of the Russian Federation in or against Ukraine, starting on or after 24 February 2022” can now be submitted by individuals, companies or the state of Ukraine.

The Register started in April 2024 and is part of a complex interconnected set of structures including a ‘Claims Commission’ which – when it gets the ratifications needed from states – will subsume the Register into itself as one component, and continue to process claims, then adjudicate upon them, while waiting for the final cog in the machine to be added: a payment system.

There’s little comparison with other claims mechanisms developed by treaty over the years, except maybe for scale, the UN Compensation Commission that dealt with post Iraq invasion of Kuwait processing more than 2 million claims over 11 years. This one has been built at rapid speed. Distinctively, it was created during the hostilities rather than after and operates digitally via app.

“It's one of the maybe underappreciated aspects of our work,” says the Register executive director Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi. “We don't have a precedent to rely on for how to build a mechanism while the war not only is ongoing, but in many ways is as intense as at any point in the past almost 5 years.” The different challenges include availability of documentation, and the fact that “some evidence is simply lost,” he notes. “It's already becoming, at times, difficult to reconstruct events in the beginning of the war in 2022. So, from that perspective, I feel quite justified that we have started work early.”

The RD4U is based in The Hague, where so much of the old and new architecture of international justice is being created. It is completely separate from the new Special Tribunal on Aggression against Ukraine, “politically and virtually in any other way,” stresses Kliuchkovskyi. “They have different mandates, different purposes, different memberships.” He acknowledges that both are “under the Council of Europe umbrella” and in The Hague. But the special tribunal “is a mechanism for individual criminal liability, whereas the compensation mechanism, including the register, is meant to pursue state liability for violations of international law”.

Kliuchkovskyi sits in a small office in the international zone of the Dutch city, a stone's throw from Europol, Eurojust, and the former premises of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. As we comment on the blandness of the furniture visible in the zoom chat, he replies: “I don't know if it's IKEA. We inherited it from the previous landlord in this space, and we haven't bothered to change it, because that's all we need. Our physical presence is kept lean on purpose. As we semi-joke, our magic happens in the digital realm.”
articles.lede: The Register of damages caused by Russia in Ukraine – also known as RD4U – has begun to operate. It has already received about 200,000 claims.

articles.title: 6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Between Official Narratives and Popular Imagination – International Law in China’s New Mainstream Films
articles.description: [Lu Yaoyao is a PhD candidate at the Faculty of Law, The University of Hong Kong.] The 2026 Chinese film Once Upon a Time in the Middle East tells the story of an ordinary Chinese protagonist caugh…
paragraphs: The 2026 Chinese film Once Upon a Time in the Middle East tells the story of an ordinary Chinese protagonist caught in a foreign conflict. Unlike earlier Chinese new mainstream films, the film approaches war through everyday experiences and personal encounters. These different cinematic perspectives invite a broader examination of how China’s changing international role is imagined and narrated in popular culture.

China’s international legal discourse has long been shaped by historical experiences of foreign aggression and unequal international relations, with an emphasis on sovereignty, non-intervention, and opposition to hegemony. As China’s global influence has grown, these commitments have come to coexist with an increasing emphasis on participation in global governance and the protection of overseas interests. These developments reflect the coexistence of historically rooted understandings of international justice and evolving conceptions of China’s role in the world.

These developments extend beyond official discourse into popular culture. China’s new mainstream films, which combine official narratives with commercially oriented storytelling, offer a distinctive space in which international affairs are translated into stories meaningful to domestic audiences. Rather than simply reproducing official positions, these films selectively reinterpret ideas of sovereignty, peace, responsibility, and international justice through familiar narratives and individual experiences. In doing so, they reveal how China’s changing international role is imagined, negotiated, and sometimes contested between official narratives and popular understandings of international order.

The significance of Once Upon a Time in the Middle East lies not simply in its overseas setting, but in how it turns a foreign conflict into a story centered on Chinese experiences. Although the film does not explicitly identify the conflict as the Iraq War, its setting evokes that historical context, with its contested questions of military intervention, sovereignty, and international responsibility. Rather than addressing these questions directly, the film approaches war through the everyday life of a Chinese civilian. Xu Fu, the protagonist, is driven by personal concerns, including the need to repay his debts and provide for his daughter. Unlike the evacuation-centered narratives of some earlier Chinese films set in overseas conflicts, Xu Fu chooses to stay. This decision shifts the focus from escaping a foreign conflict to living through it. War becomes not merely a temporary danger to overcome, but a reality within which ordinary lives and relationships unfold.

The film’s attention to individual experiences extends beyond its Chinese protagonist. Zaid’s efforts to save his daughter and the personal experiences of American soldiers reveal the human lives behind political and military identities. The restaurant is central to this narrative. Unlike the battlefield, where individuals are often defined by their national or military affiliations, it offers a space for everyday encounters across such divisions. A Chinese American soldier serving in the US military, for instance, is reminded of his mother while eating Chinese food. The director’s comparison of food with life and war with death further captures the contrast between everyday human needs and the violence of conflict. Yet the choice of a Chinese restaurant also matters. It places a distinctly Chinese space at the center of a foreign war, allowing the experiences of others to be presented through their encounters with a Chinese protagonist. A distant international conflict thus becomes something experienced and interpreted through a familiar cultural perspective. This raises questions not only about how international affairs become meaningful to domestic audiences, but also about whose experiences and perspectives shape the understanding of a conflict.
articles.lede: The 2026 Chinese film Once Upon a Time in the Middle East tells the story of an ordinary Chinese protagonist caught in a foreign conflict.

articles.title: Splitting the ICC’s Afghanistan Investigation: Judicial Oversight or Overreach?
Splitting the ICC’s Afghanistan Investigation: Judicial Oversight or Overreach?
articles.description: On 5 October 2026, Pre-Trial Chamber II of the International Criminal Court (ICC) unsealed four warrants of arrest against senior Taliban leaders in the Situation in Afghanistan. The warrants, whic…
paragraphs: On 5 October 2026, Pre-Trial Chamber II of the International Criminal Court (ICC) unsealed four warrants of arrest against senior Taliban leaders in the Situation in Afghanistan. The warrants, which were initially issued under seal on 8 July 2025 and 9 September 2025, concern the charge of gender persecution as a crime against humanity under Article 7(1)(h) of the Rome Statute. In substance, they alleged the severe deprivation, ‘through decrees and edicts, [of] girls and women of the rights to education, privacy and family life and the freedoms of movement, expression, thought, conscience and religion’, as well as the targeting of others ‘because certain expressions of sexuality and/or gender identity…’ The charges, and the identities of the suspects, raise novel issues of considerable importance, some of which have already been addressed in commentary.

At the same time, a set of curious procedural developments in the Situation in Afghanistan has received far less attention. On 15 July 2026, Pre-Trial Chamber II ordered the Prosecution to open a separate investigation into the Situation in Afghanistan concerning ‘crimes committed against women and girls after the Taliban takeover in 2021’ (para 6). This decision, which was initially issued under seal and available only to the Prosecution, appears to have been issued by the Pre-Trial Chamber (PTC) unbidden; that is, acting on its own initiative and without submissions from the Prosecution (or anyone else). This post addresses some questionable aspects of the PTC’s decision, including the fact that the very same Chamber has already issued four arrest warrants in relation to cases arising out of the existing Situation in Afghanistan, all of which pertain to crimes allegedly committed by members of the Taliban government since 2021.
We do not recount in detail the complex history of the Situation in Afghanistan here. For present purposes, it is sufficient to note:
As noted above, there are now four public arrest warrants, all of which concern the conduct of senior Taliban leaders since 2021.

In its decision of 15 July 2026, the PTC directed the Prosecution, ‘should it continue to consider that the requirements of article 53(1) of the Statute are met, to open a new investigation on the basis of the Referral submitted by the six States Parties on 28 November 2024’. The Chamber considered that the ‘principle of judicial oversight’ in relation to investigations authorised under Article 15(4), such as the ongoing investigation in Afghanistan, imposed upon it ‘an inherent responsibility to ensure that investigations … remain within the scope authorised by the Court’ (para 10).

As to the situation in Afghanistan, the Chamber explained that it was necessary to examine ‘whether, having regard to the particular features of the conduct described in the Referral, those allegations should be addressed within the existing investigation into the Situation in Afghanistan or in a separate investigation’ (para 10). The Taliban takeover of 2021 was a ‘materially different factual and institutional context, involv[ing] distinct modes of commission’, with the relevant allegations being unrelated to any armed conflict (para 14). In the Chamber’s view, the new referral ‘concerns allegations of gender and political persecution through the adoption, implementation and enforcement of discriminatory decrees, policies and restrictions made possible by the Taliban’s exercise of de facto governmental authority, rather than conduct allegedly committed by the Taliban as an insurgent armed group during the armed conflict’ (para 14). The ‘proper administration of justice and the orderly management of the Court’s proceedings’ justified a separate and new investigation.
articles.lede: On 5 October 2026, Pre-Trial Chamber II of the International Criminal Court (ICC) unsealed four warrants of arrest against senior Taliban leaders in the Situation in Afghanistan.

articles.title: France: Sweeping Bill Threatens Peaceful Protest, Rights
articles.description: A draft law that passed in its first reading by the French Senate on October 27, 2026, contains measures that would severely undermine the rights to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression, and are incompatible with France’s human rights treaty obligations, Human Rights Watch said today. The so-called “vandals pay” bill is now pending review by the National Assembly.
paragraphs: (Paris, November 12, 2026) – A draft law that passed in its first reading by the French Senate on October 27, 2026, contains measures that would severely undermine the rights to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression, and are incompatible with France’s human rights treaty obligations, Human Rights Watch said today. The so-called “vandals pay” bill is now pending review by the National Assembly.

“Penalizing people engaged in their right to peaceful protest is the wrong answer to tackling violent disorder in France,” said Eva Cossé, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Lawmakers in both houses should reject this problematic bill entirely.”

The bill was introduced by the government on September 16 under a fast-track procedure. It was pushed forward and significantly toughened by opposition conservative senators in response to weeks of nationwide high school protests over what students see as the government’s under-investment in their education, and the violence that took place alongside school and cost-of-living protests on October 17 that included significant clashes with law enforcement and widespread looting and property damage across France. The bill builds on the momentum of legislation adopted in August to address serious public disorder, developed in response to concerns over illegal dance parties, football-related rioting, and racing vehicles on the streets.

While the purpose of the current legislation is ostensibly to address and deter violence and property damage, the text adopted by the Senate introduces measures that pose a serious threat to human rights, including the essence of the right to peaceful protest, Human Rights Watch said. The French authorities have also failed to put forward evidence that existing criminal justice measures are insufficient to address violent disorder or criminal damage.

The draft law provides for joint civil liability for property damage during a protest. It would allow courts to order individual participants, including the parents of children who participated, to pay up to €10,000 in damages—or perform community service—whether or not the individual committed acts of violence or caused the damage.

People could be penalized simply for “knowingly” participating in an “unlawful assembly” ( attroupement ), defined in the French criminal code as “any gathering of people on a public highway or in a public place that is likely to disturb public order,” or for failing to disperse after the police issue orders for a second time. Legal commentators have said that the requirement for prior dispersal orders is not an effective safeguard, because such orders are in practice either not issued or are not sufficiently audible.

Being present during a protest considered an unlawful assembly, or failing to leave the area fast enough following police orders to disperse, could trigger severe financial consequences. The bill requires prosecutors to share suspects’ identities with prefects, the interior minister’s local representative, and local authorities so they can pursue damage claims in civil court, even if the prosecutor has decided not to pursue criminal charges.

articles.title: Indonesia: Alleged Excessive Force Against Protesters
articles.description: Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate allegations that military and police officers on November 10, 2026, responded to youth protests with excessive force and may have deliberately provoked violence.
paragraphs: (London) – Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate allegations that military and police officers on November 10, 2026, responded to youth protests with excessive force and may have deliberately provoked violence, Human Rights Watch said today. Security forces in the city of Yogyakarta on Java Island used rubber bullets, water cannons, and tear gas to disperse protesters, injuring several and detaining over 150 people, including children.

Student and activist groups had organized protests across several cities against corruption, environmental damage, and the rising cost of living on National Heroes’ Day, November 10, and called for the resignation of President Prabowo Subianto. Police said that some protesters hurled rocks and firebombs at the provincial parliament building, leading to heavy security force deployment with columns of troops and armored vehicles.

“Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate alleged excessive force against largely peaceful protesters in Yogyakarta,” said Meenakshi Ganguly, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Reports that the police instigated some of the worst violence are especially troubling.”

That evening, the generally peaceful protest turned violent when a group gathered outside Yogyakarta’s Legislative Council building in the Jalan Malioboro area, a commercial hub and tourist landmark. After clashes broke out between protesters and police, security forces used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds as the protests continued into the early hours of the morning.

A medical volunteer said the violence began around 7 p.m. when a group of unidentified people—suspected plain-clothes policemen and government supporters—appeared and began attacking students and other protesters. She said she saw security forces, both in uniform and in civilian clothes, assaulting at least 40 people then arresting them.

“I saw one person being beaten by 10 people,” she told Human Rights Watch. “They kicked and stomped on him repeatedly. There was blood everywhere. I tried to protect the victim and was hit as well.” She said that while she was recording the violence, an unidentified person seized her phone, and some men sexually harassed her when she was trying to assist victims.

A Papuan student was struck in the face by a teargas canister while riding a motorcycle through the area around Tugu Yogyakarta, the city’s main landmark. “I fell, immediately felt disoriented, and lost consciousness,” he said. Police subsequently arrested him and then took him to the hospital.
Overnight, police entered Gadjah Mada University to track down protesters and arbitrarily rounded up people, accusing them of violence.

“Tear gas was fired at us,” said Diana Nuraini, a student journalist from Pijar Press at the university. “Teargas canisters were also launched about 100 meters from [nearby] Panti Rapih Hospital. The crowd ran into the campus.” One protester suffered a skull fracture near the campus, while eight students were arrested.
articles.lede: Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate allegations that military and police officers on November 10, 2026, responded to youth protests with excessive force and may have deliberately provoked violence.

articles.title: Russia: Lev Shlosberg’s outrageous 11-year prison sentence for anti-war views upheld
articles.description: Expressing any anti-war sentiment is becoming increasingly dangerous in Russia.
paragraphs: Reacting to a court’s decision to uphold the guilty verdict and 11 years and one month prison sentence of Lev Shlosberg, a leading member of the Yabloko party – the only party in Russia to stand on an anti-war platform – for sharing social media posts related to Russia’s war on Ukraine, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia, said:

“According to this verdict, someone who expresses pacifist views and shares a photo of a victim of Putin’s aggression against Ukraine is guilty of ‘discrediting the Armed Forces’ and ‘spreading false information.’ This tells you all you need to know about the state of freedom of expression in today’s Russia.

“Today’s decision follows the persecution of other Yabloko members, and the disqualification of the party from the recent State Duma election. Expressing any anti-war sentiment is becoming increasingly dangerous in Russia.”

“Amnesty International calls for the immediate and unconditional release of Lev Shlosberg and all those detained solely for exercising their right to freedom of expression and demands an end to the systemic repression of peaceful political dissent.”

On 12 November, the Pskov Regional Court upheld the 17 August sentence imposed on Lev Shlosberg by Pskov City Court for allegedly posting a video of his online debate about Russia’s war against Ukraine and sharing of a social media post with a Daily Mirror front page depicting Vladimir Putin and a blood-covered Ukrainian woman. In 2026, Yabloko members have increasingly faced criminal prosecutions and election-related disqualifications with at least seven other party members including another deputy chair, Maksim Kruglov, serving prison sentences or held in pre-trial detention. In August, the Supreme Court for the first time since the foundation of the party in 1993 barred, arbitrarily, its federal candidate list from the September State Duma election.
articles.lede: Expressing any anti-war sentiment is becoming increasingly dangerous in Russia.

articles.title: ICC terminates proceedings against Sylvestre Mudacumura
6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: The Buster Call on Ohara – One Piece and the International Law of Destroying a People’s Past
articles.description: [Estéfany Rocha Monteiro is a Brazilian lawyer and researcher. She studied at the Geneva Academy of International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights and has previously worked with the Inter-American…
paragraphs: [ Estéfany Rocha Monteiro is a Brazilian lawyer and researcher. She studied at the Geneva Academy of International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights and has previously worked with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights and the United Nations.]

Since 1997, Eiichiro Oda’s One Piece has followed Monkey D. Luffy, a young pirate searching for the legendary treasure that gives the manga its name, across a world of islands, kingdoms and competing political orders. As that voyage expands, it also uncovers a history that the World Government has tried to place beyond investigation: one hundred years, known as the Void Century, are missing from the historical record, and research capable of recovering them is prohibited.

Evidence of those missing years nevertheless remains on Poneglyphs, stone inscriptions dispersed across the world and written in an ancient script that very few people can decipher. No single inscription restores the history that has disappeared, since their contents acquire meaning through comparison with other Poneglyphs and with historical materials preserved elsewhere. On Ohara, generations of archaeologists had brought those practices together around the Tree of Knowledge, an immense library in which the study of books, archaeological evidence and the ancient script had developed into a common scholarly tradition.

The consequences of the prohibition are told through Nico Robin, who grows up inside that scholarly community and learns to decipher the ancient script while still a child. When government agents discover what the Oharan archaeologists have been studying, Professor Clover is shot as he begins to explain what their research has revealed about the civilisation that existed during the missing century, while a Buster Call, a World Government military protocol authorising overwhelming Marine force against a designated target, is activated against the island. The bombardment reaches the researchers together with the place and materials through which their knowledge had been produced, accumulated and transmitted.

As the Tree of Knowledge burns, the archaeologists spend their final hours carrying books towards its windows and throwing them into the lake below. Ohara is destroyed, most of its scholarly community is killed and eight-year-old Robin escapes with knowledge that will make her a fugitive for much of her life, while the collection disappears beneath the water. The scene appears to join the fate of the books to that of the people who had worked through them, until Oda returns to Ohara many years later and allows those two histories to separate.

That return occurs through Dr Vegapunk, a scientist employed by the World Government who had known Clover and visited Ohara after its destruction. He finds that the scholars’ final effort had preserved much of the collection: giants had recovered the books from the lake and carried them to Elbaf, where Vegapunk later gained access to the materials and continued research informed by what the Oharan archaeologists had discovered. By the time another scholar can work through the collection, the books have crossed the destruction of the library that assembled them, while much of the linguistic knowledge, research memory and intellectual community that had surrounded them survives only through scattered people and relationships.
articles.lede: Since 1997, Eiichiro Oda’s One Piece has followed Monkey D. Luffy, a young pirate searching for the legendary treasure that gives the manga its name, across a world of islands, kingdoms and competing political orders.

articles.title: Haiti: More than 1,000 killed between July and September, UN report reveals
articles.description: More than 1,000 people were killed in Haiti during the third quarter of this year, as armed gangs continue to terrorize the population in the capital Port-au-Prince and beyond, the UN team in the island nation, said in its latest human rights report.
paragraphs: It details bloody turf wars, sexual violence and other horrors, noting that serious violations and abuses continue to be committed across the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and in the Artibonite and South-East departments.

“The scale of the massacres documented during this period, particularly in Kenscoff and several other localities that had previously been spared, reminds us of the absolute need to strengthen both mechanisms for protecting the population and the presence of the State in recently liberated areas,” said Carlos Ruiz Massieu, Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General in Haiti and Head of the UN Integrated Office in the country, BINUH.
The UN Security Council has authorized a Gang Suppression Force for the Caribbean country which has yet to be fully deployed.

Between July and September, at least 1,167 people were killed and 459 injured in Haiti. Gangs were responsible for more than 45 per cent of these incidents, while around five per cent were attributable to self-defence groups targeting gang members and people suspected of collaborating with them.

The report notes that more than half of all documented killings and injuries occurred during ground or aerial operations carried out by security forces against gangs, sometimes with the support of a private military company using drones.

Armed groups maintained a grip on neighbourhoods in the capital under their control, carrying out targeted killings in retaliation for security operations. They also murdered people who refused to be extorted, respect their rules or who had denounced attempts by gang leaders to interfere in the electoral process.

Gang members who had been driven out of neighbourhoods such as Bel Air and La Saline by security operations earlier in the year gradually regained a foothold in these areas and committed further abuses there.

In early August, gangs beheaded at least 19 people in the Cité Soleil neighbourhood, including 12 elderly women. Two attacks in the town of Kenscoff in July and August left at least 105 people dead, including 19 children. More than 36 victims were shot dead in the courtyard of a Protestant church.
Attacks were also carried out in the communes of Saint-Michel-de-l’Attalaye in Artibonite and Marigot in South-East, areas that had previously been largely spared from gang infiltration.

articles.title: Regulating ‘Killer Robots’: another missed opportunity?
articles.description: On 16-20 November in Geneva States will deliberate on what could form the basis of a future Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) instrument. But what does this mean for civilian protection and meeting the challenges of algorithmic warfare?
paragraphs: One glance at recent headlines on automated and accelerated decision-making in targeting in Gaza, Iran, Ukraine and elsewhere, shows how far the time required for doubt, reflection – and human witnessing – has been stripped, without a corresponding emphasis on understanding and accounting for what is lost for civilians forced to exist and survive in these conflicts.

Over the past two decades, artificial intelligence (AI) in the military domain, which includes a reliance on algorithmic decision-support systems and predictive pattern-of-life targeting, has dramatically altered how war is experienced, and how crucial parts of International Humanitarian Law (IHL) – such as civilian status – are interpreted.

In early September 2026, the final meeting of the United Nations group of governmental experts (GGE) on emerging technologies in the area of Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems concluded a final text of “elements for an instrument”, adopted by states, available to read online. The text will be presented to delegations convening in Geneva, the Swiss capital of diplomacy, at the seventh review conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons – commonly referred to as the ‘CCW’ – which will be held this month from 16 to 20th November 2026.

A reading of the text – often referred to as “regulating killer robots” – generates a disturbing disconnect from the reality of today’s wars and raises questions about whether a treaty in this forum could ever serve to restrain autonomous or artificial intelligence-assisted uses of force.

The 1980 CCW is an international treaty banning or restricting the use of weapons considered to cause unnecessary or unjustifiable suffering to combatants and indiscriminate harm to civilians, in both international and non-international armed conflicts. It operates through five annexed protocols, designed to be added to, which address specific categories of harmful weapons:

Could there be a sixth protocol on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (also known by the acronym LAWS)? Possibly. The CCW was designed to be a flexible convention, so new weapons protocols could be added to it over time. Under article 8 of the CCW, any state that has ratified the treaty has the power to propose an additional protocol relating to categories of conventional weapons not yet covered, and a conference to negotiate a protocol can proceed if a majority of states agree. Or, states can collectively decide on new protocol negotiations at a meeting.

Because the CCW operates by consensus, a decision can only be made if no member state actively objects to it. This enables broad participation on the one hand, but on the other hand means that the CCW requires the passive or explicit agreement of every single participating state, which has implications for how text is negotiated – vetoed and blocked, or compromised and diluted. Some states embrace consensus and others instrumentalise it, diluting the collective will and ambition, as Yvette Issar from the Quaker UN Office in Geneva, has reflected on.
articles.lede: On 16-20 November in Geneva States will deliberate on what could form the basis of a future Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) instrument.

articles.title: 6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Ownership of a Style – Ghibli-Style Generation and the Limits of Copyright within the Territorial Framework
articles.description: [Lakshmidevi Somanath is Partner – Litigation & Strategy at Anand and Anand, India and a PhD Scholar at IIT Kharagpur. She formerly served in the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, Go…
paragraphs: [ Lakshmidevi Somanath is Partner – Litigation & Strategy at Anand and Anand, India and a PhD Scholar at IIT Kharagpur. She formerly served in the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, Government of India as a Member Judge.]

In March 2025, the launch of native image generation together with GPT-4o created an avalanche of family photos and movie posters recreated in the unique soft hand-painted style that is specific for Studio Ghibli. The explanation given by the provider defined the line separating persons and organizations, with the model being capable of rejecting a prompt referring to a living artist but accepting those associated with more general studio styles. On the contrary, the copyright law makes no such distinction, and reactions from practicing artists confirmed this fact.

Eighteen months on, the question has moved from the timeline to the docket. In October 2025 the Content Overseas Distribution Association, whose members include Studio Ghibli, asked OpenAI to stop using members’ works for machine learning and to answer infringement claims arising from Sora 2 outputs, and the Japanese Cabinet Office made a formal request of its own. In November, the Regional Court of Munich I held that song lyrics memorised in model parameters, and reproduced in chatbot outputs, infringed German copyright.

The case provides a genuine test for three propositions put forward by clients during a single counseling session, namely: (1) style is unprotectable, (2) training is subject to the laws of the particular jurisdiction in which it occurs, and (3) moral rights arise where economic rights are inadequate. All three propositions hold true, at least in part.

First of all, this postulate is well-established and universally accepted. According to TRIPS Article 9(2), copyright covers expression rather than an idea, procedure, or method of operation. Similarly, the Berne Convention only covers the works of literary and artistic nature rather than the manner of their creation. Palette, line weight, weather depiction, and pacing of a cut belong to the latter category and are therefore not protected under Berne Convention.

This position is corroborated in all jurisdictions involved. Japan’s General Understanding on AI and Copyright published by the Cultural Council’s Legal Subcommittee in March 2024 considers the act of infringement at the output stage as involving two elements – resemblance to the concrete expression of a copyrighted work and reliance on the expression. The former is usually presumed if the work in question is included into the training data (as per Tatsuhiro Ueno, who is a member of the subcommittee). Simply being similar to the manner of expression is not enough. In the same fashion, the US Copyright Office has reached this doctrinal conclusion in Part 3 of the report on generative AI training, albeit with some shift in focus – the concept of stylistic substitution is considered as market harm under the fourth factor of fair use doctrine.

The practical consequence is that liability is assessed output by output rather than trend by trend. The forensic question is whether the image is in the style of the catalogue or of a work within it, and the answer rarely turns on the wording of the prompt. Copyright attaches to works and to the rights subsisting in them, and is indifferent to whether an aesthetic is attributable to one director or to several hundred animators.
articles.lede: In March 2025, the launch of native image generation together with GPT-4o created an avalanche of family photos and movie posters recreated in the unique soft hand-painted style that is specific for Studio Ghibli.

articles.title: A collective step forward: the outcome document on achieving meaningful protection for hospitals in armed conflict
cats: Upholding humanity in war: the Global IHL Initiative
articles.description: When war reaches hospitals, protection becomes a matter of life and death. Discover what international humanitarian law demands.
paragraphs: Hospitals and other medical facilities enjoy specific protection under international humanitarian law (IHL), yet the reality in contemporary armed conflicts is starkly different. Attacks against health-care facilities, their misuse and impediments to their functioning continue to put patients and medical personnel at risk and undermine access to essential medical care. Against this backdrop, more than 100 states from all regions came together through the Global IHL Initiative to examine what meaningful protection for medical facilities requires in practice.

In this post, ICRC Legal Advisers Supriya Rao and Alexander Breitegger examine the recently released outcome document on Achieving Meaningful Protection for Medical Facilities in Conflict, resulting from several rounds of consultations with states led by Nigeria, Pakistan, Spain, Uruguay and the ICRC. This piece highlights key parts from the outcome document, including what the specific protection afforded to medical facilities entails, the strict conditions under which that protection may be lost, and the rules that continue to constrain attacks even when it is lost. Drawing on two years of state consultations and expert discussions, it also considers areas of disagreement among states and explains how the positions reflected in the outcome document can help states translate their existing legal obligations into meaningful protection on the ground.

Hospitals and other medical facilities enjoy one of the highest levels of protection under international humanitarian law (IHL), reflecting their life-saving function and going beyond the protection enjoyed by other civilian objects. Yet there is a widening gap between the protection the law provides and the grim reality on the ground, as attacks against health-care facilities, their misuse and impediments to their functioning continue to take a devastating toll. It was in response to this gap that the protection of medical facilities was chosen as one of the workstreams of the Global IHL Initiative.

Led by four co-chairing states – Nigeria, Pakistan, Spain and Uruguay – together with the ICRC, the workstream sought to reaffirm and deepen understanding of the existing IHL rules protecting medical facilities in contemporary armed conflict. It also aimed to identify practical measures, drawing on existing law and good practices from states, to strengthen implementation of those rules. The resulting outcome document, Achieving Meaningful Protection for Medical Facilities in Conflict, does not seek to create new law and is not open for endorsement. It reflects five consultations with more than 100 participating states from all regions of the world over 18 months, complemented by two expert workshops bringing together a wealth of experience and expertise.

At a time when hospitals are increasingly targeted or otherwise affected by hostilities, the outcome document provides an important reaffirmation of the specific protection IHL affords medical facilities. It examines what that protection requires in practice and offers states a concrete tool for translating their legal obligations into meaningful protection on the ground. In doing so, it demonstrates that respecting and protecting medical facilities during armed conflict is both possible and essential to fulfilling the fundamental obligation to care for the wounded and sick. It may also contribute to countering narratives and interpretations that portray the IHL rules protecting hospitals as significantly more flexible than they actually are.
articles.lede: When war reaches hospitals, protection becomes a matter of life and death. Discover what international humanitarian law demands.

articles.title: After the ICJ ruling, who pays? Vanuatu’s fight for climate justice premieres at COP31
6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Genocide in the Canvas? International Law and the Destruction of Lumière in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
articles.description: [Dr Laurence Atkin-Teillet is a Lecturer in International Criminal and Humanitarian Law at Nottingham Law School, Nottingham Trent University.] What makes a world real? Is it the material from whic…
paragraphs: [ Dr Laurence Atkin-Teillet is a Lecturer in International Criminal and Humanitarian Law at Nottingham Law School, Nottingham Trent University.]

What makes a world real? Is it the material from which it is made, the person who created it, or the lives of those who inhabit it? And if a world contains beings who think, love, suffer, build communities and fear their own destruction, does it matter that they were painted into existence rather than born?

These questions are at the heart of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, the role-playing game developed by Sandfall Interactive. They also raise a very difficult question for international law: could the deliberate destruction of an entire population of human-like beings constitute genocide, even if those beings exist inside a painting?

The answer under existing international law is obviously not straightforward. Yet the question does show some important assumptions about the groups whom international law protects, the nature of personhood, and the boundaries between what we consider real and what we consider worthy of legal protection.

At first, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 appears to tell a story of a population living under the shadow of an existential threat. Its inhabitants live in Lumière, a city in a strange and beautiful world shaped by magic.

Each year, a figure known as the Paintress marks a new number on a distant Monolith. This number determines the age of those who will disappear in an event known as the Gommage. When the number changes to 33, everyone aged 33 vanishes, leaving families and friends to mourn those they have lost. Expedition 33 sets out to stop the Paintress and end the cycle. As the story continues, however, the distinction between reality and fiction begins to disappear.

The Canvas is not an imaginary world inhabited by characters who exist for the entertainment of an audience – it is a world created through the artistic powers of the Dessendre family. The real-world painter Verso created the Canvas; following his death, his mother, Aline, retreated into it and recreated aspects of the family she had lost. The world came to contain painted versions of people, alongside other beings with their own lives and identities.

Aline’s husband, Renoir, enters the Canvas in an attempt to bring her back to reality. Their conflict gradually threatens the survival of the world and its inhabitants. The struggle becomes even more complicated when we discover that Maelle is the real-world Alicia, who entered the Canvas and lost her former identity, while the painted Verso is a recreation of the real Verso.

The game’s ending presents a difficult choice. In Verso’s ending, often nicknamed the “ Genocide Ending ”, he defeats Maelle and destroys the Canvas. The painted world and the inhabitants whom the player has come to know disappear. In Maelle’s ending, she preserves the Canvas, but her decision also raises questions about autonomy and the right to determine one’s own existence.

The choice is between two understandings of what makes a life worth preserving. The painted inhabitants may have been created by another person, but they experience relationships, loss, fear and attachment – their lives have meaning to them. From their perspective, the destruction of the Canvas is the end of their world.
articles.lede: Is it the material from which it is made, the person who created it, or the lives of those who inhabit it?

articles.title: 6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Who Can Speak for Earth? Representative Authority and First-Contact Governance in The Three-Body Problem
cats: Declaration of Principles Concerning the Conduct of the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence
articles.description: [Shaoxuan Xu is a PhD student in international law at Fudan University Law School and holds an LLM from New York University School of Law.] When Ye Wenjie receives an extraterrestrial warning, she …
paragraphs: [ Shaoxuan Xu is a PhD student in international law at Fudan University Law School and holds an LLM from New York University School of Law.]

When Ye Wenjie receives an extraterrestrial warning, she already has the means to answer. The warning tells her that replying will let the Trisolarans locate Earth and bring conquest, yet she responds. Later, Mike Evans finances a second communications base aboard Judgment Day. Control of the channel allows two people to make choices whose consequences extend far beyond themselves (chs. 24 and 29). Read alongside public governance documents, these episodes from the trilogy’s first volume raise a question that precedes the invasion: how does control over communication acquire the appearance of authority to represent everyone affected? I argue that first-contact governance must address both representative claims and the conditions for collective decision-making. Even a sender without authority can alter everyone else’s circumstances. Scrutiny of representative claims must therefore accompany procedures that preserve an opportunity for collective consideration before transmission changes the choices available.

Although Red Coast gives Ye the equipment to receive and answer signals, receiving a signal, authorizing transmission, choosing its content and claiming to speak for humanity remain distinct decisions. Scientific verification assesses a signal’s extraterrestrial origin, while an equipment license permits specified activities under the relevant rules. Neither determination alone establishes who may choose a reply or whose position the reply expresses. Even where one institution performs several functions, authority for one task does not automatically extend to the others. The distinction between privilege and legal power explains why. A privilege denotes the absence of a duty not to act in a particular legal relationship; a power is a legally recognized ability to alter legal relations. Equipment ownership, technical ability and permission to operate therefore cannot be treated as interchangeable with representative authority. A license concerned with technical compliance does not itself establish a mandate to make political commitments. Constitutional reasoning directs attention to the source, subject matter and limits of that authority: who conferred the power, what decision does it cover, and to whom must its exercise be explained?

Replacing an individual with a state does not settle the scope of representation. Under Principle 4 of the International Law Commission’s Guiding Principles Applicable to Unilateral Declarations of States Capable of Creating Legal Obligations (2006), a declaration binds a state only when a competent authority makes it. Principle 9 prevents one state’s declaration from imposing obligations on other states without their clear acceptance. These rules provide a structural comparison about authority among human actors; they do not determine the legal status of extraterrestrial communication. Authority to speak for one state cannot simply expand into authority to speak for humanity. The inquiry must identify who instructed the operator, what mandate the sending institution holds, and whom the final message represents. A signal’s physical reach answers none of those questions. Even a message addressed to the universe can express only a limited institutional position. Reaching a wider audience does not enlarge the constituency on whose behalf the sender is entitled to act.
articles.lede: When Ye Wenjie receives an extraterrestrial warning, she already has the means to answer. The warning tells her that replying will let the Trisolarans locate Earth and bring conquest, yet she responds.

articles.title: Fair Share Obligations in Climate Change Litigation: Towards a Global Carbon Approach?
Fair Share Obligations in Climate Change Litigation: Towards a Global Carbon Approach?
articles.description: In January of this year, the District Court of The Hague’s first-instance decision in Bonaire v The Netherlands found the Netherlands to be in violation of Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convent…
paragraphs: In January of this year, the District Court of The Hague’s first-instance decision in Bonaire v The Netherlands found the Netherlands to be in violation of Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention of Human Rights (“ECHR”) for failing to take sufficient climate mitigation and adaptation measures, resulting in discrimination towards the inhabitants of Bonaire.

Bonaire is among an increasing number of domestic court decisions that interpret human and constitutional rights in light of the international climate treaties to require each State to play their “part” or contribute their “fair share” in the mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions. Such language has its origins in the early Urgenda decision of 2019, which first put forward the concept of “partial responsibility” in the context of emission reductions: “each country is responsible for its part and can therefore be called to account in that respect” (para. 5.7.5). In adopting such logic, domestic courts globally reject the drop in the ocean argument in which individual responsibility for climate harm is diluted merely because emissions are cumulative in nature ( see decisions in Australia, Belgium, Germany, and Korea ).

While still under appeal, the District Court in Bonaire took this reasoning a step further. In its assessment of Article 8 of the ECHR, the District Court considered it a negative factor that the Netherlands had not quantified its emission allowance based on the remaining global carbon budget to limit global warming to 1.5°C (para. 11.15). In assessing whether the Netherlands had sufficiently played its part in emission reductions, it endorsed a global carbon budget approach.

This post draws attention to an increasing number of domestic courts that hold governments accountable for their failure to quantify their “fair share” of emissions in line with the global carbon budget. The first part defines the global carbon budget approach with reference to the reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (“IPCC”). The second unpacks the legal reasoning of recent domestic and regional court decisions that require States to determine their “fair share” on this basis. The third examines domestic courts’ engagement with the best available science to determine methodological considerations for calculating their “fair share” of emissions apportioned to the global carbon budget. It thereby points to an emerging practice of establishing responsibility for States’ due diligence obligations to reduce emissions commensurate with global mitigation efforts and fairness considerations, without necessarily evidencing a direct causal nexus with environmental harm.

The IPCC has estimated with a 50% probability that to keep greenhouse gas emission reductions in line with the 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, only 500 GtCO 2 remains available to be released into the atmosphere from 1 st January 2020 (p. 678). Under the global carbon budget approach, States collectively had a finite quantity of CO 2 in 2020 – exactly 500 GtCO 2 – that can be used in the transition to net-zero by 2050. Thus, for a State to contribute its “fair share”, it must carve out its share of remaining emissions from the global carbon budget consistently with its obligations under the international climate change regime, such as the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (“CBDR”) and set emission reduction targets accordingly.

articles.title: Mind the Gap: The Distance Between WHO Data and International Legal Standards
articles.description: Recent report concludes that WHO attack data cannot support the legal and comparative claims routinely built on top of it.
paragraphs: International lawyers, UN bodies, and human rights organizations increasingly cite one source when they discuss violence against health care in armed conflict: the World Health Organization’s Surveillance System on Attacks on Health Care (SSA). Since its launch in 2017, the SSA has become the default empirical basis for claims about the scale and pattern of harm caused to hospitals, clinics, medical transport, and health personnel in dozens of conflicts. The UN Office of the Special Representative for the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict draws on it. Special rapporteurs cite it. Advocacy organizations build their own datasets on top of it. It now shapes the narrative of accountability for alleged attacks on health care and forms the basis for misplaced arguments about culpability for them as breaches of international humanitarian standards.

We spent months reviewing the SSA’s methodology and publicly available data. Our conclusion—in a report recently published by The Hague Initiative for International Cooperation and the Henry Jackson Society—is that the system, as currently designed, cannot support the legal and comparative claims routinely built on top of it. This is not an argument against monitoring attacks on health care, which is an important and legitimate project. It is an argument that continuing to treat SSA figures as verified, comparable, or legally dispositive risks distorting the debate it’s meant to inform.

The SSA defines an “attack” as “any act of verbal or physical violence, threat of violence or other psychological violence, or obstruction that interferes with the availability, access and delivery of curative and/or preventive health services.” This is considerably broader than the operative legal definition of “attack” found in Additional Protocol I, Article 49, which requires an “act of violence against the adversary” connected to an armed conflict.

The over-extension matters. The SSA’s event taxonomy includes categories such as “psychological” violence (insults, intimidation, threats) and “obstruction,” which by the WHO’s own methodology can include a health worker being delayed at a security checkpoint, which is not an “act of violence.” It also includes arrests, detentions, and searches; categories of State and non-State conduct that international humanitarian law (IHL) does not automatically treat as unlawful, and that may in some circumstances be required by a party’s obligation to take precautions against the misuse of medical facilities. Some of this conduct is problematic, but labeling all of it “attack,” without further qualification, imports a legal conclusion the underlying facts don’t establish.

We also found, using conflict-onset data from the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, that 39% of logged SSA events in the occupied Palestinian territory occurred during periods that would not meet standard thresholds for active armed conflict, a precondition for the legal category of “attack” to apply at all. This suggests the SSA is, at least in part, capturing lower-level friction and violence. Such conduct is distinct from attacks governed by IHL.
articles.lede: Recent report concludes that WHO attack data cannot support the legal and comparative claims routinely built on top of it.

articles.title: 25ème session de l’Assemblée des États Parties au Statut de Rome de la Cour pénale internationale, du 30 novembre au 7 décembre 2026 (AEP25)
25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma de la Corte Penal Internacional
25th session of the ICC Assembly of States Parties, 30 November
25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma de la Corte Penal Internacional, del 30 de noviembre al 7 de diciembre de 2026 (AEP25)
articles.description: Share this page Twitter Twitter Twitter Mail EN
paragraphs: Del 30 de noviembre al 7 de diciembre de 2026, los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma se reunirán en La Haya con motivo de la 25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes de la Corte Penal Internacional (AEP25).

La Asamblea es el órgano de supervisión y legislativo de la Corte. Reunidos en sesión plenaria una vez al año, los Estados Partes adoptan decisiones fundamentales para el funcionamiento eficaz de la Corte y del sistema del Estatuto de Roma en su conjunto.

La AEP25 se celebra en un momento crítico para la justicia internacional. Ante la intensificación de los ataques contra la CPI, sus funcionarios, las organizaciones de la sociedad civil y otras personas y entidades que apoyan su mandato, la Asamblea brinda a los Estados Partes una oportunidad esencial para demostrar, mediante medidas concretas, su compromiso con una Corte independiente y eficaz y para proteger la integridad del sistema del Estatuto de Roma.

La sociedad civil estará presente durante toda la sesión para seguir los debates, dialogar con los Estados Partes y los funcionarios de la Corte y abogar por una CPI justa, eficaz e independiente, procurando al mismo tiempo que las perspectivas de las víctimas, las personas supervivientes y quienes defienden los derechos humanos sigan ocupando un lugar central en las deliberaciones sobre justicia y rendición de cuentas.

En su vigésima quinta sesión, la Asamblea de los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma (AEP) elegirá a seis jueces/juezas para cubrir un tercio de los 18 puestos de magistrado de la Corte Penal Internacional, conforme al ciclo electoral trienal ordinario. Cada uno/a de los/as seis jueces/juezaselegidos ejercerá un mandato de nueve años, de 2027 a 2036.

Las elecciones judiciales figuran entre las funciones de gobernanza más importantes de la Asamblea. La calidad, independencia y diversidad de los magistrados de la Corte inciden directamente en la credibilidad de la CPI, el desarrollo de su jurisprudencia y su desempeño operativo. El Estatuto de Roma establece un marco jurídico detallado destinado a garantizar que los magistrados sean seleccionados en función de sus méritos, integridad y representatividad, mientras que las resoluciones posteriores de la Asamblea han reforzado progresivamente las salvaguardias de transparencia y diligencia debida.

En vísperas de la AEP25, organizaciones de la sociedad civil y personas defensoras de los derechos humanos de todas las regiones comparten sus prioridades y recomendaciones para fortalecer la justicia a través de la CPI y del sistema del Estatuto de Roma.

Estas contribuciones son mucho más que declaraciones: reflejan las realidades vividas por quienes se encuentran en primera línea de los esfuerzos de rendición de cuentas. A lo largo de la AEP25, #NGOVoices seguirá dando visibilidad a estas perspectivas, para que las decisiones adoptadas en La Haya reflejen las necesidades y los conocimientos de quienes trabajan por la justicia en todo el mundo.
En los márgenes de la AEP25, la sociedad civil, los Estados, la Corte y otros actores organizan numerosos eventos paralelos.
articles.lede: Del 30 de noviembre al 7 de diciembre de 2026, los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma se reunirán en La Haya con motivo de la 25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes de la Corte Penal Internacional (AEP25).
