articles.title: Breaking the silence in Mexico’s barracks
articles.description: In Mexico’s armed forces, an order from a superior is meant to be obeyed without question. For many women in uniform, investigative journalist Zorayda Gallegos found, that can include an order to step into an officer’s bedroom.
paragraphs: “If an officer says, ‘Come into my bedroom,’ she must go in, otherwise she would be disobeying an order from her superior,” she told UN News.

Her investigation into sexual violence inside the military has won her the 2026 Breach/Valdez Award for Journalism and Human Rights. It has also made her a target, in one of the most dangerous countries in the world to be a reporter.
Her story, told ahead of the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes Against Journalists on Monday, shows both why a free press matters and how much it can cost.
Her report, Sexual violence in the barracks: an X-ray of impunity, tracked more than 520 women who reported sexual offences over a 12-year period.
Only three per cent of those cases ended in a conviction. The other 97 per cent led to no effective sanctions.
This is not an isolated problem, Ms. Gallegos says, but a structural one. It reaches beyond the barracks into military schools and hospitals.
She also documented how high-ranking officials cover up abuse, and how gender inequality and institutional obstacles discourage victims from filing complaints at all.

For Ms. Gallegos, part of the problem starts with military training itself, which she describes as “a very hierarchical, top-down system where women are always taught to follow orders from their superiors”.

Deep-rooted sexism makes things worse, she maintains, shaping who gets which jobs and who gets promoted. Female soldiers are often assigned tasks associated with “caregiving and nursing, even though they are qualified for higher-ranking positions,” she explains.
articles.lede: In Mexico’s armed forces, an order from a superior is meant to be obeyed without question. For many women in uniform, investigative journalist Zorayda Gallegos found, that can include an order to step into an officer’s bedroom.

articles.title: ‘They deserve to know the truth’: UN rights chief demands probe into staffer’s death in Houthi custody
articles.description: The UN human rights chief on Saturday demanded an independent investigation into the death of a Yemeni colleague held by the Houthis for more than two years, whose family learned of his death only weeks after it happened.
paragraphs: Mohammad el Shami, a staff member of the UN human rights office in Yemen, had been arbitrarily detained by the Houthi de facto authorities since 6 June 2024. His family say he died more than a month ago but were told only recently.

“ Mohammad’s family has not received any explanation of the cause or circumstances of his death – they deserve to know the truth ,” said High Commissioner Volker Türk, who described the loss as devastating.

In a statement issued late Saturday, the UN Secretary-General António Guterres added his wholesale condemnation of the death saying “the circumstances surrounding this appalling tragedy remain unclear.”

“Since his detention in June 2024, the Houthi de facto authorities have provided neither information about his well-being nor proof of life, despite repeated requests from the United Nations. The United Nations is urgently seeking answers from the de facto authorities about the circumstances of his death.

Mr. Türk called on the Houthis to disclose all relevant medical and detention records, preserve evidence and allow independent scrutiny of any stated cause of death. “ There must be accountability for wrongdoing ,” he said in a statement.

He said he was gravely concerned about the UN personnel still being held, including seven colleagues from his own office, as well as detained humanitarian and civil society workers. He again appealed for their immediate and unconditional release.
Mr. el Shami was reportedly detained during a wave of Houthi raids in June 2024 in which 13 UN staff were seized.
As of mid-October, the UN said 71 of its personnel were in Houthi detention. In June, the Secretary-General’s office said one UN colleague had already died in detention.
Briefing the Security Council on 9 October, UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg said many detainees had serious health problems, which made their release all the more urgent.
articles.lede: The UN human rights chief on Saturday demanded an independent investigation into the death of a Yemeni colleague held by the Houthis for more than two years, whose family learned of his death only weeks after it happened.

articles.title: DPR Korea: Isolation deepens even as the country changes, says UN rights official
articles.description: The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) is building factories and hospitals, rolling out smartphones and mobile banking, and passing new laws at an unprecedented rate. But its people are more cut off from the outside world than at any point in the country’s history.
paragraphs: That is the picture painted by James Heenan, head of the UN human rights office ( OHCHR) in the South Korean capital, Seoul. His team monitors the DPRK from beyond its borders because, as he puts it, “almost no one” can get in.

Speaking to UN News in New York, Mr. Heenan described a country where hunger remains a constant, forced labour touches every family and the border with China is so tightly sealed that even illegal crossings have all but stopped.
Yet he warned against seeing the DPRK – more commonly known as North Korea – as frozen in time. “The country is constantly changing, like every country in the world,” he said.

James Heenan: Well, it’s a tricky situation because we don’t have direct access to the country. Almost no one does at the moment. It’s very closed. In fact, historically, it’s never been more closed. We monitor, therefore, from outside.
We prioritise information from direct witnesses, so people who have suffered violations themselves, or who have witnessed them, or whose family members have suffered violations.

We also rely increasingly on Government information because the Government of the DPRK publishes more and more information, particularly over the past eight or nine years. We use other sources such as satellite imagery.

James Heenan: Well, we’ve interviewed about a thousand people. That might not sound like much when you’re coming from some other parts of the world, but when you are dealing with what is possibly the most closed country in the world, that’s quite a lot.
James Heenan: There are very few people coming in or out of the country. There is very little information coming in or out of the country. That has a pretty serious impact on people.
They do not have access to the internet. They don’t know what’s going on outside or even inside the country.
articles.lede: The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) is building factories and hospitals, rolling out smartphones and mobile banking, and passing new laws at an unprecedented rate.

articles.title: GC IV Commentary Series – Article 13: The Personal Field of Application of Part II
articles.description: Careful examination undermines Article 13 as a reliable guide to the scope of the Convention’s Part II safeguards.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The author of this post served on the Reading Committee of the updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention project. He provided feedback on early versions of the Commentary and co-authored, with a project team member, the Commentary’s sections on Articles 127 and 128. This post is based entirely on the author’s review of the final published version of the Commentary over which he had no editorial authority beyond the two sections he co-authored. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

Sitting atop Part II of the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 (GC IV), Article 13 appears as a chapeau provision, framing the thirteen articles of the Convention that follow. Both military legal doctrine and scholarship frequently cite it to identify the persons who benefit from the later protective provisions of Part II of the Convention (p. 219, n. 136).

Article 13 is also thought to highlight an important structural contrast between Part II and other parts of the Fourth Convention. Where Part III protections are restricted to a discrete class of persons who find themselves in specified circumstances, Part II is thought to apply far more widely, to “entire populations” (p. 4).

The characterization is understandable. The adopted title of Part II, “General Protection of Populations Against Certain Consequences of War,” certainly suggests as much. In this respect, academic literature frequently brands Part II as exceptional—a collection of safeguards benefitting all persons—and a departure from the Convention’s otherwise carefully parsed and tailored protections for civilians (p. 223-24; see also here, p. 302, fig. 8.3.1). States’ military legal manuals are widely in accord, instructing armed forces that GC IV Part II protections apply to the whole population of the belligerents’ territory (§ 10.3.3).

Such is the accepted wisdom, including that offered by much of the International Committee of the Red Cross’s (ICRC) updated Fourth Geneva Convention Commentary. However, careful examination undermines Article 13 as a reliable guide to the scope of the Convention’s Part II safeguards. In fact, as the Commentary itself briefly concedes, most Fourth Convention Part II protections apply only to select segments of the civilian population and in very specific circumstances, leaving Article 13 as, at best, an indicator of preliminary eligibility rather than of entitlement to protection.

This post explores the updated Commentary and other sources’ approach to Article 13 and identifies an opportunity to further clarify this deceptively unedifying article of the Fourth Geneva Convention.

The provisions of Part II cover the whole of the populations of the countries in conflict, without any adverse distinction based, in particular, on race, nationality, religion or political opinion, and are intended to alleviate the suffering caused by war.

If the purpose of the article is to lay out the scope of application of Part II protections, it does an especially poor job. The article’s opening clause is simply not correct. In fact, very few of the provisions of Part II apply to the whole population of any country in conflict. Nearly all are carefully tailored to quite specific groups of persons thought to be particularly vulnerable within those populations.
articles.lede: Careful examination undermines Article 13 as a reliable guide to the scope of the Convention’s Part II safeguards.

articles.title: World News in Brief: 300,000 displaced in Lebanon, Türk ‘deeply concerned’ over Novaya Gazeta closure, $50 million refugee appeal, World Cities Day
articles.description: More than 300,000 people displaced since early March remain internally displaced in Lebanon, where the humanitarian crisis is “far from over,” according to the UN’s aid coordination office (OCHA).
paragraphs: Despite civilians’ willingness to return home, continued Israeli military activity and presence in the south are making it very difficult, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told journalists on Friday.

This week alone, further demolitions, fires and strikes by Israeli forces were reported across Southern Lebanon, both within the so-called combat zone declared by Israel – from which residents were ordered to evacuate – and beyond it.

Although close to 970,000 people have returned to their communities in the south, their situation is often dire: homes have been damaged, while essential services are disrupted and making a living has become ever more challenging.
In Nabatieh Governorate, for example, insecurity and restrictions on access to agricultural land are disrupting the olive harvest there.
In some villages, farmers have been able to harvest for only two days before being forced by the Israeli army to stop doing so.

UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Friday he was deeply concerned and saddened by the announcement that Novaya Gazeta, a “highly respected” independent Russian newspaper, is being forced to close.
He called it “yet another devastating blow for remaining independent media in the Russian Federation”.
Independent journalism in Russia has faced mounting restrictions for many years, Mr. Türk said, but the pressure has intensified significantly since the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
That has come through increasingly restrictive legislation, tighter State controls and the harassment and persecution of journalists.
articles.lede: More than 300,000 people displaced since early March remain internally displaced in Lebanon, where the humanitarian crisis is “far from over,” according to the UN’s aid coordination office (OCHA).

articles.title: UN rights office warns of deepening displacement ‘nightmare’ in Gaza
articles.description: Israeli forces continue to push Palestinians into ever-smaller areas of the Gaza Strip while destroying civilian infrastructure and attacking displacement sites, the UN human rights office, OHCHR, warned on Friday amid concerns of ethnic cleansing.
paragraphs: OHCHR said that Israel has stated that it aims to increase the area of military deployment to 70 per cent of Gaza’s territory.
The relentless contraction of space has caused new displacement in areas adjacent to the “yellow line” demarcation boundary.

Over the past two weeks, OHCHR documented the westward expansion of Israeli military deployment areas in Al Shujaiyeh, Gaza City, and in three locations in Middle Gaza – eastern Al Bureij, eastern Deir Al-Balah and eastern Al Maghazi.
In Al Shujaiyeh, at least two Israeli attacks were reported on displacement camps, while forces reportedly used explosive robots to detonate the few buildings left standing in the area.

OHCHR said that it received reports that on 25 October, an Israeli drone dropped munitions on tents sheltering displaced families at Al Shujaiyeh junction near the yellow line and the resulting fire burned for five hours.
As a result, 200 families comprising 800 people – mostly women, children and older persons - were displaced, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Public Works and Housing.
“ The nightmare of displacement in Gaza is both acute and chronic ,” said Ajith Sunghay, Head of UN Human Rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT).

“Those displaced before the announcement of a ceasefire have little to no prospect of return to the areas they fled, most of which are inaccessible because they fall beyond the so-called yellow line. And they continue to be displaced again and again.”
OHCHR said that as an occupying power, Israel must cease the forcible transfer of Palestinians within the Gaza Strip, noting that this is a war crime that may also amount to a crime against humanity.
articles.lede: Israeli forces continue to push Palestinians into ever-smaller areas of the Gaza Strip while destroying civilian infrastructure and attacking displacement sites, the UN human rights office, OHCHR, warned on Friday amid…

articles.title: Myanmar’s illicit economy fuels escalating violence, with civilians bearing the brunt
articles.description: Myanmar’s human rights situation is “catastrophic”, the UN independent expert on the country warned at a press briefing Thursday, as the war spirals with no end in sight.
paragraphs: Myanmar has been engulfed in civil war since the military overthrew the democratically elected Government in February 2021, triggering widespread armed resistance across the country.
Special Rapporteur Kelley Anne Eckels-Currie’s new report found that at least 8,384 civilians have been killed by the military since the coup, up until 15 September 2026.
Special Rapporteurs are independent experts appointed by the UN Human Rights Council who serve in their individual capacity and receive no salary for their work.
Despite the regime launching a so-called “100-day peace plan” between 20 April and 31 July 2026, the situation in the country has only deteriorated, the independent expert found.

The military continues to use weapons of war – including airstrikes and artillery – to target and destroy civilian infrastructure, including schools, healthcare facilities, religious buildings, markets and displacement camps.

“These are not accidents… This is intentional infliction of harm on civilian populations for the purpose of terrorising them and trying to force them into submission ,” Ms Eckels-Currie told journalists.
Around 753 civilians were killed during the 100 day period, with the Myanmar military and paramilitary forces responsible for 89 per cent of civilian deaths.
The military’s strategy is rooted in the “Four Cuts” doctrine, the Special Rapporteur noted: sever food, resources, humanitarian access, and support networks from any area resisting the regime.

She found that the military deliberately obstructs humanitarian operations through telecommunications blackouts, movement restrictions and checkpoints, preventing the critical delivery of food, medicine, fuel and other essential supplies to displaced communities.
articles.lede: Myanmar’s human rights situation is “catastrophic”, the UN independent expert on the country warned at a press briefing Thursday, as the war spirals with no end in sight.

Contemporary accomplices? Considering the potential liability of AI targeting system providers under the Rome Statute
articles.description: Could AI targeting system providers face criminal liability for war crimes? Explore how the Rome Statute addresses corporate complicity in international crimes.
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled targeting systems are increasingly being used in armed conflicts to process data and provide lists of military objectives. This raises a difficult question that has received little attention: Could the senior executives of the technology companies that provide these systems face criminal liability under international law when their systems contribute to serious violations of international humanitarian law?

In this post, part of our Emerging Voices series, Rosa Villar Orero, PhD candidate at the University of Aberdeen, argues that Article 25(3)(d)(ii) of the Rome Statute, as operationalized through the Katanga test, offers a potential doctrinal avenue for establishing the criminal liability of AI targeting system providers whose contribution is made with knowledge of a group’s intention to commit such crimes.

In 1946, a British military tribunal convicted Bruno Tesch for complicity in the murder of millions of people at Auschwitz. Tesch was a businessman who ran Tesch & Stabenow, a company that supplied concentration camps with a poisonous gas called Zyklon B. Although h e never entered a camp and never issued an order to kill, merely sat in his office, processed contracts, and shipped chemicals, h e was nonetheless found liable. The reasoning was simple: Tesch had knowingly provided the means by which others committed mass atrocity. Physical proximity to the crime was not relevant; what mattered was the structural relationship between his conduct and the crime.

Nearly eighty years later, the question that emerges is: what would Tesch look like today? He would not be selling chemicals. Instead, would he be selling algorithms? As AI services are increasingly used by parties to armed conflict in the conduct of hostilities, it is time to take a fresh look at the precedent for holding companies that provide products and services to warring parties accountable for their contribution, in the case that those parties commit serious violations of international humanitarian law.

In contemporary armed conflicts, AI-enabled targeting systems are being deployed to process vast amounts of data to generate lists of military objectives. These systems dramatically increase the speed and scale of target production. They correlate data, find patterns, and recommend targets – in some reported cases, at a rate that human analysts could never match.

Behind these systems stand technology corporations. Their executives are not in the field or issuing strike orders. They are sitting in urban centers often far from the physical site of attacks, approving contracts. Yet, if these systems are deployed in the commission of war crimes at a large scale, the support those technologies provide becomes legally significant, bringing the following question:
Can the senior executives of technology companies whose AI systems contribute to the commission of war crimes be held criminally liable under the Rome Statute?

Technology corporations are primarily driven by the maximization of profits. Their AI systems are designed and sold as legitimate commercial products. Accordingly, proving that a CEO approved a contract with the purpose of facilitating a war crime is, in practice, evidentially difficult.
articles.lede: Could AI targeting system providers face criminal liability for war crimes? Explore how the Rome Statute addresses corporate complicity in international crimes.

articles.title: GC IV Commentary Series – Two Answers and Two Open Questions on Taxing Humanitarian Relief
articles.description: This post disentangles the legal elements that are relevant to taxation practices concerning humanitarian relief.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

In its framework governing occupation, international humanitarian law (IHL) details the regime governing the administration of property. Part of that regime contains IHL’s unique provision on taxing humanitarian aid. This norm, embedded in Article 61 of the Fourth Geneva Convention (GC IV), stipulates that the occupying power is obliged to lift “all charges, taxes, or customs duties” on relief consignments destined for occupied territory. The prohibition has only one exception: when collecting such duties would be in the interests of the economy of the occupied territory.

Drawing on this normative content, scholars have encouraged belligerents to adopt similar behaviour outside occupation contexts (p. 27). The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)’s 2025 Commentary equally highlights that, although Article 61’s call to exempt humanitarian relief from charges is addressed to the occupying power specifically, such exemptions should be adopted by all High Contracting Parties in peacetime. As a reflection of agreement among States that taxes and other charges on humanitarian aid need to be removed, the 2025 Commentary cites several UN General Assembly resolutions.

The exact normative content of Article 61 is not completely obvious. Therefore both the scope of occupying powers’ obligations and the behaviour toward which belligerents are otherwise encouraged was indiscernible. The 2025 Commentary provides welcome expansions in this regard.

The 2025 Commentary itself does not provide a roadmap for appraising whether an occupying power’s taxation of aid is compatible with its IHL obligations. Yet, by enunciating the links between Article 61 and other components of the law of occupation, the 2025 Commentary allows us to grasp the full framework governing the collection of such charges.

Article 61 is situated among the provisions that set out the occupying power’s obligations toward the population in occupied territory, norms governing permissible legislative changes, and requirements applicable to collecting money contributions more generally. These norms bring in a panoply of considerations that must be weighed in assessing the lawfulness of taxing humanitarian relief. They lead to the conclusion that the Article 61 exception does not give States a free hand in imposing financial duties on humanitarian aid.

This post disentangles the legal elements that are relevant to such taxation practices. It starts by addressing two questions on which the 2025 Commentary sheds light: what conditions must charges imposed on humanitarian aid meet? And is the occupying power allowed to introduce new taxes, or is its authority confined to already existing ones? I then zoom in on two issues that arise with contemporary conflicts, questioning how the normative content of the law of occupation should be interpreted.
articles.lede: This post disentangles the legal elements that are relevant to taxation practices concerning humanitarian relief.

articles.title: (Past) Debates on the Legal Nature of Belligerent Occupation
articles.description: The many theories on belligerent occupation that were raging at the beginning of the 20th century are little known.
paragraphs: The many theories on belligerent occupation that were raging at the beginning of the 20th century are little known, especially in the English-speaking world. This post will shed light on competing constructions of that time-honored notion, highlighting the breadth of competing conceptualizations. These issues are no longer hotly debated. Today, the legal regime of belligerent occupation is the object of doctrinal attention, much more than its fundamental legal construction. The same is true for the divide between fully-fledged occupation under the classical Hague rules, and fragmented, though contested, functional occupation under the newer Geneva rules.

It is useful, for the contemporary reader, to recall the categories of occupation recognized by classical law. There were four such types: (1) hostile occupation or belligerent occupation, be it as an incident of warfare or as a consequence of complete surrender or debellatio; (2) occupation of a neutral or allied territory, in large part covered by the law of belligerent occupation; (3) peacetime occupation, which is created by treaty, in situations such as grant, lease, military bases, etc.; (4) armistice or mixed occupation, where the law of belligerent occupation applies subject to modifications under the armistice agreement. The very concept of an “occupation” is to superpose or to articulate the actions of two States on a single territory.

Some brief historical references may be apposite. In the classical period of international law, beginning with Hugo Grotius, war was a means of acquiring territory and property. Thus, war constituted a title to property; conquest immediately displaced the title to sovereignty. Later, with Emer de Vattel, there was a shift towards a more modern conception. The title to territory was not the conquest as a military fact, but the title created after the war by a peace treaty or the debellatio. Possession must have been “assured” to operate a transfer of title. During the war, such possession could not be assured. It would be so only once the peace treaty (after the end of hostilities) finally consolidates the situation or the defeated State is entirely defeated.

From this doctrinal position, the law of belligerent occupation developed in the 19th century. It now perfectly fits the idea of nationalities and people’s self-determination, so strong in that century, that the territory does not pass to the conqueror as a mere fact of war, but rather needs a legal imprimatur, mainly by a treaty of peace. If sovereignty does not pass automatically with the fact of military control (conquest), room is opened for a regime of belligerent occupation as an interim situation between the status ante bellum and the status post bellum, with its treaty of peace, i.e., as in the case of war not transferring sovereignty to the occupant. This was the reason for the development of the law of belligerent occupation.

Let us now interrogate the legal writings of bygone times. How is the basis of belligerent occupation configured? We will mainly consider the “deviant” theories, not the mainstream one that has imposed itself and is well known today.
articles.lede: The many theories on belligerent occupation that were raging at the beginning of the 20th century are little known.

articles.title: GC IV Commentary Series – Brain Computer Interface-Assisted Interrogations and Articles 27, 31, & 32
articles.description: This post focuses on the potential use of BCIs in connection with interrogations of persons protected under GC IV.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

Any discussion of the treatment of new technology in the 2025 International Committee of the Red Cross GC IV Commentary must properly start with an acknowledgment of the huge scholarly endeavour that the text as a whole represents. The participants and editors are to be congratulated on bringing such an ambitious project as the preparation of new commentaries on all four Conventions to a successful conclusion. The sheer scale of the undertaking is little short of breathtaking.

It is also worth saying that it is the interpretation of treaties by the States that are party thereto that is of paramount importance. Commentaries such as these will of course be of the greatest assistance to States, but it will be how States apply these provisions to the new circumstances that novel and emerging technologies bring that will, in the end, determine how legal interpretations will evolve.

The Introduction points out that technologies, unknown in 1949 and at the time of the preparation of Pictet’s 1958 Commentary, have changed the nature of warfare and must of necessity affect our understanding and interpretation of the 1949 texts (paras. 77-82). Mike Schmitt in his valuable and highly authoritative Just Security observations has noted that “new technologies are subject to existing law of armed conflict rules,” that “hand in glove” application of existing rules to new technologies is sometimes precluded, and that in such cases interpretations must “not only be made in good faith and reflect the object and purpose of the rule in question, it must also pass the straight face test.” As an example, Article 107 deals with correspondence by internees in terms of letters and cards, and the Commentary proposes, uncontroversially it is suggested, that the detaining power should also consider more modern forms of communication, listing telephone calls, emails, video calls and recorded messages (para. 5240).

The discussion in this post will centre on a different kind of new technology, namely brain technology. The brain technology on which we will focus is brain-computer interfaces. Brain computer interfaces (BCIs) detect electrical brain activity, determine from it a functional intent, such as a wish to change, move, control or interact with an object, and can then translate that intent or wish into action. The technology, which has to date primarily been applied for medical purposes in the treatment of persons suffering e.g. from advanced paralysis, locked-in syndrome and Parkinsons Disease, has evident applications in warfare and the applicable law has been considered alongside other brain technologies by the author elsewhere. For present purposes the focus will be on the potential use of BCIs in connection with the questioning by the detaining power of persons protected under GC IV, as to which consider, for example, this and this.
articles.lede: This post focuses on the potential use of BCIs in connection with interrogations of persons protected under GC IV.

Transit States and Malicious Cyber Operations: No Due Diligence Obligation
articles.description: This post argues instead that no due diligence obligation exists under international law in respect of transit States.
paragraphs: The Tallinn Manual 2.0 advances the view that a transit State has a due diligence obligation to take feasible measures to terminate malicious cyber operations that may affect the rights of other States that it knows are transiting its territory or infrastructure under governmental control (rule 6, paras. 13-14 and rule 7). This post argues instead that no such obligation exists under international law in respect of transit States. There are considerable practical difficulties in implementing such an obligation which the Tallinn Manual acknowledges, but the objections explained in this post are principally legal and legal policy objections.

For the purposes of this post, transit States are those whose territory or infrastructure carries data packets from the State of origin to the destination State. This includes States hosting routing infrastructure, data centres, submarine or terrestrial cables, fibre-optic networks, and other communications infrastructure through which data transit.
Against this background, I now turn to my legal and legal policy objections to recognising a due diligence obligation for transit States.

First, international law does not recognise a general customary right of transit or a due diligence obligation in respect of transit States. Transit is instead regulated by specific treaty regimes and context-specific rules, rather than by a general principle of customary international law ( United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea ( LOSC) arts. 17– 26; art. 40 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, Paramilitary Activities 1986, paras. 154-160). In the absence of a specific customary rule governing transit, it cannot be argued that such a rule has simply been transposed into cyberspace on the basis that existing international law applies there.

Moreover, even assuming that a customary transit rule existed, it would not be readily transferable to cyberspace. Existing transit regimes concern the movement of persons or goods through physical means across geographically defined territory. Cyber operations, by contrast, involve the transmission of data packets through a decentralised network whose routing is determined by technical protocols rather than by territorial, legal or political considerations. The two situations are therefore materially different.

Third, the Tallinn Manual supports its position with regard to transit States by formulating due diligence in terms of the “use” of territory, which seems to be a broad concept. However, not every use, or any incidental territorial connection, is sufficient to trigger the due diligence obligation. There must be a deliberate and material use of territory that contributes substantially to the malicious cyber operation.

Also, due diligence presupposes a territorial or other nexus between a State and the source of the risk by virtue of which the State concerned is able to exercise meaningful control over the source of the risk and employ its authority and power to prevent or terminate harmful conduct. The mere fact that some element of an operation has a fleeting or incidental territorial connection with a State, as in the case of transit States, does not establish such a nexus coupled taking also into consideration the fact that the perpetrators of the operation remain located in another State and are subject to that State’s power and authority.
articles.lede: This post argues instead that no due diligence obligation exists under international law in respect of transit States.

articles.title: BELARUS: Swiss Court Convicts Former Security Officer of Enforced Disappearance
articles.description: In a historic first, a Swiss court convicts Yuri Harauski of enforced disappearance in Belarus under universal jurisdiction, overturning his 2023 acquittal.
paragraphs: (St. Gallen, Paris, Minsk, Geneva, 26 October 2026) – The Cantonal Court of St. Gallen has convicted former Special Rapid Response Unit (SOBR) member Yuri Harauski of the enforced disappearance of Anatoly Krasouski in Belarus in 1999, overturning his 2023 acquittal on appeal. The court also established his participation in the enforced disappearances of Yuri Zakharenka and Viktar Hanchar, but upheld Harauski’s acquittal for legal reasons. The court reduced Harauski’s sentence from eight to a two-year suspended prison term, considering his confession and public apology to the victims.

Following an appeal trial held on 22 September 2026, the Court found Yuri Harauski guilty of the enforced disappearance of well-known Belarusian businessman Anatoly Krasouski in 1999. The Court, however, upheld his acquittal in relation to the disappearances of Yury Zakharenka and Viktar Hanchar. The former member of the SOBR was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment, suspended.

Today’s conviction marks the first time a member of the Belarusian security apparatus has been convicted abroad for crimes committed as part of the repression under Aliaksandr Lukashenka’s regime and the first time anywhere in the world that a court ruled on crimes committed in Belarus under the principle of universal jurisdiction. The case was also the first in which the crime of enforced disappearance was examined before a Swiss court.

The conviction marks a significant step towards accountability for crimes committed under Aliaksandr Lukashenka’s regime and an important development in Switzerland and beyond. “ I feel relieved to have received the guilty verdict ”, said Valeriya Krasouskaya, daughter of Anatoly Krasousky. “ After 27 years, at least one of the numerous persons involved in the abduction and murder of my father is officially recognised guilty .”

TRIAL International, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and Human Rights Center Viasna, which initiated the proceedings together with relatives of two of the disappeared men in 2021, welcome the conviction as an important step towards accountability.

“ For years, impunity for crimes committed under Lukashenka’s regime has looked unassailable. This verdict proves it is not — investigators, prosecutors and courts now have a precedent showing that accountability for Belarusian state crimes is achievable ”, said Philip Grant, TRIAL International’s Executive Director.

The significance of the judgement may extend beyond Harauski’s own case: by establishing criminal responsibility for acts carried out by a member of the SOBR, it could contribute to broader efforts to examine the chain of responsibility behind the enforced disappearances, including the role of those who ordered or directed the crimes.

“ The conviction of Yuri Harauski for his involvement in the enforced disappearance of Anatoly Krasouski in Belarus is, first and foremost, a victory for his family, who have finally seen justice served after many years of efforts ”, said Alexis Deswaef, FIDH President. “ We are grateful to the Swiss justice system for demonstrating that this is possible by advancing international justice based on the principles of universal jurisdiction .”
articles.lede: In a historic first, a Swiss court convicts Yuri Harauski of enforced disappearance in Belarus under universal jurisdiction, overturning his 2023 acquittal.

articles.title: West Bank: Hebron crackdown displaces thousands, Türk warns of ethnic cleansing
articles.description: Israel’s “aggressive operation” in the West Bank city of Hebron raises serious concerns of ethnic cleansing, UN human rights chief Volker Türk warned on Monday, as the number of Palestinians forced from their homes passed 3,000 on the eve of Israeli elections.
paragraphs: The UN aid coordination office, OCHA, said aid partners are supporting local authorities in Hebron to meet the needs of more than 3,000 people evacuated by Israeli forces since Friday.
Mr. Türk said the operation had demolished homes and commercial property, and deprived residents of the ability to move freely.
The operation began after two Palestinian gunmen opened fire on an Israeli military checkpoint near Hebron on Friday, killing two soldiers and wounding three others. Both gunmen were killed.
“ The sweeping steps taken raise grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force – which must end ,” Mr. Türk said in a statement.
The Israeli lockdown is confining many people to their homes and immediate neighbourhoods, the UN rights chief said.
“Declarations by senior Israeli Government officials indicate that the measures implemented are punitive in nature and designed to instil fear. This is unacceptable,” he said.
He called for all those displaced to be allowed to return home, and for Israel to ensure compensation and reparation for unlawful evictions and demolitions, and the displacement they caused.
“ Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law ,” he warned. “Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing.”
OCHA said the UN and its partners are responding to new displacement in both Gaza and the West Bank.
articles.lede: Israel’s “aggressive operation” in the West Bank city of Hebron raises serious concerns of ethnic cleansing, UN human rights chief Volker Türk warned on Monday, as the number of Palestinians forced from their homes…

articles.title: Ukraine: Investigators find Russia committed war crimes by targeting civilians
articles.description: Top human rights experts investigating Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine said on Monday that the Russian authorities had committed war crimes and crimes against humanity by attacking civilians and vital energy infrastructure, among other violations of international law.
paragraphs: In its latest report, the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, noted that attacks on power plants have intensified “once again” across Ukraine, where temperatures plunged to -21°C last winter.

“ The scariest thing was to fall asleep and not to wake up; it was like torture to be scared of dying from cold ,” said one 53-year-old man cited in the report, which reiterated the war’s serious negative impact on older people, too.

“I lay cold and hungry, without medicine, without anything,” said a 74-year-old woman from Kyiv, who like many senior citizens is unable to use stairs and too afraid to use lifts, making it impossible to reach a safe place during air raid alerts.
“This means that they must remain in unheated dwellings without electricity or water, with no access to life support devices or essential services,” the report’s authors insisted.

Russian commanders ordering the attacks knew full well that the heating facilities they were targeting “were indispensable to the civilian population, particularly during the winter”, the report notes.

“Russian authorities have made official declarations concerning further attacks and referred to a plan to carry them out. The independent investigators concluded that they committed war crimes of intentionally directing attacks against civilian objects .”
The Commission was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in March 2022, shortly after Russian troops entered Ukrainian territory.

For its latest report, the three-person panel relied on the accounts of 255 persons who endured winter amid dire conditions in Dnipro, Kyiv, Kharkiv, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Poltava, Zaporizhzhia and Zhytomyr oblasts, as well as Ukrainian authorities, medical doctors and non-governmental organisations.

The Commission also examined attacks by Ukrainian armed forces on energy infrastructure in Russia and in occupied areas of Ukraine. But the panel’s investigators – Erik Møse, Pablo de Greiff and Vrinda Grover – were unable to investigate the impact of these strikes in Russia as the authorities did not allow access or respond to requests for information.
articles.lede: Top human rights experts investigating Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine said on Monday that the Russian authorities had committed war crimes and crimes against humanity by attacking civilians and vital energy…

GC IV Commentary Series – Allegiance and Protected Persons in Proxy Warfare
articles.description: This post examines how principles can assist in situations not specifically envisaged at the time of their adoption, such as IAC by proxy.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

As outlined in Dr. Anaïs Maroonian’s post, principles hold a unique position in international law, with various types fulfilling specific functions within the international legal framework. Yet all principles are distinguished from rules by their level of abstraction and are frequently operationalized through concrete norms. Despite the increasingly detailed nature of its rules, as far as international humanitarian law (IHL) is concerned principles are of paramount significance. This is particularly evident in the updated Commentary on Convention (IV) Relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War (GC IV), where, whether specific to IHL or not, principles preserve the object and purpose of GC IV, guide the understanding of certain norms, ensure that a rule is interpreted consistently and efficiently, and reinforce the general coherence of IHL.

When examining “how the updated Commentary refers to, gives expression to, and relies upon principles in interpreting GC IV,” Dr. Maroonian’s post explored how the two foundational principles of IHL—humanity and military necessity—and other principles such as the preservation of status quo ante are embodied in Articles 4, 27, 53 and 64 of GC IV. In particular, she suggested that recourse to the concept of allegiance when identifying protected persons under Article 4 is not only consistent with the object and the purpose of GC IV, as stated by the updated Commentary, but may also be understood as reflecting the interplay between humanity and military necessity.

Building on Dr. Maroonian’s analysis of principles in IHL and the updated Commentary’s revised approach, this post examines how principles of international law and IHL can assist in interpreting and applying existing rules to situations not specifically envisaged at the time of their adoption. Focusing on international armed conflicts (IAC) by proxy and on the use of allegiance theory to identify protected persons under Article 4 of GC IV, it outlines how the concrete application of these principles ensures that IHL remains effective.

The updated commentaries of the four Geneva Conventions have endorsed the Tadić theory (para. 137). Accordingly, when an organized armed group is under the overall control of another State, the group becomes subordinated and the equivalent of “agents” of that State. From the perspective of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), “this means that the intervening State becomes a Party to the existing conflict in lieu of the armed group [hereinafter proxy ] and that the conflict has become entirely international in nature” (para. 343). Resorting to overall control instead of the more stringent threshold of effective control might prevent the “intervening” State from hiding behind its proxy’s veil and evading its obligations under IHL (para. 343). Likewise, when that State “exercises overall control over de facto local authorities or other local organized groups that are themselves in effective control of all or part of a territory,” it becomes an occupying power, and the territory is considered to be placed under its “ indirect effective control” (paras. 400, 402).
articles.lede: This post examines how principles can assist in situations not specifically envisaged at the time of their adoption, such as IAC by proxy.

articles.title: West Bank: Guterres alarmed as Israel imposes sweeping closures after deadly Hebron attack
articles.description: The UN said on Friday it was “extremely alarmed” by intensifying violence in the occupied West Bank, as Israel moved to seal off the territory following a deadly attack on its soldiers in Hebron.
paragraphs: Two Israeli soldiers were killed and at least five injured when gunmen opened fire near a military checkpoint outside the city, according to news reports. The two Palestinian attackers were also killed.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered Hebron sealed, pledged house-to-house raids and home demolitions, and reportedly threatened a wider assault on a scale not seen since the Six-Day War. It is the fourth time in a month that Israel has imposed restrictions across the territory.

Speaking at the noon briefing in New York, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said Secretary-General António Guterres was deeply concerned by the closures and by reports of home demolitions and possible displacement in Hebron.
“ Those closures severely restrict Palestinians’ freedom of movement, access to basic services and livelihoods ,” he said.

Mr. Guterres condemned “the violence caused by record numbers of attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in 2026”, recalling Israel’s obligation as the occupying power “to protect the Palestinian population from such attacks and to hold perpetrators to account ”.

Mayy El Sheikh, spokesperson for the UN human rights office ( OHCHR) in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said the lockdown was “ yet another episode in a never-ending stream of suffocating measures making life more and more unbearable for Palestinians .”

“It follows a pattern of collective punishment whenever Palestinians commit acts of violence against Israeli settlers or soldiers,” she said, noting that similar incidents had previously brought lockdowns, intensified raids and arbitrary detentions.
Hebron’s entrances and exits were closed after Friday’s attack, she said, and the Ibrahimi Mosque was shut, leaving worshippers unable to perform Friday prayers.

“Israeli movement restrictions are already preventing thousands of Palestinian farmers from reaching their olives for the harvest,” Ms. El Sheikh said. “ This is bound to have devastating effects on the season .”
articles.lede: The UN said on Friday it was “extremely alarmed” by intensifying violence in the occupied West Bank, as Israel moved to seal off the territory following a deadly attack on its soldiers in Hebron.

European Parliament honours ICC with prestigious Sakharov Prize amid unprecedented threats to international justice
articles.description: 2026/10/22 European Parliament honours ICC with prestigious Sakharov Prize amid unprecedented threats to international justice Introductory text: The Coalition for the International Criminal Court (CICC) welcomes the European Parliament's decision to award its highest human rights award, the 2026 Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, to the International Criminal Court (ICC). At a time where the Court faces unprecedented attacks, this award sends a powerful message of support for the independence of international justice and the fight against impunity. Author: Coalition for the International
paragraphs: Established by the European Parliament in 1988, the Sakharov Prize is awarded annually to individuals and organisations who have made an exceptional contribution to the defence of human rights and fundamental freedoms. Past laureates include Kofi Annan and the staff of the United Nations, Dr Denis Mukwege, for his work with survivors of conflict-related sexual violence in the Democratic Republic of the Congo; Nadia Murad and Lamiya Aji Bashar, Yazidi survivors of ISIS atrocities whose advocacy has been central to efforts to secure accountability for genocide.

The Coalition for the ICC welcomes the award is an important recognition of the ICC’s role in promoting and protecting human rights and the rule of law around the world by working towards justice and redress for victims of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

The award comes against a backdrop of grave attacks against the Court’s independence and civil society organisations supporting its work, including escalating attacks by the United States (US) since February 2025, the impact of which is documented in the CICC Report ‘Criminalising Accountability'. In July 2026, the US announced a new campaign to “dismantle the ICC brick by brick”, culminating in the ICC being designated as an institution under US Executive Order 14203, on 9 October 2026. The CICC, together with hundreds of organisations and individuals, has called for States Parties to take a strong stand and concrete action to support the institution they created more than 30 years ago, and civil society organisations supporting its work.

“The support expressed by Members of the European Parliament for the ICC and its officials sends an important message in defence of the rule of law in the face of these unlawful attacks.” said Zoe Paris, CICC Advocacy Director. “It is extremely worrying that despite sanctions against the Court, the European Commission continues to delay the activation of the EU Blocking Statute. The rule of law, the protection of civic space and the ability to victims to access justice is at stake.”

The European Parliament highlights how “The blocking statute protects European operators, regardless of their size or sector of activity, by nullifying within the EU the effect of any foreign judicial decision based on foreign laws, also enabling them to seek compensation in court for damages caused by the extraterritorial application of foreign laws.”

Chloé Ridel, member of the EU Parliament who lead this campaign stresses that “This is historic! The European Parliament is sending a message of hope and resistance to Donald Trump: you sanction international justice, we honour it. Now, Europe has no choice: it must finally take action to protect the Court and activate the EU Blocking Statute.”

The European Union must now turn its commitment to international justice into concrete action, words of solidarity are no longer enough. Time is of essence, the European Commission must activate the EU Blocking Statute, Council Regulation (EC) No 2271/96, countering the risk that non-US service providers, including banks, may stop rendering their services to the ICC out of fear of penalties or reprisals from the US Treasury. Such action would send an unequivocal message that the EU will not stand by sanctions that undermine the independence and functioning of the Court and threaten the work and the very existence of civil society organisations. The EU must match its words with action and demonstrate that its commitment to accountability, the rule of law, and the preservation of civic space remains unwavering, particularly when the institutions upholding these principles are under attack.
articles.lede: Established by the European Parliament in 1988, the Sakharov Prize is awarded annually to individuals and organisations who have made an exceptional contribution to the defence of human rights and fundamental freedoms.

articles.title: World News in Brief: Russian attacks intensify, UN team tours West Bank, ‘unlawful’ elderly deaths
articles.description: Long-range Russian attacks across Ukraine are intensifying, including in Kyiv, causing at least 14 civilian deaths and 78 injuries overnight into Thursday, as UN agencies continue to provide aid.
paragraphs: Seven children were wounded in the strikes, which further damaged health and energy facilities, according to Ukrainian authorities and reports from Russian-occupied areas.
In Russian-occupied areas, reports also indicate that two civilians were killed and nine were injured in the Donetsk region.
Overnight attacks damaged energy infrastructure in Poltavska, Rivnenska and Volynska oblasts, disrupting the power supply, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Hostilities also caused power cuts in six frontline areas, while emergency power outages were also reported in Kyiv.
UN agencies continue to support communities in frontline areas of Ukraine, where reaching them is complicated or dangerous.

A UN Department of Safety and Security team delivered relief supplies on Wednesday to a community close to the contact line in the Zaporizhzhia region, where they described access as “severely constrained”.

Helping with winterisation efforts, the UN Children’s Fund ( UNICEF) reported this week that it has supported nearly 70,000 families living on the frontline with cash assistance, delivered in partnership with Ukrainian authorities.

Acting UN Humanitarian Coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory Ramiz Alakbarov and 13 UN Member State representatives have visited Jenin in the West Bank to learn about challenges surrounding the ongoing Palestinian olive harvest, displacement and recurrent Israeli settler attacks, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Thursday.

In the village of Arraba, the group heard from farmers who have been subjected to recurrent settler attacks while attempting to bring in the olive harvest – which combined with Israeli access restrictions, is undermining food security.
articles.lede: Long-range Russian attacks across Ukraine are intensifying, including in Kyiv, causing at least 14 civilian deaths and 78 injuries overnight into Thursday, as UN agencies continue to provide aid.

Yesterday’s children: now is the time to repatriate the children – and the young people who have “aged out” of childhood – in the camps and prisons of north-east Syria and Iraq
articles.description: They were children when it began. The ICRC calls for their return from Syria and Iraq, including young adults left behind.
paragraphs: Several years after the Islamic State group lost its last territory in March 2019, tens of thousands of Syrians, Iraqis, and third-country nationals from around 60 countries – including many children – remained in camps and prisons in north-east Syria and Iraq. In early 2026, almost 6,000 detainees were transferred to Iraq, among them children who were caught up in a war they did not choose. Repatriation remains the best way forward for most of the third-country nationals – but a deeply disturbing trend concerns the exclusion of young third-country nationals who “age out” of childhood from repatriation efforts.

In this post, ICRC Advisers Julia Joerin, Vanessa Murphy, and Katerina Kappos lay out why states should include young adults in repatriations as a standard practice, and call on states to reaffirm their commitment to resolving what continues to be one of the most complex and protracted child protection crises of our time.

Before the political shifts that took place in north-east Syria earlier this year, tens of thousands of Syrians, Iraqis and third-country nationals from around 60 countries were held in the region’s camps and places of detention, most of them arbitrarily, and a majority women and children. They have long been collectively perceived as affiliated with the Islamic State group, regardless of individual circumstances or their age. Over the last decade, the ICRC witnessed first-hand how these places became a microcosm of suffering and despair.

But then the situation in the camps and places of detention changed rapidly – including through the transfer of almost 6,000 detainees to Iraq. There is now a window of opportunity to act in the interests of the children and young people who have been too long forgotten.

Over recent years, several states assumed responsibility for their nationals in north-east Syria and in Iraq, bringing children home, reuniting families, and showing how this can be done humanely and safely. Around 3,400 third-country nationals (including many children) were repatriated by 58 countries of origin between 2019 and 2026.
But today, across Syria and Iraq an estimated 2,000 children of third-country nationality are still stranded, waiting to go back home with their families.

In addition, many children captured during 2017-2019 military operations have since turned 18, meaning they no longer fall under the legal definition of “child”. They are now “aged out” young adults, with little prospect to be repatriated with their families and a high risk of being left behind.

For several years, the ICRC conducted regular visits to the camps in north-east Syria, and operated a medical centre in Al-Hol camp together with the Syrian Arab Red Crescent. It was also often the only humanitarian actor able to access juvenile and adult places of detention, including “rehabilitation” centres, to monitor treatment and living conditions and to address some of the most pressing humanitarian needs. The ICRC’s visits offered detainees and people held in camps the possibility to exchange family news with their loved ones. The ICRC also notified states of the whereabouts of their nationals held in camps and places of detention, as per the wishes of the latter, who in most cases want to be repatriated to their country of origin.
articles.lede: They were children when it began. The ICRC calls for their return from Syria and Iraq, including young adults left behind.

articles.title: GC IV Commentary Series
articles.description: The updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 provides an opportunity to revisit the role of principles in IHL.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

Principles occupy a distinctive place in international law. They may constitute a source of legal obligations, express fundamental features of a legal system, underlie more specific rules, or guide their interpretation. Yet, the term “principle” also designates different legal phenomena whose nature, status, and functions should not be conflated. This is particularly relevant in international humanitarian law (IHL), where principles remain pervasive despite increasingly detailed conventional and customary rules.

The updated International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 (GC IV) provides an opportunity to revisit the role of principles in IHL. They appear throughout the updated Commentary’s interpretation of GC IV; some are expressly identified as such, while others underlie particular rules. They also operate at different degrees of generality, from principles underlying IHL as a whole to those specific to particular branches, notably the law of occupation.

This series contribution first distinguishes general principles of law, general principles of international law and general principles of IHL, before examining how the updated Commentary refers to, gives expression to, and relies upon principles in interpreting GC IV.

More generally, principles differ from specific rules in their degree of abstraction and mode of operation. While rules are ordinarily capable of more direct application, principles frequently require concretization through more specific norms.

Identification of general principles of law rests on a comparative process: different national legal orders are examined to determine whether they share a common legal principle. That process does not imply importing a particular domestic rule into international law; domestic rules are instead stripped of their specific technical or local features to identify the more general principle underlying them. A second step is then required. The principle must be capable of transposition to the international legal order.

This mechanism has traditionally been associated with the need to address gaps in international law and, in particular, to avoid situations of non liquet, in which a court would be unable to decide a dispute because no applicable rule of law could be identified. Indeed, the travaux leading to Article 38 of the ICJ Statute show that preventing non liquet was one of the purposes behind the inclusion of general principles, without granting the international judge a general power to legislate. General principles of law consequently perform a suppletive, rather than subsidiary, function. They may supply a legal solution where treaty and customary law leave a gap, but that does not translate to them occupying a hierarchically inferior position among the sources of international law.
articles.lede: The updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 provides an opportunity to revisit the role of principles in IHL.

articles.title: President Gatti Santana addresses United Nations General Assembly
articles.description: The President of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (Mechanism), Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, today presented the Mechanism’s fourteenth annual report to the United Nations General Assembly in New York. At the outset, President Gatti Santana wished His Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh every success in his role as President of the 81st session of the General Assembly, noting that his focus on peace and security, respect for international law, and commitment to multilateralism is essential in these times.
paragraphs: At the outset, President Gatti Santana wished His Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh every success in his role as President of the 81st session of the General Assembly, noting that his focus on peace and security, respect for international law, and commitment to multilateralism is essential in these times.

President Gatti Santana then referred to the award of the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay noting that she had served as the first woman Judge of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and its second President and had participated in landmark rulings that advanced accountability and justice for crimes that shock the conscience. President Gatti Santana highlighted that the justice cycle that commenced with those rulings is not complete, and that the Assembly’s support now at the end of the justice cycle is as important as the support provided to start it. She emphasized, in particular, the United Nations’ ongoing obligations to guarantee the fundamental rights of those convicted, as well as the judicial protection of thousands of victims and witnesses who courageously testified. She further stressed that the archives managed by the Mechanism are the property of the United Nations and require continued management for permanent preservation.

President Gatti Santana continued by assuring the Assembly that the responsible and appropriate conclusion of the Mechanism’s justice cycle is within reach. She referred, in particular, to the comprehensive strategic plan that the Mechanism presented to the Security Council in May 2026, which, building upon recommendations of the Secretary-General and the United Nations Office of Internal Oversight Services, provides a blueprint for the conclusion of all activities with clear implementation timelines. The plan specifically identifies which functions can end, which can be transferred, and those which must remain at the international level. In this regard, President Gatti Santana emphasised her unequivocal support for the Secretary-General’s recommendation that the authority over pardon, commutation of sentence and early release remain at the international level. She highlighted that retaining international jurisdiction on such matters safeguards the consistent application of the governing legal framework, legal certainty, and the involvement of judges familiar with the relevant cases, conflicts and sentencing practice.

However, as President Gatti Santana noted, the Mechanism requires a Security Council resolution to enact the radical transformation set out in the strategic plan. In the interim, the General Assembly has a critical role to play in ensuring that the United Nations’ investment in international criminal justice is not lost.

President Gatti Santana observed that the recent “hero’s funeral” that Mr. Ratko Mladić was accorded in Belgrade underscores the potential perils of faltering in this final phase of the justice cycle. She referred to the observations of a number of United Nations experts and special rapporteurs who warned that public actions that appear to honour individuals found responsible for atrocities “risk undermining decades of efforts to seek truth, end impunity and achieve justice and reparations for these crimes”, and that “[i]f such blatant genocide denial succeeds, it will roll back international criminal accountability gains against impunity that were forged in the fires of Nuremberg and Tokyo, and the International Criminal Tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda.”
articles.lede: The President of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (Mechanism), Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, today presented the Mechanism’s fourteenth annual report to the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

articles.title: Fate unknown of many returned to DPR Korea from China: UN independent experts
articles.description: Three years on from the reported resumption of large-scale forcible returns of nationals of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) from China, serious concerns persist about their fate, according to a group of Human Rights Council-appointed independent experts.
paragraphs: There is no information on the whereabouts and treatment of those repatriated – or those who remain at risk of return – the experts said in a press release on Wednesday.

“ These events form part of a longstanding pattern of serious human rights violations against individuals forcibly returned to the DPRK. In the absence of independent monitoring in either country, many returnees remain unaccounted for,” they said.

“For as long as their fate and whereabouts remain unknown, returnees are deprived of essential safeguards against enforced disappearance, arbitrary detention, execution, torture, forced labour, sexual and gender-based violence and other serious human rights violations,” the experts added.
Reports indicate that some women who left the DPRK – commonly known as North Korea – became victims of trafficking, forced marriage and sexual exploitation.
Among them is Kim Cheol-ok, who reportedly fled the DPRK during the 1990s famine and was trafficked into China as a child.
Despite living in China for about 25 years and establishing family ties, she reportedly faced harassment and restrictions due to her irregular status.
Detained by Chinese authorities in April 2023 without access to legal representation, she was forcibly returned in October 2023. Her fate and whereabouts remain unknown.
The Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found in 2024 that her detention by China and the DPRK was arbitrary.

Since 2023, reports have emerged of serious human rights violations against returnees, particularly those perceived as having sought asylum or who left the country without authorisation, raising concerns under the principle of non-refoulement.
articles.lede: Three years on from the reported resumption of large-scale forcible returns of nationals of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) from China, serious concerns persist about their fate, according to a group of…

articles.title: Summit in Samarkand, a boon for child wellbeing and health
articles.description: Representatives from across the international community are meeting in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, to ensure that children everywhere can thrive in a world marred by war, climate chaos and other fundamental challenges.
paragraphs: The UN-backed World Summit on Investing in Children’s Wellbeing opened on Wednesday, bringing together more than 600 participants from over 100 countries.
A child’s wellbeing depends on many factors, including health, access to education, protection from violence, family support and access to help when they need it.
In a message t o the summit, UN Secretary-General António Guterres stressed that “ when we invest in children, we invest in the future ”.
The Secretary-General’s message was read at the opening by Sabine Mahl, the UN Resident Coordinator in Uzbekistan.

Mr. Guterres warned that progress on child wellbeing is under threat. Conflicts, economic pressures, health emergencies, poverty and climate-related shocks put children at risk, particularly those from vulnerable groups.

He also noted that humanitarian and development assistance is declining, while developing countries continue to carry heavy debt burdens, which is why the summit is focusing not on a single programme or service, but on systems that need to work together.

Addressing the summit, Khalilur Rahman, the President of the UN General Assembly, called for a sharper focus on turning commitments to children into tangible results, declaring that “a target matters when a child eats, learns, receives treatment and returns home safely.” With only 36 per cent of assessable Sustainable Development Goal (SDGs) targets on track or making moderate progress, he urged countries to accelerate collective action rather than lower their ambitions.

He set out four priorities: put children before process; build services and social protection around their needs; reach those furthest behind; and match political promises with financing, responsibility and deadlines. He also called for child-centred approaches to artificial intelligence and other technologies, saying digital transformation should expand opportunity while protecting children from exploitation, discrimination, manipulation and privacy violations.

The Assembly President argued that governments should judge progress not simply by improving averages but by closing gaps for children most at risk, including those living in poverty, with disabilities, on the move or affected by conflict and climate shocks. And he challenged governments to make their commitments visible in their budgets: “ A declaration cannot vaccinate a child. A promise itself cannot pay a teacher. Applause itself cannot purchase cancer medicines .”
articles.lede: Representatives from across the international community are meeting in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, to ensure that children everywhere can thrive in a world marred by war, climate chaos and other fundamental challenges.

articles.title: PSYOP Defection Messages, Amnesty, and the Law of Armed Conflict
articles.description: PSYOPS inviting enemy personnel to defect / surrender can save lives on both sides of a conflict and weaken an armed group without an attack.
paragraphs: Calls to defect can save lives. When they promise amnesty, legal review must extend from the words broadcast to the authority behind them and the institutions expected to perform them.

This post explores recent practice with calls for enemy defection, particularly as part of psychological operations during non-international armed conflict, and briefly surveys applicable legal limits.

Psychological operations that invite enemy personnel to defect or surrender can save lives on both sides of a conflict and weaken an armed group without an attack. In December 2025, U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth directed the Department of War to redesignate “Military Information Support Operations” (MISO) with the older term “Psychological Operations” (PSYOP). The change, which the U.S. armed forces must implement by the end of 2026, revives a longstanding argument about terminology. But a message saying, in substance, “leave and you will not be prosecuted” does more than influence. It communicates a legal assurance requiring prior agreement across the military, diplomatic, and legal institutions expected to perform it.

Commanders and their legal advisers should therefore review such operations as a linked sequence of message, promise, and performance. The message must be lawful; the promisor must have the necessary authority to make the promise; and the institutions receiving, screening, and prosecuting defectors must be able to deliver the assurance under domestic law and applicable international obligations. Otherwise, a tactically successful appeal may mislead its audience, compromise accountability, and make later surrender appeals less credible.

Operation Observant Compass, which ran from 2011 to 2017, highlights the attraction of the technique. U.S. personnel supported African forces, UN personnel, civilian organizations, and communities seeking to weaken Joseph Kony’s Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA) through defection. One broadcast began with the assurance that those who left would not face prosecution. The operational premise was that Uganda had to offer amnesty, defectors had to receive fair treatment, and the messages had to ring true.

The first MISO Support Element–Uganda worked with U.S. agencies, local forces, UN personnel, and NGOs to extend radio coverage, record “come home” messages, distribute leaflets, and connect defectors with designated reporting sites. Later rotations added aerial loudspeakers and messages tailored to specific fighters, including recordings by family members. Reporting sites were managed by local forces or MONUSCO (The UN Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo), while civilians ran community defection centres. These collective efforts invited LRA members to leave a coercive armed group, expose themselves, surrender their weapons, and trust a network of institutions that no single communicator controlled.

Such a chain presents a legal problem. A message may be disseminated by actors who do not control the law later applied. It may also be heard and acted upon by people suspected of atrocities, wanted by another State, or subject to the jurisdiction of an international court.
articles.lede: PSYOPS inviting enemy personnel to defect / surrender can save lives on both sides of a conflict and weaken an armed group without an attack.

articles.title: Bangladesh: UNICEF chief calls for an end to child marriage
articles.description: At 14, Bushra faced being married off – until community leaders at a UNICEF-supported child protection hub worked with her father to prevent her from being given away against her will.
paragraphs: Her story was one of many heard by the UN children’s agency Executive Director Catherine Russell who on Tuesday called for urgent investment in Bangladesh’s children following a three-day visit to the country.

Ms. Russell urged action on three fronts: ending child marriage and keeping girls in school, delivering on the Government’s commitment to invest five per cent of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) in both education and health, and protecting quality learning for Rohingya refugee and host-community children.
“Keeping girls in school and providing them with the health, education and protection services they need will deliver a brighter future for them, for their communities, and for Bangladesh,” she said.
In Korail, Dhaka’s largest informal settlement, Ms. Russell heard from children and parents how poverty, disrupted education and limited basic services have impacted their lives.
Adolescent girls shared their ambitions and the pressures that can force them out of school and into marriage.
Nearly half – 47.2 per cent – of women in Bangladesh aged 20 to 24 were married before the age of 18, according to the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025.

Child marriage drives girls out of school, fuels early pregnancy and narrows lifelong opportunities. UNICEF is calling for girls to complete secondary school and for loopholes in national law that permit child marriage to be closed.

Meeting senior officials, including State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam, Ms. Russell welcomed the Government’s commitment to increase spending on education and health, while stressing the importance of turning promises into action.
“Budgets reflect priorities,” she said. “ Investing in children’s quality education, health, nutrition and protection is investing in Bangladesh’s future .”
