articles.lede: At 14, Bushra faced being married off – until community leaders at a UNICEF-supported child protection hub worked with her father to prevent her from being given away against her will.

articles.title: Yemen war continues to force families from homes amid hunger and disease
articles.description: More than 250,000 people have now fled renewed fighting in Yemen, the UN said on Tuesday, citing particular concern for those sheltering in the southwestern city of Taiz and the wider governorate, where access is “essentially blocked”.
paragraphs: “The Houthis’ closure of the only supply route linking Taiz to Aden is placing civilians at grave risk, blocking humanitarian aid and cutting off essential supplies,” said UN human rights chief Volker Türk.

In an appeal to Houthi fighters who he said had encircled Taiz City to allow aid in immediately, the High Commissioner for Human Rights noted that 32 civilians have been confirmed killed across the governorate, including 14 children and nine women. He warned of a significant uptick in the risk of death and injury as fighting moves closer to densely populated areas of the city.

The development follows the resumption last month of clashes between Houthi fighters – formally known as Ansar Allah – and the internationally recognized Government based in Aden, ending the relative calm brought about by the 2022 truce.
The situation in Taiz is particularly worrying because around half of those recently uprooted by the violence have sought shelter there.
“ Taiz is certainly the number one concern at the moment in an ocean of concerns ,” said Akhil Iyer, United Nations Children’s Fund ( UNICEF) Representative in Yemen.

“Many people have fled repeatedly. They are arriving in already overcrowded camps or communities with little or no food. Clean water is almost non-existent when they arrive. They’ve literally arrived with just the clothes on their backs, and they have almost nothing left to sustain themselves .”
According to the UN World Food Programme ( WFP ), wheat flour stocks in affected areas of Taiz are nearly exhausted.

“This is an alarming development in a governorate that already faces some of Yemen’s highest levels of food insecurity,” with 10 out of 16 districts already classified at emergency levels, Mr. Iyer stressed.

Briefing journalists from Aden, the UNICEF official described the deteriorating situation in conflict-affected areas, where “garbage is piling up – particularly in Taiz city – as sanitation services come to a halt”.
articles.lede: More than 250,000 people have now fled renewed fighting in Yemen, the UN said on Tuesday, citing particular concern for those sheltering in the southwestern city of Taiz and the wider governorate, where access is…

articles.title: As Sudan war spills into Central African Republic, UN warns against early peacekeeper exit
articles.description: The UN warned on Tuesday against a premature withdrawal of its peacekeepers as the war in Sudan spills over into the Central African Republic (CAR).
paragraphs: CAR continues to face a resurgence of deadly violence in the east despite the disarmament of nearly 2,000 fighters and the gradual completion of the latest electoral cycle, the Security Council heard.

Illustrating the current fragility, the top UN official in the country, Valentine Rugwabiza, highlighted an attack on 30 June by different armed groups on Am-Dafock, bordering Sudan, which killed civilians, members of national security forces, displaced 17,000 civilians and injured six UN peacekeepers.

However, without peacekeeping mission MINUSCA’s rapid response, she said, attacks in the border area with Chad and Sudan would have resulted in significantly more fatalities and State authority could not have been restored after only five days of control by the armed group, whose fighters retreated across the border into Sudan.

“In this regard, I plead with the council, as it prepares to renew MINUSCA’s mandate, to maintain MINUSCA with adequate force levels and capabilities during the critical consolidation phase ,” she stressed.

While Bangui consolidates its authority and continues disarming rebel groups, violence is multiplying in the east, driven in part by the war in Sudan that is complicating plans for a gradual MINUSCA troop drawdown, Ms. Rugwabiza said.

The situation in the northeast and southeast remained particularly worrying, notably around mining sites and along the corridors traditionally used by pastoral farmers – often the source of community tensions.

In the southeast, 26 serious incidents were recorded, attributed to suspected members of the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA – a long-established armed group of Ugandan origin – between June and September.
They included reports of rapes and sexual slavery and the abduction of 68 civilians, around 40 of them children.
At the same time, the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) militia continues to threaten local populations.
articles.lede: The UN warned on Tuesday against a premature withdrawal of its peacekeepers as the war in Sudan spills over into the Central African Republic (CAR).

articles.title: Coalition for the ICC calls for the immediate activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the ICC from US Sanctions
articles.description: 2026/10/20 Coalition for the ICC calls for the immediate activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the ICC from US Sanctions Introductory text: In an Open Letter to the European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the Coalition for the ICC calls for the immediate activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the ICC from US Sanctions
paragraphs: On 9 October 2026, the United States (US) have imposed unprecedented sanctions on the ICC as an institution, marking the gravest escalation to date in its concerted efforts to "dismantle" the Court. These measures constitute the most serious attack the international justice system has faced in the past decades. By attacking the Court, the US is directly undermining the ability of victims and survivors of international crimes around the world to seek justice and hold perpetrators to account. At stake is the preservation of the rules-based multilateral order, the independence of justice, European civic space, including the ability of civil society organisations to support the work of the Court without fear of retaliation, and the sovereignty of the 125 States Parties to the Rome Statute.

The Coalition has already witnessed how sanctions risk undermining the ability of civil society organisations to continue cooperating with the Court across all situations, including by filing briefs, providing evidence, legally representing victims, attending meetings, conducting advocacy, or funding projects, for fear of retaliation by the United States, including through the imposition of secondary sanctions.

Without the immediate activation of the EU Blocking Statute Council Regulation ((EC) No 2271/96), the EU risks enabling the continued shrinking of European civic space and undermining freedom of speech, affecting accountability efforts on all ICC investigations and cases. Executive Order 14203 prohibits US persons from providing material support or services to designated persons and entities, including financial services, and exposes non-US persons to the risk of secondary sanctions for engaging in conduct prohibited under the Executive Order.

While we acknowledge that the institutional sanctions against the Court are subject to a six-month wind-down period and that exemptions apply to certain services, this period should be used to protect the Court, its operations and those cooperating with it, including by immediately activating the EU Blocking Statute, and not become a justification for further inaction. Without this immediate step, the EU risks allowing unlawful foreign sanctions to dictate the boundaries of European civic space, chilling freedom of speech and undermining democratic freedoms and the rule of law in Europe.

The designation of the ICC as an institution creates significant risks for European natural and legal persons, including banks, financial institutions, technology companies and insurers, that provide services to or transact with the Court, as well as to civil society organisations and individuals working or cooperating with the Court, including risks of secondary sanctions, penalties and other forms of retaliation. Given the global reliance on the US financial and IT systems, even non-US service providers, including banks, may stop rendering their services to the ICC out of fear of penalties or reprisals from the US Treasury, including during the wind-down period.
articles.lede: On 9 October 2026, the United States (US) have imposed unprecedented sanctions on the ICC as an institution, marking the gravest escalation to date in its concerted efforts to "dismantle" the Court.

articles.title: Hollow Control: Cyber Compromise and Human Judgment in Lethal Autonomous Weapons
articles.description: The danger that cyber compromises pose to LAWS is that operators can make the right decision based on false information.
paragraphs: The danger that cyber compromises pose to lethal autonomous weapons (LAWS) is that operators can make the right decision based on false information. Humans may remain in command while the information that makes that command meaningful has been corrupted. Our first post argued that human control of LAWS is only as good as the picture and the abort path upon which it depends. This post accepts this difficulty as a given and narrows the question. The law of targeting does not change based upon the label affixed to the role of humans in the process. Policy does.

Soon after it first appeared in 2013, meaningful human control (MHC) quickly established itself as the language of the international debate, but is not yet a codified concept of the law of armed conflict. Meanwhile, the United States has been employing an alternative formulation: appropriate human judgment (AHJ) over the use of force.

Although both are highly useful concepts, by itself neither resolves how responsibility should be allocated when an attack was unlawful because the factual picture was false. In other words, neither is better than the integrity they presume.

As with most things that acquire a technological gloss in warfare, the law is stubbornly unchanged by the threat posed by cyber operations even though they began attracting legal attention in the late 1990s. The law still asks whether the person who planned or decided on the attack directed fire at a military objective and took feasible precautions. If the information that informs that decision was manipulated, two things are compromised at once: the quality of the decision; and the record that will later show why the attack was thought lawful. Cyber manipulation can thus do double damage as it can corrupt the decision before the weapon is released and the evidentiary record after the fact.

To be clear, the problem does not revolve around the somewhat abstract question of whether a commander can have a perfectly accurate picture. Wartime information has always been uncertain. For as long as commanders have received reports, they have had to test them against one another— in Vegetius’s words, “ to come at the truth with certainty .” The issue, then, is not whether a commander can have a perfectly accurate picture but whether a commander can reasonably assess the integrity of the information on which the legal judgment depends. Wartime uncertainty is unavoidable, but uncertainty about whether the information itself can be trusted is a different problem. This is markedly different from the all too familiar issue of erroneous intelligence or outright incompetence. The difference is that an adversary can manipulate the information environment and leave the system looking as if it remains under authorized human control while corrupting the information on which that control depends.

Should this happen, the chain of legal responsibility for an unlawful attack is a relatively long one, as it can be distributed and, potentially, diluted among multiple entities including the operator, the commander, the developer, and the acquiring State. In such a scenario, the operator almost certainly believed the information on their screens to be correct. The commander may have followed the established review process. The designer may point to tests that demonstrated the system’s envelope. The acquiring State may also assert that its legal review did not contemplate this particular compromise.
articles.lede: The danger that cyber compromises pose to LAWS is that operators can make the right decision based on false information.

articles.title: Hunger is ‘an avoidable tragedy’ in a world of plenty: Türk
articles.description: More than a quarter of humanity struggles to get enough food, even though the world produces enough for everyone, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Monday, blaming injustice and the denial of human rights for hunger in a world of plenty.
paragraphs: Addressing the UN-hosted Committee on World Food Security in Rome, the High Commissioner said that while the right to food has found its way into treaties and laws, “ for too many people, it has yet to find its way onto their dinner plates ”.
Global food supply now exceeds 3,000 calories per person per day – a historic high – yet hunger reduction has not kept pace.
“ Too much of that abundance is swallowed up by injustice and the denial of human rights ,” Mr. Türk said.
Just one per cent of the world’s farms operate more than 70 per cent of global farmland, while women farmers and Indigenous Peoples often lack government support and access to land.

Conflict is also driving acute hunger in 12 of the 13 current hunger hotspots, the High Commissioner said, with restrictions on humanitarian aid and attacks on aid workers “cutting off the last lifelines”.

He called for a human rights economy built on social protection, fair taxation and agricultural policies that reduce poverty, as well as equitable access to land, water and seeds, and meaningful climate action.
“We must do our utmost to ensure the rules of war are upheld and hunger is never used as a method of warfare,” he said.

Addressing the Committee for the first time as the independent expert on the right food, UN Special Rapporteur Sofía Monsalve Suárez said the issue that concerned her most was the rapid increase in famine and the use of starvation as a weapon of wa r.
While chronic hunger declined in 2025, acute hunger has been rising steadily since 2016, she said.
articles.lede: More than a quarter of humanity struggles to get enough food, even though the world produces enough for everyone, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Monday, blaming injustice and the denial of human rights for…

articles.title: GC IV Commentary Series – Reprisals in NIACs: What Is the Commentary’s Take?
articles.description: The Commentary implicitly concludes that if reprisals were to exist in NIACs, they would need to be available to States and armed groups.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

In its last section addressing Common Article 3, the 2025 Commentary of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) on the Fourth Geneva Convention (GC IV) addresses a matter on which the treaty text is silent: the legality of belligerent reprisals in non-international armed conflicts (NIACs). It provides a two-layered explanation. First, belligerent reprisals in NIACs do not exist. Second, even if they were to exist, belligerent reprisals in NIACs are prohibited, and this prohibition is contained in the article itself.

The Commentary’s take that the concept of belligerent reprisals does not extend to NIACs is grounded in: 1) the lack of State practice confirming an entitlement to resort to reprisals in NIACs; and 2) an explanation as to the low likelihood that States would have left open the possibility of reprisals in NIACs. With this second component, the Commentary implicitly clarifies that there is no space to discuss an imbalanced right to belligerent reprisals. The Commentary elaborates on belligerent reprisals as a tool potentially open to “belligerent Parties” (plural); and speaks of the implications of having international law permit armed groups’ resort to belligerent reprisals. Both elements indicate that the Commentary rejects the in-between understanding whereby belligerent reprisals in NIACs could be lawful but reserved for States.

In fact, the Commentary relies on Professors Milanović and Hadži-Vidanović (p. 16), for whom belligerent equality seems to be essential for rejecting the permissibility of belligerent reprisals in NIACs. This was the view of Cameroon and Nigeria ahead of the Additional Protocol II (AP II) negotiations (as accounted for by Bílková, p. 46); and can be read from certain scholars ( Newton, p. 378). By explaining that the chances of having States leave room for armed groups to carry out reprisals are close to zero, the Commentary implicitly concludes that if reprisals were to exist in NIACs, they would need to be available to both States and armed groups.

The Commentary moves on to emphasise that, even in the event reprisals in NIACs are “a tool open to the belligerent Parties,” they would be prohibited in every case where the underlying conduct contravenes common Article 3. This stance, grounded in the absolute nature of common Article 3, from which no exceptions were allowed, was already put forward in the Pictet Commentary, had already met criticism, and is not expanded further here (see, for instance, Bílková, p. 55; De Hemptinne, p. 589; Darcy, p. 148). The Commentary thus argues that acts prohibited by common Article 3 equally cannot be committed by way of reprisals.

According to the Commentary, common Article 3 implies that belligerent reprisals consisting of violations thereof are prohibited. At first glance, what broader differences can be spotted between this NIAC norm and the IAC prohibitions of reprisals?
articles.lede: The Commentary implicitly concludes that if reprisals were to exist in NIACs, they would need to be available to States and armed groups.

articles.title: Ukraine: Civilian casualty rates among ‘deadliest’ in years, as energy attacks intensify
articles.description: Civilian casualties in Ukraine remain at record levels, with intensified Russian attacks in September continuing a pattern of harm in 2026 far exceeding previous years, UN human rights monitors in Ukraine said on Friday.
paragraphs: The mission verified that at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in September – 85 per cent more than in September 2025.

Casualties were recorded across 22 regions and the city of Kyiv, where civilians were killed or injured on 22 of the month’s 30 days, more often than in any month since the start of the Russian Federation’s full-scale invasion.
The trend continued into October. On the night of 6 to 7 October alone, a Russian cruise missile and drone attack killed 22 civilians and injured 45 in Pryluky, in Chernihiv region.
“ The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years ,” said Danielle Bell, head of the human rights monitoring mission.
The high casualties came as Russian armed forces resumed systematic attacks on energy infrastructure.

On 13 and 14 October, strikes hit multiple energy facilities, including Kyiv’s three main power stations, temporarily leaving 600,000 people in the capital without electricity, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Ukrainian armed forces also targeted electricity and heating infrastructure in occupied territory and in the Russian Federation, the mission said.
“Systematically attacking electricity and heating infrastructure as winter approaches is bound to inflict significant suffering on the civilian population ,” Ms. Bell warned.
Damaged homes and attacks on energy also risk forcing Ukrainians who have returned home to flee again this winter, the International Organisation for Migration ( IOM) warned.
articles.lede: Civilian casualties in Ukraine remain at record levels, with intensified Russian attacks in September continuing a pattern of harm in 2026 far exceeding previous years, UN human rights monitors in Ukraine said on Friday.

articles.title: Call for tenders – Consultancy services to produce a briefing paper on the law and practice of universal jurisdiction in South Africa
articles.description: Call for tenders - Consultancy services to produce a briefing paper on the law and practice of universal jurisdiction in South Africa
paragraphs: TRIAL International is a non-governmental organisation that fights impunity for international crimes and supports victims in their pursuit of justice.

To support its activities, the organisation is seeking a consultant to collect information, analyse and draft, in English, a briefing paper on the law and practice of universal jurisdiction in South Africa. This briefing paper will be part of the Universal Jurisdiction Law and Practice Briefing Papers series, already comprising of 12 reports comparing the legal systems of Argentina, Belgium, Canada, England and Wales, Finland, France, Germany, Norway, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland and the United States. (a 13th, on Senegal, will be launched on 18 November 2026)

Participation in this call for tenders is open to all qualified candidates, whether natural or legal persons, regardless of nationality or place of residence. However, all candidates must meet the criteria that can be found in the full call for tenders.
For the submission requirements and selection criteria, please see the full call for tenders.
articles.lede: TRIAL International is a non-governmental organisation that fights impunity for international crimes and supports victims in their pursuit of justice.

articles.title: Military Microreactors and the Law of Targeting
articles.description: Nuclear powered microreactors may serve operational interests. However, their military usefulness does not eliminate their legal sensitivity.
paragraphs: A future military base may not only rely on diesel generators, vulnerable grids, and exposed fuel convoys for energy. It may instead be powered by a small nuclear reactor integrated into AI-enabled command nodes, electronic warfare systems, air-defense radars, counter-drone networks, and directed-energy weapons. For the law of targeting, this integration creates complexity. It also reflects broader trends towards increasingly power intensive warfare and greater vulnerability of military energy supply lines.

The United States has already moved in this direction. Project Pele seeks to design a transportable microreactor capable of providing one to five megawatts of electric power for military use. The Janus program points in a related direction by seeking secure and resilient energy for defense installations, critical infrastructure, and vital missions. Other States are exploring similar possibilities. Canada has supported research into whether microreactors could provide reliable power for remote northern defense infrastructure, while Russia is developing small modular reactors in strategically sensitive Arctic regions, where energy infrastructure, remote settlement, resource extraction, and military infrastructure often overlap.

These developments raise difficult legal questions. If a military facility is supported by the nuclear microreactor, should it be treated as an ordinary military objective, a protected nuclear installation, or a military objective with nuclear-specific targeting risk? The answer is not that every reactor-powered site becomes immune from attack. Nor is it that the presence of a military objective turns the entire nuclear-powered complex into an ordinary, lawful target. The better answer is to treat such sites as nuclear-significant military complexes containing potentially distinct military objectives, rather than a single target. Such treatment requires commanders to distinguish between the reactor, the power-distribution system, and the supported military capability before deciding what may be lawfully and prudently attacked.

The rule in Article 56 is based on a basic humanitarian concern: some objects pose special risks to the civilian population due to the dangerous forces they may release if attacked. As a result, works and installations containing dangerous forces (as well as other military objectives located at or in their vicinity) are protected from attack, even when they are military objectives, if such attacks may cause the release of dangerous forces and consequent severe losses among the civilian population.

This protection is not absolute. Under Article 56, special protection may cease in narrow circumstances, including where a nuclear electrical generating station provides electric power in regular, significant, and direct support of military operations, and an attack on the station is the only feasible option to terminate this support. This exception matters for military microreactors because a reactor that continuously supplies essential electricity to an operational air-defense radar, directed-energy weapon, electronic warfare system, or AI-enabled command node, may provide support to military operations that is regular, significant, and direct. A dedicated military microreactor might meet this standard more readily as compared to a civilian nuclear plant which is providing electricity through a connected grid.
articles.lede: Nuclear powered microreactors may serve operational interests. However, their military usefulness does not eliminate their legal sensitivity.

articles.title: Afghanistan faces record hunger levels amid rampant rights violations
articles.description: Acute malnutrition and hunger in Afghanistan have reached the highest levels ever recorded, with 15.9 million people facing acute food insecurity and conditions set to worsen in the coming months, according to a global hunger monitor report released on Thursday.
paragraphs: UN agency heads are calling for emergency support to stem the crisis, as a separate report details serious human rights violations – from public floggings to a new ban on demonstrations.

Record acute malnutrition levels for the August–October period have seen hunger levels grow for millions of Afghans – according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a global initiative aimed at informing decisions based on five phases of food security.

Economic pressures are straining households nationwide, contributing to more than 32 per cent of the population facing crisis-level acute food insecurity phase three or above, including 3.4 million people experiencing emergency phase four conditions.
The current deterioration is driven by disease outbreaks and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions, compounded by sharply reduced access to nutrition services, the report found.

The situation is expected to worsen from November to April during the winter lean season, when nearly 19.2 million people are projected to face phase three or above, including five million people in emergency food insecurity conditions.
Acute malnutrition is also set to grow significantly, with 4.04 million children under age five projected to need treatment between January and December 2027.
“Although improved rainfall and better agricultural production have supported food availability, declining humanitarian assistance is reducing households’ ability to cope,” the report warned.

The World Food Programme ( WFP) and Food and Agriculture Organization ( FAO) issued a stark message on Thursday, calling for urgent funding to scale up food assistance, emergency agricultural support and malnutrition prevention and treatment.

“We still have a window to act, but it is closing fast,” WFP country director John Aylieff said. “With urgent support, families can get through the winter with dignity. Without it, many will face impossible choices no parent should have to make.”
articles.lede: Acute malnutrition and hunger in Afghanistan have reached the highest levels ever recorded, with 15.9 million people facing acute food insecurity and conditions set to worsen in the coming months, according to a global…

articles.title: Could your brain data be used against you? UN calls for limits on neurotechnology
articles.description: Brain signals recorded by a gaming headset or a wellness gadget could one day be used as evidence against you in court, according to a new UN report which warns that neurotechnology is outpacing the laws meant to protect human rights.
paragraphs: Presenting the Secretary-General’s report to the General Assembly on Thursday, senior human rights official Claudia Fuentes Julio said the technology could threaten privacy, freedom of thought and the right to a fair trial, particularly for marginalised people.
Neurotechnology was once exclusively used for medical diagnoses or treatment, measuring, monitoring, analysing, predicting or modulating the nervous system.
The new tech gathers neural data – defined as qualitative and quantitative data about the structure, activity and function of the nervous system.

“Neurotechnology accesses, measures and analyses brain signals,” the UN chief wrote in his report. “ If these signals are treated as direct indicators of thoughts, intentions or truthfulness, the use of neural data points could undermine how we understand and value each of us as human beings .”

Once confined to clinical or research environments, these devices are now entering, or may enter, consumer markets, workplaces, schools, public services, law enforcement and justice systems, the report found.

UN Assistant Secretary-General for Human Rights Claudia Fuentes Julio highlighted a range of risks when introducing the report to Third Committee members, including the growing commercialisation of neurotechnology and the collection of large volumes of neural data by technology companies.
Marketed for wellness, gaming and productivity, wearable, so-called electroencephalography devices are now increasingly available.

As such, neural data collected through these devices could be accessed by governments or introduced as evidence in legal proceedings without adequate recognition of its highly sensitive nature, the report warned.

While these new technologies hold significant promise, particularly for medical and assistive applications, Ms. Fuentes Julio said the report “warns of risks to dignity, privacy, freedom of thought, fair trial rights, liberty and protection from ill-treatment, especially for marginalised groups”.
articles.lede: Brain signals recorded by a gaming headset or a wellness gadget could one day be used as evidence against you in court, according to a new UN report which warns that neurotechnology is outpacing the laws meant to…

articles.title: AI will not set its own limits in warfare. States must.
articles.description: AI will not set its own limits in warfare. States must establish rules on autonomous weapons.
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being developed at extraordinary speed, prompting warnings from within the technology industry itself that advances may be outpacing our ability to understand and control its risks. Nowhere are the stakes higher than in armed conflict. As militaries increasingly explore the integration of AI into weapons and military decision-making, technological capability can easily be mistaken for inevitability: if a system can be built, the assumption follows that it will eventually be deployed. History suggests otherwise. States have made choices before about which technologies of warfare to prohibit, constrain or refrain from using – and they face such a choice again today.

In this post, ICRC Director of International Law, Movement and Partnerships Cordula Droege argues that abstract debates about the need to address the risks of AI should not distract from a concrete and achievable task already before states: establishing legally binding rules on autonomous weapon systems (AWS), including those incorporating AI. Drawing on the realities of deploying complex technologies in the unpredictable conditions of armed conflict, she explains why technical safeguards alone cannot resolve the humanitarian, legal and ethical concerns raised when weapons select and apply force without human intervention. Ahead of the Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in November, she calls on states to turn more than a decade of work into clear prohibitions and restrictions on AWS, while there is still time to decide what role machines and algorithms should play in war.

Last month, American technology company CEOs made the case for somewhat slowing down the development of AI. Not for the first time, they clearly warned that the technology may be advancing faster than our ability to understand its consequences and put appropriate safeguards in place.

One week earlier, in the early hours of Saturday 5 September, in Geneva, the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons’ Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (CCW GGE on LAWS) closed its final session after three years of work.

On the face of it, these events concern quite different questions. One is about the pace of AI development, the other about international rules for weapons. But the two are connected. Trends indicate a push to integrate more complex algorithms into weapons, to increase their autonomy. The risks posed by AI – and especially the risks flagged in recent discussions that AI escapes the prediction of those who launch it – are perhaps the most consequential when it is integrated into weapons that can directly affect whether people live or die.

Both events therefore concern the question of whether the international community will act effectively to prevent potentially catastrophic harm from AI, or delay and be left to witness it once it occurs. At the recent UN Security Council meeting on 23 September, calls were made for “governance”, “frameworks” and “norm-setting”. These are welcome, but if they stay at this level of generality such calls will have no impact in reducing the suffering of people living through armed conflicts.
articles.lede: AI will not set its own limits in warfare. States must establish rules on autonomous weapons.

articles.title: GC IV Commentary Series – Navigating the Complexities of Common Article 3
articles.description: The 2025 Commentary can be described as a “commentary in miniature,” because of its comprehensive account of Common Article 3.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

The delegates who drafted the 1949 Geneva Conventions described common Article 3 (CA 3) as a “Convention in miniature.” In a very real sense, the 2025 Commentary to the Fourth Geneva Convention (the 2025 Commentary) can be described as the accordant “Commentary in miniature,” because of its comprehensive and highly beneficial account of CA 3. The drafters of the 2025 Commentary tackled one of the most complicated aspects of this update. Indeed, it is probably no exaggeration to say that the interpretation and evolution of no other article of the Conventions has been more consequential than that of CA 3. While largely identical to the text in the 2016 revision of the Commentary to the First Convention, its significance and value are beyond doubt.

That significance derives primarily from an undeniable historical anomaly: CA 3—among hundreds of Convention articles, the only one devoted to armed conflicts not of an international character—addresses what became the dominant type of armed conflict since 1949. Thus, while the drafters of the Conventions focused principally on enhancing the regulation of international armed conflicts, their brief foray into the realm of non-international armed conflicts has garnered outsized significance as the world has and continues to grapple with the humanitarian challenges in a wide array of situations falling outside the international armed conflict category.

Defining the situations to which CA 3 applies has profound consequences. Not only will it impose the obligation to comply with the article’s humanitarian mandate, but it will also be viewed as justifying the invocation of authorities derived from the law of armed conflict. As noted in the Commentary,

[T]he wording agreed upon does not resolve the persistent question of the scope of application of common Article 3. The intentional lack of detail on this point may have facilitated States’ adoption of common Article 3. However, clarity as to its scope of application is important, as whether or not a given situation is an “armed conflict not of an international character” entails significant consequences (para. 458).

Indeed, it is naïve to ignore the reality that States perceive the obligation to comply with CA 3’s humanitarian provisions as opening the door to the lawful use of military power beyond what is permitted outside armed conflict. And, according to the Commentary, that view is understandable, “[w]hen common Article 3 is applicable, other rules of international humanitarian law, including those on the conduct of hostilities, with different restraints on the way force may be used compared to peacetime law, also apply” (para. 542). This includes: the authority to employ lethal force as a measure of first resort; the authority to employ such force based on status determinations and not the threatening conduct of the object of “attack”; the authority to detain captured enemy personnel for the duration of hostilities; and perhaps the authority to utilize extraordinary military tribunals to sanction alleged violations of the laws and customs of war by those same captives.
articles.lede: The 2025 Commentary can be described as a “commentary in miniature,” because of its comprehensive account of Common Article 3.

articles.title: Colombia: UN independent experts call for Ecopetrol to provide reparations to victims of armed conflict
articles.description: UN independent experts welcomed on Wednesday a recent landmark corporate accountability ruling involving the Ecopetrol oil company by Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace, calling for reparations for victims.
paragraphs: The Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) ruling related to the Macro-Case 08, which recognises the responsibility of several State agents and a director of the State-owned company for their involvement in acts related to serious human rights violations, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the armed conflict in Barrancabermeja, Colombia’s oil capital.

“The JEP’s decision represents a significant step forward for truth, justice and accountability regarding the impacts of corporate activities in conflict-affected contexts,” the experts said. “It also opens an unprecedented opportunity to place victims at the centre of reparation and restoration efforts.”

The experts welcomed the cooperation provided by Ecopetrol during the proceedings and encouraged the company to deepen that commitment through ongoing dialogue and concrete actions for reparation and restoration aimed at the affected individuals and communities.

“Companies have a responsibility to respect human rights and to participate in redressing the negative impacts they have caused or contributed to, in accordance with the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights ,” they noted.

The experts urged Ecopetrol to continue engaging in good faith in a constructive dialogue with the victims and their representative organisations, adopting a restorative approach that allows for the identification of the harms suffered, expectations for reparations and the measures necessary to help restore the rights violated.

“Victims should not be mere observers of the reparation processes, they must be active participants in their design and implementation,” they said. “Effective reparations require meaningful participation, acknowledgment of harm and a sustained commitment to restoring rights and rebuilding trust.”
As the majority shareholder of Ecopetrol, the experts highlighted the role of the Colombian State in this process.
“When it comes to State-owned enterprises, business responsibilities to respect human rights converge with the State’s duty to protect such rights,” they said.

“Colombian authorities must ensure the company participates fully in efforts towards truth, justice, reparations and guarantees of non-repetition and that this process effectively contributes to strengthening public trust in institutions,” the experts said.
articles.lede: UN independent experts welcomed on Wednesday a recent landmark corporate accountability ruling involving the Ecopetrol oil company by Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace, calling for reparations for victims.

articles.title: Hollow Control: Cyber Compromise and Human Judgment in Lethal Autonomous Weapons
articles.description: What happens to meaningful human control (MHC) if the information gathered is corrupted before a decision?
paragraphs: Observing that modern warfare is ever more reliant on networks, data, sensors, and software, all of which are vulnerable to attack, has the novelty factor of a field manual explaining that the enemy gets a vote. The more interesting and indeed pressing discussion revolves around the circumstances in which the adversary gets a vote unnoticed.

A legally problematic cyber operation against lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS) is not one that blacks out the screen and brings the system down. It is a compromise that does nothing at first glance, yet convinces the operator that they are in control. These sort of compromises that hollow out human control are the kind that corrupt the picture on which a human decision rests or interrupt the path by which that decision is supposed to constrain the weapon.

Articles of War recently concluded a series on LAWS that examined how meaningful human control (MHC) can be built into systems and assessed as a matter of design and procedure. These two posts ask a prior question: what happens to MHC if the information gathered is corrupted before a decision? MHC is only as reliable as the information and control pathways on which it depends. If either is manipulated, the architecture of control remains and the judgment does not.

Dependence creates a fundamental vulnerability: LAWS rely upon the integrity of information, models, sensors, and the connection between them, all of which may be compromised by cyber and electronic attacks. The more ways a system gathers information, the more accurate its picture may become. However, each added source is another input that must be secured, authenticated, and checked.

This vulnerability is far from being theoretical. On the contrary, it has been known since at least 1997 (which by drone and AI standards equals the Jurassic period) when Hezbollah claimed to have intercepted analog video from Israeli drones over Lebanon. In 2009, insurgents in Iraq used commercial software to receive live video from Predator unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV). They were not able to assume control of the aircraft but could watch its live video feed, the very same picture the operator was using.

Thus, compromised data is already a problem for the law of targeting, not a problem beside it. Although it would be tempting to assume otherwise, cyber operations and electronic warfare do not create a separate body of targeting law.

If they are used in an armed conflict, cyber operations and electronic warfare remain means or methods of warfare. Distinction, proportionality, and precautions apply where the operation is an attack, and the rest of international humanitarian law (IHL) continues to govern where it is not. This idea is reflected in the Department of Defense (DoD) Law of War Manual, in the International Committee of the Red Cross’s (ICRC) position on cyber operations, and in the Tallinn Manual 2.0.

These legal frameworks are well established. What matters for autonomous weapons is a much narrower issue, as an adversary’s cyber operation does not need to cause physical damage or take down a power grid to create problems among adversaries. The picture can be subtly altered while the heading continues to look like what the operator expects; an “ ILOVEYOU ,” not necessarily a black screen. For control to fail, it is enough that the person who must apply the law does not realize that the picture, the model, or the command path is no longer theirs.
articles.lede: What happens to meaningful human control (MHC) if the information gathered is corrupted before a decision?

articles.title: India: UN rights office urges release of ‘arbitrarily detained’ protesters
articles.description: The UN human rights office (OHCHR) has voiced concern over reports of mass detentions in India of demonstrators, protest leaders, civil society members, lawyers and journalists, before and during large-scale protests in Delhi on Saturday.
paragraphs: The demonstration was called by a youth-led movement that is seeking electoral reforms ahead of state elections, with its chief demand being the resignation of the official heading India’s election commission.
Protesters have criticised the body’s revision of the national voter roll, which has reportedly removed tens of millions of names in a bid to avoid duplicates and discrepancies.
Political opponents argue it is an exercise to keep the ruling nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in power.
Police refused permission for Saturday’s protest to take place at the movement’s planned venue in the capital, and heavy security and road closures were reported.
UN human rights office spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan called on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is “fully respected and fulfilled”.
“Restrictions on peaceful protests must meet strict tests of necessity and proportionality,” he said.
He urged law enforcement officers to show “utmost restraint” in responding to peaceful protesters, in keeping with India’s democratic traditions and its human rights obligations.
Mr. Al-Kheetan said that anyone arbitrarily detained must be released immediately and unconditionally.
He also encouraged the authorities to engage in meaningful dialogue to address what he described as broadly held concerns.
articles.lede: The UN human rights office (OHCHR) has voiced concern over reports of mass detentions in India of demonstrators, protest leaders, civil society members, lawyers and journalists, before and during large-scale protests in…

articles.title: GC IV Commentary Series – The Prohibition of Deportation and Forcible Transfer
articles.description: This post explores the meaning of forcible displacement and the temporal applicability of Article 49 of GC IV.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

When Russian forces reached a town in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region in 2022, many of its residents filled the streets in pro-Ukrainian rallies. In testimony recorded by The Reckoning Project (para. 55), one woman detailed the fate of those who dared to oppose the invasion. One morning, uniformed men arrived at her home and took her, “handcuffed and with a bag over her head,” to a detention centre. She was kept in inhumane conditions, beaten, sexually abused, and intimidated. On one occasion, her captors threatened her with “an elephant”: “the placement of a gas mask over her face, with soldiers intermittently blocking the air.” The soldiers released her only after forcing her to record a propaganda video for Russia. The day after her release, she took her daughter and fled to a government-controlled area of Ukraine, leaving her home, family, and life behind.

There are countless stories of displacement in times of armed conflict. In the words of an ICRC report, “displacement is part and parcel of war.” In some cases, individuals flee areas of hostilities because of a generalised state of violence and uncertainty. Faced with the risk of harm in their homes, they make the difficult, almost impossible, choice of leaving in the hope of security elsewhere. In others, people are forced to leave against their will, either by being physically taken away or compelled into departure through other means.

Article 49 of Geneva Convention IV (GC IV) is titled “Deportations, transfers, evacuations.” Located in Part III, Section III on occupied territories, it provides the clearest regulation of displacement in international armed conflict under international humanitarian law. In its first paragraph, it prohibits “[i]ndividual or mass forcible transfers, as well as deportations of protected persons from occupied territory to the territory of the Occupying Power or to that of any other country, occupied or not, … regardless of their motive.” While other rules of international humanitarian law, such as the obligations falling within the list of fundamental guarantees, bear on the process and effects of displacement, Article 49 prohibits forcible displacement as a distinct wrong.

Despite its significance, interpretative uncertainties about the applicability and scope of the provision persist. The ICRC’s Updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention (2025 Commentary) makes an important and timely contribution to the clarification of Article 49. Even a cursory comparison between the Commentary on Geneva Convention IV Relative to the Protection of Civilians in Time of War (1958 Commentary) and the 2025 Commentary demonstrates the detail and depth of the 2025 project. This reflects both the numerous legal developments since the publication of the 1958 Commentary and the monumental work of the ICRC. It consolidates existing interpretations and solidifies and specifies understandings of key elements of the provision. It takes a stand on the contentious question of the temporal application of Article 49. And while, as I argue below, it leaves some points of substance and methodology under-specified, implicit, or dispersed in the Commentary, there is no doubt it has, in a reasoned and substantiated manner, taken the text of the Convention to the realities and demands of 21st century conflicts.
articles.lede: This post explores the meaning of forcible displacement and the temporal applicability of Article 49 of GC IV.

articles.title: Mechanism congratulates Judge Pillay on receiving Nobel Peace Prize
articles.description: The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (Mechanism) warmly congratulates Judge Navi Pillay on receiving the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In her long and distinguished career, Judge Pillay served as Judge and President of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR).
paragraphs: During her 8-year tenure (1995-2003) at the ICTR, Judge Pillay played a critical role in the early formation of the Tribunal and the interpretation and application of international criminal law. She was elected in 1995 as one of the Tribunal’s first six judges, and its only woman judge during its first four years. She served as the ICTR’s second President from 1999 to 2003, which coincided with a period of rapid expansion and increased productivity. Notably, she played an essential role as a judge in the conduct and completion of seven trial proceedings. In particular, her work as a member of the bench on the Jean-Paul Akayesu case established that rape and other forms of sexual violence could amount to genocidal conduct. She participated in the landmark conviction and sentencing of Jean Kambanda, the former Prime Minister of Rwanda, the first head of government held accountable for genocide and crimes against humanity. Judge Pillay also presided over the Ferdinand Nahimana et al. trial which held the Rwandan media, both radio and print, responsible for fomenting ethnic hatred, genocide, and other international crimes.

The Mechanism’s President, Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, praised Judge Pillay as a “trailblazer in international criminal justice, who broke barriers as a woman judge and President of the ICTR, helping to shape a legacy of courage, integrity, and principled leadership. Her contributions continue to inspire generations of jurists and reaffirm the vital role of justice in upholding human dignity and lasting peace”.
Arusha Tel: +255 (0)27 256 5376 The Hague Tel: +31 (0)70 512 5037 Email: mict-press@un.org

The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (Mechanism) was established by UN Security Council Resolution 1966 (2010) to complete the remaining work of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia after the completion of their respective mandates. The Mechanism has two branches, one in Arusha, Tanzania, and one in The Hague, Netherlands.
articles.lede: The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (Mechanism) warmly congratulates Judge Navi Pillay on receiving the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.

articles.title: World News in Brief: ‘Horrific’ attack in Sudan, Israeli incursions in Syria intensify, most women and girls homeless in Gaza
articles.description: A suspected drone strike has left at least 40 dead in Sudan’s Blue Nile State – near the Ethiopian border - according to initial reports from the ground, according to UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric. Most of the casualties were women and girls.
paragraphs: Fighting in the region has escalated in the last few months as clashes have intensified between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Government.
They are fighting over strategic towns and bases near the Ethiopian border, as part of the broader battle for control of Sudan that has been ongoing since April 2023.
In recent weeks, thousands of civilians have been displaced in the area due to sustained attacks.
Mr. Dujarric condemned the “horrifying reports” stressing that attacks directed towards civilians are prohibited under international humanitarian law.

Israeli military incursions into southern Syria are intensifying, with some 280 incidents recorded in September alone – the highest monthly figure this year, the UN human rights office ( OHCHR) said on Friday.
The incidents include reported raids on homes, restrictions on movement, harassment of civilians and arbitrary detention.
Spokesperson Shabia Mantoo said 49 Syrians are believed to remain in Israeli custody, though the figure has not been independently verified.

Former detainees describe detention lasting over a year in some cases, no reasons given and transfers to unknown facilities. They also allege torture and ill-treatment, including beatings, prolonged forced standing and threats to their families.
On Monday, a 22-year-old man from Jaba town in Quneitra governorate was killed by Israeli forces near Al-Hamidiyah.
articles.lede: A suspected drone strike has left at least 40 dead in Sudan’s Blue Nile State – near the Ethiopian border - according to initial reports from the ground, according to UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric.

articles.title: Livestreaming US execution would breach prohibition of torture, UN rights office warns
articles.description: The UN human rights office (OHCHR) on Friday warned that livestreaming a planned execution by firing squad in the United States would amount to a public execution and breach the absolute prohibition on torture.
paragraphs: The statement came after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth vowed to publicly execute Nidal Malik Hasan, who was sentenced to death by a military jury after being convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 in a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
OHCHR’s Shabia Mantoo was responding to a question from journalists at a press briefing in Geneva.

She noted that the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, in response to public executions in Afghanistan and Iran had previously stressed that such executions “constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.

“ Failure to respect this prohibition would inevitably render the execution arbitrary in nature, and result in a violation of the right to life and the absolute prohibition of torture ,” the spokesperson added.

UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said during Friday’s press briefing in New York that the “possibility of…a government executing someone in public or in front of live cameras, frankly, is abhorrent”.

Earlier this month, OHCHR also called on the authorities in the US state of Tennessee not to pursue any further attempts to execute Christa Pike, saying her case highlights why the death penalty should be abolished.

“ The death penalty has no place in any society, and Christa Pike’s case lays bare the multiple reasons why capital punishment should be abolished ,” said UN Human Rights Office spokesperson Ravina Shamdasani.
“Her prolonged suffering is abhorrent, and cruel. Key fair trial concerns remain unresolved ,” she said.
Responding to the botched execution, Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada has said he will be stepping down at the end of this month.
articles.lede: The UN human rights office (OHCHR) on Friday warned that livestreaming a planned execution by firing squad in the United States would amount to a public execution and breach the absolute prohibition on torture.

articles.title: Former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
articles.description: South African jurist and former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay was on Friday announced as the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.
paragraphs: She was honoured “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”, the Norwegian Nobel Committee said in a statement.

The committee said the award was going “to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order,” noting that she “has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted .”

Ms. Pillay served as the UN human rights chief from September 2008 through August 2014, but her career has spanned more than 50 years - from fighting apartheid in her homeland to defending civilians in conflict zones.

She is a former chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and was appointed a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) and the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Hague, in addition to serving as an ad hoc judge with the International Court of Justice ( ICJ ), the UN's highest court.

“ A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time ,” the Nobel Committee said.

In a statement congratulating the new Nobel laureate, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said Ms. Pillay has shown “that the force of law must prevail over the law of force and that defending human rights is the surest safeguard against injustice.”

He hailed her as “a champion of international law and human rights, and a steadfast, independent voice of justice”, adding that “in its citation, the Nobel Committee reminded the world that peace must be built on lasting principles, not the will of the powerful."
Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was born in South Africa in 1941 to a Tamil Indian family and was the first non-white woman to establish a legal practice in the country.
As a lawyer, she acted as a defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists, exposing torture, and helping to establish key rights for prisoners on notorious Robben Island.
articles.lede: South African jurist and former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay was on Friday announced as the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.

articles.title: ICC: what does Said’s judgment mean?
Influencer, gamer, soldier, spy: the online era of child recruitment and its implications in international law (Part II)
articles.description: Online child recruitment is entering the digital age. From gaming to social media, discover how technology is changing the way children are drawn into armed conflict.
paragraphs: As social media and gaming platforms create new interfaces between tech-savvy children and armed actors, new questions should be asked regarding how the law prohibiting child recruitment and use in hostilities can be promoted and enforced online.

In this two-part post, ICRC Advisers Vanessa Murphy, Siobhan Sparkes McNamara, and Tilman Rodenhäuser consider how the digital environment is transforming more traditional forms of child recruitment, give a rough typology of related trends in the information and communications (ICT) environment, identify the relevant international law, and propose recommendations to improve compliance with these laws in the digital age.

In recent years, states have expressed concern about the use of ICTs for the recruitment of children into armed forces and armed groups, and their use in hostilities. Such acts are subject to widely-applicable international legal obligations, and this law applies online as well as offline: today, there is general agreement that “IHL rules and principles … serve to protect civilian populations and other protected persons and objects, including against the risks arising from ICT activities”, and that “children must not be allowed to take part in hostilities during armed conflict, including through ICT activities”.

But the intricacy of the rules governing child recruitment and use in hostilities is sometimes underestimated. In the second part of this post, we present some of the most relevant provisions and encourage states to take a range of measures to improve compliance with them.

Since the Geneva Conventions were adopted in 1949, international law has developed in bursts to advance the protection of children in armed conflict. Numerous treaties articulate in one way or another the general rule that these children are entitled to special respect and protection. This universal concern has birthed a more elaborate body of law to keep children away from the primary purveyors of violence in wartime – armed forces and armed groups.

Most states are bound by more than one of the following instruments governing child recruitment and use in hostilities, and all states are bound by at least one. When more than one norm applies to a given set of facts, the rules apply concurrently, meaning that the highest standard must be complied with. For example, many states are bound by prohibitions on child recruitment under the age of 15 ( API Art. 77.2, APII Art. 4.3.c, CRC Art. 38) as well as the higher age of 18 ( OPAC Art. 2 and declaration under Art. 3.2, ACRWC Art. 22.2 ). In such cases, a state must abide by the age 18 standard.

The Optional Protocol on the Protection of Children in Armed Conflict (OPAC). The 173 States Parties to OPAC are prohibited from unlawfully recruiting children to their own armed forces, including using online means, in line with the specifications in OPAC Articles 2 and 3. They must also “ take all feasible measures to prevent” the recruitment or use in hostilities of persons under 18 by non-state armed groups, “ including the adoption of legal measures necessary to prohibit and criminalize such practices” (Art. 4.2). For their part, non-state armed groups are prohibited from recruiting or using in hostilities anyone under 18 (Art. 4.1). Finally, under Article 6.1 and 6.2, States Parties must take “ all necessary legal, administrative and other measures to ensure the effective implementation and enforcement of the provisions of the present Protocol within its jurisdiction ”.
articles.lede: Online child recruitment is entering the digital age. From gaming to social media, discover how technology is changing the way children are drawn into armed conflict.

articles.title: GC IV Commentary Series
articles.description: In its recently updated commentary of Geneva Convention IV, the ICRC explains its interpretive methodology.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.
In its recently updated commentary of Geneva Convention IV, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) explains the interpretive methodology it has adopted as follows:

The updated Commentary applies the methodology for treaty interpretation set out in the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (hereinafter ‘Vienna Convention’), in particular Articles 31-33. These rules are now generally considered to reflect customary international law. As such, they are applicable to the interpretation of the Geneva Conventions, even though the Conventions were concluded before the entry into force of the Vienna Convention (para. 98. Internal references omitted).

This methodology underpins the commentary’s frequent recourse to subsequent practice as an aid to interpretation, including its use as a supplementary means of interpretation where the practice in question falls short of establishing a general agreement among the parties as required under Article 31(3)(b) of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.

Such an interpretive approach reflects two propositions that have emerged in recent decades. First, the rules of treaty interpretation set forth in Articles 31-33 of the Vienna Convention are regarded as reflecting customary international law and, as such, are applicable to earlier treaties, including 1949 Geneva Conventions, which were adopted prior to the Vienna Convention’s entry into force in 1980. Second, the applicable rules of interpretation permit recourse to subsequent practice in the application of a treaty, even where that practice does not establish the agreement of the parties regarding the treaty’s interpretation, as a supplementary means of interpretation in the sense of Article 32 of the Vienna Convention.

These propositions are by no means unique to the ICRC’s commentaries. They are frequently assumed in legal scholarship and have increasingly found endorsement in official documents and institutional practice. However, their growing and often unqualified acceptance, without critical reflections, has long troubled me. In this post, I take the opportunity to explain my reservations concerning these two propositions and to suggest reasons for exercising caution when reading or relying on this commentary.

The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 entered into force in 1950, three decades before the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties entered into force in 1980. As a technical matter, therefore, the interpretive rules codified in Articles 31-33 of the Vienna Convention are not directly applicable to the Geneva Conventions, given the principle of non-retroactivity set forth in Article 4 of the Vienna Convention.

The first of the interpretive propositions introduced above seeks to overcome this difficulty by drawing a distinction between the treaty rules embodied in the Vienna Convention and their equivalent in customary international law. According to this view, the interpretive rules codified in Articles 31-33 did not originate with the Vienna Convention but rather reflected pre-existing customary law that was already binding when the Geneva Conventions were adopted and entered into force.
articles.lede: In its recently updated commentary of Geneva Convention IV, the ICRC explains its interpretive methodology.

articles.title: Asia-Pacific Journal Series – Dignitary Design: Embedding Human Dignity into Military AI
articles.description: Respect for human dignity should become a guiding principle in the design and governance of military AI itself.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: This post appears as part of a series highlighting articles in a recent volume of the Asia-Pacific Journal of International Law, on which presentations were made at a workshop hosted by National University of Singapore’s Centre for International Law. Introductory post by Samuel White, Danielle Yeow, and Jonathan Kwik can be found here.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the way military operations are planned and conducted. Systems capable of processing enormous quantities of data now assist commanders in identifying potential targets, predicting civilian presence, assessing collateral damage, and recommending operational courses of action.

Although these technologies remain, in formal legal terms, decision-support tools rather than autonomous legal actors, they increasingly shape the informational environment within which military decisions are made. As a result, the central challenge confronting international humanitarian law (IHL) is no longer confined to regulating autonomous weapons. My article engages with the broader question of how IHL should respond when human judgment itself is progressively mediated by algorithmic systems.

Contemporary debates on military AI have largely focused on whether IHL is adequate to regulate emerging technologies, how meaningful human control should be preserved, and who should bear responsibility when AI-assisted operations produce unlawful outcomes. While these discussions have generated important insights, they share a common premise: they treat AI as a technological reality to be regulated after it has already been developed, rather than asking what normative values should shape its design from the outset.

This is the idea underlying what I describe as dignitary design. The concept rests upon a straightforward proposition: respect for human dignity should not function merely as a standard against which military operations are evaluated after harm has occurred. Rather, dignity should become a guiding principle in the design and governance of military AI itself. Instead of viewing human dignity exclusively as a legal value protected through judicial review, accountability mechanisms, or reparations, dignitary design understands it as an ex ante constraint that shapes technological development before operational decisions are ever made. If military AI increasingly structures battlefield decision-making, IHL cannot remain concerned solely with the legality of outcomes; it must also engage with the architecture through which those outcomes are produced.

This proposal builds upon the normative foundations of IHL itself. The principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution all presuppose that human beings possess an intrinsic value that cannot simply be reduced to strategic utility. Likewise, the Martens Clause reminds us that even where treaty law is silent, military operations remain governed by the principles of humanity and the dictates of public conscience.
Together, these rules reflect a legal order whose legitimacy depends not merely upon regulating violence efficiently but upon preserving the humanity of those affected by armed conflict.
articles.lede: Respect for human dignity should become a guiding principle in the design and governance of military AI itself.

articles.title: Asia-Pacific Journal Series – Can We Design Military AI to Follow IHL by Default?
articles.description: Can we design artificial intelligence (AI) systems to automatically follow core principles of international humanitarian law?
paragraphs: Editors’ note: This post appears as part of a series highlighting articles in a recent volume of the Asia-Pacific Journal of International Law, on which presentations were made at a workshop hosted by National University of Singapore’s Centre for International Law. Introductory post by Samuel White, Danielle Yeow, and Jonathan Kwik can be found here.

Can we design artificial intelligence (AI) systems to automatically follow core principles of international humanitarian law (IHL) in similar ways to Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics? A recent proposal from the Institute for Law & AI suggests that future agentic military AI systems should be designed to consult “AI-Guiding Treaties” and to refuse human instructions that would violate the designated treaties.

This idea of Treaty-Following AI (TFAI) is appealing for military agentic AI systems. It would effectively sidestep the long overdue responsibility gap debate regarding ex post attribution of responsibility and turn the focus toward an ex ante design duty that could prevent an AI henchman from loyally carrying out human orders without questioning their legality.

This post highlights my argument from a previously published article contending that some areas of IHL are particularly difficult to codify as legal constraints because States deliberately left their meanings ambiguous.

In quantum mechanics, light can exist as both a wave and a particle, a phenomenon known as superposition. Light collapses into one state only when it is observed (the observer effect). I argue that IHL exists under similar conditions because it holds two logically irreconcilable visions at once: military necessity; and humanity. The meaning of these rules is suspended until we decide which rule wins out.

The difficulty in applying the TFAI proposal to IHL lies precisely in the fact that IHL’s fundamental provisions, such as the principles of precaution, distinction, and proportionality, can be legitimately interpreted differently according to two opposing moral reference points. The danger of TFAI is that it rests on the need to collapse the superposition ex ante to provide objective guidance to the AI, which would inevitably privilege one vision over the other as an infrastructural reality while obscuring the political nature of that choice.

There is nothing novel in the claim that some rules of IHL are indeterminate. My article distinguishes four established forms of indeterminacy in existing accounts: (1) linguistic indeterminacy, arising from open-textured languages; (2) legal indeterminacy, arising from questions of sources, interpretation, and application (such as whether military manuals count as State practice? What counts as “direct participation in hostilities”? How many civilian casualties are considered “excessive” to the military advantage anticipated?); (3) structural indeterminacy, arising from IHL’s dual role in both legitimising and restraining violence; and (4) practice-based indeterminacy, arising from a divided IHL interpretive community between military and human rights lawyers. Each account describes a form of legal indeterminacy, but none fully explains why indeterminacies in IHL have proved so resilient.
articles.lede: Can we design artificial intelligence (AI) systems to automatically follow core principles of international humanitarian law?
